1840s-france-the-socialists-bastiat-was-.context_blurb:
In the late 1840s France was a pressure cooker, and the Paris journalist and deputy Frédéric Bastiat fought on two fronts at once. On one side stood the high border taxes that sheltered French industry. On the other stood a brand-new crop of socialists who promised that the state could guarantee every man a job and abolish the cost of borrowing. Their schemes gave Bastiat his best material.

A tariff is a tax charged on goods as they cross into a country. The July Monarchy, France's government until 1848, laid heavy tariffs on iron, cloth and grain, so French makers could charge more without losing their customers to cheaper imports. The socialist Louis Blanc pushed a different promise. In 1839 he had argued that only the state could cure unemployment, through "social workshops" organized trade by trade. When revolution toppled the king in February 1848, Blanc joined the new Provisional Government and pushed the decree that created the National Workshops, open to any jobless man. A wage guaranteed to all who ask must be paid by someone, and that someone is everybody else, who has to be taxed heavily to fund the payroll.

By May the workshops had swelled past 100,000 men. The treasury had real productive work for only a few of them, so most were paid to do almost nothing, and the wage turned into a straight handout. Then the government shut it down. Thousands of men whose income vanished overnight took to the streets in the June Days of 1848, and General Cavaignac crushed the rising with heavy loss of life.

Bastiat's most stubborn opponent was Pierre-Joseph Proudhon, the first thinker to call himself an anarchist. In 1840 Proudhon had asked what property is and answered with a line that rang through the century: property, he said, is vol, which means theft. From October 1849 into March 1850 the two men traded open letters in Proudhon's paper, La Voix du Peuple. Proudhon dreamed of a People's Bank that would offer free credit. Bastiat answered that interest is no robbery but a price, the real market price of time preference: the reward a saver earns for lending his savings and waiting. Because it is a genuine price, no law can decree it down to zero.

Bastiat's sharpest weapon was laughter. In 1845 he published a mock plea from France's candle-makers, begging the Chamber to make the law close up windows, skylights and shutters, because a foreign rival was flooding the country with light at an impossibly low price: the sun. His target was every live argument that called a competitor's natural advantage "unfair." Others tried to escape the market altogether. Étienne Cabet wrote a novel about a perfect communist republic called Icaria, and in 1848 he led several hundred believers to America, to Texas and at last to Nauvoo, Illinois, a town the Mormons had abandoned. Like most of the dozens of little communist colonies that sprang up in nineteenth-century America, Icaria broke apart within a few years amid quarrels and shortages.

That same February of 1848, in London, the German exiles Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels published a pamphlet of twenty-three pages for the Communist League: the Communist Manifesto, summoning the workers of the world to unite and seize the factories and fields from their owners. The pamphlet grew into the bible of a movement whose regimes killed somewhere between 65 and 100 million people over the following century, by the count of The Black Book of Communism. Against Blanc's workshops, Bastiat kept pressing one move. Each franc handed to a workshop man had first been taken, through taxes or loans, from some other citizen who never saw where it went: the wage was seen, and the taxpayer's lost spending was unseen. That September his essay The State boiled the point down to a famous definition: the state is the great fiction by which everyone tries to live at the expense of everyone else.

aig-the-182b-backdoor-bank-rescue.context_blurb:
American International Group, founded in 1919, was one of the largest insurance companies in the world. In September 2008, in the middle of the financial panic, the Federal Reserve and the Treasury threw it the biggest single rescue in American history. To economists in Bastiat's tradition and the public-choice school, the most revealing part of the story is where the money actually went.

AIG's Financial Products unit had sold a kind of insurance on mortgage bonds, called credit default swaps, to nearly every major bank. Insurance works when trouble strikes a few customers at a time: one bank has a bad year, the insurer pays and carries on. When home loans sour everywhere at once, every customer claims together, and an insurer that sold far more coverage than it could ever pay simply runs out of money. Lehman Brothers collapsed on September 15, 2008. The very next day the Fed lent AIG about 85 billion dollars and took nearly four-fifths of the company in return.

That first loan was only the beginning. Over the following months the commitment kept climbing until it peaked at about 182 billion dollars, the largest government rescue of a single firm in the nation's history. Follow the money, though, and the rescue changes shape. AIG passed the borrowed cash straight on as collateral, at full face value, to the banks that had bought swap protection from it, so the true beneficiaries were AIG's counterparties, and every major dealer was made whole.

The biggest checks went to the biggest banks, the ones that had placed the largest bets: Goldman Sachs collected about 12.9 billion dollars, Société Générale about 11.9 billion, Deutsche Bank about 11.8 billion and Merrill Lynch about 6.8 billion. Congress had set up a watchdog to track the bailout money, an inspector general known by the clumsy initials SIGTARP. Its chief, Neil Barofsky, published reports from 2009 to 2011 tracing how the AIG money flowed to those banks, and he later told the story in his book Bailout.

How did a giant insurer fall so fast? Its top-grade AAA rating meant customers had accepted AIG's promises without demanding cash up front, and no regulator required it to hold any. But its own contracts said that if the rating fell, AIG had to post collateral. When the rating agencies cut its rating in September 2008, AIG suddenly owed billions in collateral that it could not raise. The rest of Wall Street drew the obvious lesson, the one economists call moral hazard: if the government will catch you when you fall, the sensible move is to take even bigger risks next time. Timothy Geithner, who as head of the New York Fed designed the rescue, became Treasury Secretary in January 2009.

The rescue was presented as protection for ordinary families' insurance policies. That was the seen. The unseen was that most of the money ran straight through AIG to the big creditor banks, a bank bailout routed through an insurer, which spared officials the sight of paying Goldman and Deutsche Bank directly. Public-choice economists warn of two lasting results whenever a rescue hides its real winners: the big risk-takers come to expect more rescues, and public trust in government drains away. The AIG pipe worked in the moment, but it taught every future gambler that appearances can be managed while the counterparties get paid.

anthony-de-jasay-the-state-1985.context_blurb:
Anthony de Jasay, a Hungarian born in 1925, escaped Communist rule in 1948, eventually reached Oxford and later settled in France. In 1985 he published a short, startling book that asked a question most political theory had stopped asking: if the state is self-interested, as public-choice economists assume, what could ever make it respect limits on its own power?

The book came out from Basil Blackwell, an Oxford publisher, and its author, Anthony de Jasay, opened it by asking readers to imagine what they would do if they were the state. He gave it a title of one stark word, The State, because that was his single great subject. Once a government exists, he argued, it will use and enlarge its power in ways no theory of a neutral umpire or a kindly public servant predicts.

In the 1960s James Buchanan and Gordon Tullock had built a new branch of economics by asking how to write rules that would restrain self-interested politicians in office. That branch, which asks whether politicians, judges and bureaucrats serve the public or serve themselves, is called public choice economics. De Jasay thought its founders had skipped a step. Before designing any constraint, he asked why a state, presumed self-interested, would ever honor a constraint at all, since a rule binds only if the one it binds accepts it.

He also went after the social contract, the story told in different forms by John Locke, Thomas Hobbes and John Rawls, that the state's authority flows from its citizens' consent. De Jasay answered with history rather than theory: no such consent ever took place, because real states were founded by conquest or by groups seizing power, and the contract story was a rationalization added afterward.

Over the following fifteen years he pressed further, against political rule as such, in Social Contract, Free Ride (1989), Choice, Contract, Consent (1991), Against Politics (1997) and Justice and Its Surroundings (2002). The Austrian economist Peter Boettke later helped carry his work to a wide audience. Strangest of all, de Jasay never held a permanent academic post. While most great names of his tradition were tenured professors, he earned his living in a wine business in Normandy and wrote his books entirely outside the universities.

arthur-burns-nixons-political-pressure-a.context_blurb:
A celebrated Columbia professor and expert on business cycles, Arthur Burns had once led the National Bureau of Economic Research. In 1970 Richard Nixon put him at the head of the Federal Reserve, America's central bank, which controls how many dollars exist and what it costs to borrow them. Burns held the job until 1978, and his years there became known as the Great Inflation.

A president who phones the Fed demanding cheaper money wants voters to feel richer by election day. The hidden cost arrives later: printing extra money pushes prices up, so the pleasant boom is paid for with inflation. Nixon wanted easy credit timed for his November 1972 reelection, and he leaned hard on Burns to keep rates low; the White House tapes and Burns's own private notes record the pressure. Burns kept a diary through those years. Long after his death in 1987, it appeared in 2010 as Inside the Nixon Administration: The Secret Diary of Arthur Burns 1969-1974, a real-time record that confirmed what the tapes had shown.

Money stayed cheap while prices climbed. Arab producers squeezed the oil supply in 1973, and the Iranian Revolution choked it again in 1979. Consumer prices rose 11 percent in 1974, more than 11 percent in 1979 and about 13.5 percent in 1980, the peak year and the worst peacetime inflation in American history. The leading Keynesian guide of the day said that could not happen; it grew from a paper that A.W. Phillips, an economist from New Zealand, published in 1958. The Phillips curve held that inflation and unemployment trade off, so that when one climbs the other falls. In the 1970s both rose together, and newspapers coined a word for it: stagflation.

Milton Friedman had seen it coming in his presidential address to the American Economic Association in December 1967. Printing money to cut unemployment works only until workers catch on. Once they start expecting next year's higher prices and bargain for raises to match, the trade-off breaks: unemployment drifts back up, and inflation stays high as well.

Austrian-school writers such as Murray Rothbard refused to blame mere bad luck or one feeble chairman. Any institution empowered to expand credit, they argued, will be captured by politicians who profit from a quick boost, whatever the long-term cost. Burns himself came close to agreeing. A year after he left the Fed, in a 1979 lecture in Belgrade on the anguish that central bankers live with, he admitted that a central banker finds it hard to hold the line, because elected leaders keep pushing for cheap credit to help win the next election.

Burns also eased too early. When the first wave of inflation subsided he cut rates, expectations came loose, and a second, worse wave rolled in at the end of the decade. Breaking it took extraordinary rate hikes, with Paul Volcker, chairman from 1979, driving rates above 20 percent. Austrian analysts warn that any central bank that cuts too soon invites the same sequel: a second inflation wave that only Volcker-style hikes can crush. The appointment lesson is just as hard. Burns had every credential, and his own theory told him what loose money would do, yet under political pressure he caved and produced the very inflation his training warned against. In the Austrian reading the fault lies in the structure, not the man, which is why they say monetary rules should outrank monetary leaders.

bastiat-and-slavery-the-1848-abolition-v.context_blurb:
In February 1848 a revolution in Paris drove out King Louis Philippe and created France's Second Republic. Within weeks the new government moved against the oldest injustice in its empire, slavery in the colonies. The economist Frédéric Bastiat, about to enter politics, had attacked slavery in print for years, and his reasoning shows his method at its sharpest.

The abolitionist Victor Schoelcher, who had campaigned against slavery for two decades, drafted the decree, and the Provisional Government issued it on April 27, 1848, freeing the enslaved people of Martinique, Guadeloupe, French Guiana and Réunion. Free workers choose their own jobs, can quit and keep their wages, and over time free labor proves more productive than forced labor, because people work harder when the work is their choice and the pay is theirs.

This was France's second abolition. The Revolution had first ended colonial slavery in 1794, but in 1802 Napoleon Bonaparte, eager to restore the sugar profits of Saint-Domingue and the other Caribbean colonies, sent soldiers to force slavery back on them. In April 1848 the voters of Landes, Bastiat's native department in the southwest, elected him to the new National Assembly, and he took his seat in May.

Defenders of plantation slavery pointed to the cotton and the wealth it produced. Bastiat pressed what they failed to see: a slave has no incentive to be productive, forced labor corrupts the master's own character, and the free market for labor is strangled. The abolition followed a British model. When Britain's Parliament ended slavery across most of its empire in 1833, it bought off the plantation lobby with twenty million pounds paid to the former slave owners, while the freed people received only a period of so-called apprenticeship. France, too, compensated the former slave owners rather than the people who had been enslaved, a choice critics have pressed ever since.

In 1850, sick with the tuberculosis that would kill him before the year was out, Bastiat wrote The Law, a short pamphlet on how governments seize from some and hand to others while giving the seizure a lawful disguise. The idea binding it together was legal plunder: one person's labor or property seized by the force of law and handed to another, and slavery was its purest form. His own record on the 1848 abolition has a precise shape. He was elected on April 23, the decree came on April 27, and the Assembly first met on May 4, so he never voted on the decree itself; he backed abolition publicly and voted for the measures that carried it out.

berlins-2020-rent-freeze-mietendeckel.context_blurb:
In February 2020 the German city-state of Berlin froze the rents on most of its apartments for five years. The law, called the Mietendeckel, meaning rent lid, held rents at their June 2019 levels and even ordered cuts on pricier flats. Because the lid stopped dead at the city line, it handed economists a rare and clean experiment.

The first lesson holds for any city. If a law locks rents low for years, whatever heating and repairs may cost, builders stop putting up new apartments, because nobody builds for a rent he can never raise. What thrilled researchers about Berlin was the lid's border: it covered only the territory inside Berlin's city limits, while neighboring towns in Brandenburg, such as Potsdam, kept charging market rents. Economists at the ifo Institute in Munich and the DIW in Berlin compared the two sides of that line: one country, one year, one side capped and one side free.

The results came quickly. Inside the city, rental listings fell sharply, while listings in the towns just beyond the line went up. Landlords held flats off the market, let them as furnished shares that the freeze did not cover, or sold them. That is why a newcomer, say a nurse arriving for a hospital job, found almost nothing to rent, and what she did find cost more than before. The freeze had shrunk the pool of listings, so every mover now competed for the few that were left. Bastiat would sort it neatly: the protected sitting tenant is seen, while the mover facing a smaller, fiercer market is not.

On April 15, 2021, Germany's Federal Constitutional Court in Karlsruhe struck the law down. The judges never weighed its economics. They ruled on federalism, holding that rent regulation belongs to the national government and that the state of Berlin had lacked the authority to pass it, and tenants then owed back the rent the lid had suspended. Thanks to that clean border, good statistics and a sharp before-and-after window of some fourteen months, the Berlin freeze has become the standard modern case study of how housing supply responds to a sudden rent-control shock.

bootleggers-and-baptists-in-the-modern-e.context_blurb:
In 1983 the Clemson economist Bruce Yandle gave a name to an old American alliance: the moralist who wants a rule for principled reasons, and the business that wants the same rule because of how it is written. The pattern has not gone away. It shapes today's fights over electric cars, online sales taxes, legal marijuana and tobacco.

Yandle took the name from Southern Sunday-closing laws, which devout Protestants defended on moral grounds and moonshiners defended because legal Sunday sales would have ruined their trade: Bootleggers and Baptists. The two partners need not share a philosophy, a party or a background. What they must share is an identical position on the rule's specific design, because the moral side supplies cover and the commercial side supplies money and lobbying muscle, and both need exactly the same detailed policy to win.

Take California's rule that new cars sold there from 2035 must be zero-emission, set as a goal by a 2020 order and approved by the state's air board in August 2022. Frédéric Bastiat would point to what the rule's fans rarely examine, such as the strain on the power grid, the mining supply chain and the poorer drivers who can no longer afford a new car; in his 1850 essay he called such hidden effects the unseen. Big established carmakers such as GM and Ford publicly backed the goal, alongside environmental groups. The reason is that they can afford the costly switch while smaller rivals and independent parts suppliers cannot, so the rule works as a moat.

In June 2018 the Supreme Court, in South Dakota v. Wayfair, let states make out-of-state online sellers collect sales tax. Revenue officials and level-playing-field advocates supplied the moral case, while big brick-and-mortar retailers and Amazon, which already collected the tax, quietly welcomed a ruling that raised compliance costs on small rivals, who now face more than forty-five state tax systems. Legal marijuana shows the pattern too. Since Colorado and Washington led the way in 2012, many states have legalized it but hemmed in the legal trade with scarce licenses, heavy taxes and piles of paperwork. In California in 2023 about two-thirds of the cannabis sold still came from the untaxed illegal market, a gift both to anti-drug campaigners and to licensed incumbents who like having few competitors.

In 1998 the big four of American tobacco signed a Master Settlement Agreement with the attorneys general of forty-six states. It looked like a punishment, but its payments on every pack made new entry ruinously expensive, so the four largest tobacco firms and public-health advocates found themselves allies: the advocates got a stream of money, and the big four got a moat. Yandle and his co-author Adam Smith gathered such modern cases, from banking to green rules to the tobacco deal, in a 2014 book for the Cato Institute titled Bootleggers and Baptists.

Yandle's habit for analysts is simple. When reformers with a moral cause and quiet commercial interests line up behind one new rule, never stop at the moral story out front; look one layer down for the business with a concentrated stake that is sheltering behind the moralist. The lesson is not that moral advocates are insincere, for often they mean every word. It is that the moral reasons given seldom tell the whole story of who actually pushes a rule through, and the identity of the commercial winner often predicts better whether a rule passes and in what form.

bryan-caplan-the-myth-of-the-rational-vo.context_blurb:
In 2007 Bryan Caplan, an economist at George Mason University, published a book that pushed an old idea about voters in a less flattering direction. Anthony Downs had argued in 1957 that voters stay uninformed because one vote rarely matters. Caplan argued that they are not merely uninformed but systematically wrong, and he named the ways.

Start with arithmetic. When millions of people vote, a lone ballot practically never tips the result, so voting from muddled economic ideas costs the voter nothing personally. That suggests that what the typical voter believes about the economy can be quite wrong, precisely because being wrong in the voting booth is free. His title called the rational voter a myth, and his subtitle promised to explain why democracies choose bad policies.

His main evidence came from a 1996 survey that put the same economic questions to ordinary Americans and to economists with doctorates. Comparing the answers, Caplan found four biases that voters share and that economists of every party do not. The first two are an anti-market bias, which underrates what markets deliver, and an anti-foreign bias, which underrates the gains from trade. The third is make-work bias: treating jobs as valuable in themselves rather than for what they produce, so that cutting a wasteful job looks like a loss even when it frees resources for better use. It fuels opposition to labor-saving machines, automation and free trade. The fourth is pessimistic bias, in which voters keep overestimating how bad the economy is and how fast it is getting worse, so polls show gloom even in booms. The survey was the Survey of Americans and Economists on the Economy, or SAEE, commissioned by the Washington Post together with Harvard and the Kaiser Family Foundation.

Caplan's name for the mechanism is rational irrationality. A single mistaken belief sways one vote among tens of millions, so its private cost is essentially zero, and it becomes rational, in a narrow sense, to cling to a comforting error such as the idea that trade destroys jobs. His sharpest contrast sets two arenas side by side. A consumer who believes something foolish about a product pays for it from his own wallet, so he thinks before he buys, while a voter who believes something foolish about a policy pays almost nothing, so he can afford to indulge it. That, Caplan argues, is why democracies choose bad policies.

Caplan works at George Mason University in Virginia, which became the main home of the public choice school founded by James Buchanan and Gordon Tullock. His colleagues there have included Peter Boettke, Alex Tabarrok and Tyler Cowen; the university runs the Mercatus Center, and Cowen and Tabarrok write the economics blog Marginal Revolution.

carl-menger--who-he-was.context_blurb:
Carl Menger, born in 1840, founded the Austrian school of economics. Trained in law, he was working in the press office of Austria's prime minister when he published his Principles of Economics in 1871, and the book won him a chair at the University of Vienna in 1873. From there his ideas spread through students who carried them into the next century.

Menger taught that worth lies in the wants of the person judging a good, not in the toil that made it, and the circle that grew around him in Vienna became known as the Austrian School. He was not alone. Within a few years Jevons, working in Manchester, and Walras, in Lausanne, reached the same insight separately: a good's value springs from the usefulness of one more unit of it to the person acquiring it, and labor has nothing to do with it. Historians call that breakthrough the marginal revolution.

In 1876 Emperor Franz Joseph chose Menger as private tutor to his son, Crown Prince Rudolf, and Menger traveled with the prince through Europe until 1878. His lesson was the lesson of his book: a good's value comes from the personal wants of its buyers and from how much of it they already hold. Rudolf's death at Mayerling in 1889 grieved his old teacher deeply. Menger's two brightest students, Eugen von Böhm-Bawerk and Friedrich von Wieser, wrote most of the next chapter of Austrian thought, on capital, on how value passes from goods back to the factors that make them, and on refuting Marx's labor theory of value. The two men also married a pair of sisters.

Menger came to economics through law, not mathematics. After earlier study in Prague, he took his doctorate in jurisprudence in 1867 at the Jagiellonian University in Kraków, Poland's oldest university. His civil-service job of reading the daily commodity reports showed him that prices did not follow the labor put into goods. Price, he concluded, comes from the subjective usefulness of the last unit of a good to each individual buyer.

Picture two friends at a food truck. One orders a taco, his favorite; the other, who has no taste for tacos, orders nothing, though the price and the ingredients are the same for both. The scene shows that value is subjective, depending on the person and not on the object. Menger's son Karl, born in Vienna in 1902, became a mathematician of the Vienna Circle, and a three-dimensional fractal, a cube hollowed again and again by ever smaller cubes, bears his name: the Menger sponge.

In 1892 Menger wrote his second most-cited work, an essay on the origin of money, Über den Ursprung des Geldes. It shows money arising from barter without any ruler's decree: traders learn which goods others take most readily and drift, step by step, toward the most saleable of all. Menger also gathered a vast private collection of economics books, pamphlets and journals, among the biggest anywhere in Europe. After his death in 1921 his heirs sold it abroad, and it survives as the Menger Library at Hitotsubashi University in Tokyo.

certificate-of-need-the-hospital-that-ne.context_blurb:
In about thirty-five American states and Washington, DC, no hospital may add a wing, open a facility or buy an expensive scanner until a state board agrees that it is needed. The permission slip is called a Certificate of Need, and the rules that require it are known as CON laws. Their stated aim is efficiency, but economists who study their record tell a different story.

Critics in the public-choice school see a racket in the Certificate of Need: it hands established hospitals a way to stop cheaper newcomers before a single patient walks in. Backers defend the laws as a guard against duplicative healthcare investment, arguing that proof of need prevents wasteful overbuilding and steers patients to busier, more efficient facilities.

In practice, whenever someone applies to build, the hospitals already there turn out at the hearing in force to swear that no more beds are needed, because they do not want the competition. Their objections can delay an approval for years or kill it outright. Economists such as Matthew Mitchell of the Mercatus Center have compared states that keep these rules with states that scrapped them or never had them. The CON states end up with fewer hospitals for their population, and they charge more. Year after year, with incumbents holding a loud voice, boards turn applicants away, so fewer hospitals open, fewer MRI scanners get bought and prices climb, the opposite of the promised savings.

George Stigler explained the pattern in a 1971 paper, The Theory of Economic Regulation: over time, regulators end up working for the very firms they oversee instead of for the public. The idea is now called regulatory capture, and Certificate of Need boards are a textbook case of it.

The same rule reaches beyond hospitals. In many states, anyone hoping to start a home-health-care office must prove need before a board where firms already in business can argue against letting it in, so the law mostly protects existing businesses from new competition. In Kentucky, a lawsuit brought by the Institute for Justice, the Bogdanchik case, argues that such a rule violates the Fourteenth Amendment's protection of the right to earn a living.

concealed-carry-fees-the-victim-who-coul.context_blurb:
Carrying a hidden pistol for protection is regulated very differently from one American state to the next. Some states require nothing at all, while others demand fees, training and long lists of forbidden places. Economists in Bastiat's tradition ask who pays for those rules, and who never shows up in anyone's count.

In a growing number of states, any law-abiding adult may carry a concealed handgun with no permit whatever: no fee, no application, no required class. Supporters call this constitutional carry and say it restores what the Second Amendment originally meant; about 27 states allowed it by 2024. The debate turns on incentives. A burglar who knows that some homes may hold an armed occupant has a reason to think twice, while one who knows that no home is armed has less to fear, because incentives change behavior. The economist John Lott's 1998 book More Guns, Less Crime is the most-cited, and most disputed, study of carry laws.

When one state cut its fees and paperwork, the people who signed up in much greater numbers were lower-income and minority families living in high-crime neighborhoods, residents who cannot count on the police arriving quickly. On June 23, 2022, the Supreme Court decided the case known as Bruen, brought by the New York State Rifle and Pistol Association. It struck down New York's may-issue law, under which officials could deny a permit unless an applicant showed a special need, and Justice Clarence Thomas, writing for the majority, held that the right to bear arms extends beyond the home into public places. Gun-rights supporters rank Bruen beside the Heller decision as a landmark.

California, New Jersey and New York, which had kept permits scarce, did not give up after Bruen. They shifted from refusing permits outright to making them costly and limited: higher fees, extensive training requirements, and long lists of sensitive places where carrying is banned. Bastiat's method looks for the person who is harmed but never counted. The seen side of such rules is the fee revenue and the training certificate. The unseen side is the victim who could not afford the fee, a woman being stalked, say, who could not pay hundreds of dollars and give up twenty hours to classes, and so faced her attacker unarmed.

The fiercest empirical fight concerns how often Americans use guns in self-defense. In 1995 the criminologists Gary Kleck and Marc Gertz published a national household survey estimating about 2.2 million defensive gun uses a year, far more than the number of gun crimes, and gun-control groups still dispute the figure.

craig-wright-s-fraudulent-satoshi-claim-.context_blurb:
Bitcoin's creator, who wrote as Satoshi Nakamoto, published the white paper in 2008, mined the first coins and then vanished without ever showing a face. Many people have since claimed the name. The loudest was Craig Wright, a computer scientist from Australia, and his story became a lesson in what counts as proof in a system built to replace trust with mathematics.

Experts ask any claimant for one simple demonstration: move some of the coins Satoshi mined in Bitcoin's first days, which works as a signature only the true owner could make. Just as decisive is signing a fresh message with a private key known to belong to Satoshi, a proof that takes seconds and cannot be forged. Wright never did either.

In May 2016 Wright invited a few reporters to private sessions in London and walked them through what looked like a cryptographic proof. Within hours the security researcher Dan Kaminsky and others showed that it was an old Satoshi signature copied, not a new one, because anyone with a computer can verify a Bitcoin proof for himself. Rather than retreat, Wright doubled down. In November 2018 he helped launch a coin that split from Bitcoin Cash and carried his claim in its very name: Bitcoin Satoshi's Vision, or BSV.

Wright also threatened and sued developers who called him a fraud. So programmers and crypto firms joined forces in the Crypto Open Patent Alliance and took him to the High Court in London, and in March 2024 the case, COPA v Wright, ended with Mr Justice James Mellor ruling that Wright was not Satoshi. The judge's language was unusually blunt: the documents and messages he had put forward as proof had been forged and backdated, many with fonts and metadata that could not have existed on the dates claimed.

Why pool their resources? Fighting a wealthy litigant costs more than any single small developer could bear, but the cost becomes bearable when it is split across many. The alliance, launched in 2020, was founded and largely funded by Jack Dorsey's company Square, later renamed Block. Bitcoin developers stress that the simplest check on any would-be Satoshi costs nothing: ask him to sign a message with a private key from the earliest Bitcoin blocks.

After the ruling Wright kept repeating his claims, and the court held him in contempt and referred him for possible criminal prosecution for perjury and forgery. Bitcoin teachers draw one lesson from the saga. Old writings, speeches and court papers prove nothing, because in a system whose whole security rests on private-key signatures, cryptographic proof of key control is the only identity claim that means anything.

de-gaulle-s-gold-drain-and-the-london-go.context_blurb:
The postwar Bretton Woods order pegged other money to the dollar, and only the dollar to gold, at thirty-five dollars an ounce. By the 1960s America was issuing dollars faster than its gold could back them. From 1965 to 1968 the France of Charles de Gaulle put the American promise to the test, and the test exposed what was already broken.

Washington was paying for two huge undertakings at once, the Vietnam War and Lyndon Johnson's Great Society programs such as Medicare and the War on Poverty, and the dollars it printed made the peg ever harder to defend. In February 1965 Charles de Gaulle, president of France, told a Paris press conference that the arrangement handed America a huge and unfair advantage, and he announced that France would swap its dollars for real gold and bring the bars home.

The famous phrase for that advantage, the exorbitant privilege, is often credited to de Gaulle, but it was coined by his finance minister, Valéry Giscard d'Estaing, who became president of France himself in 1974. The privilege was this: because central banks everywhere held dollars as their main reserve, the United States could import real goods and pay for them in freshly printed dollars that other countries were obliged to hold.

France began cashing in dollars at the US Treasury and converted about $150 million in the first year, forcing America to defend its peg with real bullion; larger conversions followed, and other central banks copied France more quietly. The bars waited first in the Federal Reserve Bank of New York's gold vault at 33 Liberty Street, cut deep into Manhattan's rock, eighty feet below the street, where foreign central banks keep their gold.

The peg had another line of defense. When private bidders in London pushed gold's price past $35 at the end of the 1950s, eight central banks of the West, with Washington and London in the lead, agreed in 1961 to pool their gold and sell into every private run to pin the price down. They called the arrangement the London Gold Pool. France quit it in June 1967, and the buying pressure kept mounting until the remaining members gave up and dissolved the pool on March 17, 1968.

From then on gold traded at two prices at once: central banks could still swap at the official $35, while private buyers paid whatever the market demanded. Monetary historians call this a two-tier gold market. A Bastiat-style reading says France did not break the peg; it revealed one already broken. Once the dollars issued had outrun the gold behind them, the peg was arithmetically impossible to sustain and would snap the moment any large holder tested it, and de Gaulle was simply the tester. Nixon's closing of the gold window on August 15, 1971, finished the story.

deng-xiaopings-reform-and-opening-1978.context_blurb:
Mao Zedong's China owned every farm and factory and told each village what to grow. After Mao's death in 1976, Deng Xiaoping, twice purged and twice restored, took charge, and in December 1978 the Communist Party's Third Plenum launched his turn toward markets. Four decades of change followed, the largest natural experiment the debate over socialist calculation ever received.

Historians call the program Reform and Opening, because real prices came back, first in farming and then in industry, and the country opened to the world. Farmers were allowed to sell some of their harvest, some private shops reopened, and foreign companies built factories in special coastal zones. Set beside Mao's rules, Deng's China was far more market and far less central planning.

The first change came in the villages. Under the communes the state had taken every crop; now a household might keep or market everything it raised beyond the state's quota, and farmers worked much harder because the extra was now theirs. It began illegally. In December 1978 eighteen families in the poor village of Xiaogang, in Anhui province, secretly divided their commune's land into family plots, risking arrest or worse, so that each family would be rewarded for the food it grew rather than the village as a whole. They even pledged to raise one another's children if any of them were taken away.

The results stunned Deng's own officials: between 1978 and 1984 China's grain output rose by about 34 percent on essentially the same land and labor. In 1980 four small coastal cities, Xiamen, Shantou, Zhuhai and Shenzhen, became Special Economic Zones, walled-off experiments where foreign firms could invest and the market set prices; Shenzhen grew from a fishing town of some 30,000 people into a metropolis of more than 17 million. Industry changed by halves. A steel mill still delivered its state quota at the old fixed price but could sell anything beyond it at market prices, a hybrid called dual-track pricing that let market signals reach production without scrapping the plan overnight.

When the old guard accused him of betraying Mao, Deng answered with a folk saying from a 1961 speech: whether a cat is black or white makes no difference, so long as it catches mice. Results, not appearances, were what counted. He also refused grand blueprints, the kind that had produced the Great Leap Forward and its tens of millions of dead. His method, in a phrase he made famous, was to cross the river by feeling for the stones: test a policy in one place, watch whether it works, and move on only once it has.

By the World Bank's count, from 1981 to 2015 about 800 million Chinese climbed above the line of extreme poverty, the largest sustained fall in poverty ever measured. The pattern inside China tells the same story. The market-priced parts of the economy, family farms, township workshops and coastal export factories, grew fastest, while the state-owned banks and factories that the planners kept in their grip grew slowest.

east-germanys-trabant-the-calculation-de.context_blurb:
The Trabant, a name meaning little satellite, was the small car turned out by the state-owned works at Zwickau, in communist East Germany, between 1957 and 1991, some three million in all. It was slow, smoky and shoddy, and for most families it was the only new car on offer. Austrian economists call it the calculation debate on wheels.

One government plant built it and no other firm was allowed to make cars, so buyers waited years for a vehicle that arrived noisy and sluggish. The lesson is plain: where no rival is allowed, quality stops improving. Planners could not secure enough sheet steel, so the body was made of Duraplast, a hard resin reinforced with waste cotton fibers, cheap, light and rustproof. That improvisation shows the limit of planning, since one small group cannot plan every material a whole country needs.

The state set the Trabant's price far below what buyers would have paid and rationed the cars through a waiting list. The wait ran from ten to fifteen years, so some parents put their names down when a child was born. Bastiat would see two prices. The seen price was the affordable sticker; the unseen price was the ten- to fifteen-year queue, along with a used market in which a secondhand Trabant cost more than a new one, because it could be driven home today.

For more than three decades the car barely changed, because no rival maker could enter the East German market and force a redesign, and so the state factory felt no competitive pressure to improve it. When the Berlin Wall's guards stepped aside on the evening of November 9, 1989, and in the weeks that followed thousands of puttering Trabants rolled through the checkpoints into West Berlin. The fall of the Berlin Wall turned the little car into a symbol of East Germany's collapse; within months used Western cars flooded in and the Trabant all but vanished.

The car is Ludwig von Mises's argument made physical. In his 1920 German essay, Economic Calculation in the Socialist Commonwealth, the Vienna economist predicted that planners without market prices could not know what to build or when a design needed updating. Its bigger cousin, the Wartburg from the Eisenach plant, had queues of its own. The pattern has one cause: with no competing makers, there is no reason to build more or to build better.

The frozen design joins two Austrian moves to the seen-and-unseen queue. One is the knowledge problem, because planners could not learn what buyers wanted or when to update; the other is the incentive-to-improve problem, because without rivals nobody had any reason to pay for a redesign.

elinor-ostrom-governing-the-commons-1990.context_blurb:
For most of the twentieth century, economists told a gloomy story about shared things. A pasture, a fishery or a forest that nobody owns, they said, is doomed to be stripped bare. One political scientist from Indiana spent her life going out to look for herself, and what she found in mountain villages and fishing harbors won her the highest prize in economics.

The gloomy story had a famous name. In 1968 the biologist Garrett Hardin set it out in the journal Science as "the tragedy of the commons." Picture a village green open to every herder. Each extra cow puts its whole gain in one herder's pocket, while the damage from overgrazing is split among everyone, so every herder keeps adding cows until the shared pasture is overused and finally ruined.

Elinor Ostrom, who taught for decades at Indiana University in Bloomington, would not accept that story until she had checked it against the world. In 1990 she published Governing the Commons, a book packed with real cases in which local people had run shared land, water and fish for centuries without wrecking them. In 2009 the Nobel committee gave Elinor Ostrom its economics prize, shared with Oliver Williamson, and no woman had ever won that prize before her.

What held those commons together? The users themselves wrote the rules, kept an eye on one another, and punished cheaters with fines, gossip and lost privileges. Local rules and social pressure, invented and enforced by the very people who depend on the resource, did the job that textbooks had handed to a government or a private owner.

Her best-known example sits high in the Swiss Alps. In the village of Törbel and its neighbors in the Valais, herders have shared the summer pastures since the 1200s under rules they wrote themselves, including limits on how many cows each family may send up the mountain. Nobody owns the slopes outright, yet they were never grazed to ruin. The lesson Ostrom drew is that a community can look after a shared resource well when it makes its own rules and enforces them.

She also pointed to the lobster coast of Maine. There, informal "harbor gangs" divide the sea among their own boats, and an outsider who sets traps in claimed water soon finds his buoy lines cut. Her collaborator James Acheson described these gangs in his 1988 book The Lobster Gangs of Maine.

Comparing case after case, Ostrom pulled out eight design principles that the long-lived commons had in common. Among them were clear boundaries around the resource, rules suited to the local setting, low-cost means of resolving quarrels, and higher governments willing to leave the users' decisions alone. She found the list by comparing real cases, not by deducing it from theory.

In 1973 Elinor and her husband, Vincent Ostrom, founded the Workshop in Political Theory and Policy Analysis at Indiana University. Generations of scholars trained there, and its approach became known as the Bloomington School.

Vincent had coined a word in 1961 that Elinor made central to her work: polycentricity. Picture neighboring farm groups along one river, each running its own irrigation canal by its own rules and meeting the others to settle problems they share; that web of many centers of decision at many levels is polycentric.

Textbooks offered only two cures for a commons: hand it to the state, or carve it up among private owners. From the irrigation canals of Nepal to the pastures of Switzerland, Ostrom's fieldwork documented a third path that works in practice: user groups governing the resource themselves, provided their institutions are designed well. In the classical-liberal reading her work sits beside Hayek's argument about dispersed knowledge, because the people on the spot devise arrangements that no distant authority could design.

Yet Ostrom never claimed to have proved Hardin wrong. His tragedy is real, she argued, but it is a conditional outcome rather than an inevitable one: it strikes when users cannot talk, watch one another or enforce rules, and her cases showed it avoided wherever they could.

eugen-von-boehm-bawerk--who-he-was.context_blurb:
Vienna around 1900 was the capital of a great empire and one of the liveliest places on earth to argue about economics. At its center stood Eugen von Boehm-Bawerk: a finance minister who refused to spend money the state did not have, a teacher whose seminar trained famous economists, and the critic who did more than anyone to take apart Karl Marx's theory of value.

He was born in 1851 in Brno, a city of Moravia in the old Austrian Empire; today Brno is the second city of the Czech Republic. As young men he and his friend Friedrich von Wieser became followers of Carl Menger, who had started the Austrian school. The friendship became family when Boehm-Bawerk married Wieser's sister Paula, and as brothers-in-law the two men carried Menger's ideas forward together for decades.

Boehm-Bawerk was a scholar who also governed. He served three separate times as Austria's finance minister, and he held that a government must live within its budget. In 1904 the army pressed for more spending than the budget could bear, and Eugen von Boehm-Bawerk resigned from the emperor's cabinet rather than approve the deficit.

He returned to the University of Vienna, where his seminar of 1905-06 became legendary. Two of its Austrian students went on to become household names of twentieth-century economics: Ludwig von Mises and Joseph Schumpeter.

His great work Capital and Interest, whose first two volumes appeared in 1884 and 1889, explains interest through a plain human trait. People value a good now more than the same good later, so a lender must be paid to wait; a hungry hiker gives more for a sandwich in hand than for the promise of one next month. Economists call this time preference, and in Boehm-Bawerk's account the interest rate is its price.

In 1896 he turned on Marx. Marx's labor theory of value held that a good's worth comes only from the work spent making it. In an essay whose German title is Zum Abschluss des Marxschen Systems, known in English as Karl Marx and the Close of His System, Boehm-Bawerk argued that the theory falls apart when you read Marx's own Capital all the way through.

The contradiction runs like this. The first volume of Capital, from 1867, ties prices to hours of labor. The third, which Engels pieced together from Marx's papers and brought out in 1894, says competition must give every industry the same rate of profit. Since industries use very different mixes of machines and workers, profit rates could not be equal if labor alone set prices, so both claims cannot hold at once. That gap is known today as the transformation problem, and Marxists have proposed rescues for more than a century.

The famous seminar was also famous for its Marxists. Week after week Boehm-Bawerk pressed his critique against two young Austro-Marxists who defended Marx: Otto Bauer and Rudolf Hilferding. Bauer later became Austria's foreign minister and Hilferding the finance minister of Weimar Germany, and the young Mises, future champion of free markets, sat in the same room.

Boehm-Bawerk died on 27 August 1914. Historians note the date because the First World War had begun only a month before, when Austria-Hungary declared war on Serbia, and the spending discipline he had fought for in cabinet was about to dissolve into war finance. His work on capital, interest and time became the foundation on which Mises and Hayek built.

fdrs-gold-seizure-executive-order-6102-a.context_blurb:
Executive Order 6102, which Franklin Roosevelt signed on April 5, 1933, commanded Americans to surrender almost all the gold they held, whether coins, bullion or gold certificates, paid for in paper dollars at the official rate of $20.67 per ounce. What followed over the next year is one of the starkest lessons in American history about who wins and who loses when a government takes control of money.

Why gather up every citizen's gold? As long as Americans could swap paper dollars for gold, the metal limited how much paper money the government could create. With the gold locked in its own vaults, the government could print more paper money with no gold limit to stop it.

The order was presented as a way to stop "hoarding" during the Depression. Anyone who kept a large stash risked up to ten years in prison and a fine as high as $10,000, though small amounts, up to $100 in coins, and rare collectors' coins were allowed.

Then came the twist. On January 30, 1934, Roosevelt signed the Gold Reserve Act, and the next day his proclamation fixed gold at $35.00 an ounce. The same stroke cut the gold content of a dollar from roughly 23.22 grains to 13.71, nearly half, so every dollar already in a pocket or a bank account was suddenly worth less in gold overnight.

Savers who had obeyed the order received $20.67 for each ounce the government now valued at $35. Gold's dollar price had jumped by about 69 percent, which meant the dollar had lost about two-fifths of its gold value, and that slice of the savers' wealth passed to the US Treasury. Nobody who had handed in gold could buy it back at the old price.

Many private contracts and government bonds had promised payment in gold. In the Gold Clause Cases of 1935 the Supreme Court split 5 to 4. It called the cancellation unconstitutional for the government's own bonds, yet ruled that bondholders could collect no damages, so in practice the government could shrink the real value of what it and other borrowers owed to savers.

Owning gold stayed illegal for ordinary Americans for more than four decades. Congress finally lifted the ban with effect from the last day of 1974, December 31, when Gerald Ford was president.

The seized metal needed a fortress. In 1936 the Treasury completed the Fort Knox Bullion Depository on an Army post in Kentucky, and it still holds most of America's official gold.

Bastiat's lens sorts the episode cleanly. The seen side was the official purpose, a sounder banking system protected from gold hoarding. The unseen side was the transfer: middle-class savers who had prudently kept gold saw their wealth moved to the Treasury through the devaluation.

Austrian economists draw a lasting lesson from 1933. A determined state can make it a crime to hold hard money, seize the holdings that already exist, and then devalue its currency against the metal it has collected. Governments have reached for that tool again and again, as John Law did in France in 1720.

for-a-new-liberty-1973-and-the-ethics-of.context_blurb:
Murray Rothbard, a New York economist who studied in Ludwig von Mises's seminar, pushed the Austrian school's defense of freedom further than almost anyone. In two books, one popular and one philosophical, he argued for a society with no government at all. Few readers accept that conclusion, but his reasoning shaped the modern libertarian movement and still starts arguments.

In 1973 the publisher Macmillan brought out his most popular book, For a New Liberty, subtitled The Libertarian Manifesto. It sketched a whole libertarian society, with private courts and roads, no military draft and no income tax. The worldview it defends, libertarianism, is the belief that most decisions, about how to live, work, worship and trade, should be left to individuals rather than to governments.

Everything in the book rests on one rule, a rule known as the non-aggression principle: no one, whether a single person or a group, may start the use of force against another person or against what that person owns. Rothbard applied the rule to the state as strictly as to a street criminal, so in his eyes taxation and the draft count as aggression too.

Followed to its end, the rule led Rothbard to reject even a minimal government. He called his position anarcho-capitalism, a stateless society in which every service, from courts and police to roads, is paid for by voluntary choice instead of taxes. To the obvious worry that this means lawlessness, he answered that it means law supplied in a different way. Police, courts, roads and even national defense would come from rival private firms, each held to contracts grounded in property rights; his chapter on private roads is the book's famous test case.

That same year David Friedman, Milton Friedman's son, published The Machinery of Freedom. He reached the same stateless goal by another road, arguing from practical results and weighing costs against benefits instead of appealing to natural rights, and the two 1973 books founded the two branches of the movement.

Nine years later, in 1982, Rothbard published his philosophical foundation, The Ethics of Liberty. It roots libertarianism in the tradition of the seventeenth-century English philosopher John Locke, the conviction that each of us owns himself, his work and its fruits, prior to any state.

That Lockean idea has a name: natural rights, rights a person holds by nature rather than by a government's permission. The Harvard philosopher Robert Nozick built his famous 1974 book, Anarchy, State, and Utopia, on the same foundation, but he drew a different conclusion. In Nozick's view a state ought to exist but do only three things: guard people against violence, guard them against theft, and enforce contracts. A government shrunk to those bare duties is called a night-watchman state. Rothbard rejected Nozick's reasoning and insisted that any state violates rights.

In Part IV of The Ethics of Liberty, Rothbard examined four rival defenders of freedom in turn: Ludwig von Mises, Friedrich Hayek, Isaiah Berlin, and Robert Nozick. He argued that Mises's utilitarian reasoning, Hayek's rule-of-law liberalism, Berlin's famous two concepts of liberty and Nozick's minimal state each fell short of a fully consistent defense of liberty.

friedmans-1968-aea-address-the-natural-r.context_blurb:
For twenty years after the Second World War, many economists believed they had found a dial for the economy. A government willing to accept a little more inflation could buy a little less unemployment, and turn the dial back again when it liked. In one lecture Milton Friedman argued that the dial was an illusion, and the 1970s proved his point.

The dial came from a chart. In 1958 the New Zealand-born economist A. W. Phillips plotted British data showing that wages rose fastest when unemployment was low. Governments read his curve as a menu: hire more workers, accept higher prices.

In December 1967, as president of the American Economic Association, Friedman gave the group's annual address, published in 1968 as The Role of Monetary Policy. Printing money to drive joblessness lower, he warned, works only briefly; before long the general level of prices begins to climb. That steady, general rise in prices is inflation.

The heart of his argument was a floor under unemployment. In the long run, Friedman said, the jobless rate is set by real features of the economy rather than by money: how long workers take to find new jobs, how well their skills fit what employers need, how freely wages adjust, and rules such as the minimum wage. He called that floor the natural unemployment rate. Working separately, the Columbia economist Edmund Phelps reached the same conclusion in a 1967 paper, and he later won a Nobel Prize for it.

What Phillips had left out was belief. Friedman and Phelps added inflation expectations, meaning what people expect prices to do in the coming year. If everyone expects prices to rise 4 percent, workers demand 4 percent more pay, and the extra money buys no extra jobs.

So the surprise wears off. Once people catch on and build the coming inflation into their wages and prices, joblessness drifts back up to its natural level, and the country is left with the higher inflation as well. In the long run, Friedman concluded, the old trade-off would collapse.

A central bank that keeps trying anyway faces a harsh logic. To keep fooling people it must push inflation higher every year, 4 percent, then 8, then 16. Holding unemployment below its natural floor, the theory predicts, requires inflation that speeds up without end, until the money itself breaks down.

The 1970s ran the experiment. Through that decade the Fed kept money loose to keep jobs plentiful, and by 1980 consumer prices were rising over 13 percent a year, up from about 2 percent in 1965. Unemployment stayed high as well, a mix that older theory said could not happen. Economists named this combination of high inflation and high unemployment stagflation, a word the British politician Iain Macleod had coined in 1965.

Friedman received the Nobel Prize in 1976, and his address still shapes how central banks work. Starting with New Zealand in 1990, most developed countries' central banks adopted inflation targeting: they publicly commit to holding inflation at a set low number so that people's expectations stay anchored and stable.

george-stigler-1971-the-theory-of-econom.context_blurb:
For generations, civics classes told a simple story about regulation: when an industry grows too powerful, the government steps in to protect the public. In 1971 the University of Chicago economist George Stigler turned that story upside down, and the work helped win him the Nobel Prize in 1982.

His paper, The Theory of Economic Regulation, appeared in the spring of 1971 in The Bell Journal of Economics and Management Science, a journal backed by the research arm of AT&T.

Stigler argued that, as a rule, an industry acquires its own regulation, and the rules are designed and run mainly for that industry's benefit. Firms lobby for the rules, help write them and then live comfortably under them.

The pattern has a name. When a regulator gradually becomes the servant of the businesses it was set up to watch, hiring their former lobbyists and writing rules that suit the biggest firms, economists call it regulatory capture.

Why do industries win? Picture a sugar tariff that hands a few big producers millions of dollars a year while adding a couple of dollars to each family's grocery bill. The producers hire lobbyists and fight, and most families never notice. The cost is dispersed, spread thinly over millions of people, while the benefit is concentrated in a few hands.

Mancur Olson had worked out the logic in his 1965 book The Logic of Collective Action. When a rule means millions to a small group and pennies each to a huge one, the small, well-organized group with much to gain usually wins, because its members have every reason to organize and the many have almost none.

Occupational licensing follows the same logic. When a state debates requiring interior designers to pass a hard exam and pay a yearly fee before they may work, the people who crowd into the capitol to support the law are the designers already in the business. The rule keeps newcomers out and their own earnings up.

Stigler made licensing his sharpest test. If licenses existed to protect customers, quality should rise where they are required. Instead, Stigler, and later Morris Kleiner, found that licensing lifts the incomes of those already in a trade with no measurable gain in quality, just as capture theory predicts.

He found the pattern elsewhere too. When Stigler studied the state commissions that fixed electricity and gas rates, he found they did little to hold prices down for households, and the regulated utilities themselves kept coming out ahead.

The oldest federal example is the Interstate Commerce Commission, created in 1887 to police the railroads and later given control of trucking as well. For decades it set truckers' rates and routes and made entry very hard for newcomers, shielding the established companies, and it became a textbook case of regulatory capture.

Stigler's analysis fed a wave of reform. President Jimmy Carter signed the Airline Deregulation Act in 1978, letting airlines set their own routes and fares, and the Motor Carrier Act in 1980, which did the same for interstate trucking.

His deepest move was a change of question. Welfare economists had asked what regulation society ought to want. Stigler treated regulation as a product with its own market and asked instead what regulation interest groups actually demand, and what government supplies in return for votes, campaign money and future jobs.

greshams-law-bad-money-drives-out-good.context_blurb:
Whenever two kinds of money must by law be accepted at the same value, but one is really worth more, something predictable happens to the better one. The pattern carries the name of an Elizabethan merchant, but people noticed it long before him, and Americans watched it happen in their own pockets in the 1960s.

Sir Thomas Gresham, a London merchant, advised Queen Elizabeth I on the crown's money in the 1500s and founded the Royal Exchange. He observed what happens when coins of equal face value hold different amounts of precious metal, and his observation was later boiled down to a short saying: bad money drives good money out of circulation.

Picture a king who saves money by mixing cheap metal into his new coins while declaring them worth as much as the old, purer ones. His subjects notice at once that the new coins are lighter and duller. Families hide the old coins at home and spend only the debased ones, so good money disappears from the market while bad money circulates.

Put two shillings in one pocket, both worth a shilling by law, one of full silver and the other secretly half silver. A sensible shopper spends the half-silver shilling and keeps the full-silver one, every time. Merchants end up holding only debased coin, while the good coins are hoarded, melted or sent abroad.

The pattern is far older than the name. Around 1360 the French scholar Nicole Oresme, later a bishop, explained it in a short book on coinage, De Moneta. If a ruler shrinks the gold in his new coins while insisting they are worth as much as the old, Oresme showed, people hide the older, purer coins and spend only the cheap new ones.

In 1526 the astronomer Nicolaus Copernicus described it again in his treatise on coinage, Monetae cudendae ratio, written for Prussia's rulers. Not until 1858 did the Scottish economist Henry Dunning Macleod attach Gresham's name, and the rule is still taught today as Gresham's Law.

Why did three men in three countries, two centuries apart, find the same rule? Because it describes a real pattern that repeats whenever rulers debase their coins: give people a legal choice between paying with something worth less and something worth more, and they will pay with the cheaper one.

Americans saw it in the 1960s. For most of the country's history its dimes and quarters had been ninety percent silver, but the Coinage Act of 1965 took the silver out and replaced it with a sandwich of copper and nickel. The older silver coins soon disappeared from cash drawers and pocket change, because people pulled them from circulation and hoarded them or melted them down for their metal.

The law needs one condition to work. Both coins must be declared legal tender at the same face value, so a seller is forced to accept the worse coin as equal to the better. Without that rule, people would simply price each coin by its real metal, and the good coin would trade at a premium instead of hiding in a drawer.

hayeks-collectivist-economic-planning-19.context_blurb:
In 1920 Ludwig von Mises published an argument in German that would shake the economics profession: a socialist economy, he said, cannot plan rationally at all. For fifteen years few English-speaking economists read it. Then Friedrich Hayek, newly settled at the London School of Economics, put it in front of them.

The challenge is easy to picture. Abolish markets and prices, and a single bureau in the capital must settle every year what the nation will produce, from boots to farm machinery. With no prices formed by buying and selling, its officials have no signal of what consumers value or which materials are scarce, and that obstacle is the calculation problem.

Mises put it in terms of choices. If the state owns every factory, it must still decide how much steel goes to trucks, how much to tractors and how much to bridges. It cannot make that choice rationally, Mises argued, because without private buyers and sellers there are no market prices to compare one use with another.

Others had imagined a way around this. Enrico Barone, an Italian, had shown in a 1908 paper that a planning ministry might, on paper, fix all prices correctly, provided it could work through a vast system of simultaneous equations. Mises and later Austrians pointed to the practical flaw: no planner could ever gather all the information those equations need, and certainly not in time.

In 1935 Hayek gathered the debate into a book published by Routledge in London, called Collectivist Economic Planning, with a long subtitle about the possibilities of socialism. Its centerpiece was the first English translation of Ludwig von Mises's Economic Calculation in the Socialist Commonwealth, the 1920 essay that had until then circulated only in German. The book also reprinted Barone's paper.

Hayek wrote two essays of his own to frame the translation. His introduction traced the origins of the problem, and his closing essay, The Present State of the Debate, surveyed what the planners' defenders had proposed since.

The volume provoked the most famous reply of the debate, the Polish economist Oskar Lange's market-socialist papers of 1936 and 1937. Hayek kept pressing, adding that the knowledge an economy runs on is dispersed among millions of people and can never be collected in one head. His essays on calculation and knowledge were gathered in 1948 in the book Individualism and Economic Order.

indias-license-raj-1947-1991.context_blurb:
When India won its independence in 1947, its leaders chose to steer the economy from New Delhi. For more than four decades a business needed government permission for almost everything it did, and the results became one of the twentieth century's great natural experiments in what permits cost a nation.

Indians called the system the License Raj, rule by permit. A firm needed approval to open a factory, to expand it, to import a machine, to hire beyond a certain size, to make a new product or to change its prices, often eighty or more separate stamps in all. When officials must approve every step of every business, the economy is being run by central planning.

Growth crawled. From 1950 to 1980 India's output per person crept up by roughly 1 percent annually, a pace the Indian economist Raj Krishna mocked with a self-critical label, the so-called Hindu rate of growth.

Meanwhile Hong Kong, Singapore, Taiwan and South Korea traded freely with the world and grew many times faster. Those four booming economies earned the nickname the Four Asian Tigers, and their success is the standard comparison for what India gave up.

Where did all the energy go? When a permit is worth more than the business it allows, people pour their time and money into chasing permits, hiring fixers, courting officials and paying bribes, instead of building better products. In 1974 the American economist Anne Krueger, drawing on India and Turkey, gave this its modern name: rent-seeking. The real resources burned up in that chase add nothing to output, and economists call the waste rent-seeking dissipation; Krueger put India's at several percent of national income.

In 1991 India nearly ran out of foreign currency to pay for its imports. Under Prime Minister Narasimha Rao, his finance minister, Manmohan Singh, began tearing down the permit system. Once the licenses were gone, new businesses could start far more easily and the economy grew faster.

The reform was real but gradual. Big state-owned firms survived, many rules stayed on the books, and tariffs fell only slowly, yet growth sped up dramatically without any overnight transformation.

Over the three decades after 1991, India's real income per person rose year after year, and by 2020 it had more than quadrupled as hundreds of millions of people climbed out of extreme poverty.

The standard scholarly account is India: The Emerging Giant, published in 2008 by the Columbia University economist Arvind Panagariya.

jeff-booth-and-the-price-of-tomorrow-tec.context_blurb:
Jeff Booth spent thirty years building and selling companies, including the online building-materials firm BuildDirect, before he turned to writing about money. His 2020 book, written during the COVID lockdowns, makes a surprising claim: falling prices are a gift, and central banks are hiding it from us.

The book is titled The Price of Tomorrow: Why Deflation Is the Key to an Abundant Future, and it has become one of the most widely read modern books on Bitcoin.

Booth starts from a plain observation. Technology makes things cheaper over time: computer chips, solar power and data storage all fall steadily in cost as engineers improve them. That ought to make ordinary paychecks stretch further each year, so Booth calls it the misunderstood gift of the modern economy.

Why don't families feel it? Booth's answer is that central banks fear falling prices and expand the money supply to stop them. The new money does not vanish; it pushes up the prices of stocks, houses and bonds, so asset prices climb instead of consumer prices falling.

Bastiat's method makes the loss visible. Suppose a saver's wages have risen only a little since 2010 while the stock market has more than tripled. The seen fact is a calm consumer price index that seems to prove the Fed succeeded. The unseen fact, in Booth's reading, is that the technology-driven cheapening she should have felt in her cost of living was absorbed into asset prices instead, enriching people who already owned assets.

Booth's way out is Bitcoin. Because its supply is capped at 21 million coins, no authority can expand it to hide falling prices, so the natural deflation from technology could finally reach savers.

Booth is regularly paired with two other leading voices of the Bitcoin monetary argument: Michael Saylor, the software executive who moved his public company's treasury reserves into Bitcoin, and Saifedean Ammous, author of The Bitcoin Standard.

judge-by-results-not-intentions.context_blurb:
Every law arrives wrapped in good intentions: helping the poor, protecting renters, keeping customers safe. Milton Friedman, the Nobel laureate of 1976, spent decades urging people to look past the wrapping. The question that matters, he insisted, is not what a policy hopes to do but what it really accomplishes once it meets the world.

His rule is easy to remember. One of the great mistakes, Friedman said again and again, is to judge a policy or program by what it intends instead of by what it achieves: always weigh results over intentions.

His favorite target was the minimum wage. An employer will not keep paying a worker more than that worker produces, so a legal wage floor set too high shuts the least-skilled people out of jobs altogether; Friedman called it, in effect, a law that forces employers to discriminate against people with low skills.

Bastiat's lens makes the two workers visible. The seen worker keeps his job and gets a bigger paycheck. The unseen worker is never hired, because the law priced his job out of existence, and nobody counts him.

Rent control is the next case. When a city caps the rent landlords may charge, apartments become cheaper for those already in them, but over the years fewer new apartments get built and the old ones are kept up worse. Friedman and George Stigler made the argument in 1946 in a pamphlet called Roofs or Ceilings? Under rent control, landlords let their buildings decay because repairs no longer pay, and new construction stops because building is unprofitable at the capped rent.

Occupational licensing is sold as protection for customers of hairdressers or interior designers. Judged by results, its main effect is to shield the income of the incumbent licensed professionals by keeping newcomers out.

Even welfare fell under the rule. The old American welfare system counted a household's combined income when deciding who qualified, so a poor couple could lose more in benefits by marrying than the marriage added in income. Friedman argued that this marriage penalty, built into the way household income was added up, quietly damaged family life among the poor.

Thomas Sowell, Friedman's student at Chicago, made the same rule his own. A law's name and stated purpose prove nothing about its effects. Instead of trusting a policy's account of itself, the honest analyst looks at what actually happened when it was put into practice.

Sowell sharpened the rule with a two-word question for anyone praising or condemning a policy: compared to what? It forces an honest comparison with the real alternative instead of with a perfect fantasy.

Put Friedman and Sowell together and you get a three-part test for any policy. What does it intend? What does it actually do? And at what cost, compared with what alternative?

karl-menger-the-younger-the-mathematicia.context_blurb:
The economist Carl Menger launched the Austrian school in 1870s Vienna, teaching that value comes from what individuals subjectively want. His son took a different road and became a leading mathematician of the twentieth century, and his life opens a window on the astonishing Vienna that both men knew.

The son was born in Vienna in 1902, when his father was sixty-two, and he carried almost the same name: Karl. To tell them apart, people call him Karl Menger the younger.

In 1924 he completed his doctorate in Vienna, with the mathematician Hans Hahn as his adviser. His field was dimension theory, the study of how many coordinates it takes to locate every point of a space: one for a line, two for a plane, three for a solid.

In 1926 he described the shape that made his name famous: the Menger sponge. Take a solid cube, cut a square tunnel straight through the center of each face, then repeat the cutting on every smaller cube that remains, forever. What is left has endless surface and almost no volume, a three-dimensional cousin of the one-dimensional Cantor set.

Because the sponge has holes at every scale, it is neither a flat surface nor a true solid. Its fractal dimension, the logarithm of 20 divided by the logarithm of 3, works out to about 2.727, between a surface's 2 and a solid's 3.

Interwar Vienna was crowded with such minds. Menger ran a famous Mathematical Colloquium where Kurt Gödel presented parts of his incompleteness work, and he sat in on the Vienna Circle, the philosophers of logical positivism. Down the street Mises and Hayek were building the Austrian school of economics. When a group's arguments settle over years into shared instincts and shared first questions, the result is a school of thought, and Vienna produced several.

Then the city's golden circle broke apart. The rise of Nazi Germany, and its takeover of Austria in 1938, drove most of these thinkers abroad.

Menger read the danger early. In 1937 he left Austria for a chair at the University of Notre Dame, the Catholic university in Indiana, a year before the Anschluss.

Late in life he wrote a memoir of the two worlds he had known, published in 1994, after his death: Reminiscences of the Vienna Circle and the Mathematical Colloquium.
