knowledge-and-decisions-1980.context_blurb:
In 1980 the economist Thomas Sowell published Knowledge and Decisions, a long book about a short question: who knows the facts, and who gets to decide? He built it on an essay by Friedrich Hayek, and Hayek himself came to call it the best general economics book in many years.

Hayek's starting point was simple. The facts an economy depends on, about tastes, skills, nearby materials, broken machines and this season's crops, are spread among millions of ordinary people. No office or computer holds them all, so no small group of planners can ever know enough to run a whole economy.

Hayek made the case in an article in the American Economic Review in September 1945: The Use of Knowledge in Society. His famous example is tin. When tin grows scarce, whether because a mine has flooded or because some new use has appeared, its price rises, and manufacturers in a dozen industries use less of it without ever learning why. No planning board could gather into one office the separate reasons millions of people have for wanting tin; the price carries that knowledge in the only form in which it can travel.

Sowell asked the same question of every institution. He put markets, elected legislatures and courts through one identical test: which facts can the process actually pick up, and which is it blind to? That is why the book is no slogan of markets good, government bad; the answers differ institution by institution.

Sowell worried about a widening gap between the people who know the particulars firsthand, the farmers, tradesmen and shopkeepers, and the people who hold the power to decide, the planners and theorists who work at a distance.

Gasoline in 1973 shows the stakes. The Arab oil embargo was a real shock, but Washington also held down what American oil and gasoline could legally sell for, and drivers waited hours in lines although national stocks were adequate. On Sowell's account the cap silenced the one signal that would have told drivers to stretch a tank and refiners to run harder. When price may not ration a scarce good, something else must, and in the autumn of 1973 Oregon's governor, Tom McCall, could not move the price, so he rationed by calendar. Cars with plates ending in an odd number could fill up on odd-numbered days and even plates on even days, a rule other states soon copied.

Sowell carried the argument into education. Racial preferences in admissions, he argued, can place a student in a program whose other students arrived much better prepared. The admissions office never checks how this particular student would do at this particular program's pace, and the issue, in his account, is the fit, not the student's ability.

In 1980 the book won the prize of the Law and Economics Center, calling it a landmark for helping readers understand how the market process and the process of government differ.

In December 1981 Hayek, then eighty-two, reviewed the book in Reason magazine under the title The Best Book on General Economics in Many a Year.

Sowell himself was proud of it, but when an interviewer asked him in 2018, as he approached eighty-eight, he named a shorter and more readable book of 1987 as his own personal favorite: A Conflict of Visions.

long-term-capital-management-and-the-199.context_blurb:
Long-Term Capital Management, founded in 1994 by the former Salomon Brothers bond trader John Meriwether, was the most celebrated hedge fund of the 1990s. Among its partners were two of the world's most famous financial economists. In 1998 it nearly brought down Wall Street, and its rescue set a precedent that critics say grew into every bailout since.

The fund's star partners, Myron Scholes and Robert Merton, won the 1997 Nobel Prize in Economics for their work on pricing options. LTCM used their kind of advanced mathematical model to place its trades. Its collapse a year later taught the world that complex math models do not guarantee safety in markets.

The fund's power came from borrowing. It held about $125 billion of positions on only about $4.7 billion of its own capital, roughly twenty-seven borrowed dollars for every dollar of its own. Using borrowed money to multiply a bet in this way is called leverage: it magnifies profits when trades go well and magnifies losses just as fast when they go badly, since the loans must be repaid either way.

For four years the strategy earned very high returns. Many of LTCM's trades bet that the small price gap between two almost identical bonds would close. Then, on August 17, 1998, Russia defaulted on its debts, investors everywhere fled to the safest assets, and the price gaps widened instead of closing. The fund nearly went bankrupt and had to be rescued to stop the damage from spreading.

The models had promised that a move that large would come only once in many centuries. What they missed is that disasters strike far more often than models fitted to quiet years predict.

LTCM had no depositors and no small savers, nothing the Federal Reserve is supposed to protect. Yet the New York Fed stepped in, and its justification was the banks: those that had traded with LTCM were so exposed that a disorderly sale of its positions could cascade into the whole banking system.

The New York Fed's president, William McDonough, summoned Wall Street's chiefs, with his deputy Peter Fisher running the details. On September 23, 1998, fourteen banks agreed to pool about $3.6 billion of their own money, not taxpayers', to take over the fund and unwind its trades slowly.

There had been another offer. Warren Buffett's Berkshire Hathaway, joined by AIG and Goldman Sachs, offered $250 million for the fund, a deal that would have wiped out LTCM's partners; the talks collapsed, and the banks' rescue came instead. Free-market critics prefer private buyouts like Buffett's because they do not teach big firms that the government will save them next time.

Critics saw the danger in that lesson. A rescue that shields risk-takers from loss encourages them to gamble more boldly in future, which economists call moral hazard, and LTCM extended the expected safety net from banks to private investment funds.

Each rescue is announced as just this once. Yet first a big bank, then an investment fund, then an insurance giant, then a money-market fund was saved, and the circle of firms considered too big to fail keeps quietly widening.

march-2020-emergency-cuts-and-unlimited-.context_blurb:
In March 2020, as COVID-19 reached the United States and markets panicked, the Federal Reserve did in a few weeks what it had taken years to do after 2008, and then went further. Austrian economists see that month as the moment a whole new level of central-bank power became normal.

The first move came on Tuesday, March 3, between scheduled meetings: an emergency cut of 50 basis points, half a percentage point, taking the target range to 1.00 to 1.25 percent. It was the first surprise cut since the crisis of October 2008.

Twelve days later, on Sunday, March 15, the Fed cut by a full percentage point more, to a range of zero to 0.25 percent, and kept rates there for two years.

On March 23 it went further, promising to buy government bonds and mortgage securities in whatever amounts were needed, with no set limit. Critics called it money printing. Their warning was the old one: when far more dollars chase the same goods, prices across the economy eventually rise.

For the first time in its history the Fed also began creating money to buy bonds issued by individual companies such as Apple, Ford and AT&T. Austrian critics, among them Peter Schiff, called it a dangerous step, because the central bank was now choosing which companies to prop up.

In April the buying stretched to riskier debt: company bonds rated investment grade until the pandemic, then downgraded to junk by the rating agencies. Wall Street calls such downgraded bonds fallen angels.

On April 9 the Fed also opened a Municipal Liquidity Facility to buy the bonds of states and cities. Together with the corporate programs, that meant the central bank itself now decided which companies and local governments got credit, a job traditionally left to legislatures.

To run its corporate bond buying, the Fed hired BlackRock, the world's largest asset manager, which also ran huge bond funds of its own. Critics on left and right saw the cozy relationship between an official body and the industry it works with as a case of regulatory capture.

All of these programs rested on Section 13(3) of the Federal Reserve Act, a clause added in 1932 that allows emergency lending to almost any borrower, beyond the usual banks, in what the law calls unusual and exigent circumstances.

The Fed's balance sheet, about $4.2 trillion before the crisis, swelled to a peak of about $8.9 trillion in the spring of 2022, the biggest expansion in its history, and inflation followed in 2021 and 2022.

Economists at the Mises Institute drew the lasting lesson: emergency programs seldom get packed away once the crisis passes. They set a new, higher institutional baseline, and the next crisis response will start from that elevated level instead of returning to normal.

teaches.b5d4dbe728: Critics on left and right saw the cozy relationship between an official body and the industry it works with as a case of regulatory capture.
teaches.9876d54561: The Fed's balance sheet, about $4.2 trillion before the crisis, swelled to a peak of about $8.9 trillion in the spring of 2022, the biggest expansion in its history, and inflation followed in 2021 and 2022.
teaches.19a8ce3cd5: All of these programs rested on Section 13(3) of the Federal Reserve Act, a clause added in 1932 that allows emergency lending to almost any borrower, beyond the usual banks, in what the law calls unusual and exigent circumstances.
teaches.da9073db57: They set a new, higher institutional baseline, and the next crisis response will start from that elevated level instead of returning to normal.

milton-friedman-brooklyn-to-nobel-1976.context_blurb: Milton Friedman was an American economist born in Brooklyn in 1912. He studied at Rutgers and Chicago, where he met his wife Rose Director. He joined the Chicago economics faculty in 1946 and remained there most of his career. His 1957 book A Theory of the Consumption Function argued that a household plans its spending around the income it expects over years and reads a one-off bonus as a one-off addition to a lifetime bank account, not as a change in the long-run income it budgets against. His 1963 Monetary History of the United States, co-authored with Anna Schwartz, became the standard reference on American monetary history. His 1979 PBS series and tie-in book Free to Choose brought his ideas to a mass American audience. In 1976 he won the Nobel Memorial Prize for consumption analysis, monetary history and theory, and the complexity of stabilization policy. His arguments against conscription included a famous exchange with General William Westmoreland. In the Chicago and Austrian traditions his method stands on measured series, money stock, prices, output, that another researcher could check.

misess-disciples-the-chain-that-carried-.context_blurb: Ludwig von Mises's two most important direct students were Friedrich Hayek and Murray Rothbard. The Austrian economist Israel Kirzner developed the Austrian theory of entrepreneurship as alertness to new opportunity. The German-born American economist Hans Sennholz carried the tradition into the small-college setting at Grove City College. Murray Rothbard's two main theoretical works are the two-volume Man, Economy, and State and the shorter America's Great Depression. The journalist Henry Hazlitt extended the tradition into popular American writing starting with his 1946 Economics in One Lesson. The California-based economist George Reisman wrote a thousand-page synthesis of the Austrian tradition after decades of teaching. Together the chain carries Mises's early-twentieth-century Vienna school through three generations of writers and across the Atlantic. In the Austrian reading, this is the human infrastructure that kept the tradition alive during the postwar decades when mainstream academic economics did not take it seriously.

nationaloekonomie-1940-the-german-precur.context_blurb: In 1940 Ludwig von Mises published a German-language systematic treatise in Geneva, with a small Swiss publishing house called Editions Union. The book was titled Nationaloekonomie: Theorie des Handelns und Wirtschaftens. It appeared in a Europe already at war; Germany and Austria were closed to it and Switzerland was neutral but inaccessible. The book attracted almost no readership on its original appearance. Mises himself emigrated to the United States in August 1940 and spent the next nine years rewriting the material in English. The result, published by Yale University Press in 1949, was Human Action: A Treatise on Economics, the Austrian-tradition anchor text of the postwar era. The two books cover the same terrain, including praxeology, the socialist calculation problem, business-cycle theory, and interventionism, but Human Action is substantially more polished and includes material responding to the previous decade's developments. The Alabama-based Ludwig von Mises Institute later made both texts freely available online. In the Austrian reading the whole episode illustrates how a great book's initial reception can be nearly nil and still be preserved by a single author's determination.

north-korea-the-arduous-march-and-the-on.context_blurb: North Korea, officially the Democratic People's Republic of Korea, has been ruled by the Kim family since its 1948 founding. Its official ideology, called Juche in Korean, is a form of nationalist self-reliance combined with central planning. In the 1990s a severe famine, called the Arduous March in the state's own stoic terminology, killed somewhere between six hundred thousand and two-and-a-half million people. The Washington-based Committee for Human Rights in North Korea has documented the regime's political-prison-camp system, in which the three-generations-of-punishment rule means an offender's parents, children, and grandchildren are all imprisoned together. The famous nighttime satellite photograph of the Korean peninsula shows North Korea nearly dark and South Korea blazing with light, with a per-capita output gap of roughly forty times. In the Austrian reading, the famine and the ongoing economic gap are a sustained demonstration of Mises's 1920 argument that without market prices the state cannot allocate food or capital rationally at scale. The DPRK is also the one remaining strict-planning economy; Vietnam and China became market-with-Communist-Party states, Cuba has introduced cautious reforms.

oskar-lange-and-market-socialism-the-rep.context_blurb: Oskar Lange was a Polish-born economist who in 1936 and 1937 published a two-part paper in the Review of Economic Studies proposing what he called market socialism. His argument was a reply to Ludwig von Mises's 1920 paper on the socialist calculation problem and to Friedrich Hayek's edited 1935 volume on collectivist economic planning. Lange suggested that a central planning board could simulate market prices by trial and error, raising and lowering administered prices in response to shortages and surpluses until supply and demand balanced. His student Abba Lerner elaborated the proposal. Lange returned to Poland after the war to become a senior figure in the Polish Communist state's economic planning apparatus. Hayek's 1945 paper The Use of Knowledge in Society was the Austrian reply that reframed the issue: the problem was dispersed knowledge, not just price arithmetic. The practical collapse of the Soviet bloc in 1989 is read in the Austrian tradition as the empirical settling of the debate.

phil-zimmermann-pgp-and-the-munitions-li.context_blurb: In 1991 the American software engineer Phil Zimmermann released Pretty Good Privacy, abbreviated PGP, a free email-encryption program. He uploaded it to the internet, from where it circulated worldwide within weeks. The US government, treating strong cryptography as a controlled export under the Arms Export Control Act and the US Munitions List, opened a criminal investigation that lasted from 1993 to January 1996. Zimmermann's response is famous in the cypherpunk tradition: he arranged for a book containing PGP's entire source code to be printed on paper and sold by MIT Press as a legally exportable publication, invoking First Amendment protection of speech applied to source code as speech. The federal case was eventually dropped. Later court rulings ultimately established that cryptographic source code counts as speech protected by the First Amendment. In the Austrian and cypherpunk reading the broader lesson is that making a piece of software already widely distributed before the state can act removes the state's leverage.

potosi-silver-and-the-price-revolution-1.context_blurb: In 1545 Spanish prospectors discovered an enormous silver deposit at a mountain called Cerro Rico, in what is now Bolivia, overlooking the town of Potosi. For the next century the Spanish treasure fleets carried Potosi silver across the Atlantic to Iberia and from there into European markets. The resulting price inflation, now called the Price Revolution, played out across the European economy for roughly a hundred years. Spain, the country with the most silver, was becoming poorer rather than richer. The theological-economic faculty at the University of Salamanca, especially the Jesuit Martin de Azpilcueta writing in 1556, worked out the earliest clean version of what economists now call the quantity theory of money: more money chasing roughly the same goods causes prices to rise. Murray Rothbard's two-volume history of economic thought argues that the classical story starting with Adam Smith in 1776 has overwritten the Salamanca contribution. In the Austrian reading the Potosi episode is the first big empirical demonstration that creating more money does not make a nation richer in real terms; in Bastiat's framing, the visible galleons of silver hid the invisible erosion of Spanish industry and savings.

prices-and-production-1931-hayeks-lse-le.context_blurb: In February 1931 Friedrich Hayek, invited by Lionel Robbins, delivered four lectures at the London School of Economics on the Austrian theory of the business cycle. The lectures were published later that year as the book Prices and Production. Robbins secured him a permanent LSE chair, the Tooke Chair of Economic Science and Statistics, on the strength of the lectures. The argument built on Ludwig von Mises's 1912 book The Theory of Money and Credit and used what is now called the Hayekian triangle, a geometric diagram of the time-structure of production, to show how a central-bank-induced credit expansion starts long, roundabout capital projects that the underlying pool of real savings cannot finish. The resulting boom was the disease; the bust the painful correction. The book put Hayek into direct intellectual conflict with John Maynard Keynes, whose two-volume Treatise on Money he had just reviewed critically, and set up the longer rivalry that ran through the 1936 General Theory. In the Austrian tradition Prices and Production is read as the moment the Mises business-cycle argument got in front of an English-reading audience, if in a difficult technical form.

public-choice-journal-founded-1966.context_blurb: In 1966 Gordon Tullock founded an academic journal to publish work applying economic reasoning to political and bureaucratic behavior. The journal was originally called Papers on Non-Market Decision Making and was renamed Public Choice in 1968. Tullock based the journal at the Center for Study of Public Choice, first at Virginia Tech and later, after 1983, at George Mason University. The Public Choice Society grew up around the journal. In 1986 James Buchanan, Tullock's longtime coauthor, won the Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences for his work on constitutional and contractual bases of economic and political decision-making. The journal's standard topics include rent-seeking, logrolling, bureaucratic behavior, constitutional political economy, and expressive voting. In the public-choice tradition the journal is the main institutional venue through which the discipline reproduces itself across generations.

regulatory-capture-at-the-sec-harry-mark.context_blurb: Bernard Madoff ran what turned out to be the largest Ponzi scheme in history, a decades-long fraud at a nominally registered securities firm that collapsed in December 2008. The independent investment analyst Harry Markopolos spent nearly a decade warning the Securities and Exchange Commission about Madoff. His formal 2005 submission to the SEC was titled The World's Largest Hedge Fund Is a Fraud. The SEC assigned the complex technical complaint to junior staff who lacked the training to evaluate it. Markopolos's book No One Would Listen, published after the collapse, is the primary first-person source. Madoff had earlier served as chairman of NASDAQ. The SEC's eventual whistleblower program pays ten to thirty percent of monetary sanctions. The total documented loss to investors was roughly eighteen billion dollars. In the public-choice and Austrian reading, the episode is a particularly stark case of regulatory capture of a different sort: staff incentives, including career paths, the risk of embarrassing establishment firms, and the revolving-door to the industry, did not align with the public mission of the agency.

robert-conquests-great-terror-1968-the-v.context_blurb: Robert Conquest was a British-born Sovietologist and poet who in 1968 published the first serious scholarly accounting of Stalin's 1937 and 1938 Great Terror. The book was based on emigre memoirs, defector testimony, and such Soviet documentation as was available in the West. A revisionist school in American academic Sovietology dismissed Conquest's estimates throughout the 1970s and early 1980s. When the Soviet archives opened in the early 1990s, the NKVD's own records vindicated Conquest's execution estimate of about seven hundred and fifty thousand, within a rounding error. His 1986 book The Harvest of Sorrow extended the method to the Ukrainian famine of 1932 to 1933. He spent his later career at the Hoover Institution at Stanford. In the Austrian and classical-liberal tradition his work is a model of empirical seriousness against ideological pressure, and his vindication by the archives is a textbook case of what Thomas Sowell calls judging a scholar's record by the facts his method eventually turned out to catch.

san-francisco-rent-control-diamond-mcqua.context_blurb: In 2019 the Stanford economists Rebecca Diamond, Tim McQuade, and Franklin Qian published a long-run empirical paper in the American Economic Review that used San Francisco's 1994 rent-control extension as a natural experiment. They were able to measure what happened to specific buildings that fell inside the extension and specific buildings that remained outside it. On the controlled buildings, rental supply fell by roughly fifteen percent as landlords converted units to owner-occupied condominiums or TIC arrangements, demolished and rebuilt, or allowed buildings to leave the rental market. Market rents in the surrounding uncontrolled stock rose by about five percent in response. The net effect was a wealth transfer from future tenants to current protected tenants. In the Austrian and classical-liberal tradition the paper is read as the single sharpest modern empirical confirmation of Milton Friedman and George Stigler's 1946 pamphlet Roofs or Ceilings? which had made the theoretical argument on the way out of the Second World War.

segwit-and-taproot-the-two-big-soft-fork.context_blurb: Bitcoin's protocol is upgraded by what the Bitcoin community calls a soft fork: a backwards-compatible rule tightening that older software can continue to accept. Two major soft forks have reshaped the protocol in the past decade. Segregated Witness, usually abbreviated SegWit, activated in August 2017 and separated transaction-signature data from the main transaction payload, which both fixed a longstanding signature-malleability issue and effectively increased block capacity. The SegWit activation debate split off a hard-fork currency called Bitcoin Cash. Taproot activated in November 2021 and bundled a new signature scheme called Schnorr signatures with new scripting primitives that improve privacy and smart-contract flexibility. In the Austrian and cypherpunk reading, the two upgrades together demonstrate that a decentralized consensus system can deliver careful technical progress when the community is broadly aligned, without any single architect deciding the rules. The specific Hayekian point is that no central architect could safely rewrite a distributed system's rules.

smoot-hawley-tariff-and-the-collapse-of-.context_blurb: The 1930 Smoot-Hawley Tariff Act, named for its congressional sponsors Reed Smoot and Willis Hawley, raised American tariffs sharply on roughly twenty thousand imported goods. A petition signed by about one thousand economists had urged President Hoover to veto the bill. He signed it anyway. World trade subsequently collapsed to roughly a third of its 1929 level over the following three years, as other countries retaliated. The teenage comedy Ferris Bueller's Day Off contains the most-quoted modern reference to the law, in a classroom scene the writer John Hughes gave to the economist Ben Stein. The eventual legislative response was the 1934 Reciprocal Trade Agreements Act, which gave the president authority to negotiate bilateral tariff reductions, and after the Second World War the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade. In the Austrian and Bastiat tradition the law is a textbook case of what Bastiat's candlemakers were parodying nearly a century earlier: visible protection for named domestic industries, hidden costs in the form of higher consumer prices, closed export markets, and retaliation that destroys more jobs than the tariff could ever protect.

sowells-compared-to-what-reasoning-move.context_blurb: Thomas Sowell's trademark analytical move is a two-word question: compared to what? The move insists that whenever an existing institution is criticized, the critic has to name the specific alternative institution that would replace it, not an imagined perfect version that exists nowhere. His 1980 book Knowledge and Decisions develops the method; the economist Harold Demsetz had earlier called the opposite move the nirvana approach. The pattern recurs across many of Sowell's arguments. On the Federal Reserve, the question is which existing alternative monetary institution would replace it. On rent control, the question is which existing public system would ration apartments better, and how. On single-payer health care, the question is which actual existing public system is being named as the model. On capitalism as judged against socialism in general, the question is which specific socialist regime is being proposed, with its actual historical record. The Nobel-winning economist Kenneth Arrow's own work on social-choice limits sits in the broader background of why no imagined perfect institution is available anywhere.

stephane-courtois-the-french-maoist-who-.context_blurb: Stephane Courtois was a French historian who in 1997 edited The Black Book of Communism, published by Harvard University Press and translated into dozens of languages. The book was a joint project with several European scholars, including the Soviet historian Nicolas Werth at the French research institute CNRS. The volume totaled the deaths caused by communist regimes in the twentieth century at roughly eighty-five to one hundred million. The book's introduction, which Courtois wrote and in which he equated communist and Nazi crimes as comparable moral catastrophes, provoked lasting public controversy inside the French left. Courtois had himself been a Maoist student militant in Paris in 1968 before becoming the leading French counter-communist historian of his generation. His own topic of specialization was Maoism. In the Austrian and classical-liberal tradition the Black Book is the standard reference for the aggregate twentieth-century communist death toll, and its specific numerical range is now a baseline figure in serious discussions.

teachers-union-public-choice-from-friedm.context_blurb: In 1955 Milton Friedman published an essay titled The Role of Government in Education in which he distinguished between funding schooling and producing it. The government might legitimately fund education, Friedman argued, without needing to run the schools itself. The essay was the intellectual origin of the modern American school-voucher and charter-school movements. Friedman's Chicago home base ran through decades of empirical work. Terry Moe at Stanford and Thomas Sowell wrote extensively on the specific political economy of public-sector education, including the organized teachers' unions as the central political actor. The California Teachers Association became the model case of a unionized interest group with disproportionate influence over state education policy. The DC Opportunity Scholarship Program, enacted in 2004, produced measurable gains in graduation rates for low-income DC students. The modern Success Academy co-location experiments in New York City became Sowell's major 2020 empirical case. In the public-choice reading the episode is a sustained demonstration of Olson's principle: which organized interest is best positioned to shape the rules.

the-1929-crash-black-thursday-and-black-.context_blurb: The American stock-market crash of 1929 took place on two famous days, Black Thursday on October 24 and Black Tuesday on October 29. The crash ended what was popularly called the Roaring Twenties and set up the long contraction of the Great Depression. The Dow Jones Industrial Average lost roughly ten percent in a single day during the crash, and by the trough in 1932 had fallen roughly eighty-nine percent from its 1929 peak. Trading volume on the panic days ran around sixteen million shares. The economist Irving Fisher had famously declared, just before the crash, that stocks had reached what looked like a permanently high plateau. The 1963 Friedman-Schwartz Monetary History argued that what turned a sharp crash into a sustained Depression was a specific policy failure by the Federal Reserve: allowing the money supply to collapse by about a third over the following three to four years rather than acting as a lender of last resort during cascading bank failures. US stock prices did not recover their 1929 peak in nominal terms until the mid-1950s.

the-2020-2024-inflation-abct-applied-to-.context_blurb: Between March 2020 and the end of 2021 the US Federal Reserve roughly doubled the size of its balance sheet and the broad US money supply grew by trillions of dollars. Federal Reserve officials, including Jerome Powell, described the rising inflation of 2021 as transitory. In June 2022 US consumer-price inflation reached nine-point-one percent year over year, the highest reading since 1981. The Austrian school, represented in the public conversation by writers in the Mises, Hayek, and Rothbard tradition, had argued throughout the preceding decade of quantitative easing that the eventual price-level adjustment would arrive on a lag of twelve to twenty-four months after the monetary expansion. The specific Austrian claim that the binding constraint on money-financed government spending is real resources, not the political willingness to spend, received unusually clear empirical confirmation. Paul Volcker's 1979 to 1982 campaign against the second 1970s inflation wave remained the historical reference for what it costs to restore price stability once expectations loosen.

the-bennett-hypothesis-federal-student-a.context_blurb: In 1987 the Reagan-era Secretary of Education William Bennett wrote a New York Times op-ed arguing that federal student aid programs allow colleges to raise tuition without losing enrollment, because the aid absorbs the price increase before the student feels it. In the following three decades the empirical literature on what has come to be called the Bennett hypothesis has grown substantially. The New York Fed's own 2015 and later studies found that a dollar increase in subsidized federal loans translates to roughly sixty cents of sticker-tuition increase. The combined US federal student-loan and Pell-Grant programs have accumulated roughly one-point-seven trillion dollars in outstanding loans. The economist Richard Vedder's book Going Broke by Degree worked out the aggregate pattern. The specific mechanism also recurs outside higher education: Section 8 housing vouchers tend to raise rents in tight rental markets, for the same reason. In the Austrian and classical-liberal reading, the Bennett hypothesis is a Hayek-knowledge-problem argument applied to a transfer program: who has the market power to price against the newly-enhanced payment capacity.

the-broken-window-applied-to-war-and-dis.context_blurb: Frederic Bastiat's broken-window parable, published in July 1850, is still the sharpest Austrian-tradition tool for thinking about war-and-disaster stimulus arguments. After the Second World War, mainstream American economists worried that the economy would slip back into depression as wartime spending was withdrawn. The actual unemployment rate stayed near four percent as resources were absorbed by private demand and investment within months of the transition. The hurricane-stimulus argument, briefly advanced by the economist Paul Krugman in the aftermath of major natural disasters, treats destruction and the production that follows it as if they were the same quantity. The specific Austrian answer, articulated by Henry Hazlitt in his 1946 Economics in One Lesson, is to count what the resources would have produced in the alternative use that destruction foreclosed. The 9/11 reconstruction consumed resources that could have built other new office buildings and other homes. The war that killed, injured, or displaced a working-age population spent a year of alternative economic activity on top of the human losses. In the Austrian reading, every war-and-disaster-stimulus argument is a broken-window parable rediscovered.

the-constitution-of-liberty-1960.context_blurb: Friedrich Hayek's 1960 book The Constitution of Liberty is his most sustained attempt to lay out, positively rather than critically, what a free society's institutions should look like. The book was written during his years on the University of Chicago's Committee on Social Thought, the interdisciplinary unit that housed him when the Chicago economics department would not. Its central concept of liberty is specifically the absence of coercion by another person, as distinct from a wider idea of positive freedom. The book argues for the rule of law against administrative discretion and makes the Hayekian value-of-innovation argument that the value of a new idea cannot be known before someone is free to try it. Hayek added a famous appended essay called Why I Am Not a Conservative, in which he argued that conservatism has no positive program, only a resistance to change from wherever society currently is. Margaret Thatcher is reported to have slammed the book down on a table during a British policy meeting with the line that this is what we believe. In the Austrian and classical-liberal tradition the book is Hayek's positive counterpart to The Road to Serfdom.

the-cypherpunk-mailing-list-hughes-may-g.context_blurb: In 1992 three San Francisco Bay Area engineers started a mailing list devoted to using cryptography to carve out privacy against the state. The three founders were Eric Hughes, Timothy May, and John Gilmore. The name cypherpunk is a 1991 coinage by the hacker and writer Jude Milhon. John Gilmore had been a very early employee of the chipmaker Intel. The mailing-list community grew up around Stanford and Berkeley through the mid-1990s and included members who would go on to build the central tools of the modern cryptographic internet, among them Adam Back, Wei Dai, Hal Finney, and Nick Szabo, and later Julian Assange. The movement's compressed slogan is Cypherpunks write code. In 2008 the thread culminated in a paper posted to a related mailing list describing a peer-to-peer electronic cash system with proof-of-work consensus. In the Austrian and cypherpunk tradition the lesson is that mathematics and code can give ordinary people privacy the government cannot take away.

the-fatal-conceit-1988-hayeks-last-book.context_blurb: Friedrich Hayek's last book, published in 1988 when he was in his ninetieth year, is titled The Fatal Conceit: The Errors of Socialism. The book argues that what Hayek calls the extended order of human cooperation, the modern market society, rests on evolved norms and institutions that no single mind could design and that any attempt to redesign them from scratch suffers from a specific intellectual error. He uses the phrase between instinct and reason to describe the character of the evolved cultural rules that make the extended order possible. The book draws on David Hume on the evolution of justice. The manuscript was heavily edited by W. W. Bartley III, Hayek's designated editor, during Hayek's declining years, and specific scholars have argued that it should be read as a joint editor-author work rather than as a pure late-Hayek statement. Still, the central move, that the market uses more dispersed knowledge than any single mind or committee could hold, is unmistakably Hayek. In the Austrian and classical-liberal tradition the book is Hayek's compressed summary of nine decades of thinking.

the-free-banking-era-and-the-national-ba.context_blurb: From 1837 to 1863 the United States operated under what historians call the free-banking era, in which state-chartered banks issued their own notes under state regulations rather than under a federal central bank. Specialized newspapers called banknote reporters printed up-to-date lists of what each bank's notes were trading at as a percentage of face value. The term wildcat bank entered the American language in this period. The Civil War ended the system; the National Banking Acts of 1863 and 1864, pushed by Treasury Secretary Salmon P. Chase, imposed federal chartering, required banks to hold Treasury securities as reserves against note issuance, and imposed a ten-percent tax on state-bank notes that effectively killed them. Modern revisionist economic history, including work by George Selgin and others, has argued that the empirical record of the free-banking era was in fact modest and comparable to later regulated eras, counter to the earlier textbook presentation. The specific missing element was a lender of last resort during panics. In the Austrian reading the whole episode is a case study in emergent-order institutions, including the banknote reporters as prices carrying reputational information.

the-halving-and-the-21-million-cap.context_blurb: Bitcoin's issuance schedule is written into the protocol. The reward paid to a miner for successfully adding a block of transactions started at fifty Bitcoin per block in January 2009 and is cut in half every two hundred and ten thousand blocks, which is approximately every four years. The first such halving happened in November 2012. By the mid-2020s the reward had fallen to three-point-one-two-five Bitcoin per block. The total supply converges to twenty-one million Bitcoin, with issuance effectively terminating around the year 2140. Each individual Bitcoin is divisible into one hundred million smaller units called satoshis. The specific feature that makes this different from any previous currency is that the twenty-one-million cap cannot be raised by any committee, politician, or emergency vote; it would require a hard fork that the rest of the network would then reject. In the Austrian reading, the fixed supply is the engineering answer to the recurring political failure of fiat currencies. A standard mainstream objection is that a truly fixed supply forces the general price level to adjust downward during a recession and could worsen such episodes.

the-law-when-legal-force-is-used-for-plu.context_blurb: Frederic Bastiat's 1850 pamphlet The Law was published in June of his final year, five months before his death. The pamphlet opens with the proposition that the proper purpose of law is to protect life, liberty, and property, and that whenever law is used for any other purpose it becomes an instrument of what Bastiat calls legal plunder. The pamphlet's specific definition of legal plunder is a situation in which the force of law takes from some persons what belongs to them and gives it to other persons to whom it does not belong. Bastiat gives several concrete nineteenth-century examples, including protectionism as a form of legal plunder of consumers for the benefit of favored producers, and corruption as the private version of the same move. The pamphlet includes the memorable line that the state is the great fictitious entity by which everyone seeks to live at the expense of everyone else. The Foundation for Economic Education issued the standard twentieth-century English translation. In the Austrian and classical-liberal tradition the pamphlet is read as the compressed moral-political argument that underlies Bastiat's later seen-and-unseen essay.

the-mises-privatseminar-1920-1934-vienna.context_blurb: From 1920 to 1934 Ludwig von Mises ran a famous private seminar in Vienna, called the Privatseminar in German. The seminar met in a conference room at the Austrian Chamber of Commerce, called the Handelskammer in German, where Mises was chief economist. Its regular attendees included Friedrich Hayek, Oskar Morgenstern, the British economist Lionel Robbins, the sociologist Alfred Schuetz, and the mathematician Karl Menger the younger. Most of the seminar's members were Jews or classical liberals who had to leave Central Europe as the Nazi party rose through the following decade. Mises himself left Vienna for Geneva in 1934 and later for the United States in 1940. His former seminar students scattered to Johns Hopkins, Princeton, and New York University, among other American institutions. In the Austrian tradition the Privatseminar is read as the specific intellectual environment that carried the Vienna school from Menger's and Boehm-Bawerk's academic chairs into its twentieth-century form.

the-nyu-seminar-1945-1969.context_blurb: After emigrating to the United States in 1940, Ludwig von Mises took a Visiting Professor appointment at New York University that paid him nothing and remained unpaid for the next twenty-four years. The seminar he ran at NYU, from 1945 to 1969, was the main American replacement for his Vienna Privatseminar. His salary was supplied by two private sources: the Kansas-City-based William Volker Fund, which also helped fund Hayek's Chicago appointment, and the New York advertising executive Lawrence Fertig, who supplemented Mises personally. The seminar's regular American students included Murray Rothbard, who became Mises's most prolific disciple, and Israel Kirzner, who developed the Austrian theory of entrepreneurship. Hans Sennholz, another Mises student, carried the tradition to the small-college setting at Grove City College in Pennsylvania. Mises retired from NYU in 1969 at the age of eighty-seven. In the Austrian tradition the seminar is read as the specific institutional bridge between Mises's Vienna years and the modern American Austrian school.

the-phillips-curves-death-and-friedmans-.context_blurb: In 1958 the New Zealand economist A. W. Phillips published a paper arguing that there was a stable statistical relationship between inflation and unemployment, now called the Phillips curve. For a decade mainstream American macroeconomic policy treated the inflation-unemployment trade-off as something policymakers could choose a point on. In 1968 Milton Friedman and, independently, Edmund Phelps argued that the trade-off was an illusion, resting on temporary mistakes about the price level. Once workers and firms updated their inflation expectations, Friedman and Phelps argued, unemployment would return to a natural rate determined by structural features of the labor market. The 1970s produced the empirical settlement of the argument. Stagflation, the simultaneous presence of high inflation and high unemployment, broke the standard Phillips curve as a policy guide. Arthur Burns, Fed chairman through most of the decade, had already been pushing the curve into territory the Friedman-Phelps argument predicted would not hold. The Phillips Machine, called the MONIAC, had been Phillips's hydraulic physical model of the economy. In the Austrian reading the whole episode confirmed Mises's older argument.

the-roman-denarius-debasement-64-ad-274-.context_blurb: The Roman denarius was a silver coin that served as the empire's main monetary unit for several centuries. Under Nero in 64 AD its silver content was reduced by about five percent. Over the next two centuries successive emperors reduced it again and again, until by the late third century AD it was effectively a bronze coin washed in silver. In 301 AD the emperor Diocletian imposed an Edict on Maximum Prices on top of the long debasement. Merchants withdrew goods from public sale, black markets emerged, and shortages appeared immediately. In the Austrian tradition the debasement is read as the earliest-documented case of a hidden tax on money holders: the ruler captures the difference between the metal's old content and its new, lower content. Diocletian's price edict rediscovered the same failure mode Julian the Apostate later rediscovered at Antioch and that Nixon's 1971 wage and price freeze later rediscovered in Washington, and that Nicolas Maduro's government rediscovered in Caracas in the 2010s.

the-soviet-gulag-solzhenitsyns-accountin.context_blurb: Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn was a Soviet mathematician, Red Army captain, and Gulag survivor. The Gulag, an acronym in Russian, was the Soviet forced-labor camp system. Solzhenitsyn's three-volume book The Gulag Archipelago, written in secret in the Soviet Union and published in Paris starting in 1973, documented the system from inside. The Soviet government stripped him of citizenship in 1974 and flew him to Frankfurt. He spent the following two decades in Vermont before returning to Russia in 1994. The historian Robert Conquest had earlier produced The Great Terror on the 1937-38 killings; the historian Anne Applebaum later produced a comprehensive postwar scholarly account. Serious scholarly estimates place the cumulative Gulag population at about eighteen million people over the system's history. The French left's post-1974 shock reading of Solzhenitsyn produced a group of young former Marxist intellectuals who were called the Nouveaux Philosophes. Solzhenitsyn's late-career Russian book, called I Told You So, You... Fools, is a title whose compressed moral energy carries over into English. In the Austrian and classical-liberal tradition the Gulag record is a specific moral benchmark against which no false equivalence with mid-twentieth-century Western failures is accepted.

the-treasury-revolving-door-rubin-paulso.context_blurb: A recurring American pattern is that senior US Treasury officials come from Wall Street firms and return to them after public service. The sequence Robert Rubin, Henry Paulson, Timothy Geithner, and Janet Yellen is the twenty-first-century version of the pattern. Rubin was co-chairman of Goldman Sachs before Treasury and earned roughly twelve-point-nine billion dollars at Citigroup after. Paulson was CEO of Goldman Sachs before Treasury and left to found a private-equity firm. Geithner joined a Wall Street firm, Warburg Pincus, after Treasury. Yellen gave paid speeches at Wall Street firms including Citadel and Goldman Sachs after leaving the Fed, at premiums of five hundred to a thousand percent over her government salary. The economist Simon Johnson's 2009 essay The Quiet Coup and the economist Luigi Zingales's book A Capitalism for the People are the two sharpest formulations of the problem. The FDA commissioner Scott Gottlieb is a parallel case in a different agency. In the public-choice reading the pattern is institutional-incentive selection rather than individual character: the pool of qualified candidates comes from the industry and expects to return to it.

the-vienna-intellectual-context-of-the-1.context_blurb: The Vienna of the 1920s and early 1930s was an unusually dense intellectual environment. The Vienna Circle, a philosophy and logic group centered on the philosopher Moritz Schlick, met weekly to work on logical empiricism. The mathematician Kurt Godel, whose incompleteness theorems reshaped twentieth-century logic, was a regular member. The economist Karl Popper, who later developed the falsification criterion of science, was adjacent but not a member. The city's politics ran through a sharp Austro-Marxist versus classical-liberal split under what the Austrian Social Democrats called their program of Red Vienna socialism. The intellectual environment ended with the March 1938 Anschluss between Austria and Nazi Germany, after which the entire scene scattered. Many of its members emigrated to the University of Chicago and the Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton. In the Austrian tradition the Vienna 1920s is read as the specific environment that produced not only the Mises-Hayek Austrian school but much of twentieth-century logic, philosophy of science, and mathematics.

time-preference-a-good-now-is-worth-more.context_blurb: Time preference is the Austrian name for the fact that human beings prefer, other things equal, to have a good sooner rather than later. The concept was developed in its modern form by Eugen von Boehm-Bawerk and extended by Ludwig von Mises. Interest, in the Austrian theory, is called originary interest in Mises's terminology; it is the market expression of the aggregate time preferences of borrowers and lenders. People who want to consume now borrow from people willing to defer consumption; the market rate that clears the two is the pure time-preference rate. Long, roundabout production processes, called roundabout production in Boehm-Bawerk's terminology, require savers to defer consumption while the capital goods are built. A society with lower average time preference can sustain a longer production structure. In the Austrian theory of the business cycle, central-bank credit expansion lies to entrepreneurs about the actual time preferences of consumers, and the bust is the painful correction. The broader social argument carried into writing by Hans-Hermann Hoppe uses the phrase decivilization to describe what happens culturally and economically when average time preference rises for structural reasons.

us-milk-supports-and-government-cheese.context_blurb: The US federal milk-support program has been in place in various forms since the 1930s. In the 1970s and 1980s the program's accumulated surplus of processed cheese reached roughly five hundred million pounds, which the federal government distributed to welfare recipients and nicknamed government cheese. The current version of the program is called the Dairy Margin Coverage system. In the public-choice tradition the dairy-support program is a textbook example of what Mancur Olson, in his 1965 book The Logic of Collective Action, called a program with concentrated benefits and dispersed costs. The specific commodity is milk, with its derivative processed dairy products. The policy is sustained politically because dairy farmers are a concentrated, organized interest that stands to lose a measurable amount from any reform, while consumers are dispersed and each one would gain only a small amount from reform, so no comparable organized consumer lobby ever forms. In the Austrian and public-choice reading the program is one of the clearest American examples of Olson's reasoning.

vincent-ostrom-polycentric-political-sys.context_blurb: Vincent Ostrom was an American political scientist who co-founded, with his wife Elinor Ostrom, the Workshop in Political Theory and Policy Analysis at Indiana University. His 1961 paper, co-authored with Charles Tiebout and Robert Warren, introduced the concept of polycentric political systems: political arrangements with multiple overlapping centers of authority rather than a single hierarchical structure. The paper was written against the then-dominant metropolitan-consolidation movement, which held that fragmented local governments should be merged into unified regional authorities. Ostrom later argued that the American founders' choice of federalism, with its deliberate separation of powers across levels of government, was itself an intentionally polycentric institutional design. His last major book argued that twentieth-century centralization was eroding the polycentric constitutional structure the founders had designed. His wife Elinor won the 2009 Nobel Memorial Prize in Economics for her related empirical work on commons governance; Vincent did not share the prize because the Nobel is not awarded posthumously and he died in 2012, shortly after Elinor died on June 12 of that year. In the Austrian and classical-liberal tradition his work is a parallel to Hayek's 1945 argument on dispersed knowledge.

western-intellectual-apologists-duranty-.context_blurb: A recurring twentieth-century pattern was the public defense of totalitarian regimes by Western intellectuals of standing. Lincoln Steffens, an American muckraking journalist, returned from a 1919 visit to Soviet Russia and told the diplomat Bernard Baruch that he had seen the future and it worked, a line he later published without the question mark. The British socialist couple Sidney and Beatrice Webb, both associated with the London School of Economics, published a two-volume defense of Soviet civilization in 1935 and 1944 in which they progressively dropped the question mark from the title between editions. Walter Duranty's New York Times reporting during the Ukrainian famine famously defended the Soviet regime's version of events. The common rhetorical move was the appearance of central planning as a rational-administrative project. The quotation about not making an omelette without breaking eggs became the pattern's compressed phrase. In Friedrich Hayek's chapter titled Why the Worst Get on Top, from The Road to Serfdom, the specific psychology of the apologist is discussed. In the Austrian and classical-liberal tradition the broader claim is that the Western intellectual class has never systematically confronted its own twentieth-century apologetics record.

yang-jishengs-tombstone-2008-the-archiva.context_blurb: Yang Jisheng is a Chinese journalist who worked for the official Xinhua News Agency for most of his career. His 2008 book, published in Hong Kong and later translated into English by Stacy Mosher and Guo Jian under the title Tombstone: The Great Chinese Famine 1958-1962, is the first archival account of Mao Zedong's Great Leap Forward famine written by a Chinese researcher from inside the Chinese provincial party records. Yang's own father, a rural schoolteacher, died of starvation in April 1959, which was the personal fact that moved him toward the project. His archival count arrived at a figure of roughly thirty-six million deaths. His method, counting from provincial party records rather than inferring from national census gaps, raised the quality of the empirical ceiling for all subsequent scholarship. The Chinese government denied him permission to leave the country to accept the Hayek Prize in person. In the Austrian and classical-liberal tradition his work is the Chinese parallel to Robert Conquest's archival vindication for the Soviet case.

1973-oil-shock-and-us-gasoline-price-con.context_blurb:
In October 1973 the Arab oil producers cut off shipments to the nations that had sided with Israel during the Yom Kippur War, and world oil prices roughly quadrupled within months. Americans remember that winter for something else: hour-long lines at gas stations that had simply run dry. Milton Friedman, Murray Rothbard and other economists in Bastiat's tradition argued that the lines came from a law in Washington as much as from the embargo.

Start with the plain economics of a cut-off. When the biggest oil exporters stop selling to a nation, buyers who still need fuel for their cars, trucks and factories bid against one another for what is left, and the price shoots up. Now imagine a government that forbids sellers to raise prices during a shortage, say with a hurricane on the way. Drivers rush to fill up at the old price, long lines snake down the road, and the pumps run empty faster than before. In the 1970s many states fell back on odd-even rules, letting cars whose plates ended in an odd number buy only on odd dates, while stations hung out NO GAS signs.

That is what Friedman and his followers saw in 1973. The United States was already living under federal ceilings on the price of gasoline, part of the wage-and-price controls Richard Nixon had imposed in 1971. The ceiling barred the pump price from rising to match the shrunken supply, so instead of charging more, stations simply emptied, and the shortage was rationed by queuing. Europe ran a natural experiment. West Germany and Switzerland had no price controls; their prices jumped, drivers cut back, and the pumps stayed full with no lines at all.

Rothbard sorted the episode into Bastiat's two columns. The seen was the low price painted on the pump. The unseen was the hours burned waiting in line, the gasoline private importers refused to bring in at a loss, and the deliveries that never happened. Behind that lay Friedrich Hayek's 1945 insight that the knowledge a market runs on is scattered among millions of ordinary shoppers, whose daily choices about price, taste and budget tell farmers and refiners what to supply. Hand all those choices to one office in the capital and it would guess wrong about what people actually want, leaving shortages in one place and waste in another. Milton and Rose Friedman made the gas lines a showcase of their 1980 television series and book, Free to Choose.

The Austrian economists put the lesson in one sharp phrase: a price cap does not abolish the cost of something scarce, it changes the currency the cost is paid in. A cost that would have been paid in money, to a seller, is paid instead in time spent in line, and nobody collects it. The caps outlived Nixon, because Presidents Ford and Carter both left them standing. On January 28, 1981, a week after taking office, Ronald Reagan used an executive order to end the last federal controls on domestic crude. Once producers could sell at real market prices, oil flowed freely, prices soon began to fall, and the lines never came back.

The pattern had already repeated. In 1979 the Iranian Revolution toppled the Shah, Iran's oil stopped flowing, and world prices spiked for the second time in the decade. The lines came back, and California's were the worst, because federal price caps still held and a federal formula divided gasoline among the states by what each had used in earlier years, which left fast-growing California with an allotment based on its smaller past use. From both episodes Rothbard drew a lesson sharper than the word shortage. Under a ceiling the shortage shows up in two dimensions at once, in space as empty pumps and in time as hours of queueing, and lifting the ceiling ends both.

airline-deregulation-1978-the-low-cost-c.context_blurb:
For forty years, from 1938 to 1978, a federal agency in Washington, the Civil Aeronautics Board, chose which American airlines flew which routes and set the price of every ticket. Its defenders called it a shield. Its critics, led by the Cornell economist Alfred Kahn, called it a textbook case of what George Stigler named regulatory capture: a regulator that ends up serving the industry it is supposed to police.

No airline could cut a fare without the Board's permission, so the established carriers never had to fear a cheaper rival, and they gained the most from the arrangement. The Board gave the public a different reason. It warned that open skies would unleash ruinous competition, a fare war that would bankrupt carriers and leave small towns stranded. Because big price gaps were treated as dangerous, airlines competed on meals, seat width and schedules instead of fares.

The shield worked too well. Between 1950 and 1974 outside firms filed 79 applications to start a scheduled airline, and the Board granted none of them; after 1960 it barely bothered to hold hearings on such requests. A few upstarts lived beyond its reach. California's Pacific Southwest and Texas's Southwest flew only within their home states, and the Board's power covered only flights between states, so it could not touch them. Free to set their own prices, they charged 30 to 60 percent less than the regulated carriers and filled more of their seats.

The cozy side of the system came out in public. Robert Timm, who chaired the Board until 1974, made it his aim that the scheduled airlines earn a 12 percent return, and he was caught accepting a Bermuda golf holiday from the very carriers he oversaw. Senator Ted Kennedy's subcommittee referred him to the Justice Department, and its 1975 hearings put the cheap fares of the in-state airlines on display. In 1977 Jimmy Carter put Kahn himself in charge of the Board. Kahn, a lifelong Democrat, joked that all airplanes looked alike to him; to him, he said, every one of them was simply a marginal cost with wings. A marginal cost is what one more passenger adds to a flight that is leaving anyway, and Kahn's point was that fares should follow it.

In the Board's day, service to small towns was paid for invisibly: travelers on crowded routes were overcharged, and the extra money propped up the lightly used ones. When deregulation ended that hidden transfer, Congress created the Essential Air Service program, paid for openly as a line in the federal budget. The lesson is Bastiat's. The cost had always been paid, by unseen passengers elsewhere, and deregulation dragged it into daylight, where lawmakers had to vote on it.

The Airline Deregulation Act, largely Kahn's design, passed both houses by enormous margins, and Carter signed it in October 1978. Those votes hid a bitter fight, and economists still point to who lost it. The fiercest resistance came from the established trunk airlines and the pilots' union, the Air Line Pilots Association: the very parties that forty years of protection had sheltered, an industry defending its own regulator. The consumer champion Ralph Nader, by contrast, backed deregulation.

anthony-downs-and-the-median-voter-theor.context_blurb:
Anthony Downs was an American economist who turned the tools of economics on politics. His Stanford doctoral thesis, written under Kenneth Arrow and published in 1957 as An Economic Theory of Democracy, asked what voters and parties do if they behave like ordinary people pursuing their own ends. His answers helped found public choice, the branch of economics that studies political behavior through incentives.

Start with one voter among a hundred million. The odds that his single ballot decides the election are about as good as a lottery jackpot, while reading up on every candidate eats whole evenings. So a sensible citizen spends very little time on research: study costs real hours, and one vote almost never settles anything. Downs's best-known idea concerns parties. When two parties compete along a single line of opinion, each keeps edging toward the citizen who stands exactly in the middle, since whoever wins that voter wins the majority. This is the median-voter theorem.

Downs made the theorem famous, but its mathematical proof had appeared nine years before his book, when the Scottish economist Duncan Black published it in 1948. The theorem explains a familiar grumble about American elections: by voting day the two big parties often sound alike on many issues, because both are chasing the same voter in the middle. Third-party campaigners like to say there is not a dime's worth of difference between them.

Downs's second big idea comes from the arithmetic of a single vote. Because one ballot among millions almost never flips the result, the private return to becoming an informed voter is near zero, even if society as a whole would gain from informed citizens. Sensible voters therefore skimp on studying bills, candidates and budgets. Downs called this rational ignorance, meaning that most voter ignorance is a reasonable response to incentives, not stupidity.

Arrow had found a deeper trap in 1951. Imagine three friends each ranking three choices for lunch. Arrow proved that no voting rule can satisfy a short list of basic fairness conditions for every possible set of rankings: some patterns of preference make every rule fail. The result, his impossibility theorem, helped earn him a Nobel Prize. Downs, meanwhile, turned to a very concrete urban headache, traffic, and wrote about cities for decades, later from the Brookings Institution in Washington. His law of peak-hour expressway congestion says that widening a highway invites more driving until the new lanes fill up again.

In 2007 the economist Bryan Caplan pushed Downs's argument further in The Myth of the Rational Voter. A mistaken vote costs the voter nothing personally, so voters indulge pet beliefs they would never risk acting on when buying groceries or a used car. Caplan concluded that voters are not merely uninformed but systematically irrational, because holding a wrong belief costs them nothing in private, a move he called rational irrationality.

asic-evolution-cpu-to-specialized-silico.context_blurb:
Bitcoin is secured by mining, a worldwide race in which computers grind through a hashing puzzle and the winner adds the next block of transactions. Since Satoshi Nakamoto released the software in January 2009, the machines in that race have changed four times, each generation more specialized than the last. The story shows an industry remaking itself, with no planner in charge, around the price of electricity.

At first, in 2009 and 2010, everyone mined on the same chip: the CPU, the ordinary processor inside every laptop and desktop. Satoshi mined that way, so did the cryptographer Hal Finney, and so could any hobbyist at home, winning 50 bitcoins a block. Then, in 2010, miners discovered that the graphics chip in a video-game card, the GPU, built for the parallel arithmetic of shading pixels, could run the hashing puzzle fifty to a hundred times quicker than a CPU. Word spread on the forums, gamers turned their rigs into round-the-clock money mints, and GPUs ruled mining through 2010 and 2011.

Next came FPGAs, chips that can be rewired after they leave the factory to perform one particular circuit. FPGA mining lasted only about a year before the first ASICs, chips built to run nothing but Bitcoin's SHA-256 hashing, shipped from Butterfly Labs and Avalon in early 2013. Every new generation won for the same reason: it did each calculation with less energy, so miners still running older gear could no longer cover their power bills. The ASIC is the extreme of that trade-off. Set against a laptop's general-purpose processor, it is vastly faster and cheaper per calculation, but it is good for nothing else, and because its silicon is fixed when it is made, it can never be repurposed.

By 2015 hobbyists could not keep up. Giant mining farms in China, many in Sichuan and Inner Mongolia, packed warehouses with ASICs thousands of times faster than any home computer, and the chief chipmakers, Bitmain and its rivals MicroBT and Canaan, were Chinese as well. That narrowness makes Bitcoin more secure, not less. A miner who has sunk millions into chips that can do nothing else has no way to walk away from Bitcoin and reuse his hardware, so his fortune rides on the network's survival. Critics call this centralization; defenders call it aligned incentives.

Then, in 2021, China banned Bitcoin mining outright, though more than half the world's hash power sat inside its borders. Over the following months, millions of machines were packed up and shipped to places with cheap, often stranded power: wind and gas in Texas, coal in Kazakhstan, geothermal heat in Iceland and the great Itaipu hydroelectric dam in Paraguay. Within nine months the network's total hash power had hit new records. No central planner ordered the move; entrepreneurs reading their electricity bills steered it themselves.

bastiat-inside-mises-s-human-action.context_blurb:
Ludwig von Mises, a Vienna-trained economist, left Austria in 1934 for a teaching post in Geneva and moved on to New York in 1940 as the Nazis overran Europe. His 1949 masterwork, Human Action, became the English-language anchor of the Austrian school. Mises saw in it the formal version of the reasoning Frédéric Bastiat had used in plain French a century earlier: trace what is seen, and then what is not seen.

The school began in 1871 with Carl Menger, a Vienna professor who taught that value is subjective. Only a person, with his own tastes and needs, can say what a thing is worth to him. A hungry child prizes a candy bar more than one who has just eaten lunch, so there is no single true price for the candy; it is worth different amounts to different children. While teaching in Geneva, Mises wrote the first, German version of his treatise, Nationalökonomie, published in 1940. When the journalist Henry Hazlitt urged an English translation, Mises chose to rewrite the book for Americans instead, and the result was Human Action.

Mises had made his name in 1920 with a paper on economic calculation under socialism. Where no one owns the factories, land and machines, they are never bought or sold, so no real market price ever shows what they truly cost, and planners are left with nothing to show them which projects deserve the resources. Friedrich Hayek pressed the point further in 1945 with an article for the American Economic Review titled The Use of Knowledge in Society: the scraps of local knowledge in millions of heads can never be gathered by any central planner. The same school traced great downturns such as the Great Depression not to markets gone mad but to central banks pushing interest rates below the level where saving and borrowing would naturally meet.

In 1946 Henry Hazlitt, who wrote editorials for the New York Times, boiled Bastiat's method down to one rule in Economics in One Lesson. Look at a policy's effect on every group, he taught, not just the group it is meant to help, and over the long run as well as the short. Mainstream economists ignored Bastiat for decades, largely because of Joseph Schumpeter, the Austrian-born Harvard economist. In his History of Economic Analysis, published after his death in 1954, Schumpeter wrote that he did not consider Bastiat a bad theorist; he considered him no theorist at all.

Murray Rothbard, the leading Austrian of the generation after Mises, answered Schumpeter in his last great work, the two-volume An Austrian Perspective on the History of Economic Thought, released by the publisher Edward Elgar in 1995, the year Rothbard died. Its pages take Bastiat seriously as a thinker in his own right, far more than a clever pamphlet writer. Read together, Bastiat's essays, Mises's Human Action and Rothbard's Man, Economy, and State of 1962 teach one move with growing rigor. Mises called his method praxeology: because human action is purposive, economic reasoning has to follow every choice through its whole chain of consequences, the unseen as well as the seen.

bitcoin-as-a-scarce-digital-commodity-th.context_blurb:
Across history, people in far-apart places have settled on gold and silver as money. The Austrian school, beginning with Carl Menger in 1871, argued that this was no cultural accident but a matter of what the metals are like. In the Austrian reading, Bitcoin's fixed supply is an engineering answer to the oldest failure of money: the people who issue it debasing it.

Shells from West African beaches, the huge stone discs of Yap, Roman gold, Chinese silver bars and the shell-bead belts of North America look nothing alike. Yet every one of them shared a single trait: each was hard to produce more of, so it held its value, while goods that were easy to make flooded the market and lost theirs. In 2009 Satoshi Nakamoto launched Bitcoin with a hard limit in its code: no more than 21 million coins can ever exist, and no central bank, committee or future programmer can raise it.

Menger asked why one good, rather than another, becomes money. Its beauty, size or toughness matters less, he answered, than its marketability: the good that the most people accept most readily in trade gradually becomes the money everyone uses. Historically, high marketability went hand in hand with difficulty of production. Mines from Nevada to South Africa and Australia add only about 1 to 2 percent each year to all the gold ever dug up and still held in vaults and jewelry, and Austrian economists see that slow growth as the real strength of a gold standard.

Gold is only relatively scarce, because its stock keeps creeping upward. Bitcoin is the first money whose code fixes a final ceiling on the total, a property called absolute scarcity; no metal and no paper currency ever had one. Saifedean Ammous, in The Bitcoin Standard, popularized a yardstick for how hard a money is to inflate: divide the whole supply already in existence by the new supply added each year. That figure, the stock-to-flow ratio, stands at about 60 for gold, and the higher it climbs, the harder the money.

Bitcoin's ratio keeps rising because of the halving. Each time another 210,000 blocks are mined, roughly once in four years, the miner's reward is cut in half, so after about thirty-three halvings the reward rounds down to nothing and new issuance ends around the year 2140; miners will then live on transaction fees alone. In 2019 a Dutch analyst writing as PlanB turned stock-to-flow into a price model that forecast very high prices after the 2020 halving. It looked accurate for a while and then missed badly from 2021, a reminder that a formula tuned to old prices may not forecast new ones. The monetary idea of hardness survived; the price forecast did not.

The Austrian case for Bitcoin is narrower than world conquest. Every past currency, from Diocletian's Roman denarius to the Weimar mark of 1923 to the paper money issued since 1971, lost value through the same channel: debasement by the authority that issued it. Bitcoin's cap closes that channel, because no one holds the power to decide the supply. The whole line of argument traces back to one book, Carl Menger's Principles of Economics, published in Vienna in 1871, and every later Austrian work on money builds on it.

bretton-woods-1944-the-dollar-gold-ancho.context_blurb:
In July 1944, with the Second World War still raging but nearly won, delegations from forty-four Allied nations spent three weeks at a resort in New Hampshire's White Mountains, designing the money system for the postwar world. The arrangement they built anchored the world's currencies on the dollar, and the dollar on gold, and it lasted until 1971. Austrian economists argue that its end was written into its design.

The delegates met from July 1 to July 22 at the Mount Washington Hotel, in the New Hampshire village of Bretton Woods, which gave the system its name. Every Allied currency was pegged at a set rate to the American dollar, while the dollar itself was fixed by law to gold at $35 an ounce, so foreign central banks could turn in their dollars at the American Treasury for gold at that price. The conference also founded two institutions to run the system, both still at work today: the International Monetary Fund, to keep exchange rates stable, and the World Bank, to finance the rebuilding of a shattered world.

Britain's delegation was led by John Maynard Keynes, who pushed a rival plan. His design called for a reserve money belonging to no single country, issued by a new International Clearing Union to square the trade accounts of nations, and he named that currency the bancor. The American design, drafted by the Treasury official Harry Dexter White, won instead. Its aim in tying everything to a dollar anchored in gold was to keep exchange rates steady and to stop governments from printing money without limit, since any country that inflated would see its currency strain against its fixed rate.

White's own story turned dark. In 1948 the former Soviet courier Whittaker Chambers named him before a congressional committee. From 1995 the National Security Agency released files from the Venona project, a wartime effort that had cracked Soviet cables, and they identified White as a Soviet source under the code names Jurist and Richard. The episode exposes a hidden risk in letting a small circle design the world's money: a handful of insiders, pursuing aims no one else can see, can write rules that bind all the rest.

The gold promise held for twenty-six years after the war. On Sunday evening, August 15, 1971, Richard Nixon announced on television that the gold window was closed, and from then on the dollar was a paper currency backed only by the government's word. Austrian writers such as Murray Rothbard and Saifedean Ammous argue that the collapse was arithmetic, not bad luck. To supply the world with the dollars it needed, the United States had to keep running deficits in its own currency, and once the dollars it owed abroad outgrew its gold, the peg was doomed, whatever leaders said or did.

Strictly speaking, Bretton Woods was never a classical gold standard like Britain's before 1914, when ordinary people could hand paper money across a bank counter for gold coins. Private citizens had no such right; only foreign central banks could swap their dollars for the metal, which made it a gold-exchange standard.
