buchanans-1986-nobel-prize.context_blurb:
In October 1986 the Nobel prize in economics went to a single winner, James Buchanan, who had grown up in Tennessee and now taught in Virginia at George Mason University. His achievement was to turn the ordinary tools of economics on government itself. The prize put public choice theory on the world's academic map.

For much of the twentieth century, economists pictured politicians and bureaucrats as selfless servants maximizing the public welfare. Buchanan and his colleague Gordon Tullock called that a fairy tale: officeholders chase votes, agencies chase larger budgets and voters chase benefits, all pursuing their own interests just as people do in markets. The branch of economics built on that insight is public choice. The Swedish academy worded its citation with care, naming the idea rather than the school: it honored Buchanan for developing the contractual and constitutional foundations of the theory of economic and political decision-making.

On December 8, 1986, at sixty-seven, Buchanan gave his Nobel lecture in Stockholm under the title The Constitution of Economic Policy. Its point was that arguing about this or that tax rate misses the prior question of what rules frame the arguing, so policy should be judged by the rules that govern choices and not only by the outcomes of particular choices. What public choice adds about people in government is plain: officials and politicians react to rewards and penalties exactly as shoppers and business owners do.

Many economists disliked that framing, because it strips away the comfortable assumption that officials always act for the public good. When the prize was announced, Paul Samuelson reportedly grumbled that it was really for political science, which was exactly Buchanan's point: the wall between the economics of markets and the economics of politics was itself the mistake. The British economist Ronald Coase, who won the Nobel in 1991, noticed that if bargaining were free, neighbors would settle any quarrel over noise or smoke on their own. In real life bargaining costs time, effort and lawyers. Coase called that friction a transaction cost, and it helps explain why companies exist at all, and why the law's assignment of property rights matters so much.

By the 1990s this rules-of-the-game tradition, often called new institutional economics, had won three Nobels: Buchanan in 1986, Coase in 1991 and the economic historian Douglass North in 1993. In 2009 Elinor Ostrom of Indiana University joined them, the first woman to win the economics prize, for demonstrating that ordinary communities can govern shared pastures, fishing grounds and irrigation canals by themselves, with neither state ownership nor privatization. The tradition also explains everyday politics. A senator backs a bridge back home that enriches a handful of local firms and costs every taxpayer a few dollars, because the benefits fall on a few who notice and reward him, while the costs are spread thin over many who barely notice. Tullock, Buchanan's co-author on The Calculus of Consent in 1962 and the pioneer of rent-seeking analysis, never won a Nobel, a sore point among public-choice scholars.

Whether the subject was a constitution, a property right, a court system or a village's rules for a shared fishery, Buchanan, Coase, North and Ostrom all built on a move Buchanan had made decades earlier: treating institutions themselves as serious objects of economic study. The rules of the game, he insisted, deserve as much analysis as the play within them.

carters-windfall-profits-tax-on-oil-1980.context_blurb:
In April 1980 Jimmy Carter signed a federal Windfall Profit Tax on crude oil, a levy on American oil producers' earnings above a set base price. Its backers promised to capture an undeserved bonanza without changing anyone's behavior. Bastiat's method asks first what the tax raised, and then what never happened because of it.

The 1979 revolution in Iran overthrew the Shah and choked off much of Iran's oil, setting off the second oil crisis; world crude climbed from about $15 a barrel in 1978 to more than $35 by 1981. Carter and Congress argued that domestic producers should not keep that jump as pure profit, so they reached for a windfall tax, a special levy on unusually large profits.

A decade later the Congressional Research Service, Congress's nonpartisan research arm, reported in 1990 what the tax had done. By raising the cost of every extra barrel, it had kept marginal wells from being drilled, so domestic production fell by roughly 3 to 6 percent while imports rose to fill the gap. A country anxious about energy independence ended up producing less of its own oil.

Picture a Texas senator in 1985 complaining that the tax had thrown thousands of Texas oilmen out of work. An economist in Bastiat's tradition would name the unseen part: the tax works like a price ceiling on what producers earn, so the barrels never drilled and the workers never hired are its hidden cost. The tax had been projected to bring in tens of billions of dollars, but producers cut output and sank fewer new wells, since every barrel now returned less after tax. Taxes change behavior, so the money actually collected often falls far short of the plan. When world oil prices collapsed in the mid-1980s the tax brought in almost nothing, and Congress repealed it in 1988, after Ronald Reagan had campaigned against it.

The idea keeps coming back. It was proposed for banks after the 2008 crisis and for drugmakers in the pandemic year of 2020, and Britain imposed one on North Sea oil firms through its Energy Profits Levy of 2022. Each time Bastiat's question returns with it: what will the taxed producers do less of, and who will bear that cost without ever seeing it? A tax on the reward for producing during a shortage weakens the incentive to produce at the very moment it is needed most.

chinas-household-responsibility-system-1.context_blurb:
In December 1978, two years after Mao's death, eighteen families in Xiaogang, a poor village in Anhui province, gathered at night by the light of a kerosene lamp and signed a secret pact. They would split the commune's land into family plots, hand the state its quota and keep whatever was left. Private farming was still forbidden, and they knew they were risking their lives.

Under Mao's collective farms they had been starving. Once each family worked its own plot and kept the surplus, their harvest shot up, far beyond anything the commune had ever grown. The commune had left Xiaogang's families permanently hungry though they toiled every day; for years villagers had gone begging for food in other counties, and memories of the great famine of 1959 to 1961 were still fresh. The signers even promised to raise one another's children if any of them were jailed or executed.

The gamble paid off at once. In the first year the village's grain output rose about six times over, too much for local officials to hide, and neighboring villages copied the idea county by county. The arrangement was tolerated, then imitated, and by 1983 it was legal across China as the Household Responsibility System, under which every family delivered a set grain quota to the state and could keep or sell everything above it.

Across the country, grain output rose by about a third over the following six years. The economist Justin Yifu Lin later found that roughly half of that gain came from the change in incentives rather than from fertilizer, weather or better seed: farmers worked harder and grew more because the extra was theirs. Economists call that right to the leftover, once fixed obligations are paid, the residual claim, and it is the incentive at the heart of private property.

Deng Xiaoping, China's new paramount leader, quietly backed the reform and defended it with a saying he had first used in 1961: the color of a cat, black or white, does not matter as long as it catches mice. Results, not ideological purity, became the test of his Reform and Opening. Austrian economists see a natural experiment confirming Ludwig von Mises's 1920 argument on economic calculation: without real prices and property, planners cannot weigh costs, and the failure of the communes, admitted by China's own Communist Party, bore him out.

The crumbling contract, marked with the farmers' red thumbprints, is today honored as one of modern China's treasures and is displayed at the National Museum in Beijing. The lesson it carries is simple. Same land, same farmers, same seeds, and far more grain, because the only change was who kept the surplus; Austrian economists boil the episode down to two words, incentives matter.

continental-illinois-1984-and-the-birth-.context_blurb:
In May 1984 one of America's biggest banks, Chicago's Continental Illinois, came close to collapse. Regulators saved it with a guarantee that went far beyond the ordinary limits of deposit insurance. Economists in the Austrian and public-choice traditions see that rescue as the template for every big bailout since.

Continental Illinois National Bank, the nation's seventh-largest, with about $40 billion in assets, had piled into energy loans in the oil fields of Oklahoma and Texas, many of them bought from the failed Penn Square Bank of Oklahoma. The collapse of oil prices turned those loans sour. The run that followed was a new kind. Instead of savers queuing at teller windows, big companies and foreign banks pulled their money by electronic wire, billions at a time, and no one needed to set foot in a lobby. Economists call that a wholesale run, and it moves far faster than the old-fashioned kind.

To halt the panic, Washington pledged to make good every account at the bank, even balances far above the $100,000 insurance limit of the day, and big depositors got everything back. A rescue that covers creditors the law never promised to cover, because the bank is thought too large to be allowed to fail, is a too-big-to-fail bailout. Todd Conover, who as Comptroller of the Currency regulated the national banks, testified to a House banking committee that September that the government would not let any of the country's eleven largest banks fail. At that same hearing Congressman Stewart McKinney summed up the new policy in four words that have stuck ever since: too big to fail.

Mergers among large banks sped up after the rescue, and small banks were bought out or squeezed. The four biggest American banks held about 10 percent of deposits in 1984; by 2020 Citigroup, Wells Fargo, Bank of America and JPMorgan Chase together held over 45 percent.

The Austrian and public-choice critique centers on what the rescue taught. Big banks learned that regulators would shield uninsured depositors and creditors in a crisis, so larger risks had become safer to take. The same logic applies to deposit insurance itself. The FDIC, created in 1933 after the bank runs of the Depression, promises to repay depositors if a bank fails, and critics call the result moral hazard: the bank keeps the profits from its big bets, while taxpayers cover the loss if it fails. The FDIC itself took majority ownership of Continental Illinois, which Bank of America finally absorbed in 1994.

The deeper lesson is about precedent. A discretionary exception granted once, and described at the time as a one-off, hardens into a structural rule that shapes every later risk-taking decision in the industry. Long-Term Capital Management in 1998, Bear Stearns and the TARP program in 2008 and Silicon Valley Bank in 2023 all followed the 1984 pattern. The Austrians press one step further. A guarantee that only the biggest banks will be saved is itself a subsidy to them, because depositors sensibly prefer the protected bank, and so the guarantee drives ever-greater concentration in banking.

cubas-special-period-1990-1994.context_blurb:
For three decades the Soviet Union kept communist Cuba afloat with billions of dollars a year, chiefly fuel sold below world prices and sugar bought above them. When the Soviet Union dissolved in December 1991, that support ended almost overnight. What followed tested whether a planned economy could adapt to a sudden shock.

Between 1990 and 1994 Cubans went short of food, fuel and power, and hunger reached every province. Fidel Castro's government gave the crisis an official name: the Special Period in Time of Peace. Daily calories per person fell from about 3,100 in 1989 to about 1,900 in 1993, and medical journals later reported that the average adult lost somewhere from five to twenty-five pounds.

Meat all but vanished from Havana's ration books, and the city's cats and dogs nearly disappeared as well; hungry residents caught and ate some, and many others starved or were abandoned. The recovery did not come from more planning. Castro kept most price controls and ration books, but he reluctantly opened two small doors to the market: small city vegetable plots together with legal self-employment in certain trades, and permission for ordinary Cubans to hold and spend US dollars. Where the market was let in, calories followed.

A Mises-influenced economist prizes the episode as a natural experiment. The Soviet subsidy simply vanished while the rest stayed put: the planning apparatus remained, the weather was ordinary, and the American embargo was nothing new, having been in force since 1962. That isolates a single question, whether central planning can adapt to a supply shock, and it plays out Mises's 1920 prediction in body weight.

In 1993 Fidel Castro, ruler since 1959, gave speeches finally admitting the hunger, and he blamed the US trade embargo rather than the central planning he had kept in place. Critics call that blaming a constant for a sudden change, since the embargo had coexisted with a stable food supply for three decades.

death-in-rome-christmas-eve-1850.context_blurb:
Frédéric Bastiat, born in Bayonne in 1801, crammed a lifetime of writing into his last five years. By 1850 tuberculosis of the throat had left him barely able to speak, and his doctors sent him south in search of warmer air. He spent his final months in Italy, still writing, and died there at forty-nine.

His most famous essay begins with a broken shop window and a crowd that cheers the glazier's new job. Bastiat's point is what the crowd forgets: the shopkeeper's money now goes on glass, so he can no longer spend it on shoes or bread. He reached Rome, then the capital of Pope Pius IX's Papal States, in September 1850, and on Christmas Eve he died.

In his Roman sickroom he kept correcting the proofs of Economic Harmonies, his one attempt at a complete positive theory, a book he did not live to finish; his friend Prosper Paillottet edited an expanded edition from his papers in 1851. The book argued that when strangers buy and sell freely, no person or committee needs to be in charge, because a working system emerges in which each person's needs are met without a central planner.

He was buried in Rome's French national church, San Luigi dei Francesi, near Piazza Navona, where a memorial plaque marks his tomb. The same church holds three paintings by Caravaggio, his cycle on the life of Saint Matthew from around 1600, which any visitor may stroll in and see at no charge. Put up for sale, they would fetch hundreds of millions of dollars, a reminder that value comes from what people are willing to pay, not from whether a thing is being sold today.

Weak and coughing, Bastiat had raced in his final months to finish the essay that sums up his method, That Which Is Seen, and That Which Is Not Seen. Its lesson is that every tax, subsidy or ban has effects beyond the obvious one, and an honest thinker traces them all, counting the hidden effects that almost no one mentions.

difficulty-adjustment-the-homeostatic-cl.context_blurb:
Bitcoin's design calls for one fresh block of transactions roughly every ten minutes. Miners come and go all the time, yet the pace holds. The secret is a rule that every computer on the network runs in exactly the same way, with no one in charge, recalibrating how hard the mining puzzle is.

One block may come after sixty seconds and the next after half an hour, but the long-run average stays near ten minutes because of the difficulty adjustment, which raises or lowers the puzzle's difficulty as miners join or leave. Every 2,016 blocks, which is two weeks at exactly ten minutes a block, each node measures the time the previous batch actually took and sets the new difficulty from the blocks' own timestamps. That interval is a separate constant from the 210,000-block spacing between halvings.

When a batch of 2,016 blocks arrives in less than two weeks, the network raises the difficulty at the next retarget. The target number shrinks, so miners must find hashes with more leading zeros, valid answers grow rarer, and blocks slow back toward ten minutes; if blocks have been slow, the adjustment runs the other way.

The rule met its sternest test in 2021. When China banned Bitcoin mining in May and June, roughly half the world's mining power went dark within weeks and blocks slowed down. With no human decision at all, the retarget of July 3, 2021, cut the difficulty by about 28 percent, the largest drop in Bitcoin's history, and blocks returned to their ten-minute pace. A Hayekian economist names the property, one that no central bank has: the homeostatic self-correction of a rule-based network that needs no human decision-maker. No agency could set the right difficulty in real time for a worldwide industry it did not know intimately, but the rule gathers the scattered information automatically.

The displaced miners shipped their machines to Texas, Kazakhstan and elsewhere, and within about nine months of the ban, by March 2022, the network's total mining power had climbed back to a new all-time high.

economic-calculation-in-the-socialist-co.context_blurb:
In 1920 Ludwig von Mises, a thirty-nine-year-old economist at the Vienna Chamber of Commerce, published an essay that started one of the great debates of the century. Its question was not whether socialism was kind or cruel but whether it could work at all. Seven decades later, the collapse of the planned economies settled the argument in his favor.

The essay, Die Wirtschaftsrechnung im sozialistischen Gemeinwesen, was the work of Ludwig von Mises, whose private seminar the young Friedrich Hayek, then a student, would later attend. Mises set aside every moral objection, laziness and corruption included, to press one technical claim: rational economic calculation under socialism is impossible. It appeared in volume 47 of a journal that Max Weber had helped edit before the First World War, the Archiv für Sozialwissenschaft und Sozialpolitik. In 1922 Mises expanded the argument into a book, Die Gemeinwirtschaft, translated in 1936 simply as Socialism, whose central claim is that planners deprived of free-market prices have no way to work out the true cost of anything.

Picture a Soviet planner in 1925 choosing between rolled steel and aluminum for a new railway. Both would work, and each draws labor and materials from other uses, but with the state owning every mine and mill, the metals are never bought or sold, only shuffled between state enterprises. What is missing is prices generated by exchange for the capital goods involved, and more statisticians or better forecasts cannot replace them. Friedrich Engels had promised that a socialist society could keep its accounts simply, by tallying the hours of labor that went into each product, a locomotive or a sack of grain. Mises quoted him and answered that labor hours say nothing about how scarce each material input is, since two goods may each take ten hours while one devours scarce iron ore and the other uses plentiful clay.

The argument, pressed by Mises and later Hayek through the 1920s and 1930s, became known as the socialist calculation problem. Hayek's 1935 collection, Collectivist Economic Planning, first put it before English-speaking economists. Two economists replied in the late 1930s. Oskar Lange and Abba Lerner proposed that the state own the factories while managers copied market prices by trial and error, adjusting output until shortages and surpluses disappeared, a scheme known as the Lange-Lerner model of market socialism. Mises and Hayek answered that imitation without real ownership still lacks the discipline of profit and loss that makes prices informative.

In 1945 Hayek recast the argument in The Use of Knowledge in Society, published in the American Economic Review: prices squeeze what millions of people privately know into signals that no planner could ever gather. History supplied the test. At their peak Soviet planners set some 22 million prices, yet stores ran out of basics while warehouses filled with goods nobody wanted. When the planned economies fell between 1989 and 1991, Western economists such as Robert Heilbroner, writing in The New Yorker in 1990, admitted that the 1920 argument of Mises had been vindicated; Mises, Heilbroner wrote, was right.

emperor-julians-grain-price-ceiling-in-a.context_blurb:
In the summer of 362 the Roman emperor Julian rode into Antioch, one of the richest cities of the eastern empire, to prepare a war against Persia. He found bread scarce and dear. What he did about it, and what the grain did next, has become one of history's oldest lessons about controlling prices.

Antioch owed its wealth to where it stood. It was a crossroads where trade routes from the sea and caravan roads from the desert came together, so merchants arrived from every direction and goods flowed through its markets.

A legal maximum that no seller may charge above is called a price cap. Julian's grain order was one. So, sixty years earlier, was the sweeping order of Emperor Diocletian, which barred sellers across the empire from charging more than prices the emperor himself had fixed.

Eager to win the favor of the poor, Julian ordered every sack of grain in Antioch sold at a low fixed price. The market answered at once: the city's merchants and the farmers of the countryside held their grain back rather than sell it at a loss. Julian shipped in grain from imperial stores, but buyers snapped it up, often to resell it on the black market, and the shops emptied again.

The cap itself caused the shortage. Hauling grain to Antioch now cost sellers more than the law let them charge, so supplying the city stopped paying and the grain dried up. Over the following months merchants stopped sending grain to Antioch at all, and the shortage grew worse instead of better.

Julian did not lift the cap. He blamed the sellers' greed, and early in 363 he wrote Misopogon, or "Beard-Hater," a mocking pamphlet aimed at the people of Antioch, who had laughed at his philosopher's beard. It is one of the very few first-person books by a Roman emperor to survive. Critics of price controls have a name for his mistake: blaming the messenger for the message. Empty shelves are the message, news that the legal price is too low, and the seller who carries that news gets punished for it.

The American economist Thomas Sowell, who sets the Julian and Diocletian episodes side by side in Basic Economics, teaches a habit that cuts through such blame. He asks, "Compared to what?" Before you praise a policy or condemn it, name the real alternative: the choice in Antioch was never cheap grain against dear grain, but high prices with grain on the shelves against low prices with none.

Julian is remembered for something else as well. He turned away from the Christian faith that Constantine had championed and tried to restore the old gods of Greece and Rome. After his death, Christian writers fixed on him the hostile name that stuck in the history books: Julian the Apostate, the man who abandoned the faith. He was killed fighting the Persians in June 363, a few months after leaving Antioch.

Austrian economists pair Julian with Diocletian, whose Edict on Maximum Prices emptied markets across the whole empire in 301, because both cases follow one pattern that keeps returning. The ruler sets a low price, the goods vanish, and the ruler blames the seller. The same three steps reappear in Nixon's controls of 1971 and in Venezuela after 2013.

every-fiat-currency-dies-the-5-000-year-.context_blurb:
Money backed by nothing but a government's word has a long history, and most of it is unhappy. From medieval China to modern Zimbabwe, rulers who could print money have printed too much of it. Austrian economists and Bitcoin advocates read that record as a pattern with a cause, not as a string of bad luck.

The story starts in Sichuan, in western China, in the 1000s. Merchants weary of lugging heavy iron coins along the roads began trading printed paper notes called jiaozi instead, and around 1023 the government of the Song dynasty took over issuing them.

Europe's first great paper experiment came seven centuries later. Between 1716 and 1720 the Scottish financier John Law ran France's royal bank for the boy-king Louis XV and flooded the country with notes to pump up the Mississippi Company, a venture built on French claims in North America. His paper money was John Law's Banque Royale livre, and when the bubble burst it lost almost all its value.

When a government prints money so fast that prices climb out of control, the result is called hyperinflation. The worst case ever measured struck Hungary just after the Second World War: by July 1946 prices in pengő were doubling about every fifteen hours, so bread cost more at supper than at breakfast. Zimbabwe under Robert Mugabe came close in its 2008 crisis, when the central bank ended up printing a single note for one hundred trillion Zimbabwe dollars, a note too feeble to pay for bread.

For most of history, paper money could at least be swapped for metal. Under the Bretton Woods system set up in 1944, a foreign government could turn in dollars at the American Treasury and receive gold at a fixed price. On August 15, 1971, President Richard Nixon closed that gold window. He called the suspension temporary, but it was never undone, and the Nixon shock cut the last real tie between money and gold.

The dollar, the euro, the yen and the pound have all been fiat money ever since: paper made legal tender by government order, with no metal behind it. Measured in gold, a 1913 dollar, from the year the Federal Reserve was created, now buys only about two cents' worth, and fiat money is what made that slow leak possible, since nothing stops a government from issuing more paper. The arrangement Nixon's shock left behind is called the fiat standard, and the whole world still runs on it.

Defenders of paper money sometimes point to the British pound, which admirers call 1,300 years old, as proof that a currency can last. The Austrian reply is that the pound has lost about 99.5 percent of its buying power since 1750, and its coins have changed metal, from silver down to nickel. A medieval silver penny and today's paper pound share a name, not a money.

Austrian writers see political power over the economy at its most extreme in the communist states. The Black Book of Communism, written by a team of French scholars under Stéphane Courtois and published in 1997, tallied the deaths caused by communist regimes from the Soviet Union and China to Cambodia and North Korea at between 65 and 100 million people.

Why does fiat money keep failing? Mises and Rothbard, and after them Joseph Salerno and Saifedean Ammous, answer that the cause lies in incentives, not in the personal character of particular bankers. Politicians promise citizens more than taxes will cover, the monetary authority fills the gap by printing, the printing debases the currency, savers silently absorb the loss, and the cycle builds until confidence breaks.

From that record they draw a conclusion about reform. Sound money, they argue, is an engineering problem to be solved with fixed rules that nobody can bend, not a political problem to be solved by finding better leaders. That is the thinking behind Bitcoin's 2008 design, which replaces trust in officials with cryptography and a rule-bound network.

fed-treasury-accord-and-william-mcchesne.context_blurb:
For almost nineteen years, from 1951 to 1970, William McChesney Martin Jr. ran the Federal Reserve, America's central bank, longer than anyone else has. He is remembered for one image, a party and a bowl of punch, and for the harder thing behind it: telling presidents no when they wanted cheap money.

The story begins in the Second World War. To keep Washington's borrowing cheap, the Fed pinned interest rates low, buying up as many government bonds as it took and in effect creating new dollars to lend to the Treasury. When the war ended and price controls came off, all that new money was still in circulation, and prices rose as too many dollars chased the same supply of goods.

Even after the war the Fed stayed tied to the Treasury's needs. The Treasury-Fed Accord of March 4, 1951, finally gave the central bank back its power to set interest rates by itself. Economists draw a lesson from the episode: in wartime a central bank surrenders its independence to paying the government's bills, and winning that independence back afterward is a political fight that has to be fought openly, never simply assumed.

There was a twist. Martin had helped negotiate the Accord as a Treasury official, arguing the Treasury side. So when President Harry Truman chose him to chair the Fed in April 1951, Truman expected a loyal ally. Instead Martin became a fierce defender of the Fed's independence, and Truman felt betrayed.

Martin had grown up inside the system. When the Fed opened for business in 1914, the first governor of the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis was Martin's own father, who bore the same name, and thirty-seven years later the son took charge of the whole system. He went on to serve five presidents in a row: Truman, Eisenhower, Kennedy, Johnson, and Nixon.

In October 1955 Martin addressed a gathering of investment bankers in New York and found the image that defined him. The Fed, he said, is like the chaperone who orders the punch bowl carried away at the very moment the party is starting to warm up. The punch stood for cheap credit, the easy money that makes a boom feel lively. Martin meant that the Fed must cut off the easy money before the boom can end in a crash.

Financial writers turned his line into shorthand for a particular job: restrictive monetary policy, imposed during a boom and against political pressure, lifting rates to calm an economy running too hot. That is also why the job is so hard. Tightening is always unpopular at the moment it matters most, because it arrives exactly when everyone is enjoying the good times.

Martin felt that pressure in the late 1960s. President Lyndon Johnson paid for the Vietnam War and his Great Society programs at once without raising taxes to cover them, while the Fed kept rates low enough to keep government borrowing cheap. A country that combines big unfunded spending with cheap central-bank money tends to get high inflation a few years later, and the Great Inflation of the 1970s, which Martin's successor Arthur Burns made worse, followed.

frederic-bastiat-the-journalist-economis.context_blurb:
Frederic Bastiat was a French farmer, journalist and politician who wrote economics for ordinary readers. In just six years, from 1844 until his death in 1850, he produced the essays that still teach people to hunt for the unseen costs of every policy. He was born in Bayonne in 1801, lost both parents young, and was raised by his grandfather on the family estate at Mugron in southwestern France.

For some twenty years Bastiat farmed at Mugron and read deeply about trade and money, hardly known beyond his district. Then, in October 1844, the Journal des Economistes, the Paris flagship of the French free-trade school, printed his article comparing English and French tariffs, and almost at once he was famous.

Across the Channel, Britain's Corn Laws kept bread dear for the poor by loading foreign grain with heavy duties. The Anti-Corn Law League, which Richard Cobden and John Bright had launched in Manchester in 1838, fought those duties with rallies, pamphlets and speeches; it was a free-trade movement of national reach, and in 1846 it won repeal. Bastiat visited England, befriended Cobden and went home to build a French version.

Bastiat wrote in plain, lively French that ordinary working people could follow. He refused, on purpose, the mathematical formalism of equations and graphs, wanting every reader to check each step of an argument without algebra; wit, stories and satire were his tools instead.

After the revolution of 1848 toppled King Louis-Philippe, Bastiat won a seat in the Assembly the revolution created, kept it in the election that followed, and served on its finance committee. In speech after speech he went after the socialists of Louis Blanc and Pierre-Joseph Proudhon, whose national workshops and free-credit bank he believed would ruin France.

In the summer of 1850, already gravely ill with tuberculosis, he sent two short works to the printer within weeks of each other. La Loi, The Law, came out in June, and in July came Ce qu'on voit et ce qu'on ne voit pas, the essay on what is seen and what is not seen.

The second holds his most famous story. A boy breaks a shop window, and onlookers cheer that at least the glazier will get work. Bastiat pointed to the sale nobody sees: the shopkeeper must now spend his money on glass, so he cannot buy the new shoes he intended, and the shoemaker loses that sale.

Judging every choice against the alternative given up is what modern textbooks call opportunity cost, and they credit Bastiat with its first clear statement. Together with the broken window, it is his lasting gift to economics.

Bastiat hoped to be remembered for something larger: Harmonies economiques, his reply to the socialists, meant to prove that free exchange breeds cooperation instead of class war. Only the first part appeared before he died, and the remainder was pieced together afterward from his notes.

That autumn his doctors sent him south for the mild Italian winter. He went first to Pisa and then on to Rome, and there, on Christmas Eve, 1850, he died at forty-nine; he lies buried in the French church of San Luigi dei Francesi. His friend Prosper Paillottet, who was at the bedside, reported that in his last hour Bastiat kept murmuring two words, "la vérité, la vérité," the truth, the truth. His friends took the phrase as the summary of a life spent refusing to lie about consequences.

friedrich-hayek-who-he-was.context_blurb:
Friedrich Hayek was born in Vienna in 1899 and died in Freiburg, Germany, in 1992, and in between he lived through the century's great contest between planned economies and free ones. More than anyone, he explained why the planners kept failing. His answer was not mainly a moral one. It was about knowledge: what it is, and where it lives.

As a young economist in 1920s Vienna, Hayek went to the private seminar that Ludwig von Mises ran every second Friday at the Chamber of Commerce, where Mises worked, and he always credited Mises with teaching him real economics.

In 1931 Lionel Robbins invited Hayek to London to give four lectures. Published as Prices and Production, they laid out his theory of the business cycle, the claim that booms built on cheap central-bank credit are bound to collapse into busts. The lectures went so well that the London School of Economics gave him a chair, which he held until 1950.

While German bombs fell on London, Hayek wrote The Road to Serfdom, published in 1944 for British and American readers, and it became a bestseller in both countries. Its warning was that a government trying to direct an entire economy from above, however kind its intentions, slides step by step toward controlling more and more of ordinary people's lives, because every plan needs someone to enforce it.

In 1947, with central planning fashionable everywhere, Hayek brought about forty classical-liberal scholars together at a resort high above Lake Geneva. They founded a society named after the mountain, the Mont Pelerin Society, to keep the free-market tradition alive.

In 1950 Hayek moved to the University of Chicago, but its economics department would not hire him. Chancellor Robert Hutchins found him a professorship elsewhere, on the interdisciplinary Committee on Social Thought, paid for by the William Volker Fund.

His central idea is the knowledge problem. A modern economy runs on millions of scraps of local knowledge, about what is wanted, what is scarce and what things cost, scattered in millions of heads, and no committee, however brilliant, can ever gather them in one place. Market prices carry that knowledge instead. In 1974 Hayek shared the Nobel Prize in Economics with Gunnar Myrdal.

In his prize lecture in Stockholm that December he took aim at his own field. His fellow economists, he said, had borrowed the trappings of physics, its formulas and confident forecasts, without the knowledge that would justify them. He called the lecture The Pretence of Knowledge.

His final book, The Fatal Conceit, appeared in 1988, when he was eighty-nine. In it he argued that morality, the family, property and markets evolved over countless generations into an order too intricate for any planner to rebuild. The fatal conceit, in his phrase, is the confidence that human reason can design from a blank page what took history ages to evolve.

Hayek also refused to call himself a conservative. In "Why I Am Not a Conservative," the postscript to his 1960 book The Constitution of Liberty, he found "libertarian" an unattractive label too and preferred to stand with the Old Whigs. What his tradition defends is the conviction that prices, laws and customs grew up over centuries and cannot be redesigned from nothing.

gordon-tullock-the-lawyer-who-co-founded.context_blurb:
Gordon Tullock, born in Rockford, Illinois, in 1922, helped found one of the most important ideas in modern economics without ever earning a doctorate in the subject. He was a lawyer and a diplomat first. What he saw inside real governments convinced him that politicians and officials respond to incentives like everyone else.

Tullock took a law degree at the University of Chicago in 1947 and then spent nearly ten years in the US Foreign Service, posted in Tianjin during the Communist takeover of China, in Hong Kong and in Korea. He later said those years of watching officials scheme and bargain taught him more about how political incentives work than any economics class ever could.

That insight became a whole branch of economics. It treats officials, legislators and the citizens who elect them as self-interested human beings who want votes, larger budgets and promotions, not as saints serving the common good, and it is called public choice, or public-choice economics. A mayor who puts promised new parks in swing districts, where grateful voters can reward him, rather than in the poor neighborhoods that need them most, is behaving exactly as public choice predicts.

In 1958 Tullock joined James Buchanan at the University of Virginia, and in 1962 the two published The Calculus of Consent, the book that launched the field. In 1966 Tullock started the field's own journal, first called Papers on Non-Market Decision Making and renamed Public Choice in 1968, and he edited it for more than thirty years.

In 1965 Tullock turned the same tools on government offices in The Politics of Bureaucracy, showing how officials build careers, enlarge their agencies and defend their turf; William Niskanen's 1971 study of bureaus built directly on it. The head of a government office usually wants more staff, prestige and power, so year after year he asks for a bigger budget, even when its workload is falling. Offices like his try to grow, and almost never volunteer to shrink.

In 1967 Tullock described another hidden cost of government. When the state hands out a few valuable permits that let only certain firms do business, companies pour money into lobbying for the permits instead of into better products, and all that effort creates nothing. Anne Krueger, studying India's import licenses in 1974, gave the behavior its modern name: rent-seeking.

Tullock even applied the tools to dictatorship, in a 1987 book. A dictator, he and later thinkers such as Bruce Bueno de Mesquita argued, does not need to please the masses. He needs to keep a narrow circle of generals and courtiers well rewarded, because if those insiders turn on him, he falls.

In 1986 Buchanan won the Nobel Prize for founding public choice, and Tullock, his co-author, was left out. Colleagues remember his bitter quip that co-writing The Calculus of Consent apparently did not count. The two had moved their Center for Study of Public Choice to George Mason University in 1983, where Tullock taught until 2008; he died in 2014.

hal-finney-first-node-first-transaction-.context_blurb:
When Bitcoin came to life in January 2009, almost nobody noticed. One of the few who did was Hal Finney, a California programmer who had spent two decades building tools for private communication and digital cash. He became Bitcoin's first partner, its first customer, and in the end one of its most moving witnesses.

Bitcoin was the creation of an unknown inventor who called himself Satoshi Nakamoto. It is money that exists only on computers and that no government prints; a worldwide network of computers solving math puzzles maintains the record of ownership that a bank would otherwise keep. Money of that kind, run by computers and cryptography, is called a cryptocurrency.

Finney was ready for it. For years his day job at PGP Corporation had been writing code for Pretty Good Privacy, software that scrambles a message so only the holder of the right secret key can read it. A government agency that intercepts such a message sees only gibberish, and that scrambling is called encryption.

He had also wrestled with digital cash himself. In 2004 he published a design called Reusable Proofs of Work, which he shortened to RPOW. Like other early digital-cash systems, it depended on one central trusted server, and that was its weak point: if that server is shut down or corrupted, the whole currency breaks.

Satoshi released the Bitcoin software in early January 2009, and Finney started it on his own computer a day or so after the network went live, making his machine the second Bitcoin node ever. On January 11 he tweeted just two words about what his machine was busy with: "Running bitcoin."

A day later Satoshi sent him 10 coins, the first time bitcoin had ever passed from one person to another. That small transfer mattered because it proved the new digital money actually worked the way its design promised.

Later in 2009 Finney learned he had amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, or ALS, the disease that slowly paralyzes the body and is often called Lou Gehrig's disease. By 2013 he could type only by moving his eyes across a screen. That March, using eye-tracking software, he posted an essay on the bitcointalk.org forum titled "Bitcoin and Me," telling the whole story from the first node to his illness. He died in 2014, and, true to his lifelong interest in extending life, his body was cryopreserved by the Alcor foundation in Arizona.

Because he was there at the very start, Finney was often accused of secretly being Satoshi. Two lines of evidence rule it out. Finney denied it plainly himself, and the timeline does not fit: while Satoshi was busy sending emails, Finney was training for a marathon and posting his running times.

hazlitts-economics-in-one-lesson-bastiat.context_blurb:
Henry Hazlitt (1894-1993) was never a professor, yet his short book of 1946 has taught more Americans to think like economists than almost any textbook. A journalist all his life, he took one idea from a French pamphleteer of the 1840s and applied it to every policy of his own day.

The idea came from Frederic Bastiat. A rule must be judged by its effects on everybody, the hidden losers as well as the visible winners. Bastiat called it the method of what is seen and what is unseen, and Hazlitt preached it for twelve years in his New York Times editorials.

The essay Hazlitt carried forward was Bastiat's That Which is Seen and That Which is Not Seen, written in 1850 by a man dying of tuberculosis, months before his death.

Hazlitt's book was Economics in One Lesson, published in 1946 by Harper & Brothers. It has sold more than a million copies and has never gone out of print.

The method has one big lesson: always hunt for the hidden cost of a policy, not just the benefit everyone can see. The mistake it warns against is judging a policy only by the short-term help it gives one favored group.

Hazlitt put the rule in a single sentence. The art of economics, he wrote, is to trace a policy's consequences not just for one group and not just at the immediate moment, but for all groups and over time. Friedman and the congressman Ron Paul each recommended it as the first economics book a newcomer should read, and generations of American libertarians started there.

The same year, 1946, Hazlitt joined Leonard Read in founding the Foundation for Economic Education at Irvington-on-Hudson, often counted the first free-market think tank in the country; Read was its president and Hazlitt sat on its founding board.

From 1946 to 1966 Hazlitt also wrote the Business Tides column in Newsweek, and Milton Friedman, who later took a Newsweek slot of his own, called him the model. A magazine that keeps a writer for twenty years is itself a small lesson: readers can cancel any day and take their money elsewhere, so market competition keeps the editors working hard to please them.

In 1959 Hazlitt published The Failure of the New Economics, a reply to John Maynard Keynes that worked through the 1936 General Theory chapter by chapter and answered each argument in turn.

Friedrich Hayek admired the 1946 book, and his short verdict, a brilliant performance, has been printed on later editions.

ineptly-defended-the-line-sowell-borrowe.context_blurb:
In 1840s France, Frederic Bastiat wrote witty pamphlets defending free trade against a powerful protectionist lobby. He also left a rule about how to argue that writers still borrow today, the economist Thomas Sowell among them.

Bastiat warned that clever enemies are not a good cause's greatest danger. The worst thing that can happen to a good cause, he wrote, is not to be attacked skillfully but to be ineptly defended.

So he set himself a discipline. Nearly every essay in his 1845 collection Economic Sophisms first lays out the protectionist argument fairly, even sympathetically, in its strongest form, and only then answers it.

Today that move has a one-word name. Around 2010, writers in the online rationalist community, on sites such as LessWrong and Slate Star Codex, began calling it the steelman, in contrast to the straw man. A debate coach who tells students to restate a rival's idea as well as its own supporters would, before attacking it, is teaching steelmanning. The habit is worth building because it stops you from defeating a weak version of an argument while the strong version still stands.

The same essay shows Bastiat's other great habit, counting the unseen. When a town spends tax money on a new stadium, everyone sees the ribbon-cutting. Bastiat wanted the other side of the ledger counted: everything the taxpayers would otherwise have bought or built with that money, purchases and projects that now never happen.

Thomas Sowell, born in Gastonia, North Carolina, in 1930 and later a scholar at the Hoover Institution, has named Bastiat among the formative influences on his method. In 2000 he published Basic Economics, a plain-language guide to the whole field with no graphs or jargon; it went through five editions and sold widely to students and adults alike.

Sowell's 1987 book A Conflict of Visions applies the steelman to politics itself. It maps two rival worldviews: a constrained vision, in which human nature is flawed and wisdom lives in tested traditions, and an unconstrained vision, in which people can be perfected if the right experts are in charge. Sowell presents each in its strongest terms before tracing how they lead to different policies.

jekyll-island-the-secret-meeting-that-dr.context_blurb:
In November 1910 a few of the country's mightiest bankers, a senator and a Treasury official boarded a private railroad car in New Jersey and rode south to Jekyll Island, a millionaires' hunting club off the coast of Georgia. For about nine days they worked in secret, and what they wrote became the blueprint for the Federal Reserve.

They were drafting a central bank, an institution whose main job is to manage the nation's supply of money: how much money exists, and at what price it can be borrowed.

The party was led by Rhode Island's Senator Nelson Aldrich, who chaired the National Monetary Commission. With him came Paul Warburg of the investment house Kuhn Loeb, an expert on European central banks, Benjamin Strong of Bankers Trust and the Treasury official Piatt Andrew. Frank Vanderlip came as president of the National City Bank of New York, the bank tied to the Rockefeller fortune that later became Citibank. Henry Davison, a senior partner at J.P. Morgan and Company, drafted most of the written plan.

Secrecy was total. The men called one another by first names only so the staff would not learn who they were, kept the curtains drawn and said nothing in public for years. Their work became the Aldrich Plan of 1911. A plan like that becomes law only one way: Congress must pass it, and in modified form it did. President Woodrow Wilson signed the Federal Reserve Act on December 23, 1913, creating America's first central bank since the Second Bank of the United States lost its charter in the 1830s.

Critics later raised one central worry. A money system that would shape the lives of every American had been designed by a few insiders, not in public. Public-choice economists put it more sharply: the bankers who would live under the new rules had drafted those rules themselves, a vivid case of regulatory capture at an agency's very birth.

Their wider lesson concerns who designs a central bank. The particular men who drew up the plan led the very New York institutions, and represented the very fortunes, that its structure would benefit, and they kept the whole trip secret.

The story stayed hidden for a quarter of a century. In 1935 Vanderlip finally told it in print, in an article for the Saturday Evening Post. He admitted that on that trip he had been as secretive, indeed as furtive, as any conspirator.

judy-shelton-the-austrian-tradition-fed-.context_blurb:
In 2020 the Senate fought over Judy Shelton, an economist President Donald Trump had picked for a seat on the Fed's Board of Governors, which runs America's central bank. The fight that followed was unusual. It turned on an old question that had not shaped a Fed nomination in decades: whether money should be tied to gold.

To see why, start with the gold standard. Until 1933 in America, and nearly everywhere before 1914, a citizen could swap paper money for a set amount of gold. A government could issue only as much paper as its gold could cover, so the rule stood guard against endless money printing.

Shelton had spent decades arguing for that kind of discipline. Critics and defenders alike placed her in the Austrian tradition and called her gold-standard-curious, a rare outlook for a Fed nominee. In her 1994 book Money Meltdown she warned that central banks were creating money far too freely, and she defined sound money as money that holds its value because no one can print it at will.

She had also called a bigger collapse early. In The Coming Soviet Crash, published in 1989, she argued that the Soviet economy would fail, which it did in 1991. The reasoning followed Friedrich Hayek: the planners in Moscow could never collect the countless facts about goods, prices and labor that a working economy depends on, the obstacle known as the knowledge problem.

Her writings had also questioned how far the Fed should stay independent of elected leaders. Many economists defend that independence for a plain reason: it keeps decisions about money from being bent to help one politician win the next election. Her doubts about the Fed's independence from the White House alarmed Democrats and some Republicans.

The resistance was fierce. Over a hundred people who had once worked at the Fed put their names to a public letter opposing her, and among the signers were seven former chairs and vice chairs of the Fed itself.

The Senate Banking Committee approved her, but in November 2020 the full Senate stopped her nomination, when Republicans Susan Collins, Mitt Romney and Lamar Alexander joined every Democrat to deny her a vote. Above all, the fight was about whether linking the world's money to gold is a respectable policy choice at all.

Austrian-tradition analysts read a public-choice lesson in her defeat. A candidate who openly proposes to constrain the institution she would join tends to be blocked by that institution's own alumni network.

Her warnings were being tested even while the Senate debated. In the first COVID lockdowns of spring 2020, the Fed pledged to purchase government bonds without limit, pouring new dollars into the economy. Austrian critics call that a hidden tax: the new money makes every existing dollar worth less, so savers quietly lose buying power.

katyn-1940-and-the-molotov-ribbentrop-pa.context_blurb:
In the summer of 1939 the two great dictatorships of Europe, which had spent years denouncing each other, suddenly made a deal. Within a year one of them had murdered much of a neighboring nation's leadership in secret, and then lied about it for half a century.

In Moscow on August 23, 1939, Vyacheslav Molotov and Joachim von Ribbentrop, the two foreign ministers, signed a non-aggression treaty for their governments: Nazi Germany and the Soviet Union. In public it promised peace between them. A secret protocol carved Poland, the Baltic states and part of Romania into German and Soviet spheres.

On September 1 Hitler's armies crossed Poland's western border, and the war in Europe began. On September 17 the Soviet Union invaded from the east, and the two powers divided the country between them. In June 1940 Moscow also annexed Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania.

Stalin's secret police, the NKVD, then rounded up Polish army officers, policemen, priests, professors, teachers and lawyers. On March 5, 1940, the Soviet Politburo ordered them shot, and that April and May NKVD squads executed about 22,000 of these prisoners, in the Katyn Forest near Smolensk and at the prisons of Kalinin and Kharkiv, burying the bodies in mass graves.

The victims were chosen on purpose. A regime that wants to rule a conquered people goes after its educated class first, because officers, teachers and priests are the ones who could organize resistance to the new masters.

Taken together, the pact, the joint invasion, the seizure of the Baltics and the massacre establish a hard fact about the twenty-two months before Hitler turned on Stalin in June 1941. In those months the Soviet Union was not a neutral bystander but a co-belligerent of Nazi Germany.

After German troops found the graves in 1943, Moscow blamed the Nazis, and it kept telling that lie for almost half a century. On April 13, 1990, under Mikhail Gorbachev and his policy of openness, the Soviet government finally admitted that Soviet police had carried out the killings.

The last proof came after the Soviet Union itself was gone. On October 14, 1992, the Russian president Boris Yeltsin handed Polish leaders the secret Politburo file. The order of March 5, 1940, bore the signature of the man who had ordered the killings: Joseph Stalin.

In 2007 the Polish director Andrzej Wajda released a film called simply Katyn, told through the families searching for their missing men. The story was his own: Wajda's father, an army officer, had been among those shot at Kharkiv.

late-talking-children-1997-and-the-einst.context_blurb:
Thomas Sowell is known for books on economics, race and history. But in the 1990s he wrote about something far from his usual subjects: bright children who start talking unusually late. The reason was in his own home, and the books ended up applying his economics to medicine.

Sowell's first rule of economics, the theme of the opening chapter of his plain-language textbook Basic Economics, is that every choice means giving up the best alternative you did not choose. A year at college costs a year of wages; a late movie costs sleep. Economists call that sacrifice the opportunity cost.

The new subject began with his son. Sowell's own son John was one of these children: specialists variously labeled the boy autistic, retarded or deaf, and all of them were wrong. John talked late and grew into a highly intelligent adult with a technical career.

Sowell gathered other families' stories and published Late-Talking Children in 1997. He saw a pattern: bright late talkers were often strong in math and music, and many came from families full of engineers, scientists and musicians. In 2001 he named the pattern after Albert Einstein, who, his family said, did not speak in sentences until about age three. He called it the Einstein Syndrome.

Sowell argued that the professionals who evaluate such children were not neutral judges. Pediatricians, therapists and school special-education offices, he said, had institutional incentives to sort children into named conditions, each with its own named treatment and its own funding stream, even when a particular child fit none of the labels.

This was Hayek's knowledge problem carried into pediatric medicine. No single specialist could see a pattern that crossed specialties, and the incentives inside each specialty rewarded intervention over patient waiting.

The same idea runs through Sowell's whole career. Big programs run by distant experts often make problems worse, he argued, not because the experts are wicked or insincere but because they are missing the detailed local knowledge held by the people on the spot.

ludwig-lachmann-radical-subjectivism-and.context_blurb:
Ludwig Lachmann (1906-1990) was born in Berlin, studied under Hayek in London and taught for some forty years in Johannesburg at Wits, the University of the Witwatersrand. He pushed one Austrian idea, that value and expectations live in individual minds, further than anyone, and he became the leading voice of what is now called radical subjectivism.

The starting point is the Austrian theory of value. What a thing is worth does not come from its materials or what it cost to make; it depends on who wants it, when and why. A cold bottle of water is precious in the desert and almost worthless in your fridge, and that is subjective value.

In 1956 Lachmann published a short, influential book, Capital and Its Structure. Lathes, delivery trucks and factory buildings are different tools with different uses that fit together in particular ways. Mainstream textbooks liked to add all of them up into one big number, called K, but Lachmann attacked the idea that capital can be squeezed into a single total, because the sum erases the very fit between tools that booms and busts disrupt.

He applied the same thinking to expectations. In the 1970s the school of rational expectations treated business owners as if they could calculate the future by probability. Lachmann, drawing on Frank Knight's 1921 distinction between measurable risk and true uncertainty, replied that the future is genuinely unknowable, so different entrepreneurs will reasonably form different expectations about it.

That has a sobering consequence. Dice have known odds, but the future holds inventions, companies and choices that do not exist yet, so no honest odds can be given. If Lachmann and the British economist George Shackle are right, a ten-year economic forecast is basically a guess and should not be trusted like a weather report.

His most radical statement came in a 1976 essay, From Mises to Shackle. Markets never settle into equilibrium; plans and expectations keep shifting, and the overall picture keeps rearranging itself, like the bits of glass in a kaleidoscope. Borrowing Shackle's word, he called this picture the kaleidic society.

He never doubted the school's core claim about planning. Mises, Hayek and their students argued that central planning fails not because planners are wicked but because the knowledge an economy needs is spread across millions of buyers and sellers, and no small group can ever collect it. Lachmann later taught at New York University, which under Israel Kirzner and Murray Rothbard became the training ground of the Austrian revival.

Lachmann also wrote The Legacy of Max Weber, in 1971. The German sociologist Max Weber had argued in his 1905 study of the Protestant ethic and the rise of capitalism that a culture's teachings, such as hard work, thrift and keeping your word, shape how its markets grow. His broad claim is that culture and shared habits shape a market as much as its formal rules do.

marginal-revolution-and-mru-cowen-and-ta.context_blurb:
George Mason University in Virginia became the home of public-choice economics when James Buchanan and Gordon Tullock moved their center there in 1983. A generation later, two of its economists carried the school's way of reasoning out of the seminar room and onto the internet.

They are Tyler Cowen and Alex Tabarrok. Their blog, Marginal Revolution, at marginalrevolution.com, began in 2003, and they have posted on it every day for more than twenty years, which makes it one of the longest-running economics blogs online.

The tradition they inherited rests on a blunt idea, which Buchanan won the 1986 Nobel Prize for developing. People in government, from legislators to agency staff, follow incentives such as votes, larger budgets and promotions, as people everywhere do; they are not selfless guardians of the common good. That school is called public choice economics.

Taking the idea seriously changes how you read any political decision. A congressman or a judge is no angel once in office, so a politician will often pick whatever helps his or her own career rather than the general good.

In 2012 the pair opened Marginal Revolution University, a free online collection of short video lessons in economics. Its great gift is access: anyone with an internet connection can learn the subject without paying college tuition, and millions have enrolled, many of them home-schooled and high-school students.

Cowen also made an argument of his own. In his 2011 book The Great Stagnation he pointed out that the decades before the 1970s brought life-changing inventions such as electricity, the car, indoor plumbing and the airplane, while far fewer have arrived since. The result, he argued, is that productivity growth slowed, and with it the growth of the whole economy.

In 2015 Cowen launched an interview podcast in which he talks for about an hour with a single guest, from economists and historians to novelists, chess players and chefs. It is called Conversations with Tyler.

Their contribution to the Mason tradition is easy to name. Buchanan and Tullock built the academic structure; Cowen and Tabarrok moved its reasoning online and into the popular conversation about economics, through the blog, the free courses, the podcast and their textbook, Modern Principles of Economics.
