minimum-wage-the-teenager-whose-job-is-p.context_blurb: The minimum wage is a legally mandated floor on hourly wages. Classical and Austrian economists from Frederic Bastiat forward have argued that such a floor eliminates jobs whose market-clearing wage lies below the floor, and that those lost jobs do not appear as fired workers; they appear as workers never hired, which makes them invisible to most observers. Milton Friedman, Thomas Sowell, and Walter Williams returned to this seen-and-unseen framing repeatedly through the postwar decades. A mainstream empirical challenge arrived in 1994 with Card and Krueger's phone-survey study of New Jersey and Pennsylvania fast-food restaurants, which found no measurable job loss. The economists David Neumark and William Wascher responded with longer-run studies based on administrative payroll records that reversed the sign of the effect. More recent episodes in Seattle after its 15-dollar floor produced visible capital-for-labor substitutions.

misess-emigration-vienna-to-geneva-to-ne.context_blurb: Ludwig von Mises left Vienna for Geneva in 1934 and left Europe altogether in July 1940, ahead of the Nazi advance. He and his wife Margit arrived in New York on August 2, 1940. For the next twenty-nine years, through his death in 1973, Mises taught a seminar at New York University that carried a Visiting Professor title but was funded entirely by private donors: the Kansas-City-based William Volker Fund and the New York advertising executive Lawrence Fertig, among others. His 1940 German-language book Nationaloekonomie, published in Geneva as Europe fell into war, went almost unread. His manuscripts were seized by the Nazi occupation of Vienna, shipped to Moscow after the war, and returned to the Mises Institute fifty years later. His 1949 English-language rewrite, Human Action, became the postwar Austrian-tradition anchor text.

ncaa-amateurism-as-cartel-obannon-v-ncaa.context_blurb: For most of the twentieth century American college sports operated under a rule called amateurism: the roughly five hundred thousand athletes at eleven hundred member institutions received scholarships, room and board, and small stipends but no cash compensation above standardized limits. A series of federal court cases in the 2010s and 2020s treated the arrangement as a price-fixing agreement among the nominally competing universities. The 2014 O'Bannon case established an athlete's property right in his own name and likeness. The 2021 unanimous Supreme Court decision in NCAA v. Alston, with a sharply worded concurrence by Justice Brett Kavanaugh, cleared the way for broader athlete compensation. On July 1, 2021 NIL compensation became legal for college athletes. The House v. NCAA settlement in 2024 opened direct revenue-sharing. In the public-choice reading, amateurism is a textbook cartel in which the output-restriction rules collapse once judicial pressure removes the legal and cultural prop.

north-koreas-public-distribution-system-.context_blurb: Between 1993 and 1998 North Korea suffered a famine that killed somewhere between several hundred thousand and three million people. The state's own term for it translates roughly as the Arduous March. The state's rationing system, the Public Distribution System, broke down in the regions farthest from Pyongyang, and ordinary North Koreans survived by trading on informal roadside markets that had been illegal under communist law. Those markets have a specific Korean name. Two major English-language studies by Marcus Noland and Stephan Haggard document the economics of the catastrophe. Two famous defector memoirs by Yeonmi Park and Hyeonseo Lee, both published in 2015, describe the market system from inside. Andrei Lankov at Kookmin University in Seoul is the leading scholarly authority on the modern survival of the market system. In the Austrian tradition the famine is read as the socialist calculation problem in acute form, resolved informally by the spontaneous order Hayek described in 1945.

oskar-morgenstern-from-mises-kreis-to-th.context_blurb: Oskar Morgenstern took his Vienna doctorate under Ludwig von Mises and Hans Mayer in 1925 and became a regular at the Mises Privatseminar. In 1931 he took over direction of the Austrian Institute for Business Cycle Research when Friedrich Hayek left Vienna for the London School of Economics. He accepted a chair at Princeton in 1938, days after the Nazi Anschluss made his continued academic work in Austria impossible. At Princeton he met the Hungarian polymath John von Neumann, and the two of them spent four years, 1940 to 1944, co-authoring a book that founded a new branch of applied mathematics and remains the toolkit of modern economics, political science, and computer science. Morgenstern also wrote on business-cycle forecasting, on the accuracy of economic measurement, and on the reflexive paradox that still carries his name.

physiocrats-and-classical-liberals-basti.context_blurb: Francois Quesnay, physician to Louis XV, led a group of mid-eighteenth-century French thinkers called the Physiocrats. In 1758 he published a diagram of economic circulation, the Tableau economique, that is now treated as the first macroeconomic model. The group's slogan, laissez faire, laissez passer, meaning let it be done, let it pass, became a shorthand for the classical-liberal policy stance of the next century. Anne-Robert-Jacques Turgot briefly served as Louis XV's economic minister in 1774 to 1776 and attempted to implement Physiocratic reforms before noble pressure forced him from office. Jean-Baptiste Say later systematized classical economics for French readers and formulated the proposition the English call Say's Law. The compressed English form of Say's claim was attacked by John Maynard Keynes and defended by the Austrians. A merchant named Le Gendre is reported to have given Jean-Baptiste Colbert the laissez-nous-faire line around 1680.

ppp-loans-2020-the-concentrated-benefit-.context_blurb: In March 2020 Congress passed the CARES Act, the largest single relief bill in American history at the time. One of its programs, the Paycheck Protection Program, lent money through private banks to small businesses that pledged to keep workers on payroll during the pandemic. The loans could later be forgiven. The MIT economist David Autor and coauthors produced the main empirical study, using administrative payroll microdata. Their estimates suggested the program had been very expensive per job actually saved, and that most of the money ultimately flowed to firm owners and shareholders rather than to workers who would otherwise have lost jobs. The Austrian reading, drawing on Hayek's 1945 paper on dispersed knowledge, is that no central agency could tell which firms actually needed emergency relief in April 2020 and which did not. In Bastiat's seen-and-unseen terms the preserved payrolls were visible to anyone who looked; the taxpayer liability for a very large share of the money that funded no additional employment was invisible.

prices-as-knowledge-signals-the-core-aus.context_blurb: Friedrich Hayek's September 1945 paper in the American Economic Review has become the most-cited single text in the Austrian tradition. The paper is an eleven-page argument that the knowledge relevant to economic allocation decisions never exists in concentrated form; it exists only as the dispersed, often tacit knowledge of millions of individual actors, each of whom knows the local circumstances of time and place that no central agency can plausibly collect. Hayek used the real-world example of a specific commodity whose supply chain crossed four continents to illustrate how prices do the coordination work that no planner could do. His phrase for the on-the-spot actor stuck. The paper was Hayek's answer to Oskar Lange's 1936 to 1937 proposal for market socialism, and it extended Mises's 1920 calculation argument into a reframing of what knowledge even is. Thomas Sowell's 1980 book Knowledge and Decisions is the most sustained modern application of the Hayek essay.

public-sector-unions-fdrs-warning-and-wi.context_blurb: Public-sector unions are organizations that bargain collectively on behalf of government employees. Franklin D. Roosevelt publicly opposed the idea during his first term in office. By 2010, public-sector union density had grown to roughly thirty-six percent while private-sector density had fallen to about seven percent. In 2011 Wisconsin Governor Scott Walker signed Act 10, which made government-worker union dues voluntary and required annual recertification votes; weeks of protests at the state capitol followed, and Democratic state senators temporarily walked out to deny quorum. After the law passed, the Wisconsin teachers' union lost most of its members. In 2018 the US Supreme Court's Janus v. AFSCME decision extended the right-to-work principle to public-sector workers nationwide. The large public pension system CalPERS manages roughly four hundred and sixty billion dollars. In the public-choice tradition, drawing on Mancur Olson and George Stigler, the public-sector-union arrangement is read as a case in which the standard adversarial-bargaining assumptions of private-sector labor relations break down because the union helps elect the officials who then bargain with it.

regulatory-capture-case-studies-icc-cab-.context_blurb: In 1971 the Chicago economist George Stigler published a paper arguing that regulatory agencies tend over time to be captured by the industries they are supposed to regulate. His student Sam Peltzman later developed the formal model. The Interstate Commerce Commission, the Civil Aeronautics Board, and the Federal Communications Commission are the classical American examples, but post-2008 financial-crisis reviews extended the diagnosis to banking regulators. The Cornell economist Marver Bernstein had already described a four-stage life cycle of such agencies in a 1955 book. The common thread across these cases is that an agency's original public-interest justification gives way, over decades, to a protective function that favors incumbent firms over new entrants. The deregulation of American aviation in 1978 and of American trucking in 1980 is the historical reversal that the Stigler-Peltzman tradition points to as proof the diagnosis was right.

ron-paul-end-the-fed-and-audit-the-feder.context_blurb: Ron Paul is a Texas obstetrician and Republican congressman who served three stretches in the US House of Representatives between 1976 and 2013. He is the only American politician in the modern era to make Austrian-tradition monetary economics a central public issue. His 2009 book argued the Federal Reserve is unconstitutional, morally objectionable, and economically destructive. He was personally close to Murray Rothbard. His legislation to audit the Fed attracted an extraordinary three hundred and twenty House co-sponsors but was gutted by Senate leadership. In 2003 he had predicted a housing bubble and crash on the floor of the House, in a speech aimed at Alan Greenspan's low-rate policy. The constitutional case he made rested on Article I, Section 8, which assigns to Congress rather than to an independent agency the power to coin money and regulate its value. In the Austrian tradition his career is read as the move that took Fed criticism from a fringe position to a mainstream Republican-primary one.

sarbanes-oxley-2002-the-small-cap-ipos-t.context_blurb: In 2002 Congress passed and President George W. Bush signed a sweeping overhaul of American corporate-accounting rules, named for the chairmen of the two congressional committees that wrote it. The law was a direct response to the Enron collapse of December 2001 and the WorldCom bankruptcy of July 2002. Section 302 made named corporate executives personally responsible for the accuracy of their companies' financial statements. Section 404 required internal-controls attestations with significant annual compliance cost. The visible effect over the next two decades was a steep decline in the number of publicly listed American companies, from more than eight thousand to roughly four thousand three hundred. In the Austrian and Calomiris-Haber traditions the law is read as a regulation whose large fixed compliance cost fell disproportionately on smaller firms, and whose effect on retail investor access to early-stage growth companies has been substantial.

self-custody-and-not-your-keys-not-your-.context_blurb: A Bitcoin private key is a roughly two-hundred-and-fifty-six-bit secret that authorizes spending from a Bitcoin address. In the Austrian and cypherpunk traditions a central lesson of the 2010s and 2020s has been that holding your own private key is categorically different from holding an IOU denominated in Bitcoin at a cryptocurrency exchange. The point was made vividly by Andreas Antonopoulos in his 2014 book Mastering Bitcoin and in his public speaking. The Mt Gox exchange collapse of early 2014 wiped out customers who had left their coins on the exchange. The FTX bankruptcy under Sam Bankman-Fried in November 2022 did the same. In both cases customers who had already withdrawn to self-custody wallets were unaffected. The technical infrastructure for safe self-custody includes hardware wallets, standardized backup phrases, and multi-signature wallets that split the authorizing power across multiple devices or people.

social-security-the-retirement-check-and.context_blurb: Social Security is the American federal retirement program created by the Social Security Act of 1935. The first monthly beneficiary, Ida May Fuller of Vermont, collected roughly twenty-three thousand dollars in benefits over thirty-five years after paying in less than twenty-five dollars. In its early decades there were about forty workers paying in for every retiree drawing out; today the ratio is under three. Milton Friedman criticized the program's rhetorical labeling in Free to Choose: the law describes payroll taxes as contributions and benefits as entitlements, but the Supreme Court's 1960 decision in Flemming v. Nestor confirmed that payroll taxes do not purchase any legal property right and that Congress may change the benefits at will. The 2025 Trustees Report projects that incoming payroll taxes alone will cover roughly eighty-one percent of scheduled benefits once the trust funds are depleted. Chile's 1981 pension privatization and President George W. Bush's unsuccessful 2005 reform attempt both tried different approaches to the same arithmetic.

sowells-late-career-charter-schools-and-.context_blurb: In 2020 Thomas Sowell published a book comparing the test-score performance of charter-school and traditional-public-school students in New York City. His key move was to compare students in the same school buildings or same neighborhoods, so that the usual sociological explanations for test-score gaps did not apply. The specific charter network he studied in most detail, Success Academy, operated dozens of schools in Harlem and the Bronx. The resulting test-score comparison was the load-bearing empirical finding of the book. Sowell applies his trademark compared-to-what question throughout. The public-choice reading he returns to is Olson's: teacher unions are a concentrated, organized interest; charter parents are a diffuse, less-coordinated one, and policy outcomes reflect that asymmetry. In 2023, at age ninety-three, he returned to the broader argument in another short book.

stockholms-twenty-year-apartment-queue.context_blurb: Stockholm has operated a rent-control system since the 1940s. The city's housing bureau, called Bostadsformedlingen in Swedish, runs a strictly first-come-first-served queue for rent-controlled apartments. The rent levels are set below what a market-clearing price would be, so demand massively exceeds supply, and the queue has grown to lengths of twenty years or more for central Stockholm addresses. Some Swedish parents enter their newborns into the queue the day they are born. The Swedish economist Assar Lindbeck, who spent most of his career chairing the Nobel Memorial Prize committee, famously described rent control as, next to aerial bombing, the surest way to destroy a city. An illegal secondary market has grown up in which sitting tenants sublet their controlled apartments at multiples of the controlled rent. In the Austrian and classical-liberal tradition the pattern generalizes: whenever a price does not clear a market, some other allocation mechanism arises to do the job, typically queueing, personal connections, or black markets.

term-limit-resistance-why-incumbents-opp.context_blurb: The American presidency has been limited to two elected terms by the Twenty-Second Amendment, ratified in 1951 after Franklin Roosevelt's four elections. Congressional term limits have polled at roughly three-quarters support for decades but have not been enacted. In 1995 the Supreme Court held in US Term Limits, Inc. v. Thornton that individual states cannot impose term limits on their federal representatives. California's Proposition 140 in 1990 did impose limits on state legislators, and researchers including Einer Elhauge documented a specific shift of power in the post-limit California legislature toward the executive branch, lobbyists, and permanent staff. In the public-choice tradition there is a self-reference problem: the people who would have to vote for term limits are themselves the ones who would be term-limited. Switzerland's rotating-presidency arrangement illustrates the solution of writing the limit into a founding constitution so that no incumbent ever had to vote to shorten his own tenure.

the-1974-nobel-prize-and-the-pretence-of.context_blurb: Friedrich Hayek received the 1974 Nobel Memorial Prize in Economics while on a trip to Salzburg. The cable from Stockholm reached him by surprise. He shared the prize with the Swedish socialist economist Gunnar Myrdal, in a joint citation covering their very different pioneering work on money, business cycles, and the interdependence of economic and institutional phenomena. The prize was awarded in a year of global stagflation that had broken the post-war Keynesian consensus. Hayek's Nobel lecture, delivered in Stockholm in December 1974, is a compressed statement of his critique of macroeconomics. In it he attacked what he called scientism, the posture of treating economics as a measurement discipline capable of guiding policy with the precision of a physical science. The lecture also returns to his central 1945 claim about the dispersed character of economic knowledge. The lecture's closing sentence invokes the free efforts of millions of individuals and warns against the destruction of a civilization no single mind has designed.

the-2020-24-everything-bubble-across-ass.context_blurb: Between March 2020 and the end of 2021 the Federal Reserve ran one of the most aggressive monetary expansions in its history, holding short-term rates at zero and buying trillions of dollars of government bonds. Across that period the US S&P 500 nearly doubled, Bitcoin rose roughly seventeen-fold, residential real estate posted its sharpest year-over-year gains in the Case-Shiller series, meme stocks surged, special-purpose acquisition companies raised record amounts, and non-fungible-token sales reached roughly twenty-five billion dollars. The financial analyst Jesse Felder popularized a particular name for this unusually broad asset-price pattern. In the Austrian tradition the pattern is read as a textbook Cantillon-effect episode: those who receive newly created money first benefit at the expense of those who receive it later. When the Fed started tightening in 2022 and 2023, the most speculative assets corrected hardest.

the-berlin-wall-1961-89-the-calculation-.context_blurb: On the night of August 12 to 13, 1961, the East German government built a barrier through the middle of Berlin to stop the flow of its own citizens into the free West. Walter Ulbricht's regime had watched roughly three and a half million East Germans, close to a fifth of the country's population, leave through Berlin over the preceding twelve years. The barrier was roughly ninety-six miles long. Its fortifications faced inward: the guns, mines, and death-strip were aimed at East Germans trying to escape, not at any invading army. The East German secret police, the Stasi, had the highest surveillance-to-population ratio of any modern state. The Berlin Wall Memorial documents roughly one hundred and forty confirmed deaths at the Wall itself, including the first, Ida Siekmann, who jumped from a fourth-floor apartment in 1961, and the last, Chris Gueffroy, shot in February 1989. The Wall fell on November 9, 1989, and the archive of Stasi files was opened to the public. In the Austrian tradition the exit-as-verdict argument reads: given free comparison across an open border for twelve years, the population had voted with its feet.

the-broken-window-the-shopkeepers-son-an.context_blurb: In July 1850, five months before his death, Frederic Bastiat published a pamphlet called Ce qu'on voit et ce qu'on ne voit pas. Its most famous chapter imagines a shopkeeper whose window has been broken by his careless son. Onlookers console him by observing that a glazier has now been given six francs of work; some glass industry employs the glazier, and so on. Bastiat shows that this consoling story leaves out the alternatives the shopkeeper could have spent his six francs on. The point generalizes. Henry Hazlitt's 1946 book is dedicated to Bastiat and extends the move to twentieth-century American policy. Milton and Rose Friedman's 1980 book and PBS series apply it across public education, welfare, consumer protection, and inflation. A famous modern illustration came in 2009, when running used cars were destroyed to qualify buyers for a new-car rebate.

the-continental-1775-1781-not-worth-a-co.context_blurb: On June 22, 1775 the Continental Congress authorized the first issuance of paper money, called bills of credit or Continentals, to fund the Revolutionary War effort. By the end of the war the paper had hyperinflated. Soldiers who were paid in Continentals watched the money their families held evaporate. The phrase not worth a Continental entered the American idiom. Congress and several state legislatures imposed wage-and-price controls, with meager effect. When the Constitutional Convention met in 1787, Madison, Hamilton, and the other delegates had personally lived through the collapse, and they wrote Article I, Section 10 to forbid any state to issue bills of credit. The French assignat episode a few years later illustrated the same failure mode with the death penalty added on top.

the-endangered-species-act-perverse-ince.context_blurb: President Nixon signed the Endangered Species Act on December 28, 1973. The act gave federal regulators sweeping authority to restrict land use on private property that harbored listed species. In the decades since, land-use scholars have documented a persistent perverse incentive: a rural landowner whose property is a plausible habitat for a listed species has a reason to make the property unsuitable before the species is formally detected there. The best-studied example involves a southeastern US woodpecker and the preemptive harvest of mature pine stands on parcels adjacent to known colonies. Dean Lueck and Jeffrey Michael's 2003 paper and Jonathan Adler's later work in the Boston College Law Review are the central scholarly treatments. Elinor Ostrom's 1990 argument about polycentric governance of common-pool resources points to a very different design, in which local user groups with clearly defined boundaries and shared stake outperform top-down uncompensated federal designations.

the-federal-reserve-act-of-december-23-1.context_blurb: The Federal Reserve System is the central bank of the United States, created by legislation that passed Congress in December 1913 and was signed by President Woodrow Wilson on December 23 of that year, after most members of Congress had already left Washington for the Christmas holidays. The system has twelve regional Reserve Banks. The paper dollars in circulation today are formally Federal Reserve Notes, backed by the Fed's assets rather than by any metal. In its early design the system drew heavily on the Jekyll Island meeting of November 1910 among senior New York bankers and the chair of the Senate's National Monetary Commission. The 1978 Humphrey-Hawkins Full Employment and Balanced Growth Act added the explicit dual-mandate language. The Fed's main day-to-day tool is open-market operations in Treasury securities. In the public-choice reading of its history, the agency illustrates a specific worry about delegating money control to insiders.

the-friedman-hayek-relationship-and-mont.context_blurb: In April 1947 Friedrich Hayek convened a ten-day meeting at the Hotel du Parc in the village of Mont Pelerin above Lake Geneva. The thirty-nine attendees were classical-liberal economists, historians, and philosophers from several countries, including Milton Friedman at age thirty-four. Ninety-three percent of the conference costs were paid by a specific Swiss commercial bank. The group adopted a Statement of Aims warning that the central values of civilization were in danger, naming individual liberty, voluntary cooperation, and private property as the goods under threat. The society Hayek founded that week has met every year since. Hayek himself had moved to the University of Chicago in 1950, not into its economics department but onto its interdisciplinary Committee on Social Thought. His salary there was partly funded by outside grants. His 1974 Nobel lecture returned to the same themes the 1947 meeting had framed.

the-hayek-keynes-exchange-1931-1932.context_blurb: In August 1931 Friedrich Hayek, who had just arrived at the London School of Economics, published the first part of a long critical review of John Maynard Keynes's A Treatise on Money. Keynes replied, Hayek rejoined, and the exchange ran across four issues of the LSE journal Economica into February 1932. The technical substance of the debate ran through capital theory and the Swedish economist Knut Wicksell's natural rate of interest. Keynes attacked Hayek's own 1931 book Prices and Production in equally sharp language. When Keynes published his General Theory in 1936, Hayek chose not to review it, a decision he later explained with reference to Keynes's famous tendency to change his mind. The two men respected each other personally; when LSE evacuated to Cambridge during the Second World War, Keynes helped find Hayek a place at King's College. The 1995 Caldwell-edited volume Contra Keynes and Cambridge collects the whole exchange.

the-liberty-fund-collected-works-bastiat.context_blurb: In 1946 Leonard Read founded the Foundation for Economic Education in Irvington-on-Hudson, New York, with Henry Hazlitt on the founding board. FEE predates the Cato Institute, the Mises Institute, and the Reason Foundation. Decades later the Indianapolis-based Liberty Fund undertook the first comprehensive scholarly English edition of the collected works of Frederic Bastiat, a six-volume project under the editorial direction of David Hart with general editors Jacques de Guenin and Jean-Claude Paul-Dejean. The Liberty Fund edition added scholarly apparatus the earlier FEE translations lacked, including introductions placing each essay in 1840s French political context, glossaries of French figures, and modern translations. The Online Library of Liberty makes every page available free.

the-modern-democratic-socialist-revival-.context_blurb: Senator Bernie Sanders of Vermont ran for the Democratic presidential nomination in 2016 and 2020, self-identifying as a democratic socialist. The Democratic Socialists of America grew roughly fifteen-fold in membership between 2014 and 2021. The movement's main policy proposals, including Medicare for All, large minimum-wage increases, rent control in high-demand cities, and government-negotiated pharmaceutical prices, drew sharp attention from the Austrian and classical-liberal traditions. The careful classical-liberal response is to name the argument an Austrian critic would press on each policy. For a minimum wage, that is Bastiat's seen-and-unseen move applied to the worker priced out of the market. For rent control it is the knowledge-problem and supply-response mechanism. For government pharmaceutical prices it is a Mises-1920 argument about the informational role of prices.

the-panic-of-1907-and-j-p-morgans-privat.context_blurb: In October 1907 a classic financial panic broke out on Wall Street. A failed attempt by the Heinze brothers to corner the stock of a copper company triggered a run on the Knickerbocker Trust Company, the third-largest trust in New York. There was no central bank. The private banker J.P. Morgan assembled the presidents of the largest New York banks in his personal library on Madison Avenue and raised roughly twenty-five million dollars in fifteen minutes to keep the New York Stock Exchange open. He personally decided which banks were worth rescuing and which were not. The episode made obvious to every observer that the United States lacked a lender of last resort. Senator Nelson Aldrich chaired a congressional commission that studied European central banking, produced the Aldrich Plan of 1911, and set up the structure that became the Federal Reserve Act of 1913. In the Charles Kindleberger reading, this is the last time an individual private banker performed in a major crisis the function that permanent central banks now provide.

the-powell-2024-pivot-and-the-second-inf.context_blurb: On September 18, 2024, the Federal Reserve cut its target interest rate by half a percentage point, an unusually large opening move compared with the traditional quarter-point starting cut. Jerome Powell's framing at the preceding Jackson Hole symposium had already signaled the shift. The committee framed the cut as a preemptive response to labor-market cooling, hoping to produce what economists call a soft landing: inflation falling to target without a recession. Inside the Fed and in commentary around it, the memory of Arthur Burns in the early 1970s, who cut rates too soon after the first inflation wave of that decade and set up a second wave Paul Volcker had to crush with twenty-percent rates in 1981, is persistent.

the-salamanca-school-16th-century-spanis.context_blurb: In the sixteenth century a group of Dominican and Jesuit theologians at the University of Salamanca in Spain wrote on price, money, labor, and just conduct in the context of the Spanish empire and the enormous flow of silver into Iberian markets from the newly colonized Americas. Francisco de Vitoria led the faculty during the crucial 1530s and 1540s. Martin de Azpilcueta, also called Doctor Navarrus, wrote a 1556 confessor's manual that contains the earliest clean statement of the quantity theory of money. The Jesuit Luis de Molina argued in De Iustitia et Iure (1593 to 1609) that the just price is what willing buyers and willing sellers would agree to in a normally functioning market, an early subjective-value move. Milton Friedman's famous dictum that inflation is always and everywhere a monetary phenomenon restated what Azpilcueta had seen four centuries earlier. Murray Rothbard's An Austrian Perspective on the History of Economic Thought argued the classical story that starts with Adam Smith in 1776 has overwritten the Salamanca contribution.

the-sowell-trilogy-on-the-intellectuals.context_blurb: Thomas Sowell has written three books that together form a sustained attack on what he calls the vision of the anointed: the 1995 book of that title, the 1999 Quest for Cosmic Justice, and the 2010 Intellectuals and Society. The core move is to identify a specific pattern in which a social problem is declared a crisis, a remedy is adopted, the remedy fails or makes things worse, and the remedy's champions respond by calling the critics simplistic and demanding proof of cause. In Sowell's reading, nothing in the professional incentives of an intellectual punishes a prediction that turns out false, because the work ends in ideas rather than in something the physical world can test. The underlying intellectual move is Hayek's knowledge problem carried into the moral realm: redressing disadvantage across groups, generations, and geographies would require knowledge no central body plausibly has.

the-universal-reach-bastiat-as-economics.context_blurb: Frederic Bastiat farmed at Mugron in southwestern France for most of his adult life and spent only his final five productive years as a public writer, publishing his most important essays between 1844 and 1850. His method is a four-part discipline: write in plain prose aimed at a general reader, start with a concrete scene, state the opponent's view in its strongest form, and then trace the unseen consequences of the proposed action past the first visible effect. Henry Hazlitt's 1946 Economics in One Lesson is a chapter-by-chapter application of the method to mid-twentieth-century American policy. Thomas Sowell's 1980 Knowledge and Decisions is the most sustained modern application of the broader classical-liberal knowledge-and-decision framework to policy questions. For other parts of the Austrian tradition a reader will need Carl Menger, Ludwig von Mises, Friedrich Hayek, Eugen von Bohm-Bawerk, James Buchanan, and Gordon Tullock.

the-vienna-university-economics-traditio.context_blurb: Carl Menger took the chair of economics in the Faculty of Law and Political Economy at the University of Vienna in 1873 and held it for thirty years. His student Eugen von Bohm-Bawerk held a parallel chair from 1904 until his death in 1914. In Bohm-Bawerk's famous 1905 to 1914 seminar sat the future greatest Austrian liberal (Ludwig von Mises), the future Austro-Marxist Finance Minister of Weimar Germany (Rudolf Hilferding), and the future Austrian Social Democratic foreign minister (Otto Bauer), all together. The Vienna chair itself passed in 1922 to Hans Mayer, who held it until the 1938 Anschluss with Nazi Germany ended the Vienna phase of the tradition. Mises had already left for Geneva in 1934 and would leave for New York in 1940. In the standard Austrian story the tradition's institutional center then moved to London, then to Chicago and New York, and eventually to George Mason University in Virginia.

transitory-powells-2021-miscall-and-retr.context_blurb: Through most of 2021 the Federal Reserve chair Jerome Powell and Treasury Secretary Janet Yellen described the rising US inflation rate as transitory, meaning it reflected pandemic-era supply-chain disruptions that would resolve on their own. By November 2021 Powell retired the word; by June 2022 the consumer price index was up roughly nine percent year over year, the highest reading since 1981. Larry Summers, writing from inside the Democratic economic-policy establishment, had warned in a February 2021 Washington Post column that the size of the Biden administration's fiscal package created substantial inflation risk, and the monetarist and Austrian traditions had made the stronger version of the same argument about the preceding years of quantitative easing. In the Austrian reading the transitory episode is a case study in institutional motivated reasoning: the Fed had run enormous monetary expansion and preferred an explanation that did not implicate its own actions. The Judy Shelton nomination episode is a related case.

venezuela-2013-present-the-modern-social.context_blurb: Hugo Chavez ruled Venezuela from 1999 to 2013 and built an economic system his successor Nicolas Maduro inherited. The system combined large-scale price controls, nationalizations of key industries, and heavy use of the central bank. By the 2010s shelves had emptied, hyperinflation had set in, and roughly a quarter of the country's population, some seven million seven hundred thousand people, had left. The International Monetary Fund estimated annual inflation at roughly one hundred and thirty thousand percent in 2018. Caracas bodegas quietly repriced goods in US dollars; salaries were paid via smartphone transfers from relatives in Miami. In the Austrian tradition the Venezuelan collapse is read as an acute, real-time, smartphone-video illustration of Ludwig von Mises's 1920 argument that without market prices for capital goods, central planners have no way to know whether a proposed use of resources creates or destroys value.

walter-durantys-pulitzer-and-gareth-jone.context_blurb: Walter Duranty was the New York Times Moscow correspondent from 1922 to 1936. He won the 1932 Pulitzer Prize for Correspondence. During the 1932 to 1933 Soviet-engineered famine in Ukraine, in which several million people died, Duranty's reporting played down the catastrophe and framed it with the memorable euphemism that there was no actual starvation but widespread mortality from diseases due to malnutrition. The Welsh journalist Gareth Jones, former private secretary to David Lloyd George, walked through Ukraine in March 1933 and published a very different account at a Berlin press conference. Jones was shot in Inner Mongolia in 1935, one day before his thirtieth birthday. Malcolm Muggeridge filed similar accounts from Ukraine in the Manchester Guardian. The Pulitzer Board reviewed Duranty's prize in 2003 and declined to withdraw it, even as the New York Times itself called his reporting some of the worst to appear in the paper. In the Austrian and classical-liberal traditions this is a canonical case of a famine engineered by a government and its coverage protected by a prestige press.

why-gold-the-convergent-monetary-propert.context_blurb: People in independent cultures across history have converged on gold and silver as money. The Austrian and Bitcoin-standard traditions argue that this convergence reflects specific physical properties of the metals rather than cultural accident. The classic property list runs through durability, portability, divisibility, fungibility, recognizability, and scarcity. Gold scores well on all six: it does not corrode, essentially all the gold ever mined is still around, it can be bitten or density-tested quickly, and its stock-to-flow ratio is among the highest of any physical commodity. Diamonds fail divisibility. Cowrie shells fail scarcity once imported in bulk. Saifedean Ammous's The Bitcoin Standard is the most widely cited Austrian-tradition argument that Bitcoin extends gold's monetary role by matching its best properties and beating it on portability, divisibility, and verifiability.

youre-right-we-did-it-bernankes-friedman.context_blurb: At a November 2002 University of Chicago conference marking Milton Friedman's ninetieth birthday, the Federal Reserve governor Ben Bernanke delivered a remarkable public concession on behalf of the central bank. Friedman and Anna Schwartz's 1963 book A Monetary History of the United States had argued that the Fed had caused the Great Depression by allowing the money supply to contract about a third between 1930 and 1933 through its failure to act as lender of last resort during cascading bank failures. Bernanke, speaking as a Fed representative, apologized directly to the ninety-year-old Friedman and promised the central bank would not repeat the mistake. Six years later Bernanke was Fed chairman when the 2008 financial crisis broke, and his crisis response leaned heavily on the Friedman-Schwartz lesson. In the Austrian reading, Bernanke avoided the 1930s mistake and may have made an opposite one. Anna Schwartz herself sharply criticized Bernanke's response in a 2008 Wall Street Journal interview.

a-conflict-of-visions-1987-constrained-v.context_blurb:
Thomas Sowell, an American economist, set out in 1987 to explain a puzzle every newspaper reader knows: why do intelligent, well-informed people keep reaching opposite conclusions about the same policies? His book A Conflict of Visions argued that the quarrel starts before any facts are weighed, in each side's picture of what human beings are. It became one of his most-cited works.

Picture two friends arguing about a city's traffic. One wants clever experts put in charge to plan it properly. The other is skeptical: he doubts that any handful of planners could hold the knowledge of every driver, every street and every day's surprises. Sowell traced quarrels like that to rival views of human nature. Some people believe that the right rules and enough schooling could make us very nearly perfect; others believe we carry permanent limits, such as selfishness, ignorance and weakness, that no rulebook will ever erase. Sowell called these pictures visions because they come before any argument, shaping which policies feel obviously right and which feel obviously naive.

He named the two pictures with one pair of words: the constrained vision and the unconstrained vision. The constrained vision sees human nature as having real limits that we must work around. Knowledge is scattered among millions of people, self-interest never goes away, and good rules grow slowly through trial and error. In this vision, which runs through Adam Smith, Edmund Burke, the American Federalists and Friedrich Hayek, politics means designing rules that channel imperfect people, not finding the wise and handing them power.

The opposite picture, the unconstrained vision, holds that human nature is flexible and can be improved by new and better institutions. Sowell traced it through William Godwin, the French revolutionaries, John Kenneth Galbraith and John Rawls; in it, politics means identifying those who see correctly and empowering them to act. Sowell's own most-quoted line sums up the constrained side: in his telling there are no solutions at all, there are only trade-offs, so every choice gives up one good to gain another. He paired it with a two-word challenge, "Compared to what?" Any policy must be judged against the real options on the table, not against a dream, so a critic who calls a policy bad has to name the actual alternative he prefers.

Sowell spent the next twelve years building the idea into a trilogy. The second volume, The Vision of the Anointed (1995), held the unconstrained vision up against modern American social policy and diagnosed what happens when self-congratulation becomes a basis for policy. The third, The Quest for Cosmic Justice (1999), followed the same hope to its utopian end: the dream of remaking every outcome to match a picture of ultimate fairness.

What the first book holds back is as striking as what it says. Sowell lays out each vision at its strongest, follows both through named thinkers and applies them to real policy fights, and then deliberately declines to declare which vision is right. His aim was to teach readers to recognize which vision is speaking. That restraint explains why economists and activists so often seem deaf to each other on the very same issue, even when neither side is short of facts. Each side is reasoning from a different picture of what human beings essentially are. To one, talk of trade-offs sounds like a failure of will; to the other, talk of solutions sounds like naive utopianism.

americas-great-depression-1963-the-austr.context_blurb:
Murray Rothbard was a New York economist of the Austrian school, the tradition of Ludwig von Mises. In 1963, at thirty-seven, he published America's Great Depression, a 361-page reexamination of the worst slump in American history. Where most accounts blamed the free market and the crash of 1929, Rothbard pointed at Washington instead: at the central bank and at the White House.

Between 1929 and 1933 thousands of American banks failed and nearly a quarter of workers lost their jobs. Rothbard named two culprits, the Federal Reserve and President Herbert Hoover. The Fed's cheap credit through the 1920s built a boom that was bound to bust, and Hoover's activism after October 1929 turned what should have been a short cleanup into a decade-long depression.

For the boom Rothbard blamed one man above all: Benjamin Strong, governor of the New York Fed and the dominant force in the system. After Britain returned to gold in 1925 at its old prewar rate, Strong worked hand in glove with Montagu Norman of the Bank of England and kept American credit loose, partly to help Britain hold on to its gold. For the long bust he blamed Hoover. Weeks after the crash, in November 1929, Hoover summoned great industrialists such as Henry Ford and Pierre du Pont to the White House and pressed them to promise not to cut wage rates. Rothbard argued that this high-wage policy blocked the very adjustment that had ended earlier American depressions in eighteen months or less.

Austrian writers point to a natural experiment, the forgotten depression of 1920 and 1921. That slump was savage, with unemployment near 12 percent and output down about a sixth, yet Warren Harding's government slashed federal spending and allowed wages and prices to drop. Within about a year and a half prices had reset and the recession was over. Hoover chose the opposite path. In June 1930 he signed the Smoot-Hawley Tariff, heavy duties on nearly every import. Trading partners answered with big tariffs of their own on American goods, world trade shrank further, and the American slump spread abroad. In January 1932 Hoover founded the Reconstruction Finance Corporation, which lent more than a billion dollars in six months to failing banks and railroads. The long-run danger of such rescues is that firms come to expect a loan whenever they stumble, and so they take bigger risks in the future. Franklin Roosevelt kept the agency and enlarged it.

This record overturns the schoolbook picture of Hoover sitting idle until Roosevelt arrived. Rothbard, and later Amity Shlaes in her 2007 book The Forgotten Man, found that Hoover himself had run large spending and price-support programs; Rothbard even called him the founder of the New Deal. His deeper move came from Austrian Business Cycle Theory. Credit made artificially cheap lures savings into projects that only look profitable while rates are held down, and when rates return to normal those projects stand revealed as malinvestment. On this reading the 1929 crash was not the disease but the correction, the unavoidable liquidation of errors the Fed had planted in the 1920s. The book was a companion to Rothbard's great treatise of 1962, Man, Economy, and State, a full textbook of Austrian economics; America's Great Depression applied its framework to a single historical case.

That same year Milton Friedman and Anna Schwartz published their Monetary History, which also blamed the Fed, but for shrinking the money supply by about a third once the crash had come. Rothbard faulted the Fed for the opposite error, committed across the whole decade before: expanding credit through the 1920s to prop up Britain's return to gold, and so seeding the malinvestment that had to bust. One account explains the contraction after the crash; the other explains the boom that came before it.

anti-price-gouging-laws-michael-munger-j.context_blurb:
In 2005 Hurricane Katrina tore across the Gulf Coast and left thousands of Mississippi homes without electricity. John Shepperson, a Kentuckian, saw a chance to help and to earn something: he bought nineteen generators, rented a truck and drove them about 600 miles south. The Duke University economist Michael Munger made what happened next the classic case against laws that punish price gouging.

Picture a town without power: refrigerators warm up, food spoils, hospitals go dark. Shepperson planned to sell his generators at roughly double what he had paid. That price is what made the long drive worth his while, and so it gave the town generators it otherwise would never have had. But Mississippi's anti-gouging statute forbade selling necessities far above their normal price. When Shepperson arrived, police arrested him, seized all nineteen generators and held him in jail for four days, while the machines sat unused in police custody and families stayed in the dark.

Economists see a hidden cost in every arrest like that. Imagine a man who spends sixteen hours driving a truck full of ice into a storm zone and charges triple to cover his fuel, his time and his risk. Arrest him, and the next time disaster strikes, fewer people bring in emergency supplies, because the trip no longer pays. Munger told Shepperson's story in a 2007 essay for Cato Unbound, using the language of Friedrich Hayek's 1945 article The Use of Knowledge in Society, which argued that prices carry knowledge no planner could ever gather.

Seen through Hayek's eyes, the high Mississippi price was a message telling a man hundreds of miles away that generators were desperately needed there. By answering it, Shepperson moved scarce capital from a low-value use at home to a high-value use in the storm zone, and Mississippi's law cut the signal that made the move possible. Munger reframed the moral argument. People on the ground, he said, never get to choose between fair and unfair prices; their real choice lies between expensive supply that arrives and cheap supply that does not exist. The 1970s showed the same mess on a national scale. Federal price caps set under Nixon and kept under Carter held gasoline below the level where supply and demand would meet, and the shortage appeared as long lines at filling stations across the country.

When Hurricane Katrina drowned New Orleans in August 2005, the Federal Emergency Management Agency moved slowly, while Walmart trucks were delivering bottled water, food and diapers across Louisiana in a matter of days, often ahead of the official convoys, as the economists Sobel and Leeson documented. The difference lay in who could decide: Walmart's local managers had authority to act without waiting for orders from headquarters, and they knew what their own towns needed. Venezuela ran the opposite experiment for years. After Hugo Chávez died in 2013, Nicolás Maduro widened controls on basics such as milk, bread and medicine, capping prices far below what they cost to produce, and the result was chronic, severe shortages, empty shelves and mass emigration.

One lesson runs through every case. Where knowledge is scattered among many people, prices are what coordinate them, and a rule that cuts the price signal makes that coordination disappear. The seen result is that nobody was gouged; the unseen cost is thousands of people left in the dark for weeks.

austrian-business-cycle-theory-abct.context_blurb:
Why do economies boom for years and then crash? Austrian business cycle theory, or ABCT, is the answer worked out in Vienna by Friedrich Hayek and the older Ludwig von Mises. It treats the boom-bust cycle as a monetary event with an institutional cause: a central bank holding interest rates where they do not belong.

In 1936 Keynes traced the swings to changing moods, the lurch from hope to fear. Mises and Hayek blamed one policy tool used badly: interest rates pushed artificially low by a central bank. Mises first set out the idea in his 1912 book The Theory of Money and Credit. Hayek built on it in the 1920s and 1930s, with Monetary Theory and the Trade Cycle in 1929 and Prices and Production in 1931; the second made him world-famous at thirty-two and launched his great debate with Keynes.

Through the 1920s the two men warned that credit held cheap for an extended stretch would breed a boom of bad investments bound to collapse, and when the Great Depression followed the crash of 1929, their admirers saw Austrian Business Cycle Theory vindicated. Mises acted on his warning. In 1929 he turned down a top post at Austria's great bank, the Kreditanstalt, telling his fiancée that a great crash was coming; in May 1931 the bank failed and set off Europe's banking crisis. That forecast came straight from his own Austrian business cycle theory.

Here is the mechanism. A developer offered loans at 1 percent launches a housing development that will take fifteen years to finish, and builders in every long-lived industry do the same. When rates climb back to 4 percent, many of those projects stop making sense, and some are abandoned half-built. Austrians call such projects malinvestments: not foolish bets, but projects that would have been sound if the interest-rate signal had told the truth. The theory met a modern test when Alan Greenspan's Fed cut its key rate from 6.5 percent at the end of 2000 to 1 percent by the middle of 2003 and held it there for a year. Austrian analysts singled out housing, above all residential real estate, as the main sink for the malinvestment, because homes are bought with long mortgages and so respond to long-term rates more than any other big market.

Peter Schiff, an investment adviser who learned his Austrian economics from his father, Irwin, warned again and again on business television that a housing crash was coming, and studio guests often laughed at him. Arguing on Fox News on New Year's Eve 2006, he predicted that American real-estate prices would come crashing back to earth in 2007, and the crash arrived in 2007 and 2008. Rothbard read the 1920s the same way: the Fed under Benjamin Strong held rates artificially low, partly to help Britain back onto gold. In the Austrian account, cheap central-bank credit always fuels a boom that ends in a crash once the bad bets are exposed.

The policy conclusion follows. Suppose a lending boom leaves a town full of empty office towers that no buyer will take at boom prices. If the government buys them at those prices, the correction stretches out, since failed projects are propped up rather than cleared away. Clearing them frees capital and workers for uses people truly want, and Rothbard argued that the interventions of Hoover and Roosevelt prolonged the very depression they were meant to cure.

The yardstick behind it all comes from the Swedish economist Knut Wicksell. In a market where no central bank meddles, rates would settle where the saving people want to do matches the borrowing businesses want for real projects, and economists call that level the natural rate. Push the bank rate below it, and credit outruns real saving. Keynes's rival account, in his 1936 General Theory, made the driver psychological instead: spontaneous urges to act, swinging between confidence and panic, which he named animal spirits. For Keynes the cycle was psychological; for the Austrians it was monetary, with a specific cause and a specific cure.

bastiat-vs-proudhon-the-1849-50-debate-o.context_blurb:
Over the winter of 1849 and 1850, two Frenchmen fought a duel in print over one question: may a lender rightly ask for interest? One was Frédéric Bastiat, the free-trade economist. The other was Pierre-Joseph Proudhon, the socialist who had become the first thinker to call himself an anarchist. Their letters became the first popular statement of a theory the Austrian school would later make its own.

Proudhon had been famous since 1840, when he published a book asking what property is and answered in three words: property is theft. He meant property that draws rent or interest without labor, not a workman's tools, a distinction later socialists often blurred. At the end of January 1849 he opened the Bank of the People in Paris, which was to lend to workers without interest, paying in notes that members swapped for goods; when Proudhon was jailed, the bank was shut down. The debate ran almost entirely in Proudhon's own Paris daily, La Voix du Peuple, which he kept editing from his cell in Sainte-Pélagie prison, so Bastiat argued in front of Proudhon's readers.

Bastiat's case did not rest on lenders deserving a reward. Interest, he argued, is a price, the price of the lender's going without the use of his money for the term of the loan. On a loan of a thousand francs for a year, the interest pays for that year of doing without; a century later Austrian economists would call this time preference. He then pressed a consequence Proudhon would not accept. Force interest to zero by law, and savers simply stop lending and keep their cash, so savings no longer flow into loans and there is nothing left to borrow. Proudhon replied that he needed no force at all. Let mutual banks owned by their members multiply and compete freely for borrowers, he claimed, and competition among such lenders would drive the rate down to zero by itself. Bastiat answered that competition can push interest down only as far as the value people place on time, and no further.

In 1850 Bastiat gathered the exchange into a book from the Guillaumin house in Paris and gave it an ironic title borrowed from Proudhon's own slogan for free lending: Gratuité du crédit. The two editions do not match. Bastiat's runs to fourteen letters, opening with one by Proudhon's disciple Chevé and closing with a final reply from Bastiat that Proudhon refused to answer. Proudhon's rival edition, Intérêt et principal, simply left out Bastiat's closing letter and so contains thirteen.

The idea was set out in full, formal dress in Austria. Eugen von Böhm-Bawerk's Capital and Interest, Kapital und Kapitalzins in German, appeared in parts from 1884 onward, and he counted Bastiat among the theory's forerunners. Then in 1949 Ludwig von Mises, a Viennese exile teaching in New York, brought the argument to English readers at the heart of a thousand-page treatise, Human Action. The book presents time preference as a basic feature of all human choosing, present in anyone's weighing of today against tomorrow, and no mere quirk of capitalism.

bitcoin-as-fifth-amendment-money-the-mem.context_blurb:
Every bitcoin is controlled by a secret number so long that nobody could memorize it or copy it by hand without mistakes. In 2013 a handful of developers, among them Marek Palatinus and Pavol Rusnak, published a free open standard, BIP-39, that turns the number into a short list of ordinary words. The result is a kind of wealth no earlier age could have imagined: money you can carry in your head.

Nearly every wallet today turns its secret into a seed phrase, a sequence of twelve or twenty-four common English words that can be written on paper and locked away, and from which every key in the wallet can be rebuilt. The words all come from one fixed dictionary of exactly 2,048 English words, used alike by hardware makers such as Ledger and Trezor and by countless phone wallets, so a backup made by one wallet can be read by any other.

That makes a strange journey possible. Cross a border with no wallet, no paper and no phone, only the words in your memory, and customs officers can find nothing at all, because no search can read what is inside your head. Yet on the far side, any internet-connected computer can rebuild the wallet from those words, and the coins can move again.

The law has had to catch up. Police can seize a phrase written on paper, but when it exists only in memory, American defense lawyers argue that the state cannot force a person to say it aloud, and they cite the Fifth Amendment, which shields every person from being forced to bear witness against himself. Courts have split over phone and laptop passwords. Some judges refuse to compel a suspect to unlock a device; others order it under the foregone-conclusion doctrine, which holds that when the state already knows the material exists, where it is and that it is genuine, unlocking it reveals nothing new.

Because the standard was published free, for anyone to use without permission or fees, so many wallet makers adopted it that a user can move his funds between wallet brands without ever losing access. So if the company behind a hardware wallet shuts down for good, its owners need not panic. They simply restore their phrase into any other wallet that follows the same open standard, since no company's server ever held their coins.

Every earlier money sat somewhere physical, whether as metal in a pouch or a strongroom or as a number in a banker's books. A memorized phrase lets savings live inside the owner's own memory, with no physical or digital trace anywhere outside his head. That answers a specific threat. Gold sets off scanners, cash draws currency-sniffing dogs, and a bank balance can be frozen from a distant office, but a memorized phrase offers none of them a target: it blocks seizure by physical search, by currency detection and by remote freezing of accounts.

brics-and-the-dollar-alternative-movemen.context_blurb:
In 2001 Jim O'Neill, a British economist at the bank Goldman Sachs, coined a catchy label for four big emerging economies: Brazil, Russia, India and China, the BRICs. What began as an investment idea became a political bloc that now talks openly of trading without the US dollar. Austrian economists read its rise less as a story about rivals than as a story about the choices of the dollar's own issuer.

O'Neill picked the four because they had huge populations and plenty of room to catch up with richer countries, so their economies looked set to grow fast for twenty years. In 2009 the four began meeting as a formal group, and when South Africa joined in 2010 the forum became BRICS, a rival club to the older G7. On January 1, 2024, the bloc took in Egypt, Ethiopia, Iran and the United Arab Emirates. Its members want trade channels of their own for a plain reason: they fear the United States could freeze their dollar reserves if it disagrees with them.

The fear had a precedent. When Russian troops crossed into Ukraine at the end of February 2022, Washington, the European Union, Britain and Japan froze roughly 300 billion dollars of Russian central-bank reserves held in Western banks, the largest such action in modern history, and every reserve holder outside the West took note. Russia and China moved fast. Their trade with each other now settles overwhelmingly in rubles and yuan, over 90 percent by Chinese customs figures, up from a small fraction before 2022, and India began paying for Russian oil in rupees and UAE dirhams.

The dollar's grip is loosening only slowly. Its share of central banks' reserves fell from 71 percent in 2000 to about 58 percent by 2024, yet no rival has caught up, and nearly nine in ten currency trades still involve a dollar. Valéry Giscard d'Estaing, France's finance minister in the 1960s, coined the famous name for that special position: the exorbitant privilege, the advantage of a country that can pay its bills in money it issues itself.

Debt is the other half of the story. The federal government of the United States now owes more than 34 trillion dollars, about as much as everything the nation produces in a year or more. Ludwig von Mises warned where such a road can end. When a government that cannot tax enough to carry its debts inflates instead, people at last see that the inflation will never stop and stampede out of money into real goods until the currency collapses; Mises called that final stage the crack-up boom. Central bankers have answered with the one neutral reserve that no government controls. Their gold purchases hit a fifty-five-year high of about 1,082 tonnes in 2022 and stayed above 1,000 tonnes in each of the next two years.

Analysts in the Austrian camp, among them Luke Gromen, Lyn Alden and Saifedean Ammous, read the gold buying and the debt together: a slow shift toward neutral assets is under way, but the dollar is not about to be replaced. Historians of fallen trading currencies, from the Venetian ducat and the Spanish dollar to the Dutch guilder and the British pound, see a pattern. Rivals lurk for decades, and what finally tips the balance is the issuing country's own conduct, overspending or seizing other nations' savings. In that reading, the BRICS story is less about the yuan or the rupee than about the choices Washington made.

buchanans-constitutional-political-econo.context_blurb:
James Buchanan, who won a Nobel for founding public choice, made one move that set his work apart: he split political argument into two levels. At the lower level, people fight over particular outcomes under the rules that already exist. At the higher level, they choose the rules themselves, and Buchanan believed most policy debates go wrong by mixing the two.

Picture children quarreling every recess over who gets the ball, when they could settle once and for all the rule for who gets it each day. Buchanan built a whole field on that second kind of choice and called it constitutional political economy, which examines the rulebook itself rather than each decision made under it. Haggling over whether a tax should be 20 or 25 percent makes each new law a fresh brawl that draws lobbyists and favor-seekers every time. Buchanan wanted the argument lifted one step, to the rules that govern how policy gets made, such as whether any tax increase should need a supermajority, because a rule binds majority and minority alike in a way no single policy fight can.

In 1985, the year before his Nobel, Buchanan and the Australian philosopher-economist Geoffrey Brennan published The Reason of Rules, the standard modern statement of why firm rules, rather than officials' goodwill, must bind government. Its key device asks people to pick the political rulebook as if they had no idea whether fortune would make them wealthy or poor, mighty or humble, so that the rules stay fair to whoever lands where. Buchanan and Brennan called this the veil of uncertainty, a cousin of John Rawls's veil of ignorance. The same book explained why a fixed rule, like a posted speed limit, beats letting officials judge case by case: fixed rules limit favoritism and let ordinary citizens plan their lives ahead, while wide discretion invites the abuse of power.

In 1977 Buchanan and Richard Wagner published Democracy in Deficit: The Political Legacy of Lord Keynes. They argued that for well over a century an unwritten constitutional norm of balanced budgets had disciplined American politicians. Once Keynes's teaching licensed deliberate deficit spending, that norm dissolved and deficits ratcheted upward ever after. For Buchanan the trouble was never this or that deficit; it was the loss of the rule that had restrained everyone.

The whole tradition grew from a 1962 book by Buchanan and Gordon Tullock, The Calculus of Consent, the founding text of public choice. It brought the economist's way of reasoning to bear on how constitutions are built, and it showed why bare majority rule cannot by itself protect a minority.

The move is easiest to see on a playground. Before the kickball teams are chosen, the whole class settles how score will be kept; once the teams exist, each side knows which rules help it. Judging a rule from the moment before you know your team moves the argument from picking winners to picking fair rules: from asking whether a policy is good to asking whether we would have agreed to the rules that produced it.

cash-for-clunkers-2009-690-000-used-cars.context_blurb:
In the summer of 2009, with new-car sales crushed by the financial crisis, Washington launched a scheme officially named the Car Allowance Rebate System. Buyers who traded in a running older car got a rebate toward a new, more fuel-efficient one, and the old car was destroyed. To economists in Bastiat's tradition it is a modern worked example of his oldest parable.

President Barack Obama signed the program into law in June 2009, with rebates of $3,500 to $4,500. So that no trade-in could ever be resold, the rules spelled out its fate: the dealer poured sodium silicate, a kind of liquid glass, into the oil to seize the engine, and then the car was crushed. Everyone knew the program by its catchy nickname, Cash for Clunkers, and it burned through its $3 billion in about two months.

The program matches the most famous parable in Bastiat's 1850 essay, the broken window: destroying a usable good does not create wealth, however busy the glazier's shop, or the car dealer's, may look. Some 690,000 running cars were destroyed, most of them in the cheap price range where low-income families and students shop. As Austrian economists predicted, the price of used cars climbed roughly 10 percent in the following year, according to the Manheim index of used-vehicle values.

In 2013 Ted Gayer and Emily Parker of the Brookings Institution found that most of the program's new-car sales were purchases buyers would have made in the next six to nine months regardless. People had just bought sooner to catch the rebate, an effect the two economists called pulled-forward sales. They also found no lasting gain in jobs, and carbon savings that cost far more per ton than official estimates of the harm carbon does. The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration, part of the Department of Transportation, wrote the program's rules and certified each car's destruction.

The seen benefit was obvious: a new car in a buyer's driveway. The unseen victims, critics from the Austrian and Chicago schools pointed out, were poor households who buy in the used-car market, which the destruction had thinned out, since they now found fewer cheap running cars, at higher prices.

Critics found the whole argument laid out long before, in 1946, by Henry Hazlitt, a financial journalist who wrote for the New York Times and later Newsweek, whose book Economics in One Lesson applied Bastiat's seen and unseen to make-work projects. Beyond the wrecked cars and the priced-out buyers lay a larger loss. Every one of those $3 billion had to come from a taxpayer or a lender, and the alternative goods and jobs that money could have supported, had it stayed with them, are the program's biggest unseen cost.

coase-1937-the-nature-of-the-firm.context_blurb:
In 1937 Ronald Coase, a twenty-six-year-old British economist at the London School of Economics, asked a question most of his profession had never thought to ask. If prices coordinate markets so well, why does so much economic life happen inside companies, where managers give orders instead? His answer launched a whole field and, more than half a century later, won him the 1991 Nobel prize.

He published the paper in the journal Economica under a plain title, The Nature of the Firm. The idea had begun years earlier on a traveling scholarship in 1931 and 1932, when Coase, still an undergraduate, toured America's great integrated companies to learn why so many tasks were handled within single firms. In Detroit he visited Ford, the giant carmaker of the day.

His answer was that using the market is not free. Finding partners, haggling, writing contracts and checking the work all cost time and money, so a carmaker keeps salaried workers rather than hiring someone new for each bolt tightened or letter typed: using the market for every tiny task carries its own hidden costs. The same costs set a company's size. A firm keeps bringing jobs in-house, such as cleaning, accounting or deliveries, until doing one more inside costs the same as buying it from an outsider, and there it stops growing.

Economists later built a whole subfield on that insight and named it after the quantity at its center: transaction cost economics. Oliver Williamson extended it into a study of markets and hierarchies and shared the 2009 Nobel. The burdens themselves, finding the right supplier, signing a contract, watching the work and going to court when things go wrong, are what economists call transaction costs.

Coase's idea also explains how industries change. When shipping and the internet made dealing with outside firms far cheaper, the boundary of the firm moved. Apple, which once built much of its own hardware, now designs chips in California and has contract factories in Asia build them, part of a broad shift away from vertical integration toward outsourced supply chains. His Nobel citation named two papers: the 1937 paper on the firm and a 1960 paper on social cost, which changed the economics of smoke, noise and neighborly quarrels by focusing on externalities and property rights.

For any deal, say a carmaker buying steel, Coase's framework asks one comparative question: why does this exchange happen inside a company instead of across a market? The answer always lies in the relative transaction costs of the two arrangements. Coase earned his commerce degree at the London School of Economics in 1932, and he credited his teachers there, especially Arnold Plant, who taught him to distrust the planning schemes then in vogue among British intellectuals.

corporate-income-tax-who-actually-pays.context_blurb:
Politicians like to talk about making corporations pay their fair share. Economists in the classical and Austrian traditions answer with a basic lesson about any tax: whoever writes the check to the government is often not the one whose income actually shrinks. The American corporate income tax is the clearest test of that lesson.

Congress's 2017 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act lowered the federal rate on corporate profits from 35 percent to 21 percent, where it stands today. Milton Friedman liked to point out that a corporation is a legal fiction, not a human being, and so it cannot truly pay a tax at all. Every dollar of corporate tax comes out of the pockets of real people: workers, customers, or the company's owners.

Economists call the party the law names as payer the legal, or statutory, incidence of a tax. Once prices, wages and returns adjust, the party whose income really falls may be someone else, and that real-world burden is called the economic incidence. Applied to the corporate tax, Bastiat's question has a striking answer: much of the burden lands, unnoticed, on workers, through lower wages.

The reason is an asymmetry between the two great inputs of production. Capital is more mobile across borders than labor: money can leave a high-tax country, or demand a higher return to stay, while most workers cannot move abroad, so the burden slides onto the people who cannot leave. The standard modern study appeared in 2016 in the American Economic Review, where Juan Carlos Suárez Serrato and Owen Zidar used data on local job markets across the states to measure who really bears state corporate taxes.

Part of the burden does fall on the owners of capital, but those owners are not only the rich. Pension funds holding the retirement savings of teachers, firefighters and other public employees own enormous amounts of American stock, so the share that lands on capital hits ordinary retirement accounts too. The political trick, in this reading, is that corporate-tax talk names a legal payer the public is happy to punish while hiding the real people who carry the cost.

david-chaum-s-digicash-and-the-microsoft.context_blurb:
David Chaum, an American cryptographer, dreamed of digital money as private as cash in a pocket. In 1989 he founded DigiCash in Amsterdam to build it, and for a few years the world's biggest technology companies came calling. Its collapse in 1998 taught the cypherpunks the lesson that later shaped Bitcoin.

The foundation was a trick Chaum invented in 1982, the blind signature. A bank could certify a digital coin while, in effect, blindfolded, never seeing the particular coin it approved, so that when the coin was later spent at a shop nobody could trace it back to the person who had withdrawn it. His aim was to protect the buyer's privacy. Chaum expected banks and merchants to rush in. Instead the banks dragged their feet, few merchants signed up, and customers never came in numbers, because for most people paper money and credit cards already did the job well enough.

DigiCash's system used those blind signatures to let the bank confirm that a coin was genuine and had not been spent twice, without ever learning who had received it. The cypherpunks, though, saw one deep flaw, which they spent the next decade trying to remove: the system still required a trusted bank to issue and back the coins, and without a partner bank there were no coins at all.

In the mid-1990s Microsoft, racing to launch Windows 95, reportedly offered Chaum a nine-figure sum, widely cited as $100 million or $180 million, to build DigiCash into the new system. The big software firms wanted the technology because private digital payments promised to let their customers shop online with no bank standing between buyer and seller. Two other giants made offers too, Netscape, whose browser then ruled the young web, and the credit-card network Visa, and Chaum turned them both down.

DigiCash filed for bankruptcy in November 1998. That same month the cypherpunk Wei Dai sketched a form of digital money with no bank behind it, in which a network of computers jointly kept the books, and he called it b-money. Wei Dai, Nick Szabo and, a decade on, Satoshi Nakamoto all drew the same moral: even brilliant anonymous cryptography fails as money if the system still needs a central issuer who can be bought, bankrupted or shut down.

When Satoshi published the Bitcoin paper in 2008, he did not merely improve on DigiCash; he removed the piece that had killed it. Bitcoin keeps signatures and units of value but has no trusted issuer whose bankruptcy could freeze the currency, since new coins come from proof-of-work and a distributed network checks every transaction. Bitcoin historians press one more lesson. Chaum's refusals of Microsoft, Netscape and Visa were ordinary business choices, yet they doomed his whole system, because the operator of any trusted issuer, however brilliant, can sink an entire project through everyday business decisions.
