deirdre-mccloskey-the-bourgeois-trilogy.context_blurb:
Deirdre McCloskey, a Chicago-trained historian of the economy, spent her teaching career at universities in Iowa and Illinois. Between 2006 and 2016 she published three books, the Bourgeois Trilogy, asking why ordinary people in one corner of the world suddenly grew rich after 1800. Her answer was not machines or money but words: how people talked about those who buy, sell and invent.

For most of history nearly every family was poor and often hungry. Then, from around 1800, first in northwestern Europe and later in America, incomes began climbing year after year, until a typical Western household was some thirty times richer than its forebears. McCloskey calls that leap the Great Enrichment. Her explanation centers on a change of attitude. In 1700 a European of standing would sneer at anyone in trade; by 1800 ordinary opinion had swung toward respect for shopkeepers, inventors and traders.

The middle volume, Bourgeois Dignity, published in 2010, carries a defiant subtitle, Why Economics Can't Explain the Modern World, because the usual inputs of capital, geography and institutions fail to explain when and where the enrichment happened. The final volume, Bourgeois Equality, published in 2016, puts her thesis right on its cover: How Ideas, Not Capital or Institutions, Enriched the World.

The shift she points to took place between about 1600 and 1800, above all in Holland and England, when merchants and inventors, long despised by nobles and churchmen, began to win moral respect, and millions of ordinary people started trying to invent things. Her one-word name for the missing ingredient is dignity: treating ordinary business people with real respect, so that innovation and trade were honored in everyday talk. Her story does not discard secure property, enforceable contracts or honest courts. In McCloskey's view the new respect for innovators works alongside good institutions instead of displacing them; she adds a missing ingredient to the list and removes none of the others.

Her interest in words began much earlier. In 1985 she published The Rhetoric of Economics, a short book that jolted her profession by showing that economists persuade one another with metaphors, stories and appeals to authority as much as with mathematics. To sharpen her later puzzle she sets Ming-dynasty China's stagnation beside Britain's Industrial Revolution: similar people, land, technology and trade, opposite results, because the culture around the merchant differed.

McCloskey borrows Bastiat's pattern. The seen inputs are capital, institutions and geography; the unseen factor that made them productive was the cultural legitimation of merchants and inventors, without which the same inputs stagnate. The scale of the result is staggering. A typical European before 1800 got by on some three dollars a day in today's money, as his ancestors had for generations; since then the real income of each person in the first industrial countries has grown about thirtyfold, roughly 3,000 percent.

diocletians-edict-on-maximum-prices-301-.context_blurb:
Rome's emperor Diocletian, in the year 301, faced prices that kept rising across his empire. For decades Rome had funded its soldiers' pay by debasing the silver denarius, melting old coins and mixing in cheap metal to stretch the silver. Diocletian's answer was the most famous price control of the ancient world, and it failed in a pattern that has repeated ever since.

His Edict on Maximum Prices set legal ceilings on more than a thousand goods and wages, from bread, wine and olive oil to boots, wagon wheels and haircuts. A merchant who asked more faced execution under the edict's own text; the Christian writer Lactantius recorded that much blood was shed over small and cheap things. Merchants would not sell at a loss, so they stashed their stock, shut up shop or quit producing, and Roman shoppers met empty shelves and shortages.

The emperor did not blame his own mint. The edict's preamble cursed the merchants instead, for their unbridled fury and their greed, though it was the cheapened coin that had driven prices up. Across the empire the result came fast: goods vanished from the public market, held back, sold only to family, or carried off to black markets in other cities.

Lactantius, a Christian who had suffered through the emperor's persecution, described the outcome in his account of how the persecuting emperors died. The edict was quietly allowed to lapse within about a decade, and Diocletian himself abdicated in 305, the only Roman emperor to step down of his own will. Bastiat's method reads the episode in two parts. The seen is the cheap official price cut into stone in the market square. The unseen is the seller who would rather hoard than sell at a loss, and the buyer who goes hungry as a result.

We know the edict so well because fragments of its stone tablets survive across the eastern Mediterranean, and the most complete copy is at Aphrodisias in southwestern Turkey, from which archaeologists have rebuilt hundreds of price lines. Murray Rothbard and Thomas Sowell treat it as the founding case of an error governments keep repeating: they blame merchants for price rises that the government's own debasement of the currency caused. The pattern recurs from Rome to Nixon's Washington and Maduro's Caracas, as rulers debase the money, blame the sellers, impose a ceiling and watch the goods disappear. The record from Lactantius and the inscriptions is plain: what followed the edict was vanishing goods and spreading shortage, until the law was abandoned.

economic-harmonies-bastiats-positive-the.context_blurb:
Frédéric Bastiat is best known for his sharp critical essays, but Economic Harmonies was his one attempt at a complete positive theory of how a free economy holds together. He was still writing and revising it in Rome when tuberculosis killed him on Christmas Eve 1850. Its argument set him against the most powerful idea of the socialists of his century.

Karl Marx would soon teach that workers and owners are class enemies locked in a fight that only one side can win. Bastiat looked at the same world of markets and drew the opposite conclusion: in a free society, people's interests are naturally in harmony rather than at war, because when exchange is voluntary one party's gain does not require another's loss.

His most famous passage on value imagines a pair of equally useful diamonds, one stumbled upon in a stream bed, the other hacked out of a mine through years of toil. Buyers want both equally, and Bastiat concluded that both have the same value, because value comes from the service a good renders to its user, not from the labor spent producing it. That idea runs straight to Friedrich Hayek, who argued in 1945 that prices work like a silent messaging system: each price tells buyers and sellers something no single planner could know, so millions of strangers coordinate without anyone giving orders.

For centuries economists had held that a thing's price came from the labor put into it. In 1871 Carl Menger and William Stanley Jevons, working independently, proposed instead that a good's worth depends on how badly someone wants one more of it, an idea called subjective value, which depends on the person rather than on the labor spent. Bastiat's diamonds had hinted at it a generation earlier. He began the book in Paris near the end of the 1840s and raced the disease to finish it, but at his death only ten chapters were complete; his friend Prosper Paillottet assembled the drafts and fragments of the rest into an expanded edition in 1851.

Bastiat's method runs through the book. Imagine a farmer's barn burns down and a neighbor cheers the work it creates for carpenters. The carpenters' wages are what everyone notices, while the plow the farmer had been saving for, now never bought and never built, goes unnoticed. Bastiat called this habit of mind looking at what is seen and what is unseen.

enver-hoxhas-albania-and-the-173-000-bun.context_blurb:
Albania is a small, mountainous country in the Balkans. For four decades one man, Enver Hoxha, ruled it as the most isolated state in Europe. Its fields and beaches are still dotted with little concrete domes, the leftovers of his fear of invasion, and they make a sharp lesson in what that fear cost the people who paid for them.

Hoxha took power in 1944 and held it until he died in 1985. Under him the state took nearly everything. Farm families were driven onto huge collective farms, private business was outlawed, food often ran short, and the borders were sealed. That system, in which a single ruling party owns and plans the whole economy, is communism.

Hoxha trusted no one, not even his fellow communists. He broke with Yugoslavia in 1948, siding with Stalin against Tito; with the Soviet Union in 1961, siding with Mao against Khrushchev; and with China in 1978, as Deng Xiaoping's reforms began. Each break left Albania more alone.

In 1967 the regime closed all the country's mosques, churches and monasteries, turned many into warehouses and gyms, arrested the clergy and banned even private prayer at home. No government anywhere had declared itself officially atheist before; Albania was the first.

The secret police, the Sigurimi, kept files on almost every family and paid informers to report on their neighbors, so a joke about Hoxha could cost years in prison. Such watching has one purpose. It makes people afraid to speak, and people who are afraid to speak cannot find one another, so no group can ever organize against the state.

Hoxha was convinced that an invasion could come any day. From the late 1960s into the 1980s his regime poured concrete into about 173,000 small pillbox bunkers on beaches, hilltops and farmland, in a country of only some 2.8 million people. That works out to roughly one bunker for every sixteen Albanians.

When the regime finally fell in the early 1990s, researchers opened the secret-police archives and camp records. Even with those papers, an honest death count is hard to reach, because regimes like Hoxha's hide deaths, record prisoners under false labels and burn their files before they lose power. Scholars still count thousands executed for political crimes and tens of thousands sent to labor camps.

In December 1990 Hoxha's successor, Ramiz Alia, decided not to shoot the students protesting in the streets, and in March 1991 Albanians voted in their first multi-party election. Once the frontier opened, ordinary Albanians could finally see what it had hidden from them: how far their planned economy had fallen behind the free-market countries next door. Albania ended the communist era with the lowest income per person in Europe.

The French economist Frederic Bastiat taught that every choice has a cost you cannot see. A Bastiat-minded economist looks at the bunkers and asks what is missing beside them. Every ton of cement and every hour of labor that went into a bunker was a ton and an hour that never became a house, a school or a factory; economists call that lost alternative the opportunity cost. The invasion never came, but the houses were never built either.

ex-im-bank-and-boeing-the-concentrated-f.context_blurb:
In 1934, with the Great Depression at its worst, Franklin Roosevelt set up a federal lender by executive order: the Export-Import Bank of the United States (Ex-Im Bank). Its task was to use taxpayer-backed credit to help foreign customers buy American products, and it became one of the clearest cases of how a small, organized interest can keep a federal program alive.

Over the decades one customer came to dominate. One think tank reviewed the bank's lending over the years 2007 to 2013 and found that roughly two-fifths of its help went to the sales of a single company: Boeing, whose foreign airline customers bought jets with Ex-Im-backed financing. Critics nicknamed the agency the Boeing Bank, a textbook example of corporate welfare.

In June 2015 FreedomWorks, the Heritage Foundation and the Club for Growth beat Boeing and the bank's other big corporate allies in Congress. Lawmakers refused to renew the bank's charter, so it lapsed for about five months, and from July until December 2015 it could not sign new deals.

Boeing had warned that American exports would collapse without the bank. The bank's critics found no measurable fall in exports during the lapse, because Boeing kept selling airliners using ordinary commercial bank loans, which cost a little more than Ex-Im's guarantees but not enough to stop the deals.

In December 2015 Congress brought the bank back by folding its renewal into a big highway bill, the FAST Act. Few lawmakers wanted to vote against road money for their districts, so voting against Ex-Im suddenly became expensive; public-choice economists call this kind of bundling and vote-trading logrolling.

Why does the bank keep surviving? Mancur Olson's 'The Logic of Collective Action', published in 1965, explains the pattern. When a program hands large benefits to a few firms and spreads its cost thinly across millions of taxpayers, the few organize and lobby hard while the many barely notice. Boeing spends millions of dollars a year lobbying, but no single taxpayer spends a weekend fighting over his few cents' share.

fee-and-the-american-rediscovery-leonard.context_blurb:
In March 1946 the American businessman Leonard Read founded the Foundation for Economic Education, known as FEE, in Irvington-on-Hudson, New York. It was the first postwar American institution devoted to teaching free-market economics to ordinary readers, and it became the bridge that carried the old European classical-liberal tradition to a new American audience.

That same year Henry Hazlitt, a journalist who sat on FEE's founding board, published Economics in One Lesson. Hazlitt reduced economics to a single rule taken from Frederic Bastiat: in judging any policy, look at both its seen and its unseen effects.

Bastiat's best-known illustration of that rule comes from his 1850 essay on the seen and the unseen. A boy hurls a rock through a shopkeeper's window, and the neighbors comfort themselves that at least the glazier will get work. Bastiat showed what they missed: the money the shopkeeper must now spend on glass can no longer buy the new shoes he had planned on, so the shoemaker's lost sale is the hidden cost.

FEE helped make Bastiat an American author. In 1950 it published Dean Russell's English translation of The Law, the short book Bastiat finished months before he died in 1850. Bastiat argued that when a government seizes property from some citizens to hand it to others, the law itself becomes legal plunder. The law's true job, he said, is to protect every person's life, liberty and honestly earned property.

In 1958 Read wrote FEE's most famous essay, I, Pencil, narrated by an ordinary yellow pencil. Its cedar is logged in Oregon, its graphite is mined far away, its eraser comes from rubber trees and its metal band from brass, and the pencil boasts that no one anywhere could make it alone. Read's point was that a free market coordinates millions of strangers with no central planner directing them. If no one can plan a pencil, no single mind could ever plan a whole economy. Prices carry the signals, so the logger, the miner and the factory hand each respond to what things cost, and millions cooperate without anyone in charge; Milton Friedman later built a segment of his television series Free to Choose around the pencil.

Why build an institution rather than run campaigns? In his 1949 essay The Intellectuals and Socialism, Friedrich Hayek argued that a country's direction is set less by elections than by the ideas that schoolteachers, reporters and authors absorb and pass on, because politicians eventually follow them. Think tanks, magazines and reading programs for students, FEE's among them, aim at something campaigns cannot reach: they work, slowly, on what the public treats as common sense about economics.

friedman-1970-business-responsibility-is.context_blurb:
By 1970 American companies were being urged to take on causes beyond making money: cleaner air, better neighborhoods, social programs. Milton Friedman, the University of Chicago economist, answered with an essay people still argue over more than fifty years later. His question was simple: whose money is a company's boss spending, and on whose behalf?

The essay ran in the Sunday magazine of the New York Times on September 13, 1970, and its title said it outright: the social responsibility of business, Friedman wrote, is to increase its profits. Admirers and critics alike now call the argument the Friedman Doctrine.

It was not a new idea for him. The essay condensed and sharpened a chapter of Capitalism and Freedom, his 1962 book arguing at length for open markets and a small state.

Friedman began with a plain fact about who works for whom. A corporate executive is an employee of the shareholders, the owners of the firm, and their interests define his job: to run the business so it makes as much money as possible for them.

The chase for profit had limits, though. The executive must keep to the basic rules of society, Friedman wrote, both those written into law and those carried in ethical custom, so he was defending honest business, not fraud.

Then Friedman drew his sharpest line. An executive's own salary is his to give away, so he may donate it to whatever cause he likes. The company's money is different, because it belongs to the owners. An executive who spends the firm's funds on some cause its owners never approved is, in Friedman's words, spending other people's money on priorities of his own, like a self-appointed tax collector who charges the owners and then decides how the money gets spent.

Friedman also saw a problem of accountability. If managers are told to serve employees, neighbors, nature and owners together, nobody can hold them to account: with so many masters they answer to none, and any decision can be defended by pointing to whichever group it helped. One clear owner to serve is what keeps managers honest.

Friedman's essay remains the chief intellectual answer to ESG investing, the push for companies to steer profits toward environmental and social goals. In Friedman's terms, that is charity with other people's money, handed out by executives whom no shareholder authorized to give it.

The rival view gathered strength. The Business Roundtable, a Washington group of top American chief executives, issued in August 2019 a statement on what a corporation is for that broke openly with Friedman's rule, and 181 CEOs signed it.

Business-school professors pressed the same case: Michael Porter of Harvard with his idea of "shared value," Colin Mayer of Oxford on what firms are for, and Rebecca Henderson of Harvard in her book Reimagining Capitalism. All three argue that the shareholder-only rule misses how companies create value over the long run, by caring for workers, communities and the environment. Friedman's side replies that shareholders are free to choose such goals themselves; what lacks a mandate is an executive imposing them.

friedrich-von-wieser--who-he-was---oppor.context_blurb:
Friedrich von Wieser helped found the Austrian school of economics and became the bridge between its founder, Carl Menger, and the generation of Mises, Hayek and Schumpeter. He gave economics two of its most-used terms. Born in Vienna in 1851 as plain Friedrich Wieser, he died in 1926 a baron, a former cabinet minister and a member of the empire's upper house.

His closest colleague was family: Eugen von Boehm-Bawerk, who had studied beside him, married Wieser's sister Paula. Wieser spent almost twenty years, from 1884 to 1903, teaching at the German-language university in Prague, where most people spoke Czech. In 1903 he came home to take over Menger's chair at the University of Vienna.

His first famous word came in 1884. When you drink one canteen of water after another, each brings you less benefit than the one before, and what drives price is the usefulness of the final unit you add. Wieser called that usefulness Grenznutzen, which in English is marginal utility; it is why a thirsty traveler in the desert pays a fortune for the first canteen and almost nothing for the tenth.

His second word names the true price of any choice. An hour at the movies is an hour you cannot spend earning money at a job, so whatever you pass over, the most valuable option you did not take, is what the choice really costs you. Wieser's German word for it was Alternativkosten, and its English form, opportunity cost, now appears in every economics textbook. A farmer who sows wheat on a field pays, in truth, with the barley he could have grown there instead.

Behind both words lay the Austrian discovery that value lives in people, not in things. Older economists said a good's worth came from the labor or the materials inside it. Wieser and Menger answered that a thing is worth however much a particular person wants it at that moment, and Wieser set out this subjective theory of value in his readable 1889 book Natural Value. Two collectors may offer fifty dollars and two dollars for the same baseball card, because value is not a fixed number but depends on each person's wants.

He also turned the labor theory upside down with his theory of imputation. The value of a train wheel does not begin with the hours of work and the coal that went into it. It begins with what the customer will use the finished product for, a working train, and is then credited back down the chain to the steel, the ore and the workers.

In 1917, halfway through the First World War, Emperor Karl I made Wieser his minister of commerce, in charge of the empire's trade, business and industry, a post he kept until the empire collapsed in November 1918. That same year the emperor raised him to the nobility, so Friedrich Wieser became Friedrich von Wieser, a baron, and gave him a seat in the imperial parliament's upper chamber, the House of Lords.

Wieser's students carried the school forward. One was the young Friedrich Hayek, who attended his Vienna seminars in the early 1920s. In a famous 1945 essay Hayek argued that planners can never collect the countless local details of who needs what, where and at what price, details that ordinary people and market prices carry through an economy, and he named that limit the knowledge problem.

Another student, Joseph Schumpeter, watched cars replace buggies and electric bulbs replace gaslight. He argued that this constant replacement of old products and firms by new ones is the market's most important trait, and he called it creative destruction.

gottfried-haberler-prosperity-and-depres.context_blurb:
Gottfried Haberler (1900-1995) grew up in the Vienna of the Austrian school and spent most of his career at Harvard. He wrote the book a whole generation used to understand why economies boom and bust, and he carried Austrian ideas into the American mainstream, at a price some of his teachers resented.

He trained at the University of Vienna in the 1920s, and his two doctoral advisors were giants of the generation after Carl Menger: Friedrich von Wieser and Ludwig von Mises. He also joined Mises's private seminar.

His early fame came from trade. David Ricardo had explained comparative advantage in 1817, the idea that each nation does best by specializing where its edge over others is largest, but Ricardo measured costs in hours of labor. In his 1933 book on international trade, Haberler restated comparative advantage in terms of opportunity cost, what a country gives up by making one good instead of another, a version Austrians could accept and the one trade textbooks teach today.

In 1936 Haberler moved to the United States, one of many Austrian-trained economists, among them Mises, Hayek and Fritz Machlup, who left Central Europe in the years when dictators took it over. What most of them brought with them was a belief in free markets and a deep skepticism of central planning.

Every economy rises through good years, crashes into a slump where factories close and jobs vanish, and then climbs back again; economists call that repeating rise and fall the business cycle. In 1937 the League of Nations, based in Geneva, commissioned Haberler to survey every serious theory of it. The result was Prosperity and Depression, whose title pairs the top of the cycle with its bottom, and it became the standard reference for a generation.

Strict Austrians, Mises among them, were unhappy with the survey. Haberler treated the Austrian theory as just one theory among several, all equally worth surveying, instead of presenting it as the correct account, and they saw that even-handedness as a first step toward compromise with mainstream economics.

Haberler also belonged to the Mont Pelerin Society, which Hayek founded in April 1947 at a meeting in the Swiss Alps above Lake Geneva, gathering defenders of classical liberalism such as Mises, Machlup and the young Milton Friedman.

After retiring from Harvard in 1971 he moved to Washington and joined the American Enterprise Institute, where he went on attacking inflation, protectionism and government controls on wages and prices until near his death.

hal-finneys-reusable-proofs-of-work-2004.context_blurb:
Bitcoin did not appear out of nowhere. For fifteen years before it, a loose band of programmers called cypherpunks tried to build digital cash, and each attempt got a little closer. One of the most important steps came in 2004 from the California programmer Hal Finney.

The story starts with the British computer scientist Adam Back. In 1997 he built Hashcash, which made anyone sending an email first solve a small math puzzle and attach the answer as a proof-of-work stamp, so that a spammer blasting millions of messages would be slowed down. But a Hashcash stamp could be used only once and could not be handed on to someone else the way a coin can.

In 2004 Finney took the idea further. His system turned each proof-of-work stamp into a token that could change hands again and again, and he named it Reusable Proofs of Work (RPOW).

Passing tokens around raised the hardest problem in digital cash: what stops someone from copying a token and spending it twice? Finney's answer was a trusted server that kept track of which stamps had already been spent and issued fresh ones to replace them. He ran it on an IBM 4758, a tamper-resistant chip, so users could check that the server was running honest, audited code.

The famous earlier attempt, DigiCash, built by the American cryptographer David Chaum in the 1990s, also routed payments through one trusted central server. Special hardware could not cure the deeper weakness both systems shared: dependence on one server that a government could switch off or an insider could corrupt.

Bitcoin took a different road to trust. Instead of special hardware, it trusts a public network of computers that all check one another's work.

Satoshi Nakamoto's 2008 white paper solved the double-spending problem without any central server. Its invention was a public ledger that many strangers keep in step using proof-of-work, so no single party can freeze the money or rewrite the record.

Satoshi launched Bitcoin on January 3, 2009. On January 12 he sent the first person-to-person transfer to Finney, recorded in block 170: ten bitcoin, written 10 BTC.

helicopter-ben-bernankes-2002-deflation-.context_blurb:
In November 2002 Ben Bernanke, then a governor of the Federal Reserve and later its chairman, gave a speech about a danger most Americans had never worried about: prices that fall instead of rise. The speech earned him a nickname for life, and six years later it read like a script for what the Fed actually did in the 2008 crisis.

Deflation means prices drop over time, so a dollar buys more next year than today. That sounds pleasant, but it can wreck jobs: people put off purchases hoping prices will fall further, sales dry up, and businesses lay off workers.

Bernanke's speech rested on one bold claim. A central bank issuing fiat money, paper backed by nothing, can always create more of it at essentially zero cost, so it can always push prices up if it truly wants to. Markets heard reassurance; Austrian economists heard a warning that nothing but political will stands in the way of printing.

To make the point vivid, he borrowed an image Milton Friedman had used: a helicopter dropping money over a town, the simplest picture of new money flowing straight into people's hands. Friedman had painted it in his 1969 essay The Optimum Quantity of Money as a thought experiment, not a policy. The press dubbed Bernanke "Helicopter Ben," and the name stuck.

Next came a menu of tools for a Fed that has already cut short-term rates to zero. At the head of the list was buying long-term Treasury bonds to push long-term interest rates down. In an extreme case, Bernanke added, a central bank could even pay for direct tax cuts by printing money. Austrian critics called that monetary financing of fiscal policy, the central bank simply creating new money to fund the government.

Austrian-minded critics attacked the speech as a road map to eventually debasing the dollar. The trio usually named is Bob Murphy of the Mises Institute, the investor and broadcaster Peter Schiff, and the commodities investor Jim Rogers.

Six years later, in November 2008, Bernanke, by then the Fed's chairman, launched the first program to buy mortgage-backed securities and long-term government debt on a vast scale, adding hundreds of billions to the Fed's holdings. It became known as QE1, for quantitative easing.

Its sequels followed. Between 2008 and 2014 the Fed carried out nearly everything the 2002 speech had previewed, chiefly through QE1, QE2, and Operation Twist, followed by a third round of buying.

Austrian and public-choice economists draw a lesson from the whole episode. When central bankers describe in public what they could do in a hypothetical crisis, they are often previewing exactly what they will do in a real one.

inflation-is-always-and-everywhere-a-mon.context_blurb:
Milton Friedman, the Nobel-winning Chicago economist, repeated one sentence for three decades: inflation is always and everywhere a monetary phenomenon. Behind those words lay a claim about cause and a century of evidence, and they won a long argument over why prices rise.

The picture is simple. Suppose a government doubles the money it hands out while the country produces exactly as much as before. Shopkeepers find extra dollars competing for an unchanged pile of goods, so they mark prices up: the cause is too much money for too few things to buy. Friedman's point was that a lasting general rise in prices comes from money, not from wages, weather or supply troubles. In his famous line, inflation is a monetary phenomenon.

He offered it as a tested finding, not a mere slogan. With Anna Schwartz he spent nearly ten years assembling American money and price figures reaching back to 1867, and in 1963 they published the results as A Monetary History. Friedman rested his claim on that century of money-supply-and-inflation data.

The book's most famous chapter, The Great Contraction, turned to the Great Depression. From 1929 to 1933 the quantity of money in America fell by about a third, and Friedman and Schwartz argued that this sudden collapse of the money supply is what made the Depression so deep. The lesson cuts both ways: when the money supply shrinks fast, businesses fail and jobs vanish along with it.

In a famous lecture in London, titled The Counter-Revolution in Monetary Theory, Friedman openly challenged the ruling school of his day, Keynesian macroeconomics, which treated money as a passive bystander.

Friedman was careful about credit. He named as roots of his framework his Chicago teacher Henry Simons, the earlier money statistician Clark Warburton, and his co-author: Henry Simons, Clark Warburton, and Anna Schwartz.

The 1970s tested him. After Nixon cut the dollar loose from gold, and with the Fed creating money fast, prices climbed year after year, yet politicians and television reporters kept pointing elsewhere: at corporate greed, at union wage demands and at the oil sheikhs of OPEC. Friedman answered that all three were effects; the cause behind them was years of monetary expansion.

The decade also brought stagflation, rising prices and rising unemployment together, which the older textbooks had said could not happen and which Friedman had predicted. By the 1980s most textbooks had come around to his monetarist view.

The Austrians agreed that inflation is monetary but parted from Friedman on the details. Friedman watched a single statistic, the growth of the total money supply. Mises, Hayek and Rothbard focused on the way fresh central-bank credit distorts the structure of investment, building booms that later bust; in short, Friedman watched the aggregate, while the Austrians studied credit-driven malinvestment.

jiaozi-and-kublai-khan-the-first-paper-m.context_blurb:
Paper money was invented in China, roughly a thousand years ago. Within a few centuries two Chinese dynasties had shown both its convenience and its great danger, and a traveler from Venice had carried the astonishing story back to Europe.

The trouble began with iron. Under the Song dynasty, merchants in the busy trading region of Sichuan paid in heavy iron coins, sometimes a cartload for one deal. So they left their coins with trusted holders and traded the paper receipts instead, and those slips grew into paper money.

In 1023 the Song government took the system over, making the notes, called jiaozi, the first paper money issued by any government. At first they held their value. But the Song state fought long wars, first against the Jin kingdom in the north and later against the Mongols, and to pay for those military campaigns it printed far more notes than its reserves could back, until the paper lost most of its worth.

The Mongols conquered China, and in the late 1200s Kublai Khan ruled it from Beijing. He issued his own paper money, the chao, backed by no gold or silver, and ordered every merchant and peasant to accept it. A ruler free to print as he pleases, and to compel everyone to accept the result, tends to print more to pay his bills, and each note buys less than the one before.

The Venetian merchant Marco Polo, who served at Kublai's court in the 1270s and 1280s, devoted a chapter of his Travels, written in 1298, to the chao. He explained that the notes were made from the inner bark of the mulberry tree, stamped in vermilion with the imperial seal. Refusing them, he reported, was punishable by death.

To a European used to coins of gold and silver, the sight was dazzling. He compared the system to alchemy: the Khan, he marveled, had the secret of turning bark into wealth.

The magic did not last. Kublai died in 1294, and the emperors after him printed chao at will to meet each new crisis, so by the 1350s the notes were worthless and the Yuan dynasty itself was collapsing.

Modern Austrian economists draw a pointed conclusion from China's two-for-two record. The very first two government paper currencies in history both ended in hyperinflation, which suggests the failure is built into the incentives of paper money rather than being a modern accident.

Bastiat's lens sharpens the story. What Polo saw was the Khan seemingly turning bark into wealth; what nobody could see was the coming collapse in prices, already written into the arrangement, that would drain the wealth of every chao holder within a generation.

julian-assanges-cypherpunk-years-and-rub.context_blurb:
Long before he founded WikiLeaks, the Australian programmer Julian Assange spent years on the cypherpunk mailing list of the 1990s, alongside Eric Hughes, Tim May and other coders who believed privacy had to be built with mathematics. His early work shows how one idea from that world, that what many copies hold no one can seize, came to matter far beyond computers.

The cypherpunks wanted tools no government could switch off, even a powerful one. If a tool is to be beyond any government's off switch, no single person or place can control it, because any single point of control is a single point of attack.

Strong mathematics has one weakness it cannot fix. Picture a diary locked with a code no computer could ever crack; a bully can still threaten you until you open it yourself. Cryptographers grimly call this rubber-hose cryptanalysis, and Bitcoin holders face it too, because the weakest link is the person who knows the key, and force applied to him can break any code.

In 1997 Assange co-wrote an encryption program for hard disks named after that threat: Rubberhose. He meant it for human-rights activists at risk of capture and torture. Its trick was to hide several encrypted volumes on one disk, so a captive could surrender one password while the others stayed invisible; an interrogator could never prove that more hidden volumes existed. Cryptographers call this plausibly deniable encryption.

The idea outlived the program. Two widely used disk-encryption tools carried the hidden-volume design forward: TrueCrypt (2004) and VeraCrypt (2013).

In 2006 Assange founded WikiLeaks, a site for publishing leaked official papers. When governments tried to force it offline, it kept coming back, because its documents were mirrored across many independent servers in many different countries.

After WikiLeaks released secret US war logs and diplomatic cables, Assange faced arrest. In 2012 he took refuge in the Ecuadorian embassy in London and was granted asylum, and he lived inside it for seven years until Ecuador revoked his asylum in 2019 and British police arrested him there. He then spent years in Belmarsh prison until a plea deal freed him in 2024.

The thread that links the 1990s mailing list to WikiLeaks, and later to Bitcoin, is distributed censorship-resistance: what many independent copies preserve, no single power can seize.

kelo-v-city-of-new-london-2005-eminent-d.context_blurb:
Susette Kelo, a nurse, loved her small pink house by the water in the Fort Trumbull neighborhood of New London, Connecticut. In 2000 the city decided her street should make way for private redevelopment, and when she refused to sell, it moved to take her home anyway. Her fight reached the Supreme Court, lost there, and then won in a different arena.

Governments have a legal power to take private land. The Fifth Amendment allows it for "public use," provided the owner receives just compensation, and the power is called eminent domain. Historically public use meant a road, a school or a military base.

New London's plan was different. The land would go to a private developer for offices, shops and housing, built to complement a large new Pfizer research center next door. The city's stated public purpose was more jobs and a bigger tax base.

Critics said that stretched public use past breaking point, because the property was being handed to another private owner rather than turned into a park or a road.

In 2005 the Supreme Court sided with the city, five votes to four, in an opinion by Justice John Paul Stevens. Justice Sandra Day O'Connor wrote the main dissent and its most quoted warning: under this ruling, she argued, nothing stops a government from swapping a cheap motel for a luxury hotel, or a family home for a mall.

The promised revival never came. Pfizer closed its New London research center within about five years, around 2009 and 2010, and the cleared land where Kelo and her neighbors had lived sat empty for more than a decade.

Public-choice economists see a familiar story. A politically connected developer captured the government's taking power and turned it against scattered homeowners, each of whom lost a great deal but who had little ability to organize. Behind any stated public reason, they say, the analyst should look for the concentrated winner and the concentrated loser: who gains a great deal, and who pays a great deal.

The homeowners did have one organized ally. Their lawyers came from the Institute for Justice, a public-interest law firm that Clint Bolick and Chip Mellor founded in 1991 and that has become the country's leading property-rights litigator.

Then came the surprise. The backlash crossed party lines, and in the ten years after the ruling roughly 45 states passed laws or constitutional amendments limiting takings for private development. Normally a concentrated interest beats a dispersed one; here the dispersed side won, because the Institute for Justice's years of lawsuits, model bills and publicity organized the scattered homeowners into a force.

law-legislation-and-liberty-1973-1979-an.context_blurb:
In his seventies, long after The Road to Serfdom had made him famous, Friedrich Hayek set out to explain what kind of order a free society actually has, and why clever lawmakers keep misunderstanding it. The result was a three-volume work, published between 1973 and 1979, whose title joins three ideas that all begin with the letter L: Law, Legislation and Liberty.

Hayek's central picture contrasts a garden with a forest. In a garden a gardener places every flower by hand; in a forest every tree finds its own place with no planner at all. Both have order, but the forest's is a grown order that nobody designed on purpose, what Hayek called kosmos, as against the made order, taxis, of the garden.

He gave such grown systems a two-word name: spontaneous order. Human language, market prices and the common law all emerge from the separate choices of multitudes, each person following his own aims and local habits, and no one plans them. The scientist Michael Polanyi had used the same phrase in 1951, and Hayek acknowledged him.

Law can grow in exactly that way. In one tradition experts write a complete code and courts apply it word for word. In the other, judges settle actual quarrels one at a time and their successors follow the precedents, so the rules accumulate over centuries. Hayek admired the second, English common law, because like the market it has no single designer and draws on a great deal of local knowledge.

The idea was old. The Scottish philosopher Adam Ferguson had observed in 1767 that many institutions come from people's actions but not from anyone's plan, a line Hayek quoted often. Language, money and law grow out of many small everyday choices, without any one person planning the whole.

The opposite mistake has a name too. Looking at a slowly grown pattern such as language, law or prices and treating it as an engine that experts could take apart and rebuild is what Hayek called constructivist rationalism, the belief that reason can build a society from nothing.

Volume 2, published in 1976 and subtitled The Mirage of Social Justice, attacked a phrase people apply to market results. Hayek argued that social justice is a category mistake: justice belongs to the deliberate acts of persons, and a market's distribution of rich and poor has no single author. He compared it to rain spoiling a picnic, a misfortune nobody chose, which it makes no sense to call unjust.

He wrote that volume partly in answer to a book that had put social justice at the center of political philosophy five years earlier: A Theory of Justice by John Rawls, the Harvard philosopher.

Volume 3, of 1979, is his most political. Fearing that majority-rule democracies were sliding from stable general laws into day-to-day bargaining, Hayek proposed a two-chamber legislature: one chamber, its members elected for long terms, to make the general rules, and another to handle ordinary government business.

Polanyi also named a kind of knowledge that fits Hayek's argument. An experienced physician recognizes appendicitis almost at a glance yet cannot list every clue; a carpenter steadies a warped board without being able to describe each finger's movement. Polanyi called this tacit knowledge, real skill passed on by practice that no manual can fully capture, and Hayek treated it as more proof that what an economy knows cannot be gathered in one place.

ludwig-von-mises-who-he-was.context_blurb:
Ludwig von Mises, born in 1881 in Lemberg, then part of the Austro-Hungarian Empire and today Lviv in Ukraine, became the central figure linking the Austrian school of old Vienna to its revival in America. He spent his life arguing that markets coordinate what no government could, and he paid for his views with years of exile and decades without a paid professorship.

He took his doctorate in Vienna in 1906, and his strongest influences were the school's founder and its great theorist of capital: Carl Menger and Eugen von Boehm-Bawerk.

Vienna's university never paid him a professor's salary; it gave him only an unpaid lecturer's title. From around 1909 for twenty-five years his salary came from the Austrian Chamber of Commerce, the body that spoke for Austrian business, where he wrote policy papers on tariffs, labor law and money.

From 1920 to 1934 he also ran a private seminar in his office every second Friday evening. Its most famous member, Friedrich Hayek, later won the 1974 Nobel Prize for, among other things, the insight that market prices carry facts scattered across millions of people that no central planner could ever collect, an idea known as the knowledge problem.

In 1927 Mises founded a research body to study the ups and downs of the business cycle, with Hayek as its first director: the Austrian Institute for Business-Cycle Research. The Rockefeller Foundation later helped fund it.

Mises's most famous argument came in 1920. Under full socialism the state holds all the means of production, so they are never bought or sold and carry no genuine prices. Without real prices, Mises argued, planners cannot tell which uses of resources create the most value, and so they cannot plan rationally at all.

Prices, in his account, carry two messages at once: what people want and what things cost to make. Abolish free prices, as communist states did, and the planners can no longer tell what is scarce or what people truly need. In a free economy that knowledge comes instead from prices set by millions of buyers and sellers making their own decisions.

He also refused to call himself merely an economist. To Mises, economics was only one part of a larger science, built by deduction, of human beings acting with purpose, which he named praxeology from the Greek praxis, action, and he preferred to be called a praxeologist.

Mises left Vienna for Geneva in 1934, married Margit Sereny in 1938, and fled Europe for the United States in 1940; from 1945 to 1969 he led a seminar at New York University. He died in 1973. In October 1982 the American organizer Lew Rockwell founded a research institute in his name, with support from his widow Margit, Ron Paul, Henry Hazlitt and Murray Rothbard, and it has stood ever since in the college town of Auburn, Alabama.

medical-licensing-friedmans-capitalism-a.context_blurb:
Before a doctor may treat patients in America, a state must grant a license. Most people assume that rule simply protects patients. Milton Friedman argued that it also protects doctors, from competition, and economists since have tried to measure how much.

Friedman made the case in Capitalism and Freedom, published in 1962, a short defense of free markets for general readers that became one of the most widely read of the century. Its ninth chapter, on occupational licensure, argued that medical licensing holds down the supply of doctors and pushes up what they charge.

Who decides? In each American state the license is granted by the state medical board, a body staffed largely by physicians, so doctors decide how many new doctors may join them.

The modern system grew from a 1910 study. Abraham Flexner, an educator writing for the Carnegie Foundation, urged states to close small medical schools that missed strict new standards and to train doctors on the model of Johns Hopkins. School after school shut: the count fell from roughly 160 schools in 1904 to 76 by 1935. With fewer new doctors entering the field relative to a growing population, doctor visits grew more expensive.

The labor economist Morris Kleiner has measured licensing far beyond medicine. In the 1950s about one American worker in twenty needed a license; today roughly one in four does, from hair braiders to interior designers. His studies find that people who hold a license earn more, by about fifteen percent on average, because new competitors are kept out, with little measurable gain in quality. Licensing, in his findings, mostly serves the existing practitioners.

The pattern has a name. In North Carolina, the dentists who controlled the state's dental licensing board went after mall kiosks where non-dentists offered cheap teeth whitening, though the kiosks harmed no one; in 2015 the Supreme Court ruled against the board. Turning the state's licensing power against competitors in this way is called rent-seeking.

Some states have tested the alternative. By 2024 about half of them let nurse practitioners, nurses with advanced clinical training, run their own primary-care clinics without a supervising doctor. Studies by RAND and others comparing those states with physician-only states keep finding lower prices for primary care with no measurable difference in quality.

Friedman did not want patients left in the dark about who was well trained. His proposal was certification rather than licensing: the state could certify that a practitioner had met a published standard, without forbidding anyone uncertified from offering services to adults who chose them.

Public-choice economists draw a default rule from all this. When nearly every seat on a licensing board belongs to the profession it oversees, your first suspicion should be that its entry restrictions serve those members' incomes more than public safety.
