mining-pools-from-solo-miners-to-global-.context_blurb: As Bitcoin mining became more competitive and specialized, individual miners found themselves unlikely to ever solve a block on their own. Mining pools emerged as cooperatives in which individual miners contribute hash power toward a shared effort and receive proportional rewards based on units of work called shares. By the 2020s a handful of pools, including Foundry USA, controlled most of the global hash rate. In 2014 the pool GHash.io briefly reached a share of the total network that would have allowed it to execute what cryptographers call a fifty-one percent attack. Individual miners voluntarily left the pool, and the pool operators publicly asked users to switch away, before any attack was attempted. The whole arrangement is a worked example of Hayek-style spontaneous order: no central authority chose the specific limit the industry stayed under.

mmt-rise-and-fall-stephanie-keltons-defi.context_blurb: Modern Monetary Theory, abbreviated MMT, is a heterodox school of macroeconomic thought that rose to visibility in the late 2010s with the publication of Stephanie Kelton's 2020 book The Deficit Myth. Its specific policy claim was that a government that issues its own fiat currency is constrained in its spending only by inflation and the availability of real resources, not by any arithmetic debt ceiling. Larry Summers called MMT the new voodoo economics in a sharply critical 2019 Washington Post piece. Warren Mosler's earlier book Soft Currency Economics was the proto-MMT text. The 2021 passage of the roughly two-trillion-dollar American Rescue Plan became the empirical test. MMT advocates had argued the plan would not produce significant inflation; by June 2022 US consumer-price inflation had reached nine-point-one percent. MMT advocates subsequently attributed the inflation to supply-chain disruptions rather than monetary or fiscal expansion. In the Austrian reading, the whole episode illustrates that there is no such thing as unused aggregate capacity that can absorb arbitrary monetary expansion without price-level consequences, and that an empirical test in the ordinary economy can falsify a school of thought faster than a decade of academic debate.

new-york-citys-rent-control-since-1943.context_blurb: New York City has operated some form of rent control continuously since 1943. The specific legal regime now runs through the Emergency Tenant Protection Act and layers of modifications. In the Austrian and classical-liberal reading, more than eighty years of continuous experience in a single American city provides the longest-running natural experiment on the subject. Milton Friedman and George Stigler's 1946 pamphlet Roofs or Ceilings was the first academic classical-liberal statement of the mechanism. In their framing the problem is that landlords with rent below cost have no reason to maintain, expand, or add rental supply, so the stock degrades, apartments go un-built, and the overall supply of rental housing shrinks over time. The specific New York City pattern includes landlords deferring maintenance, apartments warehoused off the market by owners rather than let at a loss, and in extreme cases the incentive to burn a rent-controlled building for the insurance payout. In the Bastiat seen-and-unseen reading, the SEEN beneficiary is the tenant with a controlled lease; the UNSEEN cost is paid by the apartments that are never built, by the units held off the market, and by the maintenance that never happens.

occupational-licensing-1-600-hours-to-br.context_blurb: Occupational licensing is a legal regime in which a state requires practitioners of a trade to obtain a specific state-issued license before they can offer services, usually conditioned on long training programs and tests. In some American states the required training to braid natural hair runs to over one thousand hours, more than many police academies. Classical and public-choice critics including the Institute for Justice have documented that licensing boards are typically populated by incumbent members of the regulated profession, who have an obvious interest in restricting entry by newcomers. The specific practical tests have in some documented cases been graded by competitors of the applicants, as in a case of licensed Florida florists grading would-be applicants. In the public-choice reading the whole structure is Mancur Olson's pattern applied to local trades: a few who each gain a lot organize to shape the rules; the many who each lose a little do not. The specific legal doctrine applies here: a board of active competitors keeps regulatory immunity only under genuine state supervision. Milton Friedman's preferred alternative is state certification, which does not block newcomers from entering the trade.

paul-volcker-20-rates-and-breaking-the-1.context_blurb: Paul Volcker was appointed chairman of the Federal Reserve by Jimmy Carter in August 1979 at a moment of double-digit US inflation. On October 6, 1979 Volcker announced that the Fed would target the growth of the money supply rather than interest rates, and short-term interest rates rose rapidly, eventually peaking near twenty percent in 1981. Unemployment rose to a peak of ten-point-eight percent in late 1982, in what became known as the Volcker recession. Inflation fell from double-digits to roughly three-point-two percent by late 1983. Volcker was reappointed by Ronald Reagan, who accepted the political cost of the recession. The following three decades of relative price stability became known as the Great Moderation. The later Volcker Rule, enacted after the 2008 financial crisis, carries his name on a different topic.

polands-balcerowicz-plan-1990-shock-ther.context_blurb: On January 1, 1990 Poland's new post-Communist government, under Finance Minister Leszek Balcerowicz, launched a sudden and comprehensive reform program that American economists call shock therapy. The plan liberalized prices on almost all goods overnight, imposed a hard budget constraint on state firms, made the Polish zloty convertible to Western currencies, and opened the economy to trade. The Harvard economist Jeffrey Sachs advised the Polish team. Polish GDP contracted by about twelve percent in the first year of the program. Growth then resumed and continued steadily for the next three decades; by the 2020s Polish per-capita output was roughly triple its 1990 level. Russia under Yegor Gaidar attempted a similar gradual approach without comparable hard-budget-constraint discipline, and the result was the oligarch collapse of the 1990s. In the Austrian and classical-liberal reading the Polish growth miracle is one of the clearest modern illustrations of what Ludwig von Mises's 1920 argument would predict: when market prices and hard budget constraints replace planning and soft budgets, the economy can start to allocate resources rationally.

praxeology-economics-from-the-action-axi.context_blurb: Praxeology is Ludwig von Mises's name for a method of economic reasoning that proceeds by deduction from the simple axiom that human beings act purposefully, using scarce means to attain preferred ends. The term comes from the Greek word praxis, meaning action or deed. The method is laid out in Mises's 1949 book Human Action and extended by Murray Rothbard's two-volume Man, Economy, and State. Mises's methodological argument is that human action is not laboratory chemistry; you cannot re-run 1929 with the money supply held constant and watch what happens. Historical confirmation and empirical measurement are useful, but the underlying theoretical structure is derived in advance from the action axiom. The method stands in direct contrast with the positivist methodology of Milton Friedman's 1953 essay The Methodology of Positive Economics. Mises used the companion term thymology for the empirical study of human motivation and the historical interpretation of specific episodes. The economist Hans-Hermann Hoppe extended the methodological project in his 1988 book Economic Science and the Austrian Method. The whole approach rests on methodological individualism, the view that only individuals act.

principles-of-economics-1871-mengers-fou.context_blurb: In 1871 the Vienna economist Carl Menger published a slim book called Principles of Economics, in German Grundsaetze der Volkswirtschaftslehre, from the Vienna publishing house Wilhelm Braumueller. The book was one of three independent and almost simultaneous expositions of what historians now call the Marginal Revolution; the other two were William Stanley Jevons's and Leon Walras's work in Britain and Switzerland. Menger's version grounded economic value in the subjective theory of value: the worth of a good is set by the next specific unit a chooser is ranking, not by the labor it took to produce. The reasoning extends to the pricing of productive factors as well. Menger's book was argued in prose rather than in mathematical models, which gave his tradition a distinctive methodological character. His immediate students included Eugen von Boehm-Bawerk and Friedrich von Wieser. His son Karl Menger the younger, a mathematician, worked in a related Vienna world through the 1930s. In the Austrian tradition this book is the founding text; everything that follows in the Vienna school for the next century builds on it.

qe1-the-first-bond-buying-program-2008-1.context_blurb: QE1 is the shorthand name for the Federal Reserve's first large-scale asset-purchase program, running from November 2008 to March 2010. The Fed bought roughly one-point-seven-five trillion dollars of agency mortgage-backed securities and about two-hundred-and-fifty billion dollars of Treasuries. The purchases were paid for by crediting new reserves to the Fed accounts of the seller banks, which expanded the central-bank balance sheet by about two-point-three trillion dollars over the program. The Fed's stated purpose was to prevent depression by stabilizing MBS markets and keeping mortgage rates low. The Bank of Japan had run a similar but smaller quantitative-easing program from 2001 to 2006. In the Austrian reading, the Cantillon effect, named for the eighteenth-century Irish-French economist Richard Cantillon, became the organizing framework: those who receive newly created money first, including banks, hedge funds, financial-sector employees, and asset holders, benefit at the expense of those who receive it later. Austrian-tradition critics including Peter Schiff, Bob Murphy, and Jim Grant warned at the time. By the mid-2020s, central-bank balance-sheet expansion was a standing policy tool rather than an emergency-only measure.

rent-control-the-apartment-building-that.context_blurb: Rent control is a legal regime in which local or regional authorities cap the rent landlords can charge on specified housing units. The classic classical-liberal argument against rent control runs through non-price rationing: when the price does not clear the market, something else has to, typically queueing, personal connections, or in-kind payments called key money. In the Berlin 2020 Mietendeckel case the German Federal Constitutional Court struck down the law on federalism grounds within fourteen months. New York City's regime has run continuously since 1943. The Diamond-McQuade-Qian 2019 American Economic Review paper on San Francisco's 1994 extension found a rental-supply drop of roughly fifteen percent on the controlled stock. The Swedish economist Assar Lindbeck famously called rent control the surest way, next to aerial bombing, to destroy a city, after Stockholm's twenty-year waiting lists made the mechanism visible. In the Austrian reading, the specific unseen cost is the apartment buildings a developer would have built but did not, because future rents are capped below cost. The policy helps existing tenants and harms would-be tenants who never get a lease at all.

ronald-coase-transaction-costs-and-socia.context_blurb: Ronald Coase was a British-American economist who spent most of his career at the University of Chicago Law School and won the 1991 Nobel Memorial Prize in Economics. His two most-cited papers are his 1937 essay The Nature of the Firm, which asked why firms exist at all and introduced the concept of transaction costs, and his 1960 essay The Problem of Social Cost, which argued that in the absence of transaction costs the private parties to an externality can bargain to an efficient outcome themselves, regardless of the initial assignment of property rights. The latter result is now called the Coase Theorem. The field his work founded is now called transaction cost economics; his student Oliver Williamson later won a separate Nobel for extending it. Coase lived to one hundred and two and did late-career work on the Chinese reform experience. The internal structure of a firm, in his analysis, is characterized by command relationships between manager and employee, in contrast with the voluntary exchange of market transactions.

satoshi-nakamoto-and-the-white-paper.context_blurb: On October 31, 2008, a pseudonymous individual or group writing as Satoshi Nakamoto posted a nine-page paper to the cryptography mailing list, titled Bitcoin: A Peer-to-Peer Electronic Cash System. The paper described, in twelve sections, a cryptographic protocol for sending money directly between parties without any trusted intermediary. The specific technical challenge it solved, called the double-spending problem, is that a purely digital token can in principle be copied and spent twice; Satoshi's solution combined proof-of-work with a specific chain-ordering rule now called Nakamoto Consensus. The paper credits Adam Back's Hashcash and Wei Dai's b-money among its intellectual antecedents. The cryptographer Perry Metzger moderated the mailing list on which Satoshi posted. The Bitcoin network's software was released publicly in January 2009. Hal Finney was the second-ever node operator. By the mid-2020s Satoshi's own untouched holdings were estimated at about one million BTC. Satoshi disappeared from public view in 2011 and has not posted since. In the Austrian and cypherpunk reading the specific intellectual move the paper represents is that money could exist without any central issuing authority.

signature-first-republic-and-the-march-2.context_blurb: In March 2023 three American banks failed in quick succession. Silicon Valley Bank collapsed on March 10 after a large and swift withdrawal by its concentrated technology-sector depositor base. Signature Bank, which had been expanded during the earlier crypto boom with the help of former Representative Barney Frank on its board, failed on March 12. First Republic Bank was then propped up with a thirty-billion-dollar deposit injection by the eleven largest American banks before being seized and sold to JPMorgan Chase on May 1 at a price favorable to Jamie Dimon's firm. The common cause across the failures was held-to-maturity bond losses from the Fed's 2022-23 rate-hike cycle. Silvergate Bank had voluntarily wound down days earlier. The federal rescue invoked the systemic-risk exception in the FDIC Improvement Act, extending protection to uninsured depositors well above the standard limit. In the Austrian reading the whole episode is a worked example of the central bank's circular logic: the same institution that creates assets during a QE cycle exposes those assets to loss during the subsequent tightening cycle.

solyndra-2011-the-green-loan-guarantee-t.context_blurb: In 2009 the Obama administration approved a federal loan guarantee of roughly five hundred and thirty-five million dollars to a California solar-panel manufacturer called Solyndra. The company's design used a proprietary cylindrical thin-film panel that was expected to beat traditional flat-silicon panels on cost. By 2011 the company had collapsed. The specific proximate cause was the collapse of the world price of silicon from about four hundred dollars per kilogram in 2008 to about forty dollars per kilogram in 2011, which eliminated the cost advantage the Solyndra design was built on. The company's largest shareholder was the Oklahoma oil-and-gas investor George Kaiser through his Argonaut Ventures firm, a political donor. President Barack Obama had personally visited the plant and praised the investment. In the Austrian and Bastiat reading the episode is a worked example of Hayek's 1945 knowledge-problem argument: private investors' declined bets are dispersed information a central agency does not have. The whole sixteen-billion-dollar federal loan-guarantee program also funded Abound Solar and Fisker Automotive, both of which also failed.

sowells-there-are-no-solutions-only-trad.context_blurb: A compressed line from Thomas Sowell's writing captures a central discipline of his economic reasoning: there are no solutions, only trade-offs. The line is the first lesson of economics in Sowell's framing; its routine disregard is what he calls the first lesson of politics. Any proposed remedy for a social problem has specific costs, and the discipline is to name them and the specific people who bear them. The slogan-approach, which denounces the problem without specifying either the proposed replacement or its costs, is the political failure mode Sowell most consistently attacks. In his treatment of rent control the SEEN beneficiary is the tenant with the controlled lease; the UNSEEN cost appears in buildings that landlords stop maintaining and in rents that run higher than a free market's prices would in the uncontrolled portion of the stock. The specific question Sowell poses whenever a policy is defended is at what cost. The compared-to-what move is a sister discipline: hold every institution to the record it actually has, not to an imagined perfect alternative.

tariffs-the-consumer-who-pays-and-does-n.context_blurb: A tariff is a tax on imported goods. In classical-liberal and Austrian economics the central argument against tariffs is that the stated beneficiary, a specific named domestic industry, is visible, while the dispersed cost, higher consumer prices across every household that buys the taxed good or anything that uses it as an input, is spread so thinly that no comparable consumer lobby forms. The modern illustrative cases include US aluminum and steel tariffs: Trade Partnership Worldwide estimated the 2018 steel tariffs cost roughly nine hundred thousand dollars per primary-steel job added, and the downstream job loss across American manufacturing was in the range of seventy-five jobs per primary-steel job created. The historical cases include the 1930 Smoot-Hawley Tariff Act, which the Chicago-trained Senator Paul Douglas opposed. The 1963 Friedman-Schwartz Monetary History attributed the Great Depression's depth not to Smoot-Hawley but to the Fed's failure to prevent a one-third collapse in the money stock. In Bastiat's framing, the Petition of the Candlemakers is the compressed parody. In the public-choice reading the whole pattern is Mancur Olson's concentrated-benefit, dispersed-cost structure.

terra-luna-celsius-and-voyager-the-2022-.context_blurb: In 2022 a cluster of cryptocurrency companies collapsed in quick succession. The algorithmic stablecoin project Terra, and its sister token LUNA, imploded in May after the mechanical peg between the two tokens failed; approximately forty billion dollars of nominal value vanished within days. The founder Do Kwon later fled to Montenegro and was arrested. The lending platform Celsius froze customer withdrawals on June 12, 2022 and filed for bankruptcy on July 13. Its founder Alex Mashinsky was later charged with fraud and market manipulation of the Celsius token. The hedge fund Three Arrows Capital, with roughly four-point-seven billion dollars in assets, defaulted shortly after. The crypto broker Voyager Digital collapsed in parallel. In the Austrian and cypherpunk reading the lesson is that the companies that failed were cryptocurrency companies with an issuer or a promised-yield business model, while the Bitcoin protocol itself continued to operate normally. Customers who had held their Bitcoin in self-custody rather than at the collapsed companies were unaffected.

the-1989-collapse-arc-solidarity-to-berl.context_blurb: In 1989 the Communist regimes of Central and Eastern Europe fell in rapid succession. Poland's Solidarity trade-union movement, led by Lech Walesa, won a June 1989 election decisively, taking nearly every contested seat. Hungary opened its border with Austria in August 1989, letting East Germans flee to the West. On November 9, 1989 the East German spokesman Guenter Schabowski gave a confused press-conference answer that effectively opened the Berlin Wall. Czechoslovakia's Velvet Revolution followed in November. Romania's Nicolae Ceausescu was overthrown and shot on December 25, 1989. The Kremlin under Mikhail Gorbachev did not intervene militarily. The 1989 Tiananmen Square killings in China, in June of the same year, mark the one case in which a Communist regime did suppress its own protest movement with force. The American economist Robert Heilbroner later wrote in The New Yorker in 1990 that the Austrian economists, specifically Ludwig von Mises, had been right about the socialist calculation problem. In the Austrian reading, 1989 is the empirical settling of a seventy-year debate.

the-assignat-1789-1796-french-revolution.context_blurb: The assignat was the paper currency issued by the French revolutionary government between 1789 and 1796, initially backed by seized Catholic Church lands. Over the following seven years the issuance ran to over forty billion livres, roughly one hundred times the originally promised limit, and the currency hyperinflated. Refusal to accept the paper at face value was punishable by death. A successor currency called the mandat territorial repeated the pattern. The Cornell historian Andrew Dickson White's long essay Fiat Money Inflation in France remains the standard English-language account. The 1789-1796 French assignat and the Weimar German mark of 1921-1923 are the two most-cited European hyperinflations in modern Austrian-tradition writing. The 1718-1720 John Law episode and the 1775-1781 Continental are the Atlantic-world predecessors. In Bastiat's seen-and-unseen framing the SEEN was the legal-tender decrees and the price-control statutes; the UNSEEN was the goods vanishing from shops and the savers whose paper collapsed.

the-bitcoin-fixes-this-subculture-and-st.context_blurb: A particular Bitcoin subculture emerged in the 2010s organized around the slogan Bitcoin fixes this, applied to a long list of monetary, political, and institutional failures. The subculture distinguishes itself sharply from the broader umbrella term crypto, which it reads as including altcoins that compromise the fixed-supply engineering that makes Bitcoin interesting. Each Bitcoin is divisible into one hundred million satoshis, and the practice of accumulating satoshis in small regular purchases is called stacking sats. The subculture includes anonymous podcast hosts such as Cobie, whose real name is Jordan Fish, and intellectual figures who deliver talks on monetary history, sound money, and Austrian economics rather than trading tips. In the Austrian reading the whole subculture is a worked example of Hayek's spontaneous order: no central authority chose the cultural rules; they emerged from the dispersed decisions of participants who distinguished themselves from the broader crypto scene.

the-calculus-of-consent-1962.context_blurb: The Calculus of Consent: Logical Foundations of Constitutional Democracy, published by the University of Michigan Press in 1962, was the founding text of the public-choice school. It was co-authored by James Buchanan and Gordon Tullock. The book begins by applying the standard tools of economic analysis to the behavior of voters, politicians, and bureaucrats, treating them as rational actors with their own interests rather than as impartial servants of a diffuse public good. The core methodological move is the two-level distinction between the constitutional level, where rules are chosen behind a veil of uncertainty about one's own future position, and the post-constitutional level, where specific policies are chosen under the rules. The book preceded John Rawls's 1971 Theory of Justice, which uses a related device. The book's specific topics include supermajority rules, interest-group pressure, logrolling, and rational ignorance. Its central insight is that how the rules are chosen matters more than who wins under the rules. The book was funded in part by a grant from the Ford Foundation. Buchanan was later awarded the 1986 Nobel Memorial Prize for this and related work.

the-crime-of-73-and-bryans-cross-of-gold.context_blurb: In 1873 the US Congress effectively demonetized silver, placing the country on a de facto gold standard. The move was later denounced by advocates of the free coinage of silver as the Crime of '73. Through the following two decades US farmers who had borrowed in Civil-War-era greenbacks found themselves repaying in appreciated gold dollars, and the Populist and Free Silver movements rose in response. In 1896 William Jennings Bryan delivered his Cross of Gold speech at the Democratic National Convention and won the party's presidential nomination; he lost the general election to William McKinley. Shortly afterwards major new gold discoveries in the Klondike, the Witwatersrand, and Colorado produced the modest gold-driven inflation Bryan's silver platform had been designed to produce, and the Free Silver movement collapsed. There is no neutral choice between hard and soft money. A market-determined money supply that neither government nor lobby can inflate to redistribute wealth is the Austrian preferred alternative.

the-ethanol-mandate-and-the-2007-guatema.context_blurb: The United States Renewable Fuel Standard, enacted in 2005 and expanded in 2007, requires that a specific minimum volume of ethanol derived from corn be blended into American gasoline each year. In 2007 roughly forty percent of the US corn crop was being diverted to ethanol production. The result was a sharp rise in world corn prices, and in January 2007 tortilla prices in Mexico City triggered protests. Food-import-dependent populations in several developing countries, including Guatemala, saw their basic staple food price rise significantly. In the Austrian and Bastiat reading the mandate is a worked example of seen-versus-unseen at planetary scale: the SEEN beneficiary is a specific American agricultural interest; the UNSEEN cost is spread across more than one hundred million people in food-importing nations who paid higher prices for maize staples.

the-feds-dual-mandate-and-the-austrian-c.context_blurb: The Federal Reserve operates under a legal mandate established by the 1978 Humphrey-Hawkins Full Employment and Balanced Growth Act, named for Senator Hubert Humphrey. The act added the explicit requirement that the Fed pursue both maximum employment and stable prices. In the Austrian and monetarist reading, this dual mandate rests on an assumption that was arguably already falsified by 1970s stagflation: that there is a stable long-run trade-off between inflation and unemployment that policy can choose among. Milton Friedman's preferred alternative was a single, pre-committed rule: a constant money-supply growth rate. The Austrian reading predicts an employment-side bias producing systematic inflation error, because unemployment is politically salient in a way that low-grade inflation is not. The Fed's preferred inflation measure, the core PCE price index, excludes food and energy. The 2021 transitory-inflation episode is Austrian-tradition evidence for the predicted bias.

the-genesis-block-and-the-times-headline.context_blurb: The first block ever added to the Bitcoin blockchain, mined by Satoshi Nakamoto himself on January 3, 2009, is called the genesis block. Satoshi embedded in the block's text a specific sentence from a January 3, 2009 headline from The Times of London, referring to the UK Chancellor preparing a second bailout for banks. The embedded headline serves two purposes: it is a timestamp proof that the block was not pre-mined, and it is a direct public protest against the 2008 and 2009 bank-bailout culture that triggered the entire project. The second block was mined about six days later. The genesis block's fifty-BTC reward is permanently unspendable because of a quirk of Satoshi's code, which means it permanently removes fifty BTC from the effective circulating supply. In the Austrian and cypherpunk reading the whole arrangement is a declaration of independence naming the adversary in one sentence. The specific intellectual move is that a monetary system can bind itself to a rule at issuance and refuse the political discretion to break the rule later.

the-holodomor-stalins-ukrainian-terror-f.context_blurb: The Holodomor, meaning death by hunger in Ukrainian, is the name now given to the Soviet-engineered famine of 1932 and 1933 that killed somewhere between three-and-a-half million and seven-and-a-half million people in the Ukrainian SSR. Stalin's authorities imposed a deliberately unfillable grain quota, confiscated everything down to seed grain and food from the shelves, sealed the Ukrainian border to prevent escape, and blacklisted villages that failed to meet quota. The British historian Robert Conquest's 1986 book The Harvest of Sorrow was the first major English-language scholarly account. The American historian Anne Applebaum's 2017 Red Famine extended it. The European Parliament has formally recognized the Holodomor as a genocide. The specific agricultural collectivization program had killed roughly forty percent of Ukraine's draft horses in the preceding years. In the Austrian and classical-liberal tradition the Holodomor is one of the moral benchmark cases against which the twentieth-century communist death toll of roughly sixty-five to one hundred million people, from the Black Book of Communism, is calibrated.

the-lobbying-industry-1-4b-1998-to-4-1b-.context_blurb: Spending on registered American federal lobbying has grown from about one-point-four billion dollars in 1998 to about four-point-one billion dollars in 2023. The two largest spending sectors are pharmaceuticals and health products and the US Chamber of Commerce as an organization. Senior congressional staff who move into K Street lobbying typically see salary increases of five hundred to one thousand percent, which the economists Mirko Draca, Jordi Blanes i Vidal, and Christian Fons-Rosen documented in a paper titled Is It Whom You Know or What You Know? The specific legal framework for lobbying registration is the 1946 Federal Regulation of Lobbying Act, with foreign lobbying regulated separately under FARA. In the public-choice tradition the whole industry is Mancur Olson's logic operationalized. The concept of deadweight loss captures the resources dissipated in the lobbying contest itself rather than in productive economic activity. In the Austrian reading the whole structure is a textbook demonstration that the beneficiaries of concentrated regulatory benefits are the lobbyists themselves and their clients, not the dispersed public.

the-negative-railway-break-every-rail-li.context_blurb: One of Frederic Bastiat's parliamentary pamphlets, called The Negative Railway, parodied the French Chamber's proposal to introduce a deliberate interruption at Bordeaux on the Paris-to-Madrid rail line so that porters, innkeepers, and warehousemen in that specific city would have local business. Bastiat observed that if a single artificial interruption was good for the economy, then every town through which the line passed should get its own break, until the result was a series of unconnected roads that was not a railway at all. His modern successors, including Henry Hazlitt, have extended the parody to the recurring claim that labor-displacing technology destroys net jobs: the implicit argument runs that the spade is good because it needs workers, and therefore the wheel should be banned. Modern versions of the same argument apply the make-work logic to artificial-intelligence tools displacing writing jobs. In the Austrian and Bastiat tradition the whole pattern is read as a disguised version of the broken-window parable: artificial friction creates visible local work and hides the aggregate loss.

the-paradox-of-value-dissolved-diamond-w.context_blurb: The paradox of value is a classical puzzle: water is enormously useful to human life, yet trades at a very low price, while diamonds are useless to human life, yet trade at a very high price. Adam Smith proposed the vocabulary of value in use versus value in exchange and could not fully resolve the puzzle. David Ricardo and Karl Marx tried, with the labor theory of value, to locate value in the labor embodied in production. The 1871 Marginal Revolution of Carl Menger, William Stanley Jevons, and Leon Walras resolved the paradox by relocating value from a property of the good to a property of a choice: value is set by the ranking a specific chooser assigns to a specific additional unit against alternative uses. Water is abundant, so the marginal glass serves only a trivial use; diamond stock is near zero, so the marginal diamond ranks near the top of each buyer's priority list. In a desert the ranking reverses: one more glass of water now ranks above any additional diamond. The example of a farmer with five sacks of grain, each devoted to a progressively less urgent use, illustrates the general case. In the Austrian tradition the move dissolved the labor theory of value and the whole project of locating value in an objective property of the good itself.

the-powell-tightening-11-hikes-in-16-mon.context_blurb: Between March 2022 and July 2023 the Federal Reserve raised its target interest rate at eleven consecutive meetings, taking the rate from near zero to a range of five-point-two-five to five-point-fifty percent. Several of the hikes were seventy-five basis points each, unusually large by post-1980s standards. The Fed also conducted what it called quantitative tightening, reducing the size of its balance sheet. Short-term rate futures had been pricing a lower terminal rate just months earlier. The core consumer price index, excluding food and energy, remained the preferred inflation measure. In March 2023 the collapse of Silicon Valley Bank was the first visible financial-system casualty of the tightening cycle. In the Austrian reading the Fed is caught in a specific dilemma: raise rates enough to kill inflation and you break the financial system built on cheap money; hold rates lower and inflation stays elevated. A Fed operating alongside roughly one hundred and twenty percent federal debt-to-GDP faces a much lower ceiling on how high it can raise rates before the government's own interest cost becomes politically unsustainable. US stock markets had drawn down roughly twenty percent in 2022.

the-scholarly-rebuttal-to-macleans-democ.context_blurb: In 2017 the Duke historian Nancy MacLean published a book titled Democracy in Chains that portrayed James Buchanan and the public-choice tradition as a conspiracy to constrain American democracy on behalf of wealthy donors. The book became a New York Times bestseller and a National Book Award finalist. Economists and historians across the political spectrum, including the Austrian-adjacent Michael Munger at Duke in a Journal of Economic Literature review, documented systematic quotation out of context and misrepresentation of Buchanan's actual public-choice project. In the Austrian and classical-liberal tradition the episode has become a worked example of a specific pattern: when a work receives wide media acclaim but is met by systematic detailed rebuttal from experts across political affiliations, the specific pattern of the rebuttal is informative about the method of the original work. The underlying public-choice project it attacked is the thirty-year collaboration of Buchanan and Gordon Tullock on the Calculus of Consent and related books.

the-state-is-the-great-fiction-the-most-.context_blurb: Frederic Bastiat's most-quoted single line comes from an 1848 Journal des Debats essay titled The State: the state is the great fiction through which everyone endeavors to live at the expense of everyone else. The essay was aimed at the specific liberal-Orleanist bourgeois readership of the paper and worked by walking the reader through the arithmetic of what any promised state benefit must actually cost. Bastiat uses his recurring everyman character Jacques Bonhomme as a stand-in for the ordinary French citizen. The economist James M. Buchanan drew on the specific sentence in his later framing of the Virginia school of public choice. The companion 1850 pamphlet The Law extends the moral-political argument. The essay's specific target was the finance-committee practice of listing new state benefits without listing the corresponding tax or borrowing. In the Austrian and classical-liberal tradition the sentence is read as the compressed moral core of the whole fiscal-economics argument.

the-us-sugar-program-candy-jobs-that-fle.context_blurb: The US sugar program maintains domestic American sugar prices well above the world market level through a combination of import quotas, tariff-rate quotas, and loan guarantees. The specific legal architecture is called the Sugar Act in its various iterations. The predictable result is that American candy manufacturers, including Ferrara Pan and Brach's, have moved production to Montreal, where sugar is cheap. In Bastiat's seen-and-unseen framing, the SEEN beneficiary is the small, politically concentrated group of American sugar growers, most prominently the Fanjul family of Florida; the UNSEEN cost is paid by every American consumer of sugar and by every American candy worker whose job moved to a jurisdiction with free world-price sugar. In the public-choice reading the whole program is Mancur Olson's concentrated-benefits-and-dispersed-costs structure in textbook form. Bastiat's own Petition of the Candlemakers is the compressed classical parody.

the-white-papers-twelve-sections.context_blurb: Satoshi Nakamoto's October 2008 Bitcoin paper is about nine pages long and is organized into twelve numbered sections. The opening section opens with a sentence about commerce on the internet relying almost exclusively on financial institutions serving as trusted third parties, and the paper's central claim is that cryptography and consensus can remove that dependence. The acknowledgements credit Adam Back's Hashcash and Wei Dai's b-money. The specific technical innovations named in the paper include proof-of-work consensus, Merkle trees as a space-efficient way to summarize transaction history, and Simplified Payment Verification abbreviated SPV for lightweight client software. The paper is unusually short for the scale of its influence. The closing conclusion runs to roughly two paragraphs. In the Austrian and cypherpunk reading the specific intellectual accomplishment is that a nine-page paper from a pseudonymous author founded a monetary system whose fixed supply has become one of the most-studied monetary experiments of the twenty-first century.

trygve-hoff-and-the-1938-restatement.context_blurb: Trygve J. B. Hoff was a Norwegian economist whose 1938 book, published in Norwegian and later translated into English as Economic Calculation in the Socialist Society, synthesized the Mises-Hayek argument on the socialist calculation problem by drawing on German, Anglo-American, and Soviet-planning sources together. His book was the most comprehensive statement of the Austrian position in the late 1930s. During the Second World War the Nazi occupation of Norway arrested him, and he spent much of the war in prison and a concentration camp. After the war he was among the founding members of the Mont Pelerin Society in 1947. His book was eventually republished by the Ludwig von Mises Institute. In the Austrian tradition Hoff represents the generation of continental European classical-liberal economists whose work was interrupted by the war and who carried the pre-war Vienna tradition into the postwar institutional landscape.

venezuelas-bitcoin-mining-and-the-clap-b.context_blurb: Venezuela in the 2010s produced an unusual natural experiment in two parallel informal economies. Electricity, whose domestic price was set far below production cost by the government, made Bitcoin mining extraordinarily profitable for anyone with hardware; mining operations grew to a visible industry until the Nicolas Maduro regime sent political-intelligence police to raid and seize rigs. In parallel, a specific government food-distribution program called CLAP, standing for Comites Locales de Abastecimiento y Produccion, distributed subsidized food boxes conditioned on political loyalty, including PSUV party membership, rally attendance, and voting as instructed. The economist Alejandro Machado and the writer Jill Carlson have documented the parallel economies. In the Austrian reading the whole arrangement illustrates Ludwig von Mises's 1920 argument on economic calculation in acute real-time form: without market prices, the Venezuelan state cannot allocate food or capital rationally, and ordinary citizens respond by routing around the arithmetic through the underground global market via Bitcoin on one hand and through political loyalty via CLAP on the other.

wei-dai-and-b-money-november-1998.context_blurb: In November 1998 the American cryptographer Wei Dai, best known for the open-source cryptographic library Crypto++, posted to a cypherpunk mailing list a short description of a scheme called b-money. B-money proposed a specific alternative to Chaum-style trusted-issuer digital cash: every user would maintain a separate copy of every other user's balances, with proof-of-work tying new money issuance to real computational effort. Dai did not solve two central technical problems: how to reach consensus on transaction ordering, and how to keep ledger-keepers honest. He wrote at the time that the proposal was intended to be provocative rather than practical. Ten years later Satoshi Nakamoto emailed Dai in August 2008 asking for comments on the draft Bitcoin paper, and the eventual Bitcoin white paper acknowledges b-money alongside Adam Back's Hashcash as a direct intellectual antecedent. The later cryptocurrency Ethereum uses Dai's name for its smallest unit of account. In the Austrian and cypherpunk reading, b-money is the direct conceptual bridge between the trusted-issuer era of Chaum and the trustless-consensus era Satoshi's design made possible.

why-the-austrians-won-the-1989-verdict.context_blurb: The 1989 collapse of the Soviet bloc, visible to the world in the fall of the Berlin Wall in November, is read in the Austrian tradition as the empirical settlement of a seventy-year debate. Ludwig von Mises's 1920 essay Economic Calculation in the Socialist Commonwealth had argued that without market prices for capital goods, central planners cannot know whether a proposed use of resources creates or destroys value. The 1990s brought additional data: Mikhail Gorbachev's glasnost opened the archives, Deng Xiaoping's reforms and Vietnam's Doi Moi programs produced the market-with-Communist-Party-states that still exist today, and The Black Book of Communism counted the roughly sixty-five to one hundred million deaths across twentieth-century communist regimes. The specific technical point the Austrian tradition had made was that the dispersed knowledge of time and place held in millions of minds cannot be aggregated and processed by any central authority. The mainstream economics profession absorbed the empirical result while, oddly, keeping Oskar Lange's blackboard-arithmetic verdict in its textbooks. The specific intellectual move Hayek had made in 1945 was the knowledge-problem argument.

zimbabwe-2007-2009-the-100-trillion-note.context_blurb: Between 2007 and 2009 Zimbabwe under Robert Mugabe underwent one of the most severe hyperinflations in modern history. At its November 2008 peak the annualized inflation rate was estimated at about seventy-nine-point-six billion percent. The central bank eventually issued a one-hundred-trillion-Zimbabwe-dollar note. The specific trigger was a fiscal deficit from a collapsed tax base, combined with central-bank money-printing to close the gap. In 2009 ordinary Zimbabweans spontaneously adopted foreign currencies, including the US dollar, the South African rand, and the Botswana pula, before the government formally dollarized. The old banknotes now sell as souvenirs on collector markets for a few US dollars each. In the Austrian and Bastiat reading, the SEEN beneficiaries of the regime's money-printing were the soldiers and civil servants receiving pay; the UNSEEN cost was every existing citizen's savings destroyed. The specific empirical lesson the Zimbabwe episode left is that modern hyperinflations are not relics of the 1920s; they can still happen and did happen in the twenty-first century.

adam-back-s-hashcash-and-reference-6.context_blurb:
In 1997 Adam Back, a British cryptographer, offered a small fix for junk email that he called Hashcash. Back belonged to the cypherpunks, a scattered online circle of programmers who dreamed of digital cash without banks. Eleven years later his little trick became one of the load-bearing beams of Bitcoin. It rests on one observation: make something costly to produce but cheap to check.

Spam exists because an email costs its sender almost nothing. Back's idea was to make every message carry a stamp of computer effort, a small puzzle that keeps the sender's machine busy for about half a second. A person who writes twenty messages a day spends ten seconds of computing on them and never notices. Multiply that half-second by a million messages, though, and the puzzle work stretches into hours or days. A spammer simply could not afford to keep going, because the puzzles would swallow his machines' time.

Computer scientists call such a lopsided puzzle, slow to solve yet checked by the recipient in a blink, proof-of-work. The idea is a little older than Hashcash; Cynthia Dwork and Moni Naor had described something like it in 1993. In the mid-2000s Microsoft's mail servers tried Hashcash-style postmarks against spam through a research effort called Penny Black. The stamps never spread everywhere, because every email program on earth would have had to switch at the same moment.

Other cypherpunks saw money in the stamp. Wei Dai's b-money proposal of 1998 and Hal Finney's Reusable Proof-of-Work, or RPOW, in 2004 both leaned on Hashcash to sketch a currency made of costly computation. In August 2008 a pseudonymous programmer, Satoshi Nakamoto, emailed Back for comments on a draft, and that October he put the same puzzle-work at the heart of Bitcoin's mining. Because each new coin costs real electricity to mint, nobody can flood the network with cheap coins, and that cost is what makes the coins scarce.

Satoshi's nine-page white paper, posted on Halloween 2008, ends with a short list of eight earlier works; Back's Hashcash paper sits in sixth place, as Reference 6, while the very first entry is Wei Dai's b-money. The network that grew from the paper has no owner, no chief executive and no foundation guarding its code. Since the software is public, anyone anywhere can improve the network without asking permission, and rival teams keep one another honest. Back himself co-founded the company Blockstream in 2014, one of many teams that contribute to Bitcoin Core.

Inside Bitcoin the old spam stamp took on a second job it never had in email. Joined to the rule that the longest chain of work wins, proof-of-work became the way thousands of computers settle on one agreed order of transactions without any central coordinator. Bitcoin writers look back on Hashcash as a turning point. Before it, anything digital, a song, a photo or a game, could be copied for free. Back's stamps were the first digital tokens that cost real electricity to make yet could be checked for almost nothing: the first working taste of digital scarcity.

andrew-jackson-vetoes-the-second-bank-of.context_blurb:
Andrew Jackson, the frontier general who rode a populist wave into the presidency in 1828, spent much of his two terms trying to destroy a bank. The Second Bank of the U.S. was the nearest thing the young country had to a central bank. Jackson's war on it is a vivid reminder that a central bank is not a law of nature but a decision made by politicians.

Congress created the Second Bank in the wake of the War of 1812, in 1816, for a twenty-year term, as the successor to Alexander Hamilton's First Bank, whose charter had lapsed in 1811. From its headquarters in Philadelphia it issued notes that passed across the country and held the Treasury's money, and from 1823 Nicholas Biddle ran it. Jackson looked at the Bank's owners, wealthy men of the East and investors abroad, and saw a danger to the republic: a small group holding control over the whole nation's money.

On July 10, 1832, Jackson vetoed the recharter bill. His veto message warned that the rich and powerful too often bend the acts of government to selfish ends; a privilege like the Bank's, he wrote, helped make the rich richer and made the potent still more powerful. The struggle between Jackson and Biddle that followed, lasting until the charter ran out in 1836, is remembered as the Bank War.

Freshly reelected, Jackson began moving the government's deposits out of the Bank in 1833. Biddle fought back with the weapon he had: he squeezed credit hard across the country to bring on a recession, hoping voters would blame the president and force a new charter, a plan his own letters document. Jackson parked the federal money in a handful of state banks friendly to him, and his enemies mocked them as pet banks, political allies rewarded for loyalty.

Tradition says that in 1834, when a delegation of the Bank's directors came to plead with him, Jackson called them a den of vipers and thieves and swore he would rout them out. Historians still dispute the exact source, but the line captures his tone. Jackson won. The charter expired in 1836, and for seventy-seven years, until the Federal Reserve Act of December 1913, the country ran on private and state banks with no national central bank of any kind, though it suffered periodic panics.

Jackson's enemies were not only political. On January 30, 1835, an assailant, Richard Lawrence, came at him at the Capitol with two pistols. Each percussion cap went off, yet neither gun fired its main charge, a double misfire later reckoned at odds of about 125,000 to 1, and Jackson went after his attacker with his cane before bystanders subdued him. Jackson blamed friends of the Bank. The whole episode teaches one recognition about central banks: whether a country has one is a political choice, never a technical necessity. A determined president killed this one, and only a fresh political consensus, generations later, brought a central bank back.

applied-olson-farm-subsidies-sugar-tarif.context_blurb:
In 1965 the American economist Mancur Olson published The Logic of Collective Action, a short book that explains one of the strangest facts of politics: why a policy that helps a few people and costs nearly everyone else can survive for decades. His answer had nothing to do with conspiracy. It was simple arithmetic about who bothers to organize.

Suppose a few thousand farmers receive a government bonus for growing sugar or cotton and spreads the bill across the whole country, a few pennies per shopper. The farmers have a fortune at stake, so they fight hard to keep the payment, while each taxpayer barely notices his share, which is why such rules are almost never repealed. The modern American system dates from the Agricultural Adjustment Act of 1933, and every Farm Bill since has kept it alive. A subsidy also changes what gets planted: paid extra for a crop, a farmer grows more of it than buyers in the market would want on their own.

The purest case is sugar. Import quotas, together with price supports, shelter about 4,000 American sugar producers and push the price of sugar in the United States to about twice the world price. Those producers collect roughly a billion dollars a year from the program, while each of 330 million shoppers pays only a few extra dollars on everything sweetened. So the 4,000 producers are far easier to organize: they form trade associations and hire lobbyists, while nobody starts a club to save three dollars a year.

The same arithmetic explains occupational licensing. In 1950 about one American worker in twenty needed a state license to work; by 2020 roughly one in four did, from barbers and florists to hair braiders and tour guides. Each license hands a small group a big prize while millions of customers each pay a small hidden cost, and economists sum up that lopsided bargain in four words: concentrated benefits, diffuse costs. Licensed insiders, such as funeral directors, dental hygienists and cosmetologists, lean on state boards to make the rules stiff and expensive. The people hurt most are the would-be newcomers, and they cannot fight back, because they are not yet in the profession and so have no association to join and no members to rally. When a state makes hair braiders sit through hundreds of classroom hours and pay hundreds of dollars for a cosmetology license, competition drops, so insiders' wages rise and newcomers find it much harder to get started. The economist Morris Kleiner, often working with Alan Krueger, has measured that wage premium and entry barrier across dozens of trades and states.

The loudest voices in state capitols for these laws belong to the existing workers in each field, who want fewer competitors. The variety among states is a natural experiment: Louisiana licenses florists, tour guides and hair braiders, while Wyoming and other Western states license far fewer jobs. Olson's cases all follow one rule. Whenever a small lobby reaps large rewards and the bill is scattered in tiny amounts over a vast public that hardly notices, the lobby nearly always wins; the standard shorthand for the pattern is concentrated benefits, dispersed costs.

Picture a farm law that pays half a million farmers about $20,000 a year apiece and costs each of 100 million taxpayers about $100 a year. The farmers battle for it, and most taxpayers never hear of it: concentrated benefits, dispersed costs once again. The remedy, for Olson's heirs in James Buchanan's constitutional tradition, is to lift such decisions out of ordinary politics, where the sugar lobby wins every year, to a level that small groups cannot easily capture. Their standard tools are constitutional-level rules, judicial review, and sunset clauses that make a program expire unless lawmakers renew it in full view.

basic-economics-2000-800-pages-no-graphs.context_blurb:
Thomas Sowell studied economics at the University of Chicago after starting out as a young Marxist, and he became one of the free market's clearest defenders. In 2000, at about seventy, he wrote a book for working adults who had never sat in an economics class. The result is the book most often handed to a curious teenager as a first serious read in the subject.

Basic Books published it, and Sowell gave it the plainest title he could: Basic Economics. Over five editions it grew to around eight hundred pages, built from case studies rather than abstract theory. Its boldest choice is what it leaves out, because from cover to cover the book has no graphs, no equations and no algebra. That was a deliberate break, since Sowell's own 1971 textbook had used the usual graphs and formulas.

Rather than proceed theory by theory, Sowell groups his chapters by institution, under headings such as prices, production, work and pay, time and risk, and the national and international economy. Each part teaches through real cases, from rice farming in Ghana and American rent control to labor rules under apartheid and the economies left behind by Soviet rule. It keeps returning to the same few questions: what are the trade-offs, compared to what, what are the incentives, and who bears the unseen costs?

The backbone is a definition from the British economist Lionel Robbins, who wrote in 1932 that economics studies the use of scarce resources that have alternative uses. Because hours, money and energy always run short while wants never do, every daily decision is a trade-off, where choosing one use means giving up the others. Fans call the book the long version of a short classic from 1946, Henry Hazlitt's 'Economics in One Lesson', which a reader can finish in an afternoon. Hazlitt's single lesson was to trace a policy's effects not only on the people it obviously touches but on every group, over the long run.

Its reach comes from that plain design. The book has been translated into eight or more languages, and home-school families use it widely as their main economics text, because a student needs no math background to follow it.

bear-stearns-and-the-2-share-weekend-res.context_blurb:
Bear Stearns, founded in 1923, was one of the five biggest investment banks on Wall Street and was deep in the business of mortgage-backed securities. In March 2008 it collapsed over a single weekend. The way the Federal Reserve handled that weekend set a precedent, and the precedent shaped a far worse panic six months later.

Bear ran on borrowed money, rolled over night after night. A firm that must borrow every evening to open its doors the next morning cannot last more than a few days once its lenders take fright and refuse, and that is exactly what happened when Bear's overnight lenders stopped renewing its loans. Officials raced to arrange a sale before markets opened on Monday, because they feared the collapse would spread and frighten every other bank. JPMorgan Chase, led by Jamie Dimon, agreed to buy the wreckage with help arranged by the Fed, at an opening price of two dollars a share. Bear's stock had traded at $172 fourteen months earlier; shareholders threatened to sue, and a week later JPMorgan raised its offer to $10.

To get the deal done, the Fed set up a company called Maiden Lane, named after the New York Fed's street, which took about $30 billion of Bear's worst mortgage securities off the books, paid for with a Fed loan that could be repaid only from those same securities. The bad assets ended up with the Federal Reserve, and through it with American taxpayers. Shareholders and executives took heavy losses, but one group came through whole. Bear's creditors and counterparties, the very lenders and trading partners whose panic had caused the run, were paid in full. Critics warned at once about moral hazard: protection against a disaster makes the disaster likelier, because a bank that expects the Fed to catch it gambles with taxpayers' money instead of its own.

By September 2008, half a year on, Lehman Brothers was dying the same way. The firms still lending to it and trading with it expected the Fed to broker a similar rescue, with Lehman's creditors also paid in full. Instead, on September 15, the Fed and the Treasury let Lehman fail. Two economists from opposite camps had warned in spring 2008 that saving Bear would tempt the next bank into bigger gambles: Nouriel Roubini of New York University on the left and the Austrian-minded investor Peter Schiff on the right. Both were brushed aside at the time.

The Austrian reading turns on expectations. Every rescue rewrites what markets expect in the next crisis, so suddenly withdrawing a rescue everyone expected can cause the very panic the earlier rescue was meant to prevent; Lehman's fall was so violent partly because Bear had taught Wall Street to count on a save. The story also has a human footnote. In July 2007, as two hedge funds inside Bear collapsed, its chairman, Jimmy Cayne, was reportedly away playing in a bridge tournament. Critics drew the lesson that the leaders of giant firms can lose touch with what is really happening inside their own companies.

bitconnect-and-onecoin-the-pure-ponzi-al.context_blurb:
In the 2010s two of the largest frauds of the decade hid behind the excitement around Bitcoin. BitConnect and OneCoin dressed themselves up as cryptocurrencies, but underneath they ran one of the oldest tricks in finance. To Bitcoin's defenders they are cautionary foils, proof that a coin with a promoter at the controls is a very different thing from Bitcoin.

Start with the arithmetic of the pitch. A site promising 1 percent a day would multiply a hundred dollars about thirty-seven times over in a single year, while a United States Treasury bond, about as safe as lending gets, pays around 4 percent a year. No real business can pay that much, so a promise like that is almost always a scam. The trick has a name. Charles Ponzi, who had come to Boston from Italy, promised huge profits in 1920 from international postal coupons, paid his early investors with money from later ones, rewarded anyone who brought in new depositors, and collapsed within a year. A fraud of that shape has been called a Ponzi scheme ever since.

BitConnect, launched in 2016, claimed its returns came from a secret trading bot that no one could inspect. In January 2018 state regulators in North Carolina and Texas ordered it to stop taking money; its coin fell from about $400 to almost nothing within days, and depositors lost about $2.4 billion. Its founder, Satish Kumbhani, was indicted in the United States in 2022 and remains a fugitive. What makes such a scheme a Ponzi rather than an investment is where the payouts come from: old investors are paid with new investors' money, not with real earnings.

OneCoin was bigger still. Its founder, Ruja Ignatova, born in Bulgaria and styling herself the Cryptoqueen, launched it around 2014, filled London's Wembley Arena for promotional events and marketed it across the globe as Bitcoin's successor. When investigators took it apart, they found no working blockchain at all; the ledger was simply an internal database whose numbers her own staff typed in. Prosecutors in the United States, Britain and Germany estimate that investors poured in somewhere between 4 and 15 billion dollars, dwarfing BitConnect's losses.

On October 25, 2017, with American and German investigators closing in, Ignatova boarded a Ryanair flight from Sofia to Athens, Greece, and she has never been seen in public again. On June 30, 2022, the FBI placed her on its Ten Most Wanted Fugitives list.

Longtime Bitcoin teachers such as Andreas Antonopoulos, author of the technical guide Mastering Bitcoin, object when reporters lump every coin together as crypto. Bitcoin, they insist, is a specific 2009 protocol with a proven fixed supply, a different category of thing from most projects that borrow the word, which have an issuer who can change the rules; that power is exactly what BitConnect and OneCoin exploited. Austrian-minded writers add a historical lesson. Promising fixed high returns through a vague mechanism and paying them out of new deposits is a pattern far older than the technology it wears: these schemes were Ponzi's 1920 fraud in new clothes, and Ponzi himself needed no technology at all.

broken-window-applied-to-katrina-and-9-1.context_blurb:
Frédéric Bastiat, a French economist, told a story in 1850 that has never stopped being useful. A shopkeeper's boy breaks a window, and the neighbors console the father with the thought of all the work it gives the glazier. Every few years a disaster revives the same cheerful claim, that destruction is good for the economy, and Bastiat's essay remains the standing reply.

After a disaster flattens a city block, someone always says that at least the rebuilding will create jobs. The rebuilding is the part everyone sees. The hidden part is where that money was headed before the disaster: it was going to buy other things people wanted, so the catastrophe creates no new spending, it only diverts old spending and leaves the town a block poorer. In the original story, the whole street watches the glazier pocket his six francs, but nobody notices the coins he had meant to spend elsewhere, on a pair of shoes or a book. Bastiat's essay, Ce qu'on voit et ce qu'on ne voit pas, gives that vanished second purchase its name: the thing not seen.

Cash for Clunkers, the federal program of 2009, officially the Car Allowance Rebate System, gave dealers a voucher worth $3,500 or $4,500 for every old gas-guzzler traded in for a more efficient new car. Each trade-in was then destroyed: the dealer ran its engine on a dose of sodium silicate until it seized for good, and the car went to the crusher. The money, $3 billion, ran dry within fifty-five days that summer, by which time 677,081 vehicles had been scrapped.

Writers at the Mises Institute and the Cato Institute went looking for the unseen cost. Taking some 677,000 working cars off the used market pushed prices up at the cheap end, so the burden fell hardest on lower-income buyers, whose only choice is a used car costing a few thousand dollars. In 2013 a Brookings Institution study by Ted Gayer and Emily Parker found that the vouchers had mostly moved forward purchases that buyers would have made anyway a few months later. The summer surge in sales was largely cancelled by a slump in the months after.

The same flaw runs through cheerful talk after a hurricane. The money and time spent rebuilding a coastal town could have built something new instead, just as the shopkeeper's six francs could have bought shoes. Three days after the September 11 attacks, the economist Paul Krugman wrote that the country suddenly needed new office buildings; Bastiat's readers, among them the George Mason economist Don Boudreaux, answer that replacing what was destroyed is not growth. Boudreaux's co-blogger Russell Roberts, host of the podcast EconTalk, turned the idea into fiction in 2008 with The Price of Everything, a novel in which an earthquake strikes Palo Alto and soaring prices steer bottled water and generators to where they are needed most.

The grandest version of the fallacy says that the Second World War cured the Depression. Wartime output soared as factories turned out tanks, ships and planes, but in the 1990s the economic historian Robert Higgs looked at what households could actually buy. Meat, sugar, tires, gasoline and new cars were rationed, and everyday goods for ordinary families barely improved on Depression levels until the soldiers came home. Bastiat had packed the whole answer into the four-word French line that ends his broken-window story: Destruction n'est pas profit, destruction is not profit.

capital-and-interest--1884-1909---the-ro.context_blurb:
Eugen von Böhm-Bawerk, a student of Carl Menger in Vienna, set out in the 1880s to answer an old question: why does anyone pay interest at all? His multi-volume Capital and Interest became the classic Austrian treatise on capital and time. Its answer, that waiting is a real contribution with a real price, later became the foundation of the Austrian theory of the business cycle.

Picture a fisherman on a lake. He can splash into the shallows and snatch fish with his bare hands right away, or he can give up a whole day to knotting a net, landing nothing until it is done, and then haul in far more every day for weeks. Böhm-Bawerk called that longer path roundabout production: using tools, and tools to make tools, so that more output comes later. Eugen von Böhm-Bawerk published his first volume in 1884, and the second, in 1889, set out his own answer, later known as the time-preference theory of interest.

Karl Marx had called interest and profit a theft from the workers. Böhm-Bawerk replied that interest pays for something the saver really gives up, since by handing over his money today he postpones everything he could have enjoyed with it now. The saver, in short, is paid to wait. Why is a loaf in hand worth more to people than an identical loaf a year away? People expect to be better provided for later; they undervalue future wants, partly because they may not live to enjoy them and partly because wants shift; and a good in hand can be set to work producing still more goods. His three grounds, taken together, explain the existence of interest.

If $100 lent out for twelve months comes back as $105, the extra $5 rewards the waiting, because the lender put off enjoying his money for a year. Böhm-Bawerk traced an earlier version of this abstinence idea to the Oxford economist Nassau Senior. Behind it all lies a plain fact. The fisherman weaves before he fishes, the farmer makes his plow before he sows, and a carmaker installs its assembly line before the first car leaves the plant: production takes time. Because someone must release resources today for output that will exist only later, someone must be paid to bridge the gap.

The grounds have names. The first is the expectation of future prosperity, and the second is the habit of underestimating future wants. The third, the most disputed, is the technical edge of longer, more roundabout processes of production, which would keep interest positive even if the first two failed, since roundabout methods yield more output from the same inputs. Offer anyone $10 today or the same $10 in exactly a year, and nearly everyone takes it today. Austrians call that habit time preference: people prize goods and money now over the same sum later. The American economist Frank Fetter argued that time preference alone explains interest, which makes the third ground unnecessary.

To the modern socialist who calls interest unearned because the money only sat in an account, Böhm-Bawerk's reply needs neither risk nor entrepreneurship. The saver supplies waiting, releasing present resources so that future output can exist, and interest is the market price of that waiting. That is why Austrians object when a central bank forces rates to zero. Building on Böhm-Bawerk, Mises and Hayek treated the interest rate as the price of time itself, the measure of how much people value goods now against goods later. Push it down by decree and entrepreneurs start more roundabout projects than real savings can finish.

cato-institute-founded-1977.context_blurb:
The Cato Institute is a libertarian think tank, founded in San Francisco in 1977 and moved to Washington, DC, in 1981. It grew into a main home for economists of the free-market and public-choice schools writing about taxes, regulation and money. Its story includes an eighteenth-century pen name, a famous split, and a lawsuit brought by its own founding backers.

Three men started it: Ed Crane, a young organizer who became its first president; Charles Koch, the Kansas oil industrialist who was its chief early funder; and Murray Rothbard, the fiery Austrian economist who served as its intellectual leader. The name comes from Cato's Letters, political essays that John Trenchard and Thomas Gordon published in London's newspapers from 1720 to 1723 under the pen name Cato. They chose it to honor Cato the Younger, the Roman senator who stood against Julius Caesar, and their letters, which attacked corruption and defended liberty, were reprinted across the American colonies and helped inspire the revolutionary generation.

Rothbard did not stay. In 1981, after a bitter quarrel with his co-founders over strategy and staff, he was pushed out, and in 1982 he and Lew Rockwell founded a rival, the Ludwig von Mises Institute in Auburn, Alabama, which took a more radical Austrian line than Cato's Washington policy work. Cato's long-serving chairman, William Niskanen, put public-choice thinking at its core. His 1971 book Bureaucracy and Representative Government argued that officials push to grow their agencies' budgets and staffs, since a bigger agency brings better pay, prestige and influence, which predicts that agencies will keep expanding whether or not the problem they exist to fix ever gets solved.

In 2012 Charles and David Koch, the brothers who ran the giant private firm Koch Industries, sued Cato in a fight over control of its board. For several anxious months the case threatened the institute's independence; it was settled, Ed Crane stepped down as president in favor of the banker John Allison, and Cato stayed independent.

Cato stands apart from two older free-market groups. Leonard Read's Foundation for Economic Education, founded in New York in 1946, set out to educate the general public, and Hayek's Mont Pelerin Society, begun in 1947, was a private network of scholars gathering in Swiss resorts. Cato's specialty is day-to-day influence on Washington policy: testimony before Congress, events for congressional staff, and studies aimed at real legislation. Named for that Roman republican, whom America's founders admired as an emblem of defiance against tyrants, the Cato Institute publishes its long-form scholarship in the Cato Journal.

coase-1960-the-problem-of-social-cost-in.context_blurb:
Ronald Coase, born in England and by then teaching in the United States, published a paper in 1960 that became one of the most cited in all of law and economics. It took aim at the standard view, from the English economist Arthur Pigou, that harms like pollution call for a corrective government tax. Coase asked different questions: who holds the right, and can the two sides bargain?

It appeared in October 1960 in the Journal of Law and Economics, under the title The Problem of Social Cost. Picture a steel mill whose smoke leaves the families next door coughing, while its owner pays none of their medical bills. A cost that lands on other people instead of on the one who causes it is called an externality, and Pigou, in The Economics of Welfare of 1920, wanted a tax to correct it.

Coase's startling point was that the harm runs both ways. The smoke hurts the neighbors, but a ban on it hurts the mill just as surely, because it stops production. The real question is not who is at fault but which use of the resource creates more value. His most famous example was a rancher whose cattle stray into a neighboring farmer's crops. If the two can talk cheaply, the cattleman may pay for fencing, or the grower may pay him to fence in his herd, and either way the resource ends up with whoever values it most. The law decides who pays, not where the land and crops finally go.

When bargaining is cheap, the two sides reach the same efficient outcome whichever of them the law protects, and George Stigler named that result the Coase theorem in his 1966 textbook. Coase thought the textbook version a misreading. When bargaining is costly, as among hundreds of neighbors, government action may be worth it, he wrote in The Firm, the Market, and the Law (1988), but the government's own costs of acting must be counted too. His idea of clear, tradeable rights inspired real markets: tradeable permits to pollute, such as America's acid-rain program of 1990 and Europe's emissions market of 2005, and individual transferable fishing quotas in Iceland and New Zealand.

The paper also led Elinor Ostrom to examine how actual villages look after resources they hold in common, from mountain pastures in Switzerland and irrigation systems in Spain to fisheries in Turkey and forests in Nepal. Her 1990 book, Governing the Commons, showed communities running such resources for centuries with neither a state nor a private market in charge. Coase's two great papers, the 1937 essay on why firms exist and the 1960 one on social cost, run to only about sixty pages together. Yet the Swedish academy gave him the 1991 Nobel for discovering and clarifying the significance of transaction costs and property rights for the institutional structure of the economy.

Coase kept warning against one bad habit: setting an untidy real market beside a flawless imaginary government, or the reverse, and then declaring a winner. His rule was to compare real institutions with each other, never a real one with an idealized alternative, counting the transaction costs of firms, markets, private bargains and governments alike. The frictionless world of the textbook theorem, in his own reading, does not exist. Transaction costs are high in the real world, so who holds the rights at the start matters enormously, and so does the design of institutions.

country-level-adoption-after-el-salvador.context_blurb:
Since 2021 a handful of governments have run the first real experiments in what it means for a nation to embrace Bitcoin. They took very different paths, from legal tender in Central America and Africa to quiet mining in the Himalayas. Their stories show how much a country's circumstances matter.

On September 7, 2021, El Salvador, under its young president Nayib Bukele, became the first country to make Bitcoin legal tender beside the US dollar. Bukele had announced the plan that June at a Bitcoin conference in Miami, and on launch day the government released its Chivo wallet and gave each adult citizen $30 in bitcoin. Legal tender means that stores and businesses are legally required to accept the money as payment, so the law, and not only the market, makes it acceptable everywhere.

In April 2022 the Central African Republic followed, the second nation to make Bitcoin legal tender, but it lacked a reliable power grid, few people owned smartphones, and the International Monetary Fund objected. Its parliament repealed the law in March 2023, less than a year later, the shortest national Bitcoin experiment yet. In Argentina, voters tired of soaring prices and swollen government offices elected the libertarian economist Javier Milei in 2023. At rallies he brandished a real chainsaw, the symbol of his promise to slash government spending and cut whole agencies. He took office on December 10, 2023, and has praised Bitcoin and allowed contracts written in it, without making it legal tender.

The Himalayan kingdom of Bhutan, home to about 700,000 people and rich in hydroelectric power from its mountain rivers, chose a quieter path. Since about 2019 it has mined Bitcoin with that hydropower and built up one of the largest Bitcoin reserves held by any government, an estimated 13,000 coins or more by 2024. The International Monetary Fund pressed El Salvador to reverse its law, citing risks to financial stability. Bitcoin's supporters said the deeper reason was a feature central bankers cannot copy: no central bank controls Bitcoin's supply, so no policy can inflate it.

Which national path was right? A Hayekian economist declines to crown one, because different tradeoffs suit different countries. The Central African Republic showed that infrastructure matters as much as a legal declaration, Argentina offers deregulation without a mandate, and Bhutan turns stranded energy into savings. Its mining is run not by a ministry but by Bhutan's sovereign wealth fund, Druk Holding and Investments, which converts hydropower that would otherwise be exported or wasted into a portable asset with a fixed supply.
