david-friedman-and-the-machinery-of-free.context_blurb:
David Friedman, born in 1945, is the son of Milton Friedman, the Nobel laureate, and Rose Director Friedman. He earned a doctorate in theoretical physics before turning to economics and law, which he later taught at Santa Clara University. In 1973 he published the book that made his name, a guide to a society that does without government entirely.

That book, The Machinery of Freedom: Guide to a Radical Capitalism, argued that everything from policing and courts to highways and currency could be supplied by competing businesses and voluntary associations. Father and son disagreed about the state itself. Milton was a classical liberal who wanted a minimal state, limited to defense, courts and a few other tasks, while David is an anarcho-capitalist who argues that no state is needed at all.

Rather than simply declaring government bad, the book works through concrete machinery: private judges competing for business, rival protection agencies, money issued by private firms, roads paid for by those who drive on them. His core move is to describe how specific mechanisms would work and let the reader judge the design for himself.

Friedman shares his conclusion with Murray Rothbard but not his reasoning. Rothbard argued from natural rights, that every person owns himself and so taxation is theft. Friedman set rights aside and made a consequentialist case, that a stateless society would produce better outcomes for most people most of the time. In 2019 he and two other scholars, the George Mason economist Peter Leeson and the political scientist David Skarbek, published Legal Systems Very Different from Ours, a survey of real societies that settled disputes without a central state, from Somali xeer and the sagas of Iceland to rabbinical courts, the Amish and the Roma.

The family's line runs a generation further. In 2008 David's son, Patri Friedman, founded the Seasteading Institute, which hopes to build floating communities on the open ocean, outside every nation's laws, and Peter Thiel was an early funder. For the third edition of The Machinery of Freedom in 2014, Friedman did something the 1973 and 1989 editions had not: he released the book as an open-source text, free for anyone to read online, a fitting choice for a book about removing gatekeepers.

dekulakization-stalins-1929-liquidation-.context_blurb:
At the end of 1929 Joseph Stalin, ruler of the Soviet Union, turned the state against the most capable farmers in the countryside. The campaign, known as dekulakization, shot, deported or uprooted millions of peasants and cleared the way for collective farms. It ended in famine, and it stands among the crimes counted in The Black Book of Communism's tally of 65 to 100 million deaths under communist regimes.

Kulak, Russian for fist, was the propaganda label for any peasant a little better off than his neighbors; a second cow, a hired hand at harvest or a few extra sacks of grain could be enough. Police and soldiers seized such families by the millions, shooting many and shipping the rest to camps in Siberia and Kazakhstan, so that several million people were killed, starved or deported. In a speech in Moscow on December 27, 1929, Stalin announced that the state would liquidate the kulaks as a class, a phrase that quickly became notorious.

On January 30, 1930, the Politburo, the party's ruling council, turned the speech into policy. It sorted kulak families into three categories: those to be shot, those to be deported to the far north, Siberia or Kazakhstan, and those to be resettled locally on poor land. About 30,000 alleged kulaks were shot. From 1930 to 1932 about 2 million more were crammed into cattle cars, sometimes a whole village at once, and sent to labor settlements far to the east, while another four or five million lost their property.

Dekulakization was more than class war. It removed the most experienced farmers before collectivization, so that the collective farms into which peasants were being forced would meet no organized resistance. The secret police, the OGPU, which became part of the NKVD in 1934, ran the deportations and built the special settlements in Siberia, the Urals and the far north, where death rates in the winter of 1931 to 1932 were catastrophic. Local activists stretched the label until any villager who resisted the collective farm could be deported, a move they called unmasking, exposing the stubborn peasant as a kulak in disguise.

The historian Lynne Viola reconstructed the system from newly opened police archives in The Unknown Gulag. Its real aim was to force farmers off their land so that the state could seize every farm and run it. Ukraine, the richest grain country in the empire, was stripped of its best farmers first. Moscow kept its grain quotas high anyway, requisition squads stripped the villages of their remaining food, and in 1932 and 1933 the Holodomor famine in Ukraine killed several million people.

Party newspapers presented the campaign as seizing rich peasants' property for the sake of social justice. That was the seen. The unseen cost was the permanent loss of farming skill, the knowledge of which field to sow with which seed and when, and the famine that followed.

dodd-frank-2010-the-community-banks-that.context_blurb:
In 2010, answering the financial crisis of 2008, Congress passed the Dodd-Frank Act, named for Senator Chris Dodd and Representative Barney Frank. Running past 800 pages, it was one of the largest overhauls of financial law in American history, and it took aim at the giants of Wall Street. Public-choice economists argue that its heaviest weight fell somewhere else.

Rules like these, by which a government tells banks and companies what they may and may not do, go by the general name of regulation. The act set up a brand-new agency to watch over the loans families use most, such as home mortgages, payday loans and credit cards: the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, championed by Elizabeth Warren, then a Harvard professor. It also wrote in the Volcker Rule, named for the former Fed chairman Paul Volcker, on the principle that a bank whose deposits carry government insurance should not gamble that money by trading for its own profit.

The burden of compliance fell hardest on smaller local banks. About seven thousand commercial banks existed in 2010; by 2023 roughly 4,700 remained, a fall of about a third, and most of the missing banks were bought by larger rivals rather than closed. New banks nearly stopped appearing. Before the law, regulators approved about 130 start-up banks a year, but in the six years after it fewer than six a year won charters, though regulators had also lengthened their review of new banks in 2009.

The reason is arithmetic. Picture a rule requiring every bank to hire five more lawyers. A giant such as JPMorgan spreads that cost over sixty million customers, next to nothing per customer, while a small-town bank with a few hundred customers pays the same salaries; fixed rule costs hurt small players most, as Charles Calomiris and Stephen Haber argued in their book Fragile by Design. Bruce Yandle's name for the coalition that keeps such rules alive is Bootleggers and Baptists, after Sunday liquor bans that churches backed for moral reasons and illegal liquor sellers backed because legal stores had to close. In banking, reformers supply the moral case while the biggest banks quietly welcome rules their smaller rivals cannot afford.

The lesson recurs: rules written for the biggest players usually crush the small ones hardest. In 2018 a bipartisan law signed by President Trump eased part of the burden on smaller banks, a concession that fixed compliance costs had shrunk community banking without making the system safer.

economic-sophisms-the-wider-satire-colle.context_blurb:
Before his famous pamphlets of 1850, Frédéric Bastiat made his name with a collection of short satires, thirty-nine essays published in Paris in a first series in 1845 and a second in January 1848. Each took aim at a protectionist or socialist argument then alive in the French Chamber, stating it at its strongest and then taking it apart. He titled the collection Economic Sophisms, and many of its essays let the arguments play out through his everyman, Jacques Bonhomme.

One example runs through the book. A tax on foreign shoes lets domestic shoemakers charge more, which looks like a gift to them, but every family that buys shoes now pays more for them and so quietly funds the gift. In another satire a small-town mayor bans the sharp axe, reasoning that if woodcutters must use dull ones, chopping each log will take three men instead of one and so create jobs; the joke exposes every make-work argument.

The first series opens with an essay titled Abundance and Scarcity, which argues that the point of producing is plenty and cheapness, so a policy that makes goods scarcer and dearer has the goal backward. The best-known piece in that series is a mock petition in which the candlemakers of France beg the government for protection against an unfair foreign rival that floods the country with free light every morning: the sun. Bastiat aimed his sharpest satire at make-work schemes, which the left of his day loved, and at tariffs shielding domestic producers, which the right loved, and he turned the same method on both; that even-handedness makes the collection a lesson in method.

Back to the shoes. When foreign shoes are kept out, the shoemakers cheer and everyone else pays more, while the country's tailors, who used to sell jackets to pay for those imported shoes, lose sales too. Bastiat taught readers to look for exactly that kind of cost: the hidden one, paid by many and spread so thin that it is easy to overlook. Patrick James Stirling's English translation of 1873 was the standard text for generations, and Jane Willems's translation for the Liberty Fund is the best modern edition.

The same method reached its peak in Bastiat's broken-window story of 1850. When a crowd tells the shopkeeper that the glazier's pay will make the town richer, Bastiat answers that they count only one side: the money the shopkeeper would have spent on something else is now gone for good.

eric-hughes-and-a-cypherpunk-s-manifesto.context_blurb:
In the early 1990s, before most families owned a computer, a few programmers in California's Bay Area began meeting to talk about cryptography, the mathematics of secret codes. They called themselves the cypherpunks. Their founders were Eric Hughes, Timothy May and John Gilmore, and they asked a question that matters more every year: in a wired world, who will protect your privacy?

Their reply was that no one would, except you, armed with mathematics. A message scrambled with strong encryption can be opened only by the person it is written for, so its privacy rests on mathematics rather than on anyone's promise. Nobody needs to rely on a phone company or a state to guard the secret.

On March 9, 1993, Hughes posted A Cypherpunk's Manifesto to the group's mailing list, which Gilmore, an early employee of Sun Microsystems and a co-founder of the Electronic Frontier Foundation, hosted on his server.

The manifesto opens with a distinction. Privacy, Hughes wrote, is not the same thing as secrecy: a secret is something you want nobody to know, while a private matter is something you simply don't want the whole world to know. His most quoted line defines privacy as a power, the power to choose which parts of yourself you reveal to the world. Privacy, in other words, is your choice about what to share.

Its second claim is that nobody will hand privacy over as a gift. Hughes warned that people cannot expect governments and corporations, or any other large faceless organization, to grant them privacy out of kindness, because those are the very bodies that want to watch and track them. So the privacy-minded would have to build the tools themselves.

That leads to the manifesto's motto, three words long: "Cypherpunks write code." Hughes had no patience for privacy campaigners who gave speeches and wrote essays but never shipped a working program. Privacy would exist in the world only if someone actually built the software and gave it away.

The movement took the motto seriously. Its members wrote encryption programs and digital-cash designs, and their focus, in money as in speech, was the freedom to send messages and payments without anyone watching. Hughes and his friend Hal Finney helped build anonymous remailers, servers that took in an email, erased the return address and passed it along a chain of other machines, so an eavesdropper could not trace a message back to its author or its starting point.

Fifteen years after the manifesto, a coder calling himself Satoshi Nakamoto carried the cypherpunk playbook to its end. He published the Bitcoin paper in October 2008, launched the working network in January 2009, and by April 2011 had stepped away, leaving a system no single person controls. His path ran in four steps: a paper, working code, a live network, and then his own exit.

One historian of the movement argues that the manifesto reads less like a wish than like a working plan. On that reading, the motto is really a rule about proof: until a tool actually ships and works, the hope of privacy protects no one, and a dream of privacy is not yet a privacy technology.

fda-drug-approval-peltzman-and-the-patie.context_blurb:
Every new medicine sold in America must first be cleared by the Food and Drug Administration. That sounds like pure protection, and much of it is. But economists in Bastiat's tradition ask a harder question: what happens to the sick people who wait while a good drug sits in the queue?

The modern rules grew out of a disaster. Late in the 1950s a European drug firm marketed the sleeping pill thalidomide to expectant mothers as a cure for morning sickness, and thousands of babies were born with badly malformed arms and legs. In the United States the FDA reviewer Frances Kelsey refused to approve it, so American babies were largely spared, and President Kennedy honored her in August 1962. Lawmakers took the lesson that new medicines must be tested carefully before the public can buy them.

That same year the Kefauver-Harris Amendment became law. Until then a drugmaker only had to show a new medicine was safe; from 1962 on it also had to prove that the medicine actually worked.

Ten years on, Sam Peltzman, an economist at the University of Chicago, tallied what the rule had cost sick people who were waiting. In a 1973 study he found that the flow of new medicines to patients shrank sharply after the law. Before 1962 about forty brand-new drugs had arrived each year, and his model predicted roughly forty-one annually had the rules stayed the same. Instead the yearly count fell to about 16, a drop of some sixty percent.

Peltzman then did the accounting. On one side he set the benefit of blocking worthless drugs; on the other, the harm of good drugs delayed or never launched. He put the net result in shoppers' terms: the 1962 amendments worked like a tax of 5 to 10 percent on every prescription sold.

Why does the agency lean toward delay? In the 1970s the FDA's commissioner, Alexander Schmidt, observed that Congress had never once investigated the agency for failing to approve a drug, while hearings attacking it for approving one were too many to count. A drug that hurts people brings angry hearings and blame by name, but a delay that lets sick people die quietly brings nothing at all. That one-sided pressure gives the agency every reason to be over-cautious and slow to approve new medicines.

Alex Tabarrok, an economist at George Mason University, gave the hidden victims a place. A regulator can err in two ways: it can approve a drug that harms, or it can block one that would have saved lives. The first mistake has a name and a face. The second leaves people dying of their illness in deaths that look ordinary, so nobody counts them as the price of a decision, and Tabarrok says they lie in the invisible graveyard.

So when a senator proposes stretching drug review until no unsafe pill could ever reach a pharmacy, economists like Peltzman and Tabarrok do not call safety a bad goal. They ask Bastiat's question instead: what happens to the patients still waiting in line for treatment, and who is counting them?

fidel-castros-cuba-1959-2016-exit-as-ver.context_blurb:
On January 1, 1959, Fidel Castro's rebel army entered Havana and took power in Cuba. Castro ruled for nearly half a century, and over those decades roughly one Cuban in seven left the island, many of them gambling their lives at sea. Classical-liberal economists read that flight as a verdict: when people are able to leave, the direction they move tells you what they think of a system.

Once in power, Castro took over the island's farms, factories and stores, and the state began deciding what would be produced, where each person would work and what each would earn. A system in which the ruling party owns and directs the whole economy is communism.

One early choice shows the cost. Castro put Ernesto "Che" Guevara, a guerrilla commander with no training in business or economics, at the head of the National Bank of Cuba in 1959 and later of the Ministry of Industry. When a revolutionary state seizes the plantations and hands the economy to commanders without expertise, output of the main crop collapses, and Cuba's sugar harvest fell sharply during Guevara's years.

Dissent was punished hard. Armando Valladares, a young poet, would not put a pro-Castro sign on his desk at work; he was arrested in 1960 and spent twenty-two years in prison before French pressure won his release in 1982. His memoir, Against All Hope, changed many minds abroad, because it gave first-hand proof from a man who had lived through the prisons himself.

In April 1980 six Cubans drove a city bus through the gates of the Peruvian embassy in Havana and asked for asylum. Castro angrily withdrew the guards, and within two days some 10,800 Cubans had crowded onto the embassy grounds begging to leave.

Castro then announced that anyone who wanted to go could sail from the port of Mariel. From April to October 1980 boats crammed with families crossed to Florida in the Mariel boatlift, carrying about 125,000 Cubans, and Castro emptied prisons and mental hospitals into the flow to embarrass the United States. A mass flight like that sends a plain message: people were escaping a system that had failed them.

Then, in 1991, the Soviet Union fell apart, and with it went the subsidies, the cheap oil, the food and the money that had kept Cuba's planned economy afloat. Fuel, spare parts and fertilizer vanished, blackouts became routine, oxen went back into the fields, and the average Cuban lost about twenty pounds as output fell by about a third in three years. Castro's government gave the long crisis a gentle official name, the Special Period in Time of Peace, usually shortened to the Special Period.

In mid-1994, at the depth of that slump, tens of thousands of Cubans built rafts from inner tubes and wooden pallets and pushed off toward Florida, ninety miles away across shark-filled water. About 35,000 of these balseros, or rafters, crossed in six weeks. The shortages had become so severe that people would gamble their lives on the open sea to get out.

By 2016, the year Castro died, Cubans living abroad together with their American-born children came to roughly one and a half million people, about a seventh of the island's population of some eleven million.

friedman-and-schwartz-the-great-depressi.context_blurb:
Why did the stock-market crash of 1929 turn into the Great Depression, a disaster that lasted a decade? In 1963 two economists gave an answer that the Federal Reserve itself would one day accept: America's central bank had let the nation's money supply collapse.

The two were Milton Friedman and Anna Schwartz, and their book, known simply as A Monetary History, ran to some 860 pages covering a century of American money and banking. Ben Bernanke, a later chairman of the Fed, called its account of the Depression the finest ever written of the worst economic disaster in American history.

At its heart is chapter seven, "The Great Contraction." From 1929 to 1933, Friedman and Schwartz showed, the broad money supply, the money people held in cash and in bank accounts, shrank by about a third, roughly 33 percent, while the Fed stood aside.

Shrinking money and bank runs fed each other. Of the roughly 25,000 banks open for business when the crash came, about 9,000 failed between 1930 and 1933, and since there was no deposit insurance until 1933, each failure wiped out its depositors' savings and squeezed the money supply further.

Why did the Fed stand aside? Part of the answer was one man. Benjamin Strong, the Fed's leading figure for more than a decade, died suddenly in October 1928, and without him the regional reserve banks feuded and drifted with no clear plan, which shows how heavily a single institution can be shaped by one person.

Part of the answer was an idea. Many Fed officials followed the real-bills doctrine, which in its harsh liquidationist form told the central bank to refuse help to any bank it considered unsound and to let such banks go under, purging the system. Those were exactly the banks that needed help, so the doctrine ensured the Fed withheld the cash that could have stopped the cascade.

So Friedman and Schwartz laid the blame for the decade-long catastrophe on one institution, the Federal Reserve. Friedman won the Nobel Prize in 1976; Schwartz, his co-author, never did.

Austrian economists, led by Murray Rothbard in his own 1963 book, America's Great Depression, agreed that the Fed had failed but pointed to an earlier decade. In their reading the Fed's cheap credit of the 1920s built stocks and factories that honest interest rates would never have supported, so the crash and the Depression were the inevitable hangover that follows an artificial boom.

For decades the Fed rejected the Friedman-Schwartz charge. Then, on November 8, 2002, at a Chicago conference for Friedman's ninetieth birthday, Fed governor Ben Bernanke, himself a historian of the Depression, turned to the two authors and gave in. He told them they were right, the Fed had done it, the Fed was very sorry, and thanks to them it would not do it again.

That admission mattered. When the very institution under criticism accepts its critics' thesis, it changes how that institution thinks about its own crisis responses, for better or worse. Bernanke's Fed met the 2008 crisis with aggressive emergency lending and massive money creation, determined not to repeat the 1930s, and Austrian critics argue that in avoiding one error it planted another: years of cheap money that fed the inflation of the early 2020s.

Anna Schwartz did not join the applause. In an October 2008 interview with the Wall Street Journal, at ninety-two, she sharply criticized Bernanke's crisis response, charging that he had no real grasp of what was going on.

fritz-machlup-mises-kreis-to-princeton-a.context_blurb:
Fritz Machlup, born in Austria in 1902, was one of the Vienna-trained economists who carried the Austrian school to America. He is remembered for putting a number on something nobody had measured: how much of a modern economy consists of producing and sharing knowledge itself.

He began in Vienna. In 1923 he finished his doctorate in Vienna under Ludwig von Mises, who in 1920 had shown why socialist planners, lacking genuine prices, cannot calculate costs. Machlup became one of the youngest members of Mises's private seminar.

From Mises and Hayek he took the idea that prices are messages. When the price of bread suddenly jumps, it tells everyone, without a word from any official, that bread has grown scarcer or that more people want it, so buyers should use less and bakers should make more.

Austrian economists read trade figures the same way, looking past the headlines. When an American family buys a Japanese car or Colombian beans, its dollars go overseas, but the family has not lost anything: in exchange it gets goods it freely chose to buy.

In 1933 Machlup moved to America on a Rockefeller research fellowship, and he went on to teach at Buffalo, Johns Hopkins, Princeton and New York University. In 1947 he was among the founding members of the Mont Pelerin Society, the circle of about forty classical-liberal scholars that Hayek gathered in the Swiss mountains, which still meets every year.

In 1962, teaching at Princeton, he published The Production and Distribution of Knowledge in the United States. It was the first serious effort to measure a part of the economy no one had counted, the schools, research labs, publishers, media and information services, and he estimated that knowledge production made up about 29 percent of America's output in 1958. Machlup spoke of a knowledge industry, and his figure launched the study of what is now called the knowledge economy, years before the phrase became a business-magazine cliché.

His peers gave him their highest honor: in 1966 they elected him President of the American Economic Association, a rare summit for an economist trained by Mises.

Late in life he set out to expand the 1962 study into a vast multi-volume work, Knowledge: Its Creation, Distribution, and Economic Significance, whose volumes Princeton University Press brought out between 1980 and 1984.

greenspan-takes-over-and-black-monday-19.context_blurb:
In the summer of 1987 Alan Greenspan took charge of the Federal Reserve, America's central bank. Within weeks he faced the worst single day in the history of the American stock market, and the way he handled it set a pattern that Austrian economists say shaped the next twenty years of booms and busts.

The Fed's chairman is chosen by the President, but he cannot take office until the Senate votes to confirm him. Greenspan was confirmed and sworn in on August 11, 1987.

On Monday, October 19, 1987, the Dow Jones average dropped by more than a fifth, 22.6 percent, in one session, a far bigger one-day fall than any day of 1929. A sudden, panicked plunge like that, with everyone trying to sell at the same moment, is a market crash.

Part of the blame went to a new computer-driven strategy. In the mid-1980s Mark Rubinstein, Hayne Leland and John O'Brien had sold big investors portfolio insurance, software that automatically dumped stock-index futures as prices fell, to cap their losses. On Black Monday many firms' programs sold at the same moment, and each wave of selling triggered the next.

Early the next morning, October 20, Greenspan's Fed issued a one-sentence statement. In it the central bank declared itself ready to act as a source of liquidity, meaning cash, to support the economic and financial system. The Fed cut rates and pumped money into the banks, and within days the panic eased.

By about two years later the S&P 500 had climbed back to its peak of the summer before the crash.

The rescue worked, and that was the trouble. Whenever markets dropped hard afterward, Greenspan's Fed cut rates and supplied cash again, and traders named the pattern the Greenspan put, after the option contract that protects its owner against a fall in price.

In March 1988 President Ronald Reagan also set up a standing group of top financial officials to coordinate the response to future crises, and the press soon nicknamed it the Plunge Protection Team. Austrian critics say that repeated rescues of falling asset prices teach investors that a bailout is likely, so they feel safe taking ever bigger risks.

In the moral-hazard reading, 1987 taught markets that the Fed would step in during every major decline, and that expectation fed the appetite for risk behind the dot-com bubble of the 1990s and the housing bubble of the 2000s.

The deepest point is a tension at the heart of central banking. A rescue can succeed brilliantly in the short run and still teach markets exactly the wrong lesson about risk for the long run.

Greenspan's past made all this surprising. In the 1950s and 1960s he had belonged to the novelist Ayn Rand's Objectivist circle in New York, a hard-money, individualist movement, and in 1966 he wrote an essay for her newsletter, Gold and Economic Freedom, defending gold-backed money. The man later called the Maestro for easing whenever markets wobbled had once argued for money no central bank could print.

halving-cycles-and-market-patterns.context_blurb:
Bitcoin's supply follows a timetable written into its code, and anyone can read it decades in advance. One rule in that timetable, the halving, has lined up with a striking four-year rhythm in Bitcoin's price. Austrian-minded writers see in that rhythm an old monetary pattern, but honest analysts also warn against treating it as a promise.

Every 210,000 blocks, roughly once in four years, the protocol halves the payment miners collect for each new block they add. That scheduled event is called the halving. It has happened in November 2012, July 2016, May 2020 and April 2024, and it is why the total supply can never exceed 21 million coins.

Bitcoin's price has swung on something like a four-year beat, with big peaks that mostly came twelve to eighteen months after a halving. The approximate tops: roughly $30 in 2011, about $1,100 in 2013, near $20,000 in 2017, about $69,000 in 2021 and, in 2024, above $100,000.

Each cycle follows the same arc: a steep fall from the top, quiet buying near the bottom, a slow climb, then a wild spike. Austrian-minded writers compare it to the boom-bust cycle that Mises and Hayek tied to changes in the supply of money, a theory first set out in the early 1900s.

The best-known case for that reading is The Bitcoin Standard, published in 2018 by the economist Saifedean Ammous. He argued that Bitcoin's fixed issuance, halved on schedule, enforces a hard-money discipline no government can break.

In 2019 an anonymous analyst calling himself PlanB published a model that claimed to predict Bitcoin's price from its scarcity alone, fitting a curve to past prices. It was called the stock-to-flow model. Since roughly 2021 actual prices have drifted far away from its forecasts.

The cycle after the 2024 halving broke the old timing. Bitcoin crossed six figures late in 2024, roughly eight months after that halving rather than a year or more. Part of the reason was a new kind of buyer: US spot Bitcoin exchange-traded funds, which the SEC approved on January 10, 2024, letting ordinary brokerage accounts hold Bitcoin.

So what should a new holder make of the pattern? The honest answer is that past cycles are real observations, but the most recent one already broke the pattern, and a pattern from the past never guarantees the future.

human-action-1949-misess-magnum-opus.context_blurb:
In 1949 Yale University Press published a book of nearly nine hundred pages by an elderly Austrian refugee living in New York. Ludwig von Mises's Human Action set out to build all of economics from one starting point, and it became the book from which almost all modern Austrian economics begins.

Mises had written it once already. In 1940, living in exile in Geneva, he finished a long German version, Nationaloekonomie, just weeks before France fell; he then rewrote and expanded it in English after reaching New York.

Its first chapter opens with a short sentence on which Mises rested the whole treatise: human action, he declared, is behavior with a purpose. Everything else, he argued, can be reasoned out from that fact.

That makes economics more like geometry than chemistry. Begin with the fact that people act on purpose, every choice ranking some options above others and taking one, and reason outward step by step; Mises called the method praxeology. He rejected positivism, the view that economics should copy the natural sciences by forming hypotheses and testing them against data, and he held that history can illustrate economic laws but never prove them.

Only individuals choose. Markets, societies and economies are the results of countless individual choices that no one planned from above. Mises called this rule methodological individualism.

Value starts in people too. A glass of water means everything to a traveler lost in the desert and almost nothing to someone beside a lake, because value depends on who wants a thing and when. Economists call this subjective value.

Chapter 26 brings back the argument Mises first published in a German journal in 1920, the essay that opened the debate over whether full socialism could work: without market prices, rational calculation under socialism is impossible.

The same reasoning shapes the Austrian view of monopoly. Mises and his student Murray Rothbard argued that a lasting monopoly is almost always created by government, because only the law can keep rivals out for long. Where no law blocks them, a company that keeps its prices high soon finds new competitors coming in to undercut it.

The man behind the book lived on unusual support. At New York University Mises held an unpaid visiting post, and for many years a private foundation, the Volker Fund, covered his salary. Funding scholars the universities would not pay is a classic case of private philanthropy.

Its subtitle, A Treatise on Economics, explains its nickname. Inside the Austrian tradition, people who say "go read the treatise" mean Human Action, and Rothbard's Man, Economy, and State was written as its direct successor.

israel-kirzner-alertness-and-entrepreneu.context_blurb:
Most economics textbooks of the mid-twentieth century described markets already at rest, with every price settled. Israel Kirzner asked who moves a market toward those prices in the first place. His answer, the alert entrepreneur, became one of the Austrian school's central ideas.

Picture a girl who notices that her school cafeteria sells only cold drinks, even on freezing winter mornings. She brings a big thermos of hot chocolate, sells it by the cup at lunch, and has money left after paying for cocoa and cups. Someone who spots an unmet need and starts a business to meet it is an entrepreneur.

A Londoner by birth, in 1930, who spent his boyhood in South Africa, Kirzner came to New York for graduate school. His doctoral teacher at New York University, where he finished in 1957, was Ludwig von Mises, then teaching there after fleeing Europe, and Kirzner became the most important of Mises's doctoral students. He taught at NYU until he retired in 2002, and he is also an Orthodox rabbi.

His dissertation traced how economists over the centuries had defined the borders of their own field, and in 1960 he turned it into his first book, The Economic Point of View.

His breakthrough came in 1973 with Competition and Entrepreneurship. Its key idea fits in a single word: alertness. Two people walk past the same empty lot every day; one of them notices that families heading to the park on hot afternoons would buy cold lemonade, and his stand thrives. What he had that the other lacked was alertness.

For Kirzner, then, the entrepreneur's real skill is not bearing risk or driving hard bargains. It is noticing a chance for profit that everyone else has missed: a gap in the market, say goods selling cheaply in one place and dearly in another, or a product no one yet offers.

Kirzner wrote partly in answer to Joseph Schumpeter, who told a stormier story. In Schumpeter's account inventors of new technology sweep away established firms and entire industries, a process he called creative destruction. Kirzner disagreed about where opportunities come from. The entrepreneur does not create them out of nothing; he finds openings that already exist, waiting for someone sharp enough to see them.

Profit, in this view, carries information. Suppose a crate of oranges fetches far more in one village than in its neighbor, and a trader carts some from the cheap village to the dear one. The profit he earns signals to everyone that resources had been wasted in the low-value town, and his move pulls them to where people value them more.

In 2006, in his mid-seventies, Kirzner received the Global Award for Entrepreneurship Research, presented in Stockholm and often called the top honor in the study of entrepreneurs.

john-law-and-the-mississippi-bubble-1716.context_blurb:
In 1715 King Louis XIV died and left France nearly bankrupt from his wars. A Scottish gambler and financier, John Law, who had fled Britain after killing a man in a duel, won the trust of the regent ruling for the boy-king Louis XV. Law promised to cure France's debts with paper money, and he built Europe's first great paper-money mania.

In 1716 Law founded the Banque Generale in Paris, which issued paper notes. In 1718 the crown took it over and renamed it the Banque Royale, and its notes were guaranteed by the government. In 1717 Law also launched the Mississippi Company, which was granted the sole right to develop and trade with France's vast Louisiana territory.

Law tied the bank and the company into a loop that fed itself. The bank printed notes; investors used the notes to buy company shares; the rising share price made people want still more notes to buy with; and the bank printed them.

Between mid-1719 and early 1720 the shares soared from about 500 livres to around 10,000 livres each, roughly twenty times over. When share prices soar wildly on a tide of easy money and then collapse, the episode is called a bubble. So many small Paris shareholders grew rich on paper that the French language coined a new word for them: millionaire.

By February 1720 the bubble was cracking. Big shareholders began cashing out and demanding metal instead of paper, so Law reached for the law itself and banned private ownership of gold coin and bullion beyond small amounts. It failed within weeks.

When too much printed money chases the same goods, each note loses value fast, which is inflation, and Law's paper lost almost everything. It crashed, and thousands who had trusted the notes lost their savings when the bubble burst. Law fled France in December 1720 and died poor in Venice in 1729.

France tried again during its Revolution. In 1789 the revolutionary government seized church lands and issued paper notes, the assignats, said to be backed by that land. It printed more and more of them to pay its bills, and within a few years the notes were nearly worthless: a hyperinflation, with prices exploding as the money lost its value.

Austrian economists see Law's scheme as the earliest modern example of a pattern Mises later explained. The deeper cause of such booms and busts, they argue, is a flood of cheap money and easy credit. Credit expansion poured into one favored sector, the Louisiana company, and the whole structure collapsed the moment holders tried to redeem their paper for real money.

julian-simon-and-the-ultimate-resource.context_blurb:
In the 1970s many educated people were sure humanity was about to exhaust everything: food, oil, metals, room. The economist Julian Simon thought they had it backwards, and in 1980 he put his money where his mouth was. The bet that followed is still the most famous test of the doomsday view.

The doomsday case had a bestseller behind it. The biologist Paul Ehrlich's 1968 book, The Population Bomb, predicted that hundreds of millions would starve in the 1970s because the planet held too many people. The famines never came; farm yields kept climbing and population kept growing. The lesson is that confident predictions of doom often turn out to be badly wrong.

Simon's answer came in a 1981 book whose title named its main idea: The Ultimate Resource. The real limit on progress, he argued, lies not in oil, metal or grain but in the human mind. People are producers of ideas as well as mouths to feed, and when something grows scarce, free people invent substitutes and better methods. The ultimate resource, in short, is human ingenuity and problem-solving.

He backed the claim with prices. Over two centuries in which the number of people on earth multiplied, the inflation-adjusted prices of most raw materials, from copper and tin to wheat and iron, have fallen over the long run. If resources were truly running out, those prices would be climbing.

So in 1980 Simon offered a public bet. Anyone could choose any five metals and any period from one to a hundred years, and he would wager that their real prices would fall. Ehrlich accepted with two colleagues, John Harte and John Holdren, putting up $1,000 in all over ten years. They chose tin, tungsten, copper, chromium and nickel.

The bet ran from September 1980 to September 1990. When it closed, every one of the five had fallen in real price, so all five metals went Simon's way, and a check for the difference arrived that October.

The bet shows how to measure scarcity honestly. Headlines and forecasts can say anything, but a falling real price is the truest sign that something is growing less scarce, the most honest empirical evidence there is.

Ehrlich has argued ever since that the decade was unusual and that his broader warnings still stand. That larger debate continues, but the record of the bet itself is not in doubt: all five metals fell in real price, and Ehrlich lost on every commodity.

Simon's argument was the opposite of population control. Calls for governments to impose one-child policies belong to the alarmist camp he argued against, never to Simon's case. The British writer Matt Ridley carried his outlook forward in the 2010 book The Rational Optimist. Progress, Ridley argued, comes from ideas meeting and mating, much as people do, through free trade and exchange among millions of ordinary people, not from planners at the top.

kenneth-arrows-impossibility-theorem-195.context_blurb:
Democracies count votes and announce a winner as if the result simply reveals what the voters wanted. In 1951 a young American economist proved with mathematics that the matter is not so simple. His result still unsettles anyone who talks confidently about what the people have decided.

Kenneth Arrow published the proof in a short book drawn from his doctoral work at Columbia University: Social Choice and Individual Values. The title names the two sides of the problem, the group's choice and each person's own values.

Arrow listed a few fairness rules that any method of combining votes into a group ranking ought to obey. One says that if every voter prefers option A to option B, the group must rank A above B; it is called Pareto efficiency, or unanimity. Another, non-dictatorship, says that no single voter may decide the group's ranking whatever everyone else wants. A third, the independence of irrelevant alternatives, says the group's choice between two options should not flip because of a third.

Then he proved that no method can keep all of these rules at once. A perfectly fair procedure for turning everyone's individual votes into one group choice cannot exist; the result is known as Arrow's impossibility theorem. It helped win him the 1972 Nobel Prize, shared with John Hicks.

Picture three friends ranking pepperoni, cheese and mushrooms on pizza. Their votes can cycle, with each topping beating one rival and losing to the other, so no clear winner appears. Mathematics shows that no flawless voting rule exists, one guaranteed to be fair to every possible group.

The trouble starts only with enough options. With just two choices, simple majority rule meets every condition, but once a group of voters faces three or more options, the paradox can appear.

There is one famous escape. If every voter's preferences line up along a single left-to-right scale, majority rule picks the option the median voter prefers, a result Duncan Black proved in 1948. Arrow's student Anthony Downs applied it to elections in 1957: when two candidates care only about winning and most voters are moderate, both drift to the middle to win over the average voter.

The result shook democratic theory. If different voting methods produce different winners from the very same ballots, then the people's will, announced on every election night, is not a single thing waiting to be found; the winner is made jointly by the voters and the counting rule.

Public-choice economists such as James Buchanan drew the lesson. If no method-free group will exists, then the constitutional rules that set the method of combining votes matter enormously, because they help define the outcome rather than merely record it.

lehman-brothers-the-day-they-let-it-fail.context_blurb:
On September 15, 2008, Lehman Brothers, a Wall Street investment bank founded in 1850, filed for bankruptcy with more than $600 billion in assets, the largest bankruptcy in American history. Washington had rescued another bank six months earlier but let this one fall, and economists still argue about whether that choice caused the panic that followed.

Lehman's collapse froze credit markets around the world and helped set off the 2008 financial crisis, as it became clear that big banks had been making and hiding very risky bets on home loans.

All summer Lehman's chief executive, Dick Fuld, hunted for a buyer. Korea Development Bank negotiated and then walked away over price, and Bank of America broke off talks in early September when it chose to buy Merrill Lynch instead.

That final weekend, Treasury Secretary Hank Paulson and the Fed's chairman, Ben Bernanke, worked to line up private buyers, with Paulson and the New York Fed's president, Tim Geithner, gathering Wall Street's bosses at the New York Fed. They failed.

The last serious buyer was the British bank Barclays. When Paulson refused to put any taxpayer guarantee behind Lehman's bad assets, Barclays would have carried the whole downside alone, so on Sunday, September 14, it walked away.

The shock spread fast. The next day the Reserve Primary Fund, a money-market fund that held more than $700 million of Lehman's short-term debt, announced that its shares had fallen below a dollar. Savers who had treated such funds as safe as cash rushed to pull their money out of other money-market funds too, and the Treasury had to guarantee the whole industry.

Afterwards Paulson and Bernanke defended their decision in memoirs. Both said they had no choice: the law, they argued, did not let the Fed lend to Lehman without adequate collateral. The economist Laurence Ball, after years in the archives, argued in a 2018 book that the collateral was adequate and the refusal was a political choice.

Every rescue raises a deeper problem. A bank chief who collects huge bonuses when risky bets pay off, keeps them when the bank fails and pays nothing if taxpayers bail it out faces moral hazard: one person takes the risk while others pay for the losses. Austrian critics add that every rescue teaches bankers everywhere the same lesson, moral hazard on a national scale, because they take bigger risks knowing someone else will cover the loss.

The timing made it worse. In March 2008 the Fed had helped save Bear Stearns, a smaller investment bank. Austrian critics argue that markets had priced in a similar rescue for Lehman because of Bear, and the sudden removal of that expectation caused much of the panic that followed.

The wider lesson concerns discretion. When a central bank saves some banks and not others at its own discretion, its rescues reshape what markets expect, and that change in expectations itself becomes a source of future instability.

man-economy-and-state-1962-and-power-and.context_blurb:
In 1962 Murray Rothbard, a New York economist of thirty-six, published a two-volume treatise of nearly a thousand pages that set out the whole Austrian system of economics as one connected theory. For a generation of students it was the Austrian school's main textbook, and its story shows how unpopular ideas reached print in postwar America.

The book is called Man, Economy, and State, and the publisher D. Van Nostrand brought it out in two volumes totaling 987 pages.

It began as a smaller job. In the mid-1950s the William Volker Fund asked Rothbard to write an easier textbook version of a dense 1949 classic, Ludwig von Mises's Human Action. Under his hand the textbook grew into an original treatise of its own.

The Volker Fund, based in Kansas City, was the largest backer of classical-liberal scholarship in those decades, when most American colleges favored central planning and Keynesian economics. Private donors like these let unpopular ideas find an audience without anyone's official approval.

Rothbard followed Mises's method. His opening chapter, The Fundamentals of Human Action, starts not from statistics or equations but from an axiom, that human beings act, consciously choosing means to reach the ends they have chosen, and every later chapter deduces economic law from that starting point. Rothbard, like Mises, called this method praxeology.

Before printing, the publisher demanded one big change. The final eight chapters, Rothbard's systematic analysis of government intervention, were cut from the 1962 edition as too politically radical for a scholarly economics book.

Eight years later, in 1970, those chapters appeared as a separate book from the Institute for Humane Studies, whose title named its subject directly: Power and Market: Government and the Economy.

In it Rothbard sorted every use of state force into three kinds of intervention: autistic, binary and triangular. Autistic intervention forbids or commands an act a person does alone; binary intervention takes something directly from a person, as a tax does; triangular intervention steps into a voluntary bargain between two people and dictates its terms. The textbook example of the third is a rent-control law that caps what a landlord may charge a tenant.

In 2004 the Mises Institute finally reunited the two parts in one Scholar's Edition of about 1,500 pages, the volume Rothbard had wanted all along. It was edited by Joseph Salerno, his longtime student.

The same year as Rothbard's treatise, Milton Friedman published Capitalism and Freedom from the rival Chicago tradition. Friedman's core claim was that economic freedom is a precondition of political freedom: where officials assign work, housing and food, an election changes little in daily life, so a people cannot be politically free while the state controls the whole economy.

methodological-individualism.context_blurb:
When a news report says that a country decided something, or that a social class exploited another, economists of the Austrian school stop and ask a question: who, exactly, did it? Their insistence on that question is one of the school's founding commitments.

The rule holds that acting, choosing and deciding are things only individual persons do. A nation, a firm or a class is shorthand for the people within it, and every social outcome must be traced back to what those people did. The Austrian school, from Carl Menger through Mises and Hayek, calls this rule methodological individualism.

The rival camp treats groups, classes or whole societies as units that act in their own right, and Karl Marx's class analysis leans heavily on it. That approach is called methodological holism.

Ludwig von Mises made the rule the foundation of his 1949 treatise Human Action. An economy, on this view, is millions of individuals each pursuing aims of their own, and every price and trade is one of their choices, so economics has to start from what individual people choose to do, and why. By the logic of methodological individualism, a central plan that handles a whole country as if it were a single person cannot see what its millions of citizens actually want and choose. The philosopher Karl Popper endorsed the same rule from outside the school in 1945.

The rule has a practical payoff. When a Marxist writes that the bourgeoisie exploits the proletariat, a Misesian rewrites the sentence to name the specific persons acting in specific transactions, who hired whom, on what terms and for what reason, so the real choices and incentives come into view.

Some critics take the rule to mean that every language, market and custom must have been consciously planned by someone. That is a misreading. Hayek, drawing on Adam Ferguson of the Scottish Enlightenment, stressed that an outcome can arise from people's actions without being anyone's design.

Ferguson made the point in his 1767 Essay on the History of Civil Society: speech, law, money and trade grew from countless actions that no one planned. Hayek built on that line his idea of a spontaneous order, an order that grows without any single planner in charge.

Murray Rothbard carried the rule into his own great treatise of 1962, which begins, as Human Action did, with individuals choosing means to reach the ends they have chosen. That book is Man, Economy, and State.
