mises-institute-auburn-alabama-founded-1.context_blurb: The Ludwig von Mises Institute was founded in 1982 in Auburn, Alabama, by Lew Rockwell, with the explicit backing of Mises's widow Margit von Mises and the public endorsement of Ron Paul. The institute runs an annual summer teaching program called Mises University and publishes the Quarterly Journal of Austrian Economics. Its policy positions include one hundred percent reserve banking and the abolition of the Federal Reserve. The historian Jorg Guido Hulsmann's biography of Mises, called The Last Knight of Liberalism, is one of the institute's major publishing projects. The institute maintains the free-content website mises.org, where almost every text of the Austrian tradition is available at no cost. In the Austrian tradition the Institute is the modern American institutional home of the Rothbard-descended wing of the school, in some tension with the Cato Institute's more Washington-policy-oriented and classical-liberal profile.

mt-gox-the-first-great-custody-catastrop.context_blurb: Mt Gox was a Tokyo-based cryptocurrency exchange that at its 2013 peak handled a majority of global Bitcoin trading. The name originally stood for Magic: The Gathering Online Exchange, from the site's earlier use as a trading venue for the collectible card game. On February 7, 2014 the exchange halted withdrawals, and on February 28 it filed for civil rehabilitation in Japanese court after approximately eight hundred and fifty thousand BTC went missing. About two hundred thousand of the missing coins were later recovered. The exchange operator Mark Karpeles was later charged in Japan with embezzlement. The missing coins also included Jed McCaleb's earlier involvement in the exchange, from which he later moved on to co-found Ripple in 2012 and Stellar in 2014. By the time of the final 2024 creditor distribution, Bitcoin's price had risen so much that the recovered coins were worth many times their 2014 dollar value. In the Austrian and cypherpunk reading, Mt Gox is the first great custody catastrophe and the specific case that gave rise to the slogan not your keys, not your coins.

nick-szabo-s-bit-gold-1998.context_blurb: Nick Szabo is an American computer scientist and legal scholar who in 1998 described a scheme called bit gold on his blog. Bit gold proposed to combine proof-of-work with the time-stamped chaining of outputs to build what Szabo called a scarce digital commodity. The scheme explicitly aimed at a supply whose growth rate is governed by fixed technical difficulty, not by any issuer's discretion. Szabo did not solve two central technical problems: how to reach consensus on the ordering of new bit-gold entries across a distributed network, and how to prevent double-spending in that distributed setting. Satoshi's 2008 Bitcoin design solved both problems with the longest-chain rule combined with proof-of-work as the tiebreaker for competing histories. Szabo teaches at George Washington University and has consistently denied being Satoshi Nakamoto. In the Austrian and cypherpunk reading, bit gold is Bitcoin minus the consensus mechanism, and consensus was the single hard piece Satoshi's design added.

on-the-origin-of-money--1892---money-as-.context_blurb: Carl Menger's 1892 essay On the Origin of Money, published in English in The Economic Journal and in German as Geld, argued that money arose historically from barter without any state decree. His central concept was saleability: in a barter economy, the double coincidence of wants is a serious obstacle to exchange, and over time traders learn to accept certain goods that are especially widely desired in exchange, so that they can later re-trade them. The specific property that distinguishes money is saleability across time as well as across trading partners. Menger's position stands in direct contrast to chartalism, the view that money arises from state decree. Ludwig von Mises later built the regression theorem on Menger's foundation, arguing that the subjective valuation of money today can always be traced back through chains of past valuation to a commodity's original non-monetary use. The specific saleability properties that make a commodity suitable as money include scarcity, portability, and durability. Hayek's spontaneous-order framework is the broader methodological context. In the Austrian tradition this essay is the founding text on monetary origins.

peter-boettke-and-the-george-mason-schoo.context_blurb: Peter Boettke is an economist at George Mason University and the leading figure of the modern GMU Austrian school. He joined the GMU faculty in 1998 and became the main teacher of modern Austrian economics there. His books include Living Economics: Yesterday, Today, and Tomorrow and a study of the formative years of Soviet socialism. His student Christopher Coyne is one of the next generation. Peter Leeson's The Invisible Hook, a book on the economics of pirates, is another visible GMU product of Boettke's teaching. The Edward Elgar Handbook on Contemporary Austrian Economics, which Boettke co-edited, is the standard reference. His own methodological inheritance runs through Friedrich Hayek. The GMU school combines Austrian economics with the complementary public-choice and experimental traditions that also have institutional homes at GMU. In the Austrian tradition Boettke is the central figure in carrying the modern academic Austrian tradition forward through the current generation.

political-business-cycles-nordhaus-1975-.context_blurb: In 1975 the Yale economist William Nordhaus published a Review of Economic Studies paper titled The Political Business Cycle, arguing that elected officials have incentives to stimulate the economy before elections, which incumbent central-bank chairs with political ties face pressure to accommodate. The paradigmatic case is Arthur Burns's Fed accommodating Richard Nixon ahead of the November 1972 election, which Nixon won in a forty-nine-state landslide; the inflationary consequences then landed in the subsequent decade. Alan Greenspan's 2003 to 2004 holding of the Fed's target rate at one percent for an extended period, which many Austrians argue produced a housing bubble that would eventually burst, is a related case. The pattern Nordhaus's framework predicts is systematically pro-cyclical monetary policy relative to a fully independent central bank. Paul Volcker and Jerome Powell are the two more recent cases often cited as counter-examples who did raise rates despite political pressure. In the Austrian and public-choice reading, Fed independence is a legal structure, not necessarily an incentive structure.

price-control-failures-from-diocletian-t.context_blurb: A recurring pattern in classical-liberal economic reasoning is the specific failure mode of price controls. In 301 AD the Roman emperor Diocletian issued an edict setting maximum prices for roughly a thousand named goods and wages, with enforcement by death; an early Christian historian recorded that goods vanished from the open market. In August 1971 Richard Nixon imposed a ninety-day wage-and-price freeze, which was followed by fuel lines with odd-and-even license-plate rationing when the ceiling encountered the OPEC-era oil shock. New York City's rent control has run continuously since 1943. The Berlin Mietendeckel of 2020 was struck down fourteen months after enactment. In each case the specific failure mode is the same: a ceiling below market suffices to break the local price signal, the way full central planning breaks it everywhere, and queuing, black markets, and reduced supply emerge in response. Thomas Sowell's Basic Economics is the modern reference. In the Austrian reading the pattern is one of the clearest recurring demonstrations in the history of economic thought.

proof-of-work-and-the-digital-lottery.context_blurb: Bitcoin's consensus mechanism, called proof-of-work, is a cryptographic contest in which participating computers race to find a value, called a nonce, that when combined with a block of transactions produces a hash below a protocol-set target. Because cryptographic hashes are impossible to reverse-engineer and only produced by trial and error, the whole process effectively functions as a digital lottery that no one wins twice in a row. The specific hash function is called SHA-256. The protocol retargets the difficulty every two thousand and sixteen blocks to keep the pace of block production near ten minutes. The specific economic point is that an attacker who wanted to rewrite the blockchain would have to control more than half the network's total hash power to succeed; the resource cost of acquiring that hash power is the wall that protects every dollar of value on the network. The deeper computer-science problem the mechanism solves is called the Byzantine Generals Problem, which asks how a distributed network of actors who may include dishonest participants can reach agreement without a trusted coordinator. The specific Satoshi solution is now called Nakamoto Consensus. The miner's reward comes from the block reward. In the Austrian reading, proof-of-work is the engineering replacement for the costly physical infrastructure, including bank branches, armored trucks, printing, and the regulatory apparatus, that supports traditional money.

qe2-and-bernankes-washington-post-op-ed.context_blurb: In November 2010 the Federal Reserve launched its second large-scale asset-purchase program, called QE2, buying six hundred billion dollars of US Treasuries over several months. Fed chairman Ben Bernanke published a Washington Post op-ed explicitly justifying the program in part by its effect on the stock market, which he said would boost consumer wealth and spending through what economists call the wealth effect. The op-ed broke the Fed's long tradition of speaking only through official statements and formal congressional testimony. The German Finance Minister Wolfgang Schauble and the Texas Governor Rick Perry made notable critical responses. In the twelve months following the announcement, the S&P 500 rose approximately twenty-four percent. In the Austrian and Bastiat reading, the specific policy move was a direct application of what the tradition calls the Cantillon effect: new reserves flow into asset prices before they flow into wages or consumer prices. The SEEN benefit was the strengthening recovery; the UNSEEN cost was the asymmetric redistribution of purchasing power across the holders and non-holders of long-duration assets. In the broader reading, a central bank's public admission that it is targeting asset prices makes that goal a permanent, unhidden feature of policy.

richard-cantillon-the-1730s-essay-on-mon.context_blurb: Richard Cantillon was an Irish-French banker and economist whose Essai sur la Nature du Commerce en General, written in the 1720s and published posthumously in French in 1755, is now treated as one of the founding texts of modern economic analysis. His argument about the entry of new money into an economy was that money does not enter uniformly but at specific points, so that first-receivers of new money benefit by being able to spend at old prices before the price level has adjusted. This asymmetric mechanism is now called the Cantillon effect. In the modern application to quantitative easing, the first-receivers are banks, hedge funds, and primary dealers who sell Treasuries to the Fed, and the effect is visible in the lag between money creation and consumer-price adjustment, with asset prices moving first. Murray Rothbard rediscovered and promoted Cantillon's text in modern Austrian scholarship. Cantillon is also credited with the first analytical use of the word entrepreneur. He died in London in 1734 under disputed circumstances, possibly an insurance-fraud murder by a dismissed servant. In the Austrian reading, the Cantillon effect is the specific distributional argument against modern central-bank monetary expansion.

ross-ulbricht-dpr-the-life-sentence-and-.context_blurb: Ross Ulbricht was an American software engineer who in 2011 founded the Tor-hidden Silk Road online marketplace under the pseudonym Dread Pirate Roberts. The site allowed buyers and sellers to transact anonymously using Bitcoin. In October 2013 FBI agents arrested Ulbricht at the science-fiction section of the Glen Park branch of the San Francisco Public Library; a plant physically distracted him to keep him from locking the running laptop. He was tried in New York federal court and in May 2015 sentenced to two life sentences plus forty years without the possibility of parole. His mother Lyn Ulbricht ran a decade-long public campaign for his release. On January 21, 2025 President Donald Trump commuted the sentence to time served after about eleven years and nine months of actual incarceration, roughly two years and nine months into his life sentences. The approximately one hundred and forty-four thousand BTC seized from Ulbricht at his arrest had grown enormously in nominal value by the time of the commutation.

satoshis-disappearance-and-the-untouched.context_blurb: The pseudonymous Bitcoin creator Satoshi Nakamoto made the last widely-accepted public post on the Bitcoin forum on December 12, 2010, after passing operational control of the project to Mike Hearn and especially Gavin Andresen. Satoshi's final public communications mentioned the project's DDoS defenses as a concern. Across the roughly two years Satoshi was active, approximately one million BTC were mined from early blocks the on-chain analysis attributes to Satoshi's own machine. Not one satoshi, the smallest unit of Bitcoin's eight-decimal divisibility, from the early-mined addresses has ever moved. The Australian claimant Craig Wright was ruled by a London court in 2024 to have forged evidence of being Satoshi. In the Austrian and cypherpunk reading, the specific engineering reason Satoshi's disappearance matters is that it removes the founder's temptation to enrich himself at the expense of the currency's users. If the founder cannot or will not spend the founder's holdings, no later holder of the currency bears the overhang risk. In the mid-2020s the untouched holdings would make Satoshi the richest person on earth, and nobody knows for certain the identity, though the coins stay untouched to this day.

silicon-valley-bank-march-10-2023.context_blurb: Silicon Valley Bank was a Santa Clara, California commercial bank that primarily served venture-backed technology companies. It collapsed on March 10, 2023, with roughly one hundred and eighty-nine billion dollars in assets, after about forty-two billion dollars of customer deposits were withdrawn in a single day, the fastest run in American banking history. The specific accounting choice at the heart of the collapse was that the bank classified a large block of US Treasury bonds as held-to-maturity rather than available-for-sale, which allowed it to not mark down the bonds as rates rose, even as their economic value fell. The run was coordinated in part on social media, especially the technology-industry Twitter community. The failure was handled by the FDIC with an announcement that guaranteed all SVB deposits would be paid in full, even uninsured amounts well above the standard limit. Roughly ninety-three percent of SVB's deposits were uninsured. The bank's own Chief Risk Officer position had been vacant for most of 2022. The last American bank larger than SVB to fail was Washington Mutual in 2008.

soviet-gosplan-and-the-200-000-product-c.context_blurb: Gosplan was the central planning agency of the Soviet Union. By the 1980s the Soviet economy produced over two hundred thousand distinct product categories, and Gosplan was formally responsible for setting production quotas and prices for all of them. Standard economic estimates suggest that fully specifying the plan would have required roughly twenty billion separate quantity-and-price decisions. In practice, the system developed informal routing-around mechanisms. Factory managers employed informal fixers called tolkachi, meaning pushers, to obtain inputs when the official plan did not supply them. The practice of personal connections used to obtain goods was called blat. Factories engaged in storming, meaning rushing end-of-plan-period output to hit quotas while compromising quality. The British Sovietologist Alec Nove documented the system. The Soviet Union dissolved on December 25, 1991. In the Austrian and classical-liberal reading, the specific contrast is that market prices in the ordinary West coordinate roughly the same number of product categories with no committee needed.

sports-stadium-subsidies-the-economists-.context_blurb: The economic literature on subsidies for professional sports stadiums represents one of the clearest cases of near-unanimous agreement in applied economics. The economists Dennis Coates and Brad Humphreys have conducted the main surveys of the literature. The consensus finding is that subsidies, typically delivered through tax-exempt municipal bonds that reduce the local government's cost of financing, do not produce measurable net positive regional economic effects. The specific mechanism Austrian and public-choice critics emphasize is that stadium spending substitutes for other local entertainment spending by the same consumers; the multiplier is small. The concentrated beneficiary of the subsidy is the team owner, who has strong organizational advantages. The dispersed cost falls on taxpayers. The 2017 move of the NFL's Oakland Raiders to Las Vegas, with a subsidy structure, is a canonical modern case. The Austrian and public-choice framework for the whole pattern is concentrated-benefit, dispersed-cost combined with a jurisdictional prisoner's dilemma: any one city can refuse the subsidy, but the owner can then threaten to move to the next bidding city.

tarp-700-billion-in-a-3-page-memo.context_blurb: The Troubled Asset Relief Program, abbreviated TARP, was the main US federal response to the 2008 financial crisis. Treasury Secretary Hank Paulson submitted an original three-page memo to Congress requesting seven hundred billion dollars in discretionary spending authority. The initial version was rejected by the House on September 29, 2008, which was followed by a Dow Jones Industrial Average fall of seven hundred and seventy-seven-point-six-eight points on the day, the largest single-day point drop in history to that date. A modified package passed as the Emergency Economic Stabilization Act on October 3, 2008. The specific legal authority Paulson sought was in Section 8 of his original memo. The first TARP tranche of one hundred and twenty-five billion dollars went to nine major banks. The program was later extended to General Motors and Chrysler. FDIC Chair Sheila Bair and Senator Elizabeth Warren became visible congressional critics.

that-which-is-seen-and-that-which-is-not.context_blurb: Frederic Bastiat's pamphlet That Which is Seen and That Which is Not Seen, published in July 1850 five months before his death, is the central text of his reasoning method. The pamphlet's structural claim is that the whole difference between a good economist and a bad economist runs through what each one includes in the account: the bad economist takes into account only the effect that can be seen, while the good economist takes into account both the effect that can be seen and those effects that must be foreseen. The pamphlet's most famous chapter is the broken-window parable. The British economist W.B. Hodgson translated the pamphlet into English in 1859, and the Foundation for Economic Education issued the standard modern American translation. Thomas Sowell's phrase stage-two thinking is the modern English restatement of the discipline. Henry Hazlitt's 1946 Economics in One Lesson is a chapter-by-chapter extension of the method to twentieth-century American policy. In the Austrian and classical-liberal tradition the pamphlet is the compressed statement of the method that organizes almost every subsequent classical-liberal economic argument.

the-2004-06-rate-hikes-and-the-inverted-.context_blurb: Between June 2004 and June 2006 the Federal Reserve under Alan Greenspan raised the federal funds rate at seventeen consecutive meetings, each hike at twenty-five basis points, taking the rate from one percent to five-point-two-five percent. Greenspan announced the series would proceed at what he called a measured pace. Adjustable-rate mortgages, which many American homeowners had taken out at low teaser rates during the 2003 to 2004 period, doubled or tripled in payment size as the rate hikes took effect. The yield curve inverted in 2006. The economists Arturo Estrella and Frederic Mishkin had earlier shown that an inverted yield curve typically predicts a US recession within the next twelve to eighteen months. The subprime mortgage crisis began in late 2007. Fed Chairman Ben Bernanke stated in March 2007 that the problems were contained. In the Austrian reading the 2007 subprime episode has been called the most predictable financial crisis in American history. The deeper point is that the Fed can produce a bubble with cheap credit, then produce a warning signal by tightening, and then still be surprised by the resulting bust.

the-austrian-dispute-about-bitcoin-shost.context_blurb: The modern Austrian tradition is not internally unanimous on whether Bitcoin counts as money under Ludwig von Mises's own regression theorem. The theorem states, roughly, that a thing can only come to serve as money if it had a prior non-monetary use. The economist Frank Shostak, writing in the 2010s, applied the theorem to argue that Bitcoin lacked such a prior use and was therefore a speculative bubble that would eventually collapse. Saifedean Ammous and his co-thinkers responded that Bitcoin did have a prior non-monetary use, a cypherpunk collectible that cryptographers valued for its intellectual interest, which satisfies the theorem's requirement. The specific empirical anchor is the May 22, 2010 pizza purchase of ten thousand BTC. In the broader Austrian conversation the dispute was reasonably settled empirically by roughly 2018 to 2020. The economist Robert Murphy wrote a careful analytical treatment of the question. The commentator Peter St Onge is a modern voice on the Ammous side of the debate. In the Austrian reading the whole exchange is a worked example of how a rigorous school can disagree internally about how to apply its own theorem, and how the resolution comes out through empirical observation rather than through further armchair reasoning.

the-bitcoin-pizza-10-000-btc-for-two-pie.context_blurb: On May 22, 2010 the Bitcoin forum user Laszlo Hanyecz, a programmer, successfully arranged for another forum user to buy him two large pizzas, delivered to his house, in exchange for ten thousand BTC. The pizzas were from Papa John's. The transaction was the first documented purchase of a physical good with Bitcoin. The dollar value of the pizzas at the time was about forty-one dollars. By the mid-2020s the ten thousand BTC would have been worth over one billion US dollars. Hanyecz has publicly said that he does not regret the trade; the trade was proof Bitcoin could be spent on real goods, which was the thing that mattered. Hanyecz also wrote the first software that let a graphics processing unit, or GPU, mine Bitcoin. The anniversary is now informally called Bitcoin Pizza Day. In the Austrian and cypherpunk reading, the specific significance of the transaction is that it is the moment Bitcoin crossed from cypherpunk collectible to a medium of exchange for goods, which satisfies the historical requirement of Mises's regression theorem.

the-classical-gold-standard-1815-1914.context_blurb: The period from 1815 to 1914, from the end of the Napoleonic Wars to the outbreak of the First World War, is now called the Classical Gold Standard. The gold standard arranged that most major currencies were defined as a specific weight of gold and could be exchanged for gold at par. The British pound was defined so that one pound equaled roughly four dollars and eighty-six cents in gold-defined US dollars; because both currencies were redeemable for gold at fixed ratios, their exchange rate was essentially fixed. The specific operational mechanism was that imbalances between countries were settled in gold shipments. The French war reparations after the 1870 to 1871 Franco-Prussian War were an important stress-test the system passed smoothly. Prices across the century were stable overall; the belle epoque of 1890 to 1914 is the classic period of long-term price stability. The Austrian and classical-liberal reading highlights what the standard made impossible, which was fighting long industrial wars by inflation: the system imposed a hard budget constraint on the state and made war spending painful. The standard ended in August 1914 as the belligerents suspended convertibility. Friedrich Hayek later called it the most important instrument of the constitution of freedom.

the-cultural-revolution-1966-76.context_blurb: The Cultural Revolution was a political movement launched by Mao Zedong in 1966 and ending in 1976 at his death. The movement's youth wing, the Red Guards, held mass public struggle sessions in which political targets were humiliated, beaten, and in many cases killed. Mao called for the destruction of what he called the Four Olds: old customs, culture, habits, and ideas. The movement killed senior Communist Party leaders, including Mao's eventual successor-apparent Liu Shaoqi, who died in detention. Deng Xiaoping was also purged and sent to work in a tractor factory before his later rehabilitation. The Gang of Four, led by Mao's wife Jiang Qing, ran the movement's final years. Serious scholarly estimates place the direct death toll at roughly five hundred thousand to two million. The Chinese Communist Party's official 1981 resolution acknowledged that the Cultural Revolution was responsible for the most severe setback and heaviest losses since the founding of the People's Republic of China. Xi Jinping has rolled back some of the post-Mao distancing from the Mao era. In the Austrian and classical-liberal reading the movement is one of the central moral benchmark cases against which the Black Book of Communism's aggregate twentieth-century death toll is calibrated.

the-faa-and-boeing-737-max-certification.context_blurb: The Boeing 737 MAX is a long-serving airliner redesigned in the mid-2010s to compete with the Airbus A320neo on fuel efficiency. The redesign added a new flight-control system called MCAS, which under certain conditions could push the airplane's nose down without pilot command. Two crashes in October 2018 and March 2019 killed three hundred and forty-six people, and the aircraft was grounded worldwide for about twenty months. Subsequent investigations documented that the Federal Aviation Administration had delegated much of the airplane's certification to Boeing itself under a program called Organization Designation Authorization, abbreviated ODA. Internal Boeing communications revealed what congressional investigators called a culture of concealment. Boeing paid roughly two-point-five billion dollars in a 2021 criminal settlement. The 2024 Alaska Airlines in-flight door-plug blowout brought the ongoing problems back into public view. The 2020 Aircraft Certification, Safety, and Accountability Act partially rolled back ODA. In the public-choice reading, the lesson is that the technical expertise to certify a modern airliner resides overwhelmingly inside the regulated firm, which creates a specific capture dynamic that no formal regulatory structure fully resolves.

the-five-sowell-questions-a-distillation.context_blurb: Across Thomas Sowell's many books there is a distilled set of five analytical questions that organize his approach to any policy argument. The first is what hard evidence is there, which treats anecdotes as not data. The second is at what cost, which asks what resources the proposed policy will consume and what those resources were doing before. The third is compared to what, which insists that the critic of an existing institution name the specific real alternative, not an imagined perfect one. The fourth is and then what happens, which follows the chain of consequences past the policy's first, immediate result. The fifth is what are the trade-offs, which refuses the fiction that any gain comes without a corresponding loss somewhere. Sowell's 1980 Knowledge and Decisions received Hayek's review in which Hayek said it was the best book on general economics in years. Sowell's framework rests on a specific claim about what human beings are capable of. The 2022-2023 American student-loan cancellation proposals are an illustrative case where, with each round of partial cancellation, colleges and future students borrow expecting another cancellation. In the Austrian and classical-liberal tradition Sowell's method yields an account of what a policy costs and causes, which the reader then weighs.

the-great-leap-forward-1958-62-the-deadl.context_blurb: The Great Leap Forward was Mao Zedong's 1958 campaign to industrialize the Chinese economy at speed. The campaign abolished private landholding and organized peasants into collective organizations called people's communes. Peasants were ordered to produce iron and steel in backyard steel furnaces, destroying tools and household metal in the process. Agricultural practices were set by the Soviet pseudo-scientist Trofim Lysenko's theories, which were empirically wrong. Food production collapsed. Local party officials, under pressure to produce impressive grain reports, exaggerated. The central government, trusting the inflated reports, exported it to earn foreign currency. The resulting famine killed roughly fifteen to forty-five million Chinese between 1958 and 1962. The Chinese Communist Party vice-chairman Peng Dehuai privately criticized the policy and was purged. The journalist Yang Jisheng's 2008 book Tombstone and the historian Frank Dikotter's Mao's Great Famine are the main scholarly accounts. Liu Shaoqi and Deng Xiaoping were the leaders who later pulled the country back from the policy. In the Austrian reading, without market prices there was no signal that the commune grain reports were fantasy until the granary was empty.

the-khmer-rouge-and-year-zero-1975-79.context_blurb: The Khmer Rouge was the Cambodian communist movement that took power in April 1975 under Pol Pot. The regime called the first year of its rule Year Zero, intending to erase the previous Cambodian history and build the society over from scratch. On entering the capital Phnom Penh, the regime force-marched its entire two-million-person urban population into the countryside on foot. Educated people, including anyone who wore glasses, were systematically targeted for execution. The main interrogation center S-21, now the Tuol Sleng museum, documented the regime's methods. The agricultural fields where executions took place became known as the Killing Fields. Roughly one-point-five to two million Cambodians died, out of a population of about seven million. Several of the regime's senior figures had been educated in Paris in the 1950s. Vietnam invaded in December 1978 and ended the regime in January 1979. The Extraordinary Chambers in the Courts of Cambodia later tried surviving senior figures. In the Austrian and classical-liberal reading, the Khmer Rouge experience is one of the moral benchmark cases against which the Black Book of Communism's aggregate twentieth-century death toll is calibrated.

the-marginal-revolution-as-parallel-inve.context_blurb: In the early 1870s three economists in different countries almost simultaneously and independently produced versions of the same reorientation of economic theory. Carl Menger in Vienna published Principles of Economics in 1871. William Stanley Jevons in Manchester published The Theory of Political Economy the same year. Leon Walras in Lausanne published Elements of Pure Economics in 1874. Each reoriented the discipline around the marginal utility of the next unit to a specific chooser, rather than around the labor theory of value shared by Ricardo, Mill, and Marx. The German precursor Hermann Heinrich Gossen had worked out much of the same ground in 1854 but his book had almost no readership. The three independent arrivals are now collectively called the Marginal Revolution. Walras's version was the most mathematical; Jevons's used calculus; Menger's was argued in prose. In the Austrian tradition Menger's version is the founding text, and the tradition's distinctive methodological character, including its skepticism about reducing economics to physics-style equations, carries from his prose rather than from Walras's equations. The specific intellectual move is that economics studies purposeful human choice, which is not reducible to physics-style equations.

the-nixon-shock-august-15-1971-and-the-b.context_blurb: On Sunday evening August 15, 1971, President Richard Nixon announced on live television that the United States was closing the gold window, suspending the final remaining dollar-to-gold convertibility promise under the Bretton Woods system. The announcement interrupted a popular evening Western television show called Bonanza. The specific policy package Nixon announced also included a ninety-day wage-and-price freeze and a ten percent import surcharge. Nixon had made the decision over the preceding weekend at Camp David in a small meeting dominated by Treasury Secretary John Connally. The Great Society and the Vietnam War had been accumulating fiscal pressure for most of the preceding decade. The expected ninety-day freeze on wages and prices turned into a longer and more complex set of controls that persisted into 1972. Measured against the pre-1971 gold price, every major fiat currency has lost significant purchasing power in the fifty-plus years since. Bitcoin fans like to share charts of long-run American trends that change course in the early 1970s. In the Austrian and Bastiat reading, the specific significance is the thirty-seven-year run from the 1934 Roosevelt revaluation to the 1971 Nixon shock, after which American dollars have been fully fiat for more than fifty-four years.

the-peltzman-effect-safety-regulation-an.context_blurb: In 1975 the Chicago economist Sam Peltzman published a Journal of Political Economy paper studying the empirical effects of 1960s American automobile safety regulations, including mandatory seatbelts and padded dashboards. His finding was that drivers went faster, and crashes became more common; the regulations had produced an offsetting behavioral response. Pedestrian and cyclist deaths rose, and crashes grew more frequent. The automobile-safety activist Ralph Nader, author of Unsafe at Any Speed, was the central target of the industry; General Motors famously hired private investigators to dig up personal dirt on Nader. Similar offset effects have been documented in NFL helmet rules that produced crown-of-helmet tackling, and in childproof medicine caps that led users to leave caps off, or leave trusted bottles within reach. The underlying theoretical claim is that each person holds a target level of risk and steers back to it after a protective change. Critics have argued that the offset is a hypothesis to test case by case, not a general law, and that Peltzman's original estimate left vehicle miles travelled and driver experience out of the estimate. In the modern reading both results can stand: an offset occurred, and the law still produced a net gain.

the-rise-and-decline-of-nations-1982.context_blurb: Mancur Olson's 1982 book The Rise and Decline of Nations argued that over long periods of political stability, nations accumulate what he called distributional coalitions: organized interest groups that extract benefits from the general public through specific regulatory arrangements. Each coalition is small enough to organize effectively; the dispersed cost falls on citizens who do not organize to resist. Over time the accumulated coalitions slow growth. Major shocks, including defeat in a major war, destroy the accumulated distributional coalitions and reset the growth engine. The specific comparison Olson drew was that West Germany and Japan, both of whose pre-war distributional coalitions were destroyed by defeat in the Second World War, grew faster than Britain, whose coalitions survived. Olson's own term for the stagnation that follows coalition accumulation is a direct explanation of the 1970s American and British stagflation, high inflation coexisting with slow growth. The specific American case Olson developed in detail was the postbellum US South versus the industrialized Northeast. Margaret Thatcher's Britain 1979-90 and Roger Douglas's New Zealand 1984-88 are the two modern cases of successful political reform of accumulated coalitions. In the Austrian and public-choice reading Olson's framework explains why most societies become sclerotic over time. He explained a structural pattern; he never advocated destruction as policy.

the-so2-acid-rain-program-1990-coasean-t.context_blurb: The 1990 Clean Air Act Amendments established the first large-scale American tradable-permit program for an environmental pollutant. The pollutant was sulfur dioxide, emitted primarily by coal-burning power plants and the proximate cause of acid rain in the eastern United States. The program issued a fixed number of permits each year and let utilities trade them. Emissions fell by roughly forty percent across the first fifteen years of the program, at an estimated annual cost of four to six billion dollars, substantially below the earlier command-and-control cost estimates. The program peaked in 2006 and was later weakened by legal and regulatory changes. The EU Emissions Trading System, launched in 2005, was the European follow-on. The Harvard economist Robert Stavins is the main modern scholar of the program. The specific analytical move is Coase's: compare institutional forms on their real, transaction-cost-inclusive terms, including the risk of free-permit allocation attracting rent-seeking capture.

the-subjective-theory-of-value.context_blurb: The subjective theory of value is the foundational Austrian claim that an object's economic value is not an intrinsic property of the object but rather located in a chooser's ranking of a specific unit at a specific moment, against the alternative uses that unit could serve. The classical paradox-of-value puzzle, in which water is useful but cheap and diamonds are useless but expensive, dissolves under the subjective theory: on an ordinary day the chooser's ranking places the next specific unit of water at a trivial use while the next specific unit of diamond ranks high. A chooser with five sacks of grain, assigning each to a progressively less important use, finishes with the least important one, say parrot feed. The theory requires that the good must be scarce relative to the wants it can satisfy. Friedrich von Wieser extended the move to the pricing of productive factors in the doctrine of imputation. The specific case of a well-made five-hour suit versus a badly-made longer-labor suit resolves against the labor theory of value, which Karl Marx used in Das Kapital Volume 1. The subjective theory is also what makes Mises's 1920 socialist calculation argument work. Grice-Hutchinson's 1950 book on Salamanca scholasticism recovered the earlier Spanish version of the move.

the-use-of-knowledge-in-society-1945.context_blurb: Friedrich Hayek's September 1945 article in the American Economic Review has become the single most-cited paper in the modern Austrian tradition. The paper's central question is how to make use of knowledge that is not given to anyone in its totality, but exists only as the dispersed knowledge of the particular circumstances of time and place held by millions of individuals. Hayek's specific extended example was the global commodity tin, whose supply chain he traced across empires to illustrate how prices do the coordination work no planner could do. He called the price system a kind of system of telecommunications, and his famous closing line called it a marvel. The follow-on 1948 volume Individualism and Economic Order collects this and related papers. Hayek's 1974 Nobel lecture, The Pretense of Knowledge, returned to the central argument. The specific intellectual move the paper makes is deeper than Mises's 1920 calculation argument: not only can a planner not CALCULATE without market prices, the planner also cannot ACQUIRE the dispersed knowledge that market prices generate in the first place. In the Austrian tradition the paper is the defining text.

thomas-sowell-harlem-to-hoover.context_blurb: Thomas Sowell was born in Gastonia, North Carolina in 1930, raised in Harlem by relatives after his father's death, and left school in the eighth grade to begin delivering telegrams for Western Union. He was drafted into the Marines during the Korean War, served as a Marine Corps photographer, and used the GI Bill to attend Harvard. He studied economics at Columbia for his master's degree and at the University of Chicago for his doctorate under George Stigler. His intellectual development ran through an early Marxism, abandoned after an empirical experience at the US Department of Labor in which he tried to test whether minimum-wage law was helping the workers it was meant to help. He has been a senior fellow at the Hoover Institution at Stanford for most of his career. One of his memorable biographical lines is that he had grown up never seeing a blond-haired person and did not know blond was a hair color. His own early phrase for the knowledge-problem move is that those with the power do not have the knowledge, and those with the knowledge do not have the power. Hayek praised Sowell's Knowledge and Decisions as the best book on general economics in years. In the Austrian and classical-liberal tradition Sowell's whole corpus is a sustained application of Hayek's framework to broader policy and social questions.

tullocks-1967-paper-rent-seeking-as-dead.context_blurb: In 1967 Gordon Tullock published a short paper titled The Welfare Costs of Tariffs, Monopolies, and Theft, which the American economist Anne Krueger later renamed rent-seeking. The specific analytical move was to extend the standard calculation of the welfare cost of a government-granted monopoly or tariff. The classical calculation only counted the lost consumer surplus on units no longer produced. Tullock added the resources spent on locks, alarms, security guards, and burglary tools, and extended the analogy to the resources spent on lobbying for government-granted privileges, which also constitute real deadweight loss up to the full value of the rent being sought. Krueger's 1974 paper on Indian import licenses estimated that rent-seeking dissipation in India was costing the economy up to one hundred million dollars per year in the specific case she studied. The policy conclusion is to prefer broad-based rules that apply equally to all firms and citizens over rules that create particular privileges. Modern lobbying expenditure of over four billion dollars per year on registered federal lobbying is the empirical operationalization.

venezuelas-fair-price-law-and-the-empty-.context_blurb: In 2014 the Venezuelan government under Nicolas Maduro passed what it called the Ley Organica de Precios Justos, meaning the Organic Law of Fair Prices. The law imposed government-set maximum prices on a wide range of basic goods and provided for criminal penalties against sellers who exceeded them. Over the following three years the Venezuelan economy spiraled through severe shortages of basic goods, including the specific case of toilet paper that became the international symbol of the collapse, and inflation that eventually reached hyperinflation levels. By the late 2010s the government had introduced a fingerprint-indexed rationing system, and food distribution ran through a specific political-loyalty program called the CLAP boxes. Roughly seven-point-seven million Venezuelans had emigrated by the mid-2020s. The 2014 collapse of world oil prices, the Trump-administration sanctions from 2017, and the broader monetary chaos exacerbated the underlying problem.

weimar-hyperinflation-1921-1923-the-whee.context_blurb: Between June 1921 and November 1923 the German mark lost essentially all of its value in a hyperinflation. At its November 1923 peak the Reichsbank was printing approximately twenty-five billion marks per day. The famous period scenes include a wheelbarrow of banknotes carried to buy a single loaf of bread and a woman whose shopping basket was stolen while the money inside was thrown on the sidewalk. The stabilization was achieved under the Reichsbank president Hjalmar Schacht by the introduction of a new currency, the Rentenmark, in November 1923, at a conversion of one Rentenmark for one trillion old marks. The specific population most severely harmed by the hyperinflation was the middle class, the professionals and small savers who had held bonds and cash. In the Austrian and Bastiat reading, the SEEN was that money was still being paid; the UNSEEN was a generation's savings evaporating in twenty-seven months. The specific intellectual argument the whole episode supports is that it is Cantillon-effect asymmetric destruction playing out in real time, benefiting the first-receivers of new money and destroying the last-receivers. The remedy was the introduction of a scarce new currency the old one was replaced with, ending demand for the old paper.

william-niskanen-bureaucrats-maximize-bu.context_blurb: William Niskanen was a Chicago-trained economist who served in the Nixon administration before founding the public-choice-economics school's theory of bureaucracy. His 1971 book Bureaucracy and Representative Government, extended in his later Inside Bureaucracy, argued that bureau heads do not maximize public welfare but instead maximize what their careers reward, including the size of their agency's budget. The specific empirical pattern Niskanen traced is that agencies with clearly measurable failure tend to grow fastest, because the career incentive structure rewards budget-expanding behavior rather than mission completion. Announcing mission completion would justify budget and staffing cuts. Niskanen later served as chair of Reagan's Council of Economic Advisers and resigned over the administration's abandonment of a serious spending-cut agenda; the Reagan-era federal budget barely moved despite the political pressure. He spent most of his later career at the Cato Institute.

zimbabwes-june-26-2007-price-halving-ord.context_blurb: On June 26, 2007 the Zimbabwean government under Robert Mugabe issued an executive order requiring retailers to immediately cut all prices by roughly fifty percent. Within approximately forty-eight hours shelves had emptied in supermarkets across Zimbabwe. Within three months factories, including meat processors, dairies, and bakeries, began shutting down because they could not produce at the new mandated prices. The underlying cause of the inflation the order was intended to suppress was that the Reserve Bank of Zimbabwe was printing money to finance the government's budget. The following year the country issued a one-hundred-trillion-Zimbabwean-dollar banknote at the November 2008 peak of the hyperinflation. In the Austrian and Bastiat reading, the specific significance of this case is that the whole seen-versus-unseen chain from executive order to visible collapse ran in about forty-eight hours. The specific intellectual argument is that suppressing a price signal does not fix the underlying monetary problem that produced the price rise.

agency-budget-maximization-tsa-irs-and-t.context_blurb:
William Niskanen was an American economist who worked inside the federal government in the 1960s and noticed something odd: the agencies around him kept growing even when their work did not improve. His 1971 book Bureaucracy and Representative Government gave the public-choice school its model of why. The model accuses no one of corruption. It simply asks what the people inside an agency want.

Niskanen asked which single quantity a bureau acts as though it is always trying to enlarge, and his answer was its own budget. An official's salary, prestige, staff and chances of promotion all rise with the size of the agency, so career-minded bureaucrats push to expand it, quite rationally. Take the Transportation Security Administration, which Congress set up in November 2001, in the wake of the September 11 attacks, to screen bags at every airport. Two decades on it was bigger, not smaller, with some 60,000 employees and a budget near $10 billion a year, because new agencies almost never shrink.

Size is not the same as results. In 2015 undercover inspectors from the Department of Homeland Security tried to carry fake guns and bombs through airport checkpoints, and the screeners reportedly missed about 95 percent of them; a 2017 follow-up found little improvement. In August 2022 the Inflation Reduction Act handed the Internal Revenue Service, the national tax collector, some $80 billion spread over a decade, mostly for people rather than machines. The money was meant to pay for about 87,000 new hires.

Congress tends to answer a problem that grips the nation with a new department, and over the following decades the department's budget, staff and offices swell. Yet the problem it was built to solve often does not clearly get better. Jimmy Carter signed the Department of Education into being in October 1979; Ronald Reagan campaigned to abolish it, and it survived and grew. Real spending per pupil in American public schools more than doubled between 1970 and 2010, but the national long-term tests of reading and math for students finishing high school stayed roughly flat from 1979 to 2019. Set airport screeners, tax collectors and school officials side by side and one pattern repeats: staff and budget grow, while the results each agency exists to deliver do not clearly improve. Niskanen's model predicts exactly that.

Tie an office's budget to how many people it employs rather than to anything it finishes, and over a decade it will hire more people and invent new tasks so the budget keeps climbing. Public-choice economists such as James Buchanan spent careers tracing incentives like these, and the political scientist James Q. Wilson's 1989 book Bureaucracy showed how much an agency's behavior turns on whether its output can be measured at all. Niskanen's framework hands citizens a test for any agency that asks for more: show that the last ten percent of its old budget bought roughly ten percent of its output. If the last dollar bought far less than a dollar of results, the next dollar is even less likely to pay off, which is why Niskanen predicted agencies would resist any measurement that allowed the comparison.

Picture a school lunch service that swells from 100 staff to 400 in a decade while the number of children eating stays the same. A Niskanen reader presumes the growth reflects what the workers themselves want rather than what the job needs: internal incentives, not rising demand. After winning the 2024 election, Donald Trump put Elon Musk and Vivek Ramaswamy in charge of a drive to find bureaus bloated in just this way. He named it the Department of Government Efficiency, and its initials, DOGE, winked at a famous internet meme of a Shiba Inu dog. Bastiat would have recognized the move: grand buildings and busy hearings are easy to see, while the flat line of actual output takes effort to look up.

anne-krueger-1974-rent-seeking-gets-its-.context_blurb:
In the early 1970s the American economist Anne Krueger looked hard at two developing economies, India and Turkey, whose governments rationed the right to import foreign goods through licenses. What she found was whole departments of companies devoted not to making anything but to chasing permits. Her short 1974 paper in the American Economic Review gave that waste the name economists still use.

Picture two rival firms fighting for the only license to import some product, each spending a million dollars on lawyers and lobbyists. One wins, one loses, and nothing new has been made. The country is no richer, because the money produced nothing; it only paid for a fight over a government favor. The same thing happens when an industry, rather than making better products, pays lobbyists to persuade lawmakers to keep its foreign rivals out. Economists call that kind of profit-hunting rent-seeking. Gordon Tullock had described the mechanism in 1967, in a paper on the costs of tariffs, monopolies and theft, but Krueger gave it its permanent name.

Krueger put numbers on the waste. She estimated that the hunt for licenses swallowed about 7 percent of India's national income in 1964 and about 15 percent of Turkey's national output in 1968: effort spent courting officials, hiring lobbyists and standing in queues instead of making goods. She called that wasted effort rent-seeking, and the name stuck.

In Turkey an import permit could be worth more than the very goods it admitted, so firms behaved rationally. They staffed entire departments to lobby for licenses, cultivated officials and made side payments, and every hour spent chasing a permit was an hour not spent producing. Krueger's title named the whole pattern, The Political Economy of the Rent-Seeking Society: a rent-seeking society is one organized around that waste.

Before Krueger, the usual explanation for poverty among nations was a shortage of capital or of schooling. She added a new reason: in state-led economies, a large share of what gets measured as economic activity is really unproductive rent-seeking, ingenuity pointed at permits instead of production. Fix the rules that create the rents, her work implied, and the wasted effort turns back toward real work. India became the test. From independence in 1947 onward, for decades, its License Raj demanded official approval before a factory could expand, change what it made or grow, and businessmen haunted ministries in New Delhi instead of serving customers. In 1991 India's finance minister, Manmohan Singh, led reforms that tore down most industrial licensing and cut away the rents that fed all that lobbying, and growth sped up within a few years.

Her paper became one of the most-cited articles in economics, and others built on it. In 1982 the Indian economist Jagdish Bhagwati widened the idea into directly unproductive profit-seeking, or DUP activities: every way of earning an income without producing goods, from theft to tariff-hunting to lawsuits.

argentinas-2020-rent-control-law-and-its.context_blurb:
Argentina, a country with a long history of high inflation and populist politics, ran a rare experiment in the early 2020s. In June 2020, in the middle of the COVID lockdowns, its Congress clamped national controls on apartment rents; at the end of 2023 a new president tore them away. Because both halves happened within four years, economists could watch one market react in both directions.

The law, numbered 27,551, rewrote every lease in the country. It required leases of at least three years and allowed rents to change only once a year, by a Central Bank formula tied to wages and inflation. Within a year, brokers in Buenos Aires reported that new long-term listings had fallen by roughly 40 to 50 percent, and rents on the apartments still offered climbed steeply, tripling or more in pesos by 2023. Rather than lock an apartment into a three-year contract at a controlled rent while inflation ate the payments, landlords moved units to short-term tourist rentals on Airbnb, to unfurnished monthly lets, or onto the sale market, and some simply left them empty.

In November 2023 Argentines elected Javier Milei, an economist who campaigned brandishing a chainsaw to show how hard he would cut the state and promised to end price caps, slash spending, tame inflation and scrap the rent law. He named his school openly: the Austrian school of small government, sound money and free prices. In late December, less than three weeks after taking office, Milei issued a sweeping emergency order, a Decreto de Necesidad y Urgencia, or DNU, numbered 70/2023, that repealed or rewrote hundreds of laws at a stroke, the rent law among them. It took effect on December 29. Within a few months, new rental listings in Buenos Aires roughly tripled, and rents on new listings fell after inflation as landlords competed for tenants again.

Put the two halves together, supply shrinking with the caps on and returning with them off, and the plain lesson shows: any rule that makes supplying rental housing less profitable will shrink the amount of housing supplied. That is why the episode matters. Most studies of rent control see only the years under the caps, followed by decades of decay, which leaves defenders free to insist that removing the caps would never repair the harm. In Argentina the ceiling was removed completely and supply bounced back within months.

Opponents challenged the decree in court, and judges froze parts of it, but the section ending rent control survived every challenge. The rent law stays repealed, and Argentine leases now fall under ordinary contract law, with terms negotiated freely. Milei proudly calls himself an anarcho-capitalist and an Austrian-school economist, and he cites Rothbard, Mises and Hayek in his speeches. Frédéric Bastiat would know the shape of the story: a visible cap, invisible apartments never offered, and those apartments reappearing once the cap was gone.

bastiat-and-cobden-the-anti-corn-law-fri.context_blurb:
In the 1840s Britain's Corn Laws taxed grain brought in from abroad, keeping prices high for the landowners whose fields grew the wheat. From the factory city of Manchester rose a mass campaign to repeal them, and across the Channel a French essayist, Frédéric Bastiat, followed it with mounting excitement. The friendship that grew between them carried the free-trade argument from one country to another.

Wheat makes bread, and bread was on every table at every meal. So the grain tax fell hardest on poor families, who paid extra for every loaf while the landlords pocketed the higher price. Two Manchester cotton merchants, Richard Cobden and John Bright, led the fight through their Anti-Corn Law League and spent seven years touring the country with speeches, and both became famous names in Parliament. The families who rallied to the League wanted the grain duties gone for the plainest of reasons: the tariffs made bread dearer than it needed to be.

Their victory came in 1846. On June 25 the Conservative prime minister, Sir Robert Peel, carried repeal through Parliament against the fury of his own party's landowners, and he was out of office within days. The episode showed what a tariff really is: a help to a small group that hurts millions of ordinary buyers.

Bastiat crossed to England in the summer of 1845 to study the League's methods at its Manchester headquarters and met its leaders. Back in Paris that same year, the publisher Guillaumin brought out his book introducing the campaign to French readers, Cobden et la Ligue, packed with translations of the League's speeches and pamphlets. In February 1846 Bastiat founded a French free-trade association in the port city of Bordeaux, and it spread to Paris later that year. Its central argument was that a tariff helps a few producers a great deal but raises prices for everyone else, so most people end up worse off.

From November 1846 Bastiat edited the association's weekly paper, Le Libre-Échange. Its favorite example was a tariff on foreign shoes, under which every family pays more for its shoes so that a few shoemakers can charge more. The French campaign never won a law the way the British one had, but Bastiat's writings became its lasting legacy, and he wrote to his English friends for the rest of his short life. History named the English wing after its industrial home: the Manchester School, still a byword for classical-liberal political economy.

benjamin-strong-and-the-coup-de-whiskey-.context_blurb:
Benjamin Strong, a New York banker who had attended the secret 1910 meeting on Jekyll Island that sketched out the Federal Reserve, became the first governor of the New York Fed in 1914. Until his death in October 1928 he was the strongest personality in the young central bank. Austrian economists later saw his easy money as a root of the 1929 crash.

The Fed's chief power is over how much money circulates. When it creates a great deal of new money and pushes it into the economy, prices in the shops tend to rise, because more money is chasing the same goods. Strong pioneered the Fed's most important everyday tool, open market operations: buying Treasury bonds from banks to add reserves and push rates down, and selling them to drain reserves away.

His closest friend in finance was Montagu Norman, who governed the Bank of England for twenty-four years, from 1920 to 1944, one of the longest reigns of any central banker, and together they shaped world monetary policy through the decade. In 1925 Britain, with Winston Churchill as Chancellor of the Exchequer, went back onto gold at the prewar parity of about $4.86 to the pound. That rate overvalued the pound and brought painful deflation, strikes and unemployment, and John Maynard Keynes attacked the decision in a famous pamphlet. To help his friend, Strong kept American rates low so gold would not drain from London to New York.

In July 1927 Strong gathered Europe's central bankers in secret at an estate on Long Island. Montagu Norman of the Bank of England and Hjalmar Schacht of Germany's Reichsbank came in person, and the Bank of France, governed by Émile Moreau, sent its deputy governor, Charles Rist. Days later the Fed trimmed its discount rate, the price of its loans to banks, by half a point to 3.5 percent, to help the Europeans keep their currencies tied to gold. In private, Strong reportedly said the cut would give the stock market a little coup de whiskey. The phrase survives through the later Senate testimony of Adolph Miller, the one Fed Board member who opposed the cut.

Austrian economics explains why such a cut is dangerous. An interest rate held below the level where saving and borrowing would naturally meet tells a business owner, falsely, that people want to save more, so long-term projects such as new factories look profitable. Murray Rothbard's America's Great Depression (1963) traced the crash to the Fed's credit expansion from 1921 to 1929, when the money supply grew by roughly 60 percent, and once Strong died nobody at the Fed could rein it in. Austrians call the wasteful projects that cheap credit funded, ventures doomed once the boom ended, malinvestment.

Those who fault the 1927 cut argue that the cheap money that poured into New York fueled a stock-market bubble that burst in October 1929 and opened the Great Depression. The episode teaches one move about central banks acting in concert. When they ease together to defend a fixed exchange rate, the country doing the easing can get inflated asset prices even if its own economy needs no easing at all: Strong eased Britain's problem and created America's.

bootleggers-and-baptists-bruce-yandle-19.context_blurb:
Bruce Yandle, an economist from Clemson University, served as executive director of the Federal Trade Commission in the early 1980s and kept noticing an odd alliance behind new regulations. In 1983 he described it in a short essay for Regulation magazine, subtitled The Education of a Regulatory Economist. His two-word name for the alliance became one of the most-cited ideas in political economy.

Two groups with clashing motives can end up quietly wanting the very same rule for opposite reasons. Yandle's model case came from old Sunday liquor bans. Church members backed them because they believed drinking on the Sabbath was wrong, and illegal moonshine sellers backed them because, with the legal stores shut, thirsty customers came to them instead. Yandle named the pattern after that unlikely pair: Bootleggers and Baptists.

In the American South, devout Baptists campaigned loudly for Sunday closing as a moral crusade, while bootleggers profited quietly, because on Sundays their illegal liquor faced no legal competition. The Baptists were the moral partner and the bootleggers the profit partner. Each side needed the other. The bootleggers gained profits and helped pay for the fight, while the Baptists gave the rule moral cover, so that lawmakers could defend it without blushing.

Once seen, the coalition turns up everywhere. When a city tightens the rules on where Uber and Lyft may pick up riders or what they may charge, taxi-medallion holders, who profit from keeping rivals out, usually stand at city hall beside pedestrian-safety advocates, who supply the moral cover. Environmental rules work the same way. Sincere environmentalists support a rule to protect the planet, while domestic producers cheer it on quietly when it burdens foreign competitors more than themselves, so a green rule doubles as a trade barrier.

Economists read the nationwide alcohol ban of the 18th Amendment, which lasted from 1919 to 1933, as the biggest case of all. On one side stood moralists such as the Anti-Saloon League and the Woman's Christian Temperance Union; on the other, organized-crime beneficiaries who ran the black market and grew rich while it lasted. In 2014 Yandle expanded the idea into a full book with a co-author confusingly named Adam Smith, a present-day scholar rather than the Scot of 1776. The Cato Institute published it as Bootleggers and Baptists: How Economic Forces and Moral Persuasion Interact to Shape Regulatory Politics.

Yandle turned the insight into a habit for reading the news. In a working coalition the moral side does the visible lobbying and holds the microphone, while the profit side quietly supplies the resources and signs the checks. Regulatory economists, he wrote, spend years learning to look past the moral rhetoric to find the bootlegger.

bryan-caplan-education-signaling-and-rat.context_blurb:
Bryan Caplan teaches economics at George Mason University and has built a career on book-length arguments against ideas most readers assume are settled. He writes plainly, for educated general readers, and starts from a specific puzzle in the data rather than from a slogan. His targets have included voters, parents, colleges and the rules that keep houses scarce.

His best-known claim concerns college. The bulk of a graduate's higher pay, Caplan argues, comes not from what was learned in class but from what the diploma tells employers: that its holder can finish hard, dull tasks. Economists call this signaling, and The Case Against Education, his book of 2018, presses it hard. If he is right, students will pay a great deal for the degree itself, even when the classes taught them nothing useful, because the paper is what employers reward.

His evidence includes a jump in the data. Someone who quits one class short of graduating earns far less over a lifetime than a classmate who finished, though their coursework barely differs, so the diploma by itself seems to be worth a small fortune. Economists call that jump at the finish line the sheepskin effect. Caplan estimates that roughly 80 percent of the college wage premium is signaling, a claim that is heterodox even among friendly economists, and from it he draws his main policy recommendation: cut education subsidies. The signaling story changes what taxpayers buy. If a degree mostly shows that a student is bright and diligent, then grants, cheap loans and state universities pump up the signal without producing matching productive skills, and as more people hold the same diploma its premium wears away.

His 2007 book, The Myth of the Rational Voter, argued that voters hold systematically biased views on economics, suspicious of markets, of trade with foreigners and of saving, and keep them because a mistaken ballot costs the person casting it nothing. Caplan named the pattern rational irrationality. A shopper who believes nonsense pays for it at the checkout, but a voter who believes nonsense pays nothing, so clear thinking about politics is personally costly and privately worthless. The idea extends an older public-choice claim. In 1957 Anthony Downs argued that voters barely study the issues since one ballot in millions hardly ever decides anything, and he called that rational ignorance; Caplan's addition is that voters not only skip the homework but also indulge comfortable errors.

In 2011 Caplan used research on twins and adopted children to argue that how grown children turn out owes much less to their parents than most people believe, so raising children can be more relaxed than people fear, and he titled the book Selfish Reasons to Have More Kids.

His case for freer immigration rests on a startling gap. With an ox and hand tools, a farmer in a poor land might raise some $500 of crops a year; move that same man to a wealthy nation of tractors, good roads and reliable power, and similar work could pay around $40,000. Where people work, not just how hard they work, sets what they can produce. His 2024 book Build, Baby, Build turned to housing. When a booming city such as San Francisco smothers construction in permits, zoning and neighborhood vetoes while new jobs keep drawing residents, home prices climb steeply, because supply cannot keep pace with demand. Unusually for a tenured professor, Caplan made both of these books nonfiction graphic novels, Open Borders (2019) drawn by Zach Weinersmith and the housing book drawn by Ady Branzei. The comic form solves a problem scholarly prose cannot, reaching general readers who never open an academic book.

capitalism-and-freedom-1962-and-free-to-.context_blurb:
Milton Friedman, the University of Chicago economist who won the Nobel prize in 1976, wrote two books for ordinary readers that went on to change American policy. The first, in 1962, argued that economic and political freedom are bound together and offered a list of reforms that sounded eccentric at the time. The second, in 1980, written with his wife Rose, carried the case to television.

The 1962 book began as talks Friedman delivered in 1956 at Indiana's Wabash College, and Rose helped turn them into plain English. He called it Capitalism and Freedom, and over the years buyers took home upward of 500,000 copies. Its central claim runs in one direction only: economic freedom is necessary for political freedom, though it is not enough by itself. Once a government controls the jobs, the press and the currency, a dissenter cannot hold out, because he cannot even eat.

The book's proposals included vouchers that parents could spend at any school, a negative income tax in place of the tangle of welfare programs, an army of volunteers, floating exchange rates, and an end to licensing rules that kept newcomers out of trades. Universal single-payer health insurance, the Canadian model, was never among them. Ending the draft was the proposal that produced the sharpest exchange. In the late 1960s, at hearings of a presidential commission on the draft, General William Westmoreland objected that he had no wish to lead mercenaries, and Friedman asked whether he would rather have an army of slaves. Congress let the draft authority lapse in 1973.

Free to Choose made the same case through everyday scenes. A shopper choosing freely among thousands of items buys what her family really wants; hand the same budget to a committee of nutrition experts, and many shoppers would end up with food they did not want while the shelves filled with things nobody bought. The 1980 book accompanied a ten-part public-television series shot on location from Hong Kong to Chicago and Washington, and it became the best-selling nonfiction book in America that year. According to Friedman's memoirs, it was smuggled into the Soviet Union and Eastern Europe in underground translations, and the Czech reformer Václav Klaus later credited it as a source of his country's reforms after 1989.

The voucher idea was older than either book. Friedman first set it out in 1955 in an essay, The Role of Government in Education, in a volume edited by Robert Solo, and later folded it into Capitalism and Freedom. He had argued since 1953 for letting currencies float freely against one another. When Richard Nixon closed the gold window in August 1971, the fixed-rate system of Bretton Woods fell apart, and by 1973 the world's major currencies were floating against each other.

Looking back, historians note how many of the 1962 proposals that seemed eccentric at the time became mainstream policy: the volunteer army in 1973, floating currencies in the early 1970s, and state voucher programs from the 1990s on.

ceausescus-romania-and-the-1989-executio.context_blurb:
Nicolae Ceaușescu ruled Romania for twenty-four years from 1965, first as head of its Communist Party and later as head of state as well, with his wife Elena at his side as co-ruler. His regime joined a cult of personality to ruinous central planning. It held together for decades, then collapsed in about a week in December 1989, and he became the only communist leader shot in that year's revolutions.

By the late 1980s Romanians lived with empty shops, secret police everywhere, and heat and electricity doled out for only a few hours daily; what they threw off that December was a communist dictatorship. Ceaușescu's monument was a colossal palace in central Bucharest for the party's ruling bodies, built in the 1980s as the House of the People by 20,000 workers and 700 architects over eight years. Only one office building on earth has more floor space, and a great stretch of the old city, churches included, was flattened to make room. Today it is called the Palace of the Parliament and houses Romania's legislature.

In October 1966 Ceaușescu banned abortion and contraception, both legal since 1957, to drive the birthrate up by command. The order, Decree 770, also taxed unmarried adults and childless couples over twenty-five, and births nearly doubled within a year. The state could not care for the babies it had ordered into the world. When foreign reporters entered Romania's state institutions in 1990, they found about 100,000 children in appalling orphanages, and the footage drove reform of international adoption for decades.

In the 1980s his program of systematization bulldozed thousands of farming villages and herded families out of their old houses into identical concrete blocks near state factories. It was central planning in miniature: one small group decides how everyone should live and ignores what people actually want. The hardship had another cause too. Through the decade Ceaușescu insisted on paying off every dollar of foreign debt, exporting grain, meat and fuel for hard currency, while at home Romanians endured rolling power blackouts and rationed food, queues for meat, sugar and cooking oil, and cold apartments winter after winter.

The end began in the city of Timișoara. On December 16, 1989, townspeople gathered to stop the eviction of a pastor, László Tőkés; troops fired on them, and within a week the uprising reached Bucharest. It showed how fast public obedience can vanish once people see their neighbors dare to defy a dictator. On December 21 Ceaușescu ordered a mass rally beneath the balcony of the party's Central Committee building, carried live on national television. In mid-speech, for the first time in his rule, the crowd turned on him: boos and jeers rose, his face froze in shock, and every home in Romania watched it happen on state TV. He fled by helicopter and was caught, and on December 25, 1989, Christmas Day, a military tribunal at Târgoviște tried him and Elena in about an hour and had them shot by firing squad.

Like East Germany's Stasi, the Soviet KGB and Albania's Sigurimi, Romania's Securitate was a secret-police force with a wide network of neighborhood informants, enormous for the size of the country, built to defend the state against its own people.

comparative-advantage-in-reverse-what-pr.context_blurb:
In 1817 the English economist David Ricardo showed that voluntary trade can make both sides richer even when one of them is better at producing everything. Two centuries later, the American tariff schedule offers a sharp lesson in what overriding that insight costs, and in who pays the bill.

American tariffs on shoes are not flat. Cheap plastic and canvas sneakers carry duties of 15 to 20 percent, while fine leather dress shoes carry only 5 to 8 percent, and shoppers pay the difference at the checkout. Because poorer families spend a bigger part of their income on such low-end goods, low-income households pay more of this tax. Compare a family earning $200,000 a year with one earning $30,000. Both need shoes, shirts and pants, so the extra dollars the tariff adds are much alike, but for the poor family those dollars are a far larger slice of the budget, and so the poor family loses the bigger share of its income.

In 2002 the trade researcher Edward Gresser of the Progressive Policy Institute documented the pattern in a paper titled Toughest on the Poor. Measured against income, the tariff bill of the bottom fifth of households came to three or four times the burden of the richest fifth. Thomas Sowell of Stanford's Hoover Institution drew the political moral in Basic Economics: the people who claim to defend American workers with tariffs are the ones taxing those workers hardest.

Ricardo's idea is easy to see in miniature. Anna is quicker than Ben at both baking and sign-painting, yet it can still pay for Ben to paint while Anna bakes, and then for the two to trade. Economists call this comparative advantage: each side gains by doing what costs it least to give up, even when the other side is better at everything, and every tariff that overrides it leaves both trading nations poorer than they could have been.

A tariff on imported shirts does not fall on wages or profits directly. It raises the shelf price, so the shopper at the register pays it, which makes a tariff behave much like a consumption tax, a targeted sales tax, and a regressive one at that. The lopsided pattern was no accident. It accumulated, bill by bill, over many decades, because the domestic producers of low-end goods such as footwear and cheap apparel lobbied hardest for protection, while the scattered shoppers who paid never organized.
