covid-era-ppe-price-gouging-and-the-mung.context_blurb:
When COVID-19 struck the United States in March 2020, face masks, sanitizer and even toilet rolls vanished from the shelves, and prices began to climb. Most states answered by making it illegal to sell such goods above their old prices. The Duke University economist Michael Munger has spent years explaining why rules like that prolong shortages instead of ending them, and his favorite story involves a truckload of generators.

Laws that forbid selling emergency goods far above their usual price are called anti-price-gouging laws; most states already had them on the books and switched them on as emergencies were declared, with officials threatening fines and jail. Think of a hurricane that strips Florida's stores of bottled water, so the last bottles cost $10 instead of $2. Buyers call it gouging, but economists such as Thomas Sowell point out that the high price is doing a job: it signals sellers everywhere to rush more water to Florida, and fast.

The story comes from 2005. When Hurricane Katrina knocked out power across Mississippi in 2005, John Shepperson of Kentucky bought 19 generators, hired a truck and set off some 600 miles south, meaning to sell them at roughly twice their cost, a markup that would repay his expenses, his labor and his risk. Mississippi police arrested him under the state's anti-gouging law and confiscated the generators, which sat in custody instead of reaching anyone without power.

Bastiat's method sorts the case neatly. What everyone sees is the pleasant, low price on any generator that does get sold. The unseen part is every entrepreneur who never drives supplies into a disaster area, because the reward for doing so has been made a crime. In 2020 a few states briefly declined to enforce their gouging laws on masks and gloves, and their shelves refilled faster; economists such as Steven Horwitz argued that the higher prices told sellers to rush supply in and told buyers not to hoard. Munger packs the lesson into a slogan: in an emergency, he says, gouging is not the problem at all but the solution.

Thomas Sowell, the economist born in 1930 whose Basic Economics is read around the world, names the error at the heart of every such law: it mistakes a price signal for a moral offense, treating information about scarcity as proof of bad character. Munger adds that the real cost falls on a hidden group, the future entrepreneurs who learn from one visible arrest that carrying goods into a stricken area will not be rewarded and may even land them in jail.

So when a storm knocks out a coast's power for a week and generator prices soar, the economist in Bastiat's tradition sees the high price quietly doing its work. It tells suppliers far away that trucks and generators are worth rushing in, and it tells buyers nearby to conserve.

davis-bacon-and-prevailing-wages-paid-to.context_blurb:
In 1931, early in the Great Depression, Congress approved the Davis-Bacon Act, named for its sponsors, Representative Robert Bacon of New York and Senator James Davis of Pennsylvania. It requires that construction workers on federally funded projects be paid the local prevailing wage. Its effects, and the motives behind it, make it a classic case for public-choice economists.

The Department of Labor sets that wage by surveying local pay, and in most cities the survey settles on the union scale as its answer. Paying union rates on every federal highway, school and courthouse makes those projects more expensive, often well above what private builders in the same town pay. Studies by the Congressional Budget Office and the Beacon Hill Institute put the extra cost on federal construction at roughly 10 to 15 percent, which adds up to tens of billions of dollars in any big infrastructure package.

The 1931 debate made the original motive hard to miss. Several of the bill's backers said openly that they wanted to keep Southern Black workers, who were moving north and competing for federal construction jobs at lower wages, off federal building sites. On the House floor Congressman Miles Allgood of Alabama complained of a builder from back home who had won a federal job in New York and brought cheap colored labor north with him, labor that was, in his words, in competition with white labor throughout the country. The racial language later disappeared from talk about the law, but its exclusionary effect on lower-wage newcomers remains built into the mechanism.

Bastiat's lens shows the two sides. The seen is the union jobs on the site; the unseen is the markup every federal taxpayer pays. It fits Mancur Olson's classic pattern exactly: a concentrated benefit for the construction unions, organized and loud, and a dispersed cost for taxpayers, each paying too little to notice. That is why critics in the free-market and public-choice camps, among them Chris Edwards of the Cato Institute, have called for repeal for decades: the law raises the cost of every road, bridge and school the federal government pays for.

denationalisation-of-money-1976-hayeks-c.context_blurb:
In 1976 Friedrich Hayek, the Austrian-born economist who had shared the 1974 Nobel prize, published the most radical monetary proposal of his career. With inflation raging across the Western world, he traced the trouble to a single source, the government's monopoly on money. His remedy was to end the monopoly.

Hayek proposed letting private banks and firms put out money of their own, with customers picking whichever kept its value best, so that every issuer was forced to behave. The idea is called currency competition. The pamphlet came out in London from the Institute of Economic Affairs, Britain's oldest classical-liberal think tank, which Antony Fisher, a businessman who had made his money raising chickens, set up in 1955 on Hayek's own advice after reading The Road to Serfdom.

His single bold proposal was that governments surrender their sole right to issue money and allow private issuers to compete for people's trust. Money, he argued, is a good like any other, and competition checked by consumer choice would supply it better than a state monopoly. The pamphlet's formal title named both the reform and the historical practice behind it: Denationalisation of Money: An Analysis of the Theory and Practice of Concurrent Currencies. Concurrent currencies meant episodes such as nineteenth-century Scotland, where notes from several private banks circulated side by side.

His case rested on the historical record of government monopoly money, from Diocletian's denarius to the Weimar mark of 1923: given enough time, every such currency had been debased or destroyed, because a monopoly issuer under short-run political pressure is always tempted to inflate. What would keep private issuers honest? The same discipline every producer faces: consumers refusing to hold or accept a currency whose value was falling. An issuer whose money lost purchasing power would see it refused and would fail, while one that kept it stable would win business. Hayek predicted that only currencies that held their value would survive, so inflation would fall, and in his enlarged second edition of 1978 he added that a free market in money would settle on a few stable standards rather than an unmanageable crowd of them.

Even Murray Rothbard, who agreed that the state should not run money, drew a line here. He accepted free banking but insisted that any honest free-market money be backed by a commodity such as gold, its notes redeemable for the metal; Hayek's unbacked competing paper went further than Rothbard would. Asked why companies should compete to supply money, a Hayekian answers that the reason is the same one that lets many bakeries sell bread and many firms sell phones. Rivalry hands customers a choice and drives suppliers to serve them well, and the burden falls on the monopoly's defenders to explain why money should be the exception.

Three decades later Bitcoin's defenders, such as Saifedean Ammous in The Bitcoin Standard, hailed the pamphlet as their project's grandfather. But Bitcoin relies on a device unavailable to anyone in 1976: a supply schedule locked by cryptography, which no issuer can inflate, with its cap of 21 million coins and its halvings written into the protocol itself rather than enforced through consumer choice.

dot-com-bust-and-the-housing-bubble-setu.context_blurb:
Between 1995 and 2000 Americans rushed to buy shares in young internet firms, and the Nasdaq index of technology stocks rose about fivefold. Its crash, and the Federal Reserve's response to it, set the stage for the housing bubble and the crisis of 2008. Austrian economists read the whole sequence as one cycle feeding the next.

Any firm with a .com in its name watched its shares soar, though many of those companies had never earned a dollar of profit, and when prices collapsed in March 2000 trillions of dollars of paper wealth disappeared. A run-up of that kind followed by a crash is called a bubble. Back on December 5, 1996, the Fed chairman Alan Greenspan had told an audience at the American Enterprise Institute that investors might be in the grip of irrational exuberance. Yet he left interest rates alone and did nothing to cool the market.

From its peak of 5,048 in March 2000 the Nasdaq fell to 1,114 by October 2002, a loss of 78 percent, roughly three-quarters of its value, and hundreds of dot-com companies failed. The Fed answered with its most aggressive rate cutting in decades. Over two and a half years, from early 2001 to mid-2003, it cut thirteen times, taking its key rate from 6.5 percent down to 1.0 percent, the lowest in 46 years, and it held the rate there until June 2004.

That cheap money had a massive unintended effect: it inflated US housing. Subprime mortgages with low teaser rates drove a boom, and the Case-Shiller index of home prices in twenty cities more than doubled between 2000 and 2006. From 2005 to 2007 the investor Peter Schiff warned on CNBC and other channels that the Fed's low rates were blowing up a housing bubble, while fellow panelists chuckled. Then the housing market collapsed in 2007 and 2008, and he was proven right.

Austrian business cycle theory traces a single chain. Easy money in the 1990s fed the dot-com bubble, and the rate cuts of 2001 to 2003, the answer to that crash, were the direct origin of the 2008 crisis; the Fed, in this reading, solved one bubble by inflating a bigger one. After the crash two Boston Fed economists, Paul Willen and Kristopher Gerardi, dug into the subprime loan data and concluded that the boom grew mainly from a belief, shared by lenders and borrowers alike, that home prices could only go up.

The deeper lesson concerns how a central bank reacts. Each response to a bust plants the seeds of the next one, so there is no escape from the cycle without accepting the liquidation of bad investments that the theory says must come. Greenspan's 1996 speech carries its own moral. A central-bank chair who publicly warns of a bubble but does nothing to restrain it has in effect endorsed the speculation, and markets read his inaction as a green light.

el-salvador-the-first-country-to-make-bi.context_blurb:
On September 7, 2021, El Salvador, a small Central American country, became the first country anywhere to give Bitcoin the status of legal tender, beside the US dollar it already used. The law was the project of its young president, Nayib Bukele, elected in 2019. The experiment set a sovereign state against the international financial institutions built around government money.

Unlike the cash in your pocket, Bitcoin is issued by no government or bank; it is created by computers around the world running the same open software. The Bitcoin Law passed the Legislative Assembly on June 9, 2021, and took effect that September. El Salvador had already given up its own money, the colón, in 2001, adopting the US dollar as its official currency, and Bitcoin was added beside the dollar, not in place of it.

One big hope concerned the Salvadorans working abroad, mostly in the United States, who send billions of dollars home every year through wire services with steep fees: Bitcoin was meant to let them get money to their families faster and more cheaply than banks allowed. Bukele announced the plan in June 2021 in a video message to Bitcoin 2021, a huge conference of Bitcoin enthusiasts and developers in Miami, and pushed the law through within days.

The government launched a free national phone wallet called Chivo, Salvadoran slang for cool, built on Bitcoin's Lightning Network, a quicker payment layer riding above the main chain, so that corner shops could accept tiny payments cheaply. As an incentive, the government gave each adult who signed up $30 in bitcoin, and the bonus drove millions of downloads in the first weeks, though the app had serious early bugs.

The International Monetary Fund urged the country to abandon the law. Its stated reason was not crime or speed but price: Bitcoin's price, the Fund argued, swings far too much to safely back a nation's economy, with risks to fiscal reporting and bank supervision. Bukele mocked the Fund and pressed on. In November 2022 he announced that the country would buy one bitcoin per day for its national reserves, whatever the price, building a treasury steadily instead of trying to time the market.

Bitcoin's supply is capped at 21 million coins by its code, beyond the control of any state or central bank, so El Salvador's move defied the consensus of international financial institutions such as the IMF, which prefer that countries use state-issued money they can influence. In the Austrian reading, any successful national adoption of a money no state controls weakens those institutions' influence. El Salvador also sits on active volcanoes, and Bukele planned to mine Bitcoin with their heat, letting geothermal steam drive generators whose electricity runs the mining computers, starting at the Tecapa volcano. In November 2021 he announced a Bitcoin City near the Conchagua volcano, to be powered the same way and funded by Bitcoin bonds, though building has been slow.

esg-as-regulatory-capture-blackrock-vang.context_blurb:
Most Americans who save for retirement own a sliver of hundreds of companies without ever choosing one. Their money sits in index funds, which simply buy every stock in an index such as the S&P 500. That convenience has quietly gathered enormous voting power into a few hands, and public-choice economists ask whose goals that power really serves.

Three firms dominate the business: BlackRock, Vanguard, and State Street. Together they manage more than twenty-two trillion dollars, own roughly a fifth to a quarter of the average S&P 500 company, and cast about one vote in every four at big-company shareholder meetings. Reporters call them the Big Three.

In 2019 the legal scholars Lucian Bebchuk and Scott Hirst measured that power in the Boston University Law Review. They titled their paper The Specter of the Giant Three, echoing the line from the Communist Manifesto about a specter haunting Europe. Their specter was concentrated voting power: the trio's ownership of the S&P 500 had roughly quadrupled since 1998.

BlackRock's chief executive, Larry Fink, who co-founded the firm in 1988, writes an annual letter to the heads of companies that the financial world reads closely. In the late 2010s and early 2020s those letters pressed firms on climate and other social goals, a push that travels under the label ESG, short for environmental, social and governance. Whatever one thinks of the goals, a score like that changes behavior. Once a company's biggest owners grade it on a new score, its managers start chasing the score, not just the old work of making a useful product cheaply.

Why does Fink's letter weigh so much? BlackRock's funds own a slice of nearly every listed firm, so BlackRock can vote against a company's managers at the annual meeting when the firm shrugs the letter off.

A few employees at these firms vote the shares of tens of millions of savers who were never asked about any single ballot. In 1971 the Chicago economist George Stigler described how a regulator can come to serve the very industry it was created to watch over, a pattern he called regulatory capture. Public-choice economists see the same shape here with one twist, since no government regulator is involved at all. It is capture of the regulatory kind, running through private fiduciary infrastructure: the funds that vote on other people's behalf.

That stretches Stigler's idea in an important way. Capture does not need a government agency, because private financial gatekeepers who decide for millions can drift from those millions' wishes just as surely as regulators can.

The underlying argument is older. In a famous 1970 essay in the New York Times Magazine, Milton Friedman made the case that the people running a company are hired by its shareholders to make money for them. A manager who hands the firm's profits to causes he personally likes, Friedman said, is spending other people's money without their permission.

The same worry applies to the fund giants. A manager who votes savers' shares for causes that plenty of those savers oppose, while still charging them fees, may be serving its own goals instead of the goals of the people whose money it holds.

Some states pushed back. In 2022 Florida, where Governor Ron DeSantis had made ESG investing a target, pulled about $2 billion of state money out of BlackRock. The complaint was that BlackRock was using other people's money, Florida's among it, to push a political agenda the owners of that money never chose.

Thomas Sowell urged a simple check that fits the whole story. Whenever someone acts on others' behalf, ask whether the middlemen's incentives line up with what the people they represent actually want. Where they do not, expect the agents to follow their own preferences at their clients' expense.

fdrs-agricultural-adjustment-act-1933-an.context_blurb:
In 1933, at the bottom of the Great Depression, farm prices had collapsed and American farmers were going broke. President Franklin Roosevelt's answer, the Agricultural Adjustment Act, signed that May, tried to push prices back up by making food scarcer. Its most famous result, millions of slaughtered pigs in a hungry country, became a classic lesson in what Bastiat called the unseen.

The logic was plain supply and demand. When there is less food to sell, buyers compete for what remains and pay more for each pound, so the government paid farmers to leave fields idle, plow up planted cotton and kill livestock.

In the fall of 1933 the hog program paid farmers to slaughter about six million pigs, many of them piglets, and much of the meat, especially from piglets too small to butcher, was rendered into grease and fertilizer. Destroying useful goods to make them scarce falls hardest on hungry families, because they are the people who need those goods most.

The cities, meanwhile, were full of families already struggling to put food on the table. For them the policy did one thing: it made food dearer for people who could barely afford it. Agriculture Secretary Henry Wallace, later Roosevelt's vice president, had to defend the slaughter on national radio and was booed at his speeches.

Bastiat urged his readers to look past a policy's visible result to the one nobody sees. What everyone could see was the better price paid for the hogs that survived, a boost to some farmers' cash flow. The unseen effect was the food itself, pork turned into fertilizer while children stood in breadlines.

The payments were funded by a tax on food processors. In January 1936 the Supreme Court decided United States v. Butler, ruling that Congress had overstepped its taxing power by paying for the farm program with a levy on processors, and the law fell. Congress wrote a new version in 1938, built to survive the courts.

Harold Cole and Lee Ohanian, economists at UCLA, later rebuilt the numbers on the New Deal's farm and factory programs, including the National Industrial Recovery Act's push to lift wages and prices together. They concluded that these steps dragged the Depression out for years, because they raised the cost of food and goods just when Americans could least afford them.

Why do such programs last? Picture a rule that adds a little to the price of every bag of sugar and passes the money to a few thousand growers. Each shopper loses pennies and never notices, while each grower gains a fortune and notices every cent. Economists call this pattern dispersed costs, concentrated benefits, and Mancur Olson explained why the small group organizes while the large one never does.

William Graham Sumner, a Yale sociologist writing in the 1880s, named the person such programs leave out. When government helps one citizen by taxing another, the politician and the citizen helped get all the attention, while the taxpayer, who paid and received nothing, drops out of sight. Sumner called that taxpayer the forgotten man, and in 2007 Amity Shlaes borrowed the phrase for her history of the Depression.

The 1933 act was sold as temporary help in an emergency. Yet the programs never ended, for the 1938 law still forms the backbone of the giant farm bill Congress passes roughly every five years. Milton Friedman liked to point out that a temporary government program is about the most permanent thing there is, and the farm bill shows why: once a group depends on the checks, temporary help turns permanent.

fiscal-stimulus-and-the-multiplier-the-p.context_blurb:
In early 2009, with millions of Americans thrown out of work by the financial crisis, Congress approved a stimulus package worth $787 billion, the American Recovery and Reinvestment Act. Its backers promised that each federal dollar would multiply as it moved through the economy. The fight over how much it really did is a modern rematch of an argument Frederic Bastiat started.

That January, Christina Romer, chair of the new president's Council of Economic Advisers, and Jared Bernstein, chief economist to Vice President Biden, released a memo. With the stimulus in place, it forecast, unemployment would peak below 8 percent.

Congress passed the law in February. Unemployment kept climbing anyway, hit 10 percent by October 2009 and stayed high for years. The honest lesson is a humbling one: even brilliant experts often cannot predict what a whole economy will do.

The forecast rested on a multiplier, the number of dollars of new output each stimulus dollar is supposed to create. Romer's team assumed about $1.55. Later independent studies often found less than a dollar, which means the White House predictions had been too optimistic. A multiplier below one does not mean the economy shrank: it means government spending pushed aside some private spending, so total output rose by less than the money spent.

In 2010 Volker Wieland, John Taylor, Tobias Cwik and John Cogan redid the Romer-Bernstein calculation with standard real-world drags added, such as higher taxes later and private investment displaced by government borrowing. Their adjusted models gave a multiplier of only about 0.6 to 0.7.

The economist Valerie Ramey studied the biggest natural experiments on record, the huge bursts of federal spending in the Second World War and the Korean War, and then measured ordinary peacetime. In normal times, she found, each added federal dollar yielded under a dollar of extra economic activity. That strongly suggests ordinary federal spending usually fails to pay its own way, because it draws its resources away from somewhere else.

Bastiat taught readers to ask a stubborn question about every public dollar: where did it come from? There are only three possible answers. The government either took the dollar from a household in taxes, borrowed it from a lender, or had the central bank print it. Each path has an unseen cost: the household's lost spending, the private borrower who never got the loan, or the savers whose money now buys less.

Borrowing has a special name for its hidden cost. When a government borrows heavily, it competes with businesses and families for the same limited pool of savings, and some private borrowers are pushed aside: a factory never expanded, a house never built. Economists call this crowding-out, the modern name for Bastiat's unseen, and when it is large the multiplier sinks below one.

Henry Hazlitt pressed the point in his 1946 book Economics in One Lesson, in a chapter titled Public Works Mean Taxes. When a mayor promises a fine new bridge and plenty of jobs, the honest answer to the money question is that public works mean taxes on people who would otherwise have spent that money on something else. The ribbon-cutting is seen; the things those taxpayers never bought are not.

The objection is older than Hazlitt. On October 19, 1932, in the depths of the Depression, four economists at the London School of Economics, Hayek among them along with Lionel Robbins and Arnold Plant, warned that borrowing to pay for public works in the Keynes manner was no cure. They made their case in a letter to The Times of London.

friedman-in-chile-1975-and-the-chicago-b.context_blurb:
In September 1973 Chile's armed forces overthrew the elected socialist president, Salvador Allende, and a general took power. His military dictatorship ruled the country, a long strip of land along the Pacific, for the next seventeen years. It also handed the economy to young economists trained in Chicago, and the results, and Milton Friedman's brief part in them, are still fiercely argued.

The general who seized power in the coup of September 11, 1973, was Augusto Pinochet, and he ruled until 1990.

Since 1955 the University of Chicago had run an exchange program with Chile's Catholic University, and by the 1970s about twenty-five Chilean economists had studied in Chicago. Nicknamed the Chicago Boys, they took over economic policy from 1975, led by men such as Sergio de Castro, finance minister from 1976. Price controls and tariffs fell, state companies were sold, foreign trade and investment poured in, and the runaway inflation was brought under control.

In March 1975 Friedman spent six days in Chile at the invitation of a private Chilean foundation. He lectured in Santiago about ending the inflation that was wrecking the economy and met Pinochet for about forty-five minutes.

Back home the trip caused an uproar, and critics accused him of advising a dictatorship. Friedman answered that an economist giving technical advice was like a doctor treating a patient in a country whose government he disapproved of. Writing to Newsweek in 1976, he said that the regime was one he had nothing but dislike for.

The protests followed him to Stockholm. In 1976 Friedman received the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences, and demonstrators denounced his Chile visit at the ceremony, but he gave his lecture anyway.

Friedman pointed out a double standard. He had given similar free-market advice and lectures in China, the USSR and Yugoslavia without anything like the same protest. When he visited Communist China in 1980 and met leaders including Zhao Ziyang, almost no one objected.

Under the reforms Chile grew much richer over the following twenty years. Its poverty rate, about 45 percent in 1973, fell to around 10 percent by 2010, according to Chile's national statistics agency and the World Bank.

Pinochet's own 1980 constitution set a yes-or-no vote on whether he would stay for another term. On October 5, 1988, Chileans voted him out, and after free elections Patricio Aylwin took office in 1990, so Pinochet lost and the country returned peacefully to democracy.

The elected governments that followed were center-left, first led by the Christian Democrats and then by Socialist-led coalitions. They kept the market framework substantially in place for the next thirty years, and Chile remained the richest economy per person in South America through the 2010s.

Economists treat the whole stretch from 1973 to the 2010s as a natural experiment in a country switching to market rules. Its record is that Chile rose from a struggling economy to the richest in South America per person and, in the end, returned peacefully to democracy.

ftx-the-second-lesson-at-massive-scale.context_blurb:
In November 2022 one of the biggest names in cryptocurrency collapsed in about a week. FTX, the world's second-largest crypto exchange, based in the Bahamas and valued at some $32 billion at its peak, froze customer withdrawals and filed for bankruptcy on November 11. Its fall replayed an old lesson about trust, custody and other people's money on a massive scale.

Its founder, Sam Bankman-Fried, was an MIT graduate who had traded at Jane Street before starting a trading firm, Alameda Research, in 2017 and then FTX in 2019. Caroline Ellison, who was close to Bankman-Fried, ran Alameda.

At its height FTX seemed to be everywhere. It bought the naming rights to the arena where the Miami Heat play, for about $135 million, and paid celebrities such as Tom Brady and Shaquille O'Neal to appear in its TV ads. Splashy names like these buy a firm the look of trust before anyone gets around to asking hard questions.

The first crack appeared on November 2, 2022, when the crypto news site CoinDesk published a leaked balance sheet. Alameda's biggest asset turned out to be FTT, a token FTX had made up and could create at will. A token like that is no reserve at all, because its value depended on FTX staying in business; the moment the exchange faltered, the token would sink with it.

On November 6 Changpeng Zhao, head of Binance, the largest exchange, announced that Binance would sell all its FTT. Customers rushed to pull their money out of FTX in a classic run, and it began within hours.

There was nothing left to give them because of what had happened behind the scenes. When Alameda lost huge sums on risky bets, FTX had secretly used its customers' dollar and Bitcoin deposits to cover the losses, while promising them their money was safe. Taking money entrusted to you and spending it on yourself under false promises is fraud. In finance, mixing customer funds into a firm's own trading like this is called commingling, the same failure that sank MF Global in 2011 and the Bitcoin exchange Mt Gox in 2014.

In November 2023 a jury found Bankman-Fried guilty on every one of the seven fraud and conspiracy counts against him. In March 2024 Judge Lewis Kaplan sentenced him to twenty-five years behind bars.

Bankman-Fried had said publicly that his ethics came from effective altruism. That movement urges people to use their money and careers to help as many others as they can, for example by earning a fortune and donating it wherever it saves the most lives. He then took billions from his own customers.

Through the whole collapse the Bitcoin network itself kept running as usual, block after block. The failure was a dishonest company, not Bitcoin.

The customers who lost access had left their coins in FTX's accounts and trusted its website to say what was theirs, while people who held their own keys on their own devices were untouched. Bitcoiners sum up the lesson in a slogan about keys and coins: if the keys are not yours, neither are the coins.

greenspans-1-and-the-2005-no-bubble-spee.context_blurb:
Alan Greenspan chaired the Federal Reserve from 1987 to 2006, under four presidents, and at his peak he was hailed as the Maestro. Yet the cheap money of his last years helped build the housing bubble whose collapse set off the financial crisis of 2008, and the story is the Austrian theory of the business cycle played out in real time.

The Fed steers the economy mainly through the price of short-term loans. To encourage borrowing and spending it cuts that rate, and to cool prices that are climbing too fast, it raises interest rates.

After the dot-com bubble burst in 2000 and 2001, Greenspan's Fed cut the federal funds rate, what banks charge one another for overnight loans, again and again from 6.5 percent. By June 2003 it stood at 1 percent, the lowest in forty-six years, where it stayed for twelve months.

Cheap credit poured into housing. For decades American home prices had risen at about the pace of ordinary inflation, but in booming states such as Nevada, Florida and California prices now climbed ten to fifteen percent a year or more.

Two lenders led the rush to write risky mortgages: Angelo Mozilo's Countrywide, then the nation's biggest mortgage lender, and Ameriquest, Roland Arnall's subprime giant in Orange County, California. Their no-document loans and teaser-rate mortgages fed the demand, and both firms failed or were swallowed up when borrowers defaulted.

In a much-noticed speech to the American Bankers Association in the fall of 2005, Greenspan brushed off fears of a nationwide bubble. He allowed that some local markets showed froth, but argued that housing markets are local and varied, so a single national bubble was unlikely.

Austrian economists had been warning since 2003. Their reasoning came from the business-cycle theory of Mises and Hayek: interest rates held artificially low steer capital into long-lived, rate-sensitive projects such as housing, and the bust becomes inevitable because the real savings needed to finish those projects do not exist.

Three warning voices are usually named: Peter Schiff on CNBC, Ron Paul in congressional hearings, and Mark Thornton in his writing for the Mises Institute in Alabama. All three were brushed aside at the time.

Greenspan retired in early 2006, and in 2008 the housing market collapsed into the global financial crisis. Testifying to a House committee in October 2008, the former chairman admitted he had found a flaw in his worldview, his belief that self-interested bankers would protect their own firms from ruin, so markets would regulate themselves.

The broader Austrian lesson goes beyond one chairman. When a central bank keeps rates lower than savers and borrowers would settle on by themselves, year after year, cheap credit pours capital into rate-sensitive sectors, and the bust that follows is not a failure of the market but the correction of the earlier distortion.

The irony is sharp. In 1966, as a young private economist, Greenspan had written an essay for Ayn Rand's Objectivist newsletter calling for gold-backed money and warning that fiat paper lets governments quietly confiscate savings through inflation. Its title was Gold and Economic Freedom.

hans-hermann-hoppe-democracy-the-god-tha.context_blurb:
Hans-Hermann Hoppe, born in Peine, West Germany, in 1949, is one of the most controversial thinkers in the Austrian school. He argued that a hereditary king has better incentives to care for a country than an elected president, a claim that even many of his fellow free-market economists reject. To follow him you need one idea about time and one about ownership.

His path was unusual. In the 1970s he studied in Frankfurt under Jürgen Habermas, a famous philosopher of the left, and took his doctorate there in 1974. Over the following years his views swung toward free markets, and his story is a reminder that a person's political convictions can change over a lifetime.

In 1986 Hoppe moved to UNLV, the University of Nevada's Las Vegas campus, to work beside Murray Rothbard, and he taught there until 2008. Rothbard's vision was a society with no state at all, in which rival companies would sell protection, roads and the settling of disputes to whoever chose to buy, and he called it anarcho-capitalism.

Hoppe's own systematic case came in his 1989 book A Theory of Socialism and Capitalism, which defends private property by grounding it in the structure of deliberate human choice.

He is also known for a 1988 argument he called argumentation ethics. Anyone who argues, even someone arguing against property, is already using his own voice, flesh and time to do it, so arguing itself presupposes that each person owns his own body.

His best-known work, Democracy: The God That Failed, appeared in 2001. Its argument rests on time preference, how heavily an officeholder weighs the present against the future given how long he expects to hold power.

Hoppe made the point with an analogy from everyday property. A king owns his country, while an elected politician merely rents it for a term. An owner protects the long-run value of what he owns, but a renter is tempted to take what he can before the lease runs out.

Public debt shows the difference. A king who expects to hand the kingdom to his heir cares about its future revenue, Hoppe argued, while a president with a fixed term is tempted to borrow heavily against future taxpayers he will never have to answer to.

The book split the Austrian school. Peter Boettke of George Mason University and Joseph Salerno, long at Pace University and later the Mises Institute, accept much of Hoppe's analysis of politicians' incentives while refusing to follow him to his verdict against democracy.

In 2006 Hoppe founded the Property and Freedom Society, a libertarian conference that meets every summer in Bodrum, a resort town on Turkey's Aegean coast where he spends part of the year.

import-quotas-the-1980s-japanese-auto-ve.context_blurb:
Around 1980 Americans were buying Japanese compacts in record numbers, and the Detroit automakers were losing sales and cutting jobs. Washington's answer in 1981 became one of the clearest lessons in how a trade barrier hides its costs, and in how those costs can end up in surprising pockets.

The companies being protected were Detroit's Big Three: General Motors, Ford, and Chrysler.

Rather than slap a tariff on imported cars, the Reagan administration pressed Japan to limit its own shipments. Because Japan set the cap itself, under diplomatic pressure, the deal was called a voluntary export restraint. It began in 1981 with a ceiling of about 1.68 million cars annually, below the roughly 1.9 million Japan had sold in America in 1980, and the limit was raised during the decade before it ended in 1994.

Fewer imports meant higher prices for everyone. The economist Robert Crandall of the Brookings Institution calculated in 1987 that the restraint added about $1,000, in 1983 dollars, to the average price of a car. Later studies put the total cost to American buyers at several billion dollars a year, because Detroit raised its own prices behind the shelter.

The limit also changed the cars. Because the cap counted vehicles rather than dollars, each car Japan shipped had to earn as much profit as possible, so Japanese makers moved upmarket. The Accord, the Camry and the Maxima swelled into larger, plusher, costlier cars, the cheap little hatchback nearly disappeared, and the economist Robert Feenstra documented the upgrading in 1988.

Where did the extra money go? A tariff would have sent it to the US Treasury. Under the restraint, the Japanese companies themselves pocketed the difference as added profit on every car they sold, an income economists call quota rent.

In 1985 a senator could still defend the restraint by pointing to the Detroit jobs it had protected. A Brookings economist would answer with Frederic Bastiat's seen-versus-unseen move and name the invisible victim: the family that could no longer afford a $4,500 Japanese compact, who never testifies at any hearing.

james-m-buchanan-tennessee-farm-boy-to-n.context_blurb:
James McGill Buchanan was born in 1919 on a farm outside Murfreesboro, Tennessee, and grew up poor during the Depression. Decades later he stood in Stockholm to receive economics' highest prize for teaching the world to look at government the way economists look at markets. It was a long road from the dairy farm, and it ran through one classroom in Chicago.

Politics ran in the family. His grandfather, John Price Buchanan, was a Populist farmer-politician elected on a Farmers' Alliance platform who served as Governor of Tennessee from 1891 to 1893, and family stories of his campaigns fed the boy's early interest in public life.

After a state teachers college and wartime service on the Navy staff in Honolulu, Buchanan entered the University of Chicago in 1945 on the GI Bill. He arrived as a Southern rural Democrat who sympathized with New Deal redistribution; looking back, he called his younger self a "libertarian socialist." Six weeks in Frank Knight's course on price theory changed his mind and made him, in his own words, a market-order man.

Knight himself had drawn a famous distinction in his 1921 book. Some unknowns can be measured, like a coin flip that comes up heads half the time. Others, such as whether war will break out somewhere in the coming year, cannot be given honest odds at all, and Knight called that second kind uncertainty.

In 1955-56 a Fulbright year in Italy put Buchanan among Italian scholars of public finance, including the former president Luigi Einaudi, who wanted spending limits written into a nation's founding law. Their reasoning stayed with him: politicians face constant short-term pressure to spend and to print money, so only firm rules, set above everyday politics, can bind them.

In 1957, at the University of Virginia, Buchanan and Warren Nutter launched a research institute, naming it after the Virginian founder who had championed the small farmer and limited government: the Thomas Jefferson Center for Political Economy. Gordon Tullock joined them the following year, and in 1969 Buchanan and Tullock set up a new public-choice center at Virginia Tech, which moved with them to George Mason University in 1983.

Public choice applies the economist's toolkit, built for buyers and sellers, to officials, legislators and the citizens who vote for them. Its research on voting, lobbying and agency budgets kept reaching the same finding: people in government respond to incentives, just as people in business do. Faced with a vote on a new law, a senator will most often think first about getting re-elected. A mayor who times a ribbon-cutting for fresh pavement in a closely fought district just before the vote is showing that politicians respond to incentives like everyone else.

The Swedish Academy named Buchanan the economics laureate in October 1986, the first from the public-choice school. The committee did not use the words public choice; it honored his work on the contracts and constitutional rules that underlie the theory of how economic and political decisions are made. At the Stockholm ceremonies Buchanan made sure a portrait of his old teacher, Frank Knight, was displayed beside him.

His lesson can be put in one sentence: politicians are self-interested human beings, not benevolent planners. Buchanan himself called public choice "politics without romance."

joseph-salerno-and-the-calculation-debat.context_blurb:
In 1920 Ludwig von Mises argued that a socialist economy cannot calculate, and economists have argued ever since about what exactly he meant. Its most persistent modern student is Joseph Salerno, and his work shows how carefully one founding text can be read.

Mises's essay first ran in a German social-science journal, and in English it is called Economic Calculation in the Socialist Commonwealth.

Its core point is easy to state. Under socialism no one privately owns factories, tools or land, so no one can bid for them, and without bidding, capital goods never acquire genuine market prices. A central planner is left with no way to know which uses of resources are worth it and which waste them.

Friedrich Hayek later stressed a different side of the problem. The facts an economy runs on, about this field's soil, today's sales or a washed-out road, are spread among millions of people where they happen, and no planner could ever gather them quickly enough. Hayek called this obstacle the knowledge problem, and later Austrians such as Don Lavoie built on his reading of the debate.

Salerno, a Brooklyn native born in 1950 who taught for decades at Pace University, is now the foremost authority on the calculation debate. He defends a strict reading of Mises rather than the milder Hayekian one: the heart of the argument, he holds, is that without market prices for producer goods no cost comparison in money is possible at all, so calculation is a monetary problem first.

His key statement appeared in 1990 in the journal the Review of Austrian Economics, under the title Ludwig von Mises as Social Rationalist, and it moved many Austrians in the Mises Institute tradition toward his view.

Since its founding in 1998 Salerno has edited the scholarly journal that the Mises Institute, based in Alabama, publishes four times a year, whose plain title says exactly what it is: the Quarterly Journal of Austrian Economics.

His own essays on the Fed and the 2008 crash, written in Mises's monetary tradition, were collected by the Mises Institute in 2010 as Money: Sound and Unsound.

In 2004 he edited the scholar's edition of Murray Rothbard's great treatise, reuniting under one cover the two parts that had been split at first publication: Man, Economy, and State with Power and Market.

karl-marx-and-the-close-of-his-system--1.context_blurb:
Karl Marx's Das Kapital is one of the most influential books ever written. In 1896 Eugen von Boehm-Bawerk, of the Austrian school, published a short essay arguing that the book's central theory contradicts itself, and the argument he started ran for more than eighty years.

Marx's political aim was plain. Private ownership of factories and farms should end, and instead the state would own them on behalf of the workers.

His economics rested on one rule, set down in the first volume of Das Kapital, published in Hamburg in 1867: goods exchange in proportion to the labor-hours that went into each. A coat that took twice the socially necessary labor of a pair of shoes should trade for two pairs. This is the labor theory of value, which Marx inherited from David Ricardo.

Careful readers saw a gap at once. Real prices do not follow labor-hours: a factory full of machines sells its goods for more than its labor would predict, while a workshop full of hands sells for less. Converting labor values into the prices people actually pay became known as the transformation problem, and Marx promised to solve it in a later volume.

When Marx died in London in 1883, the solution was still in his drawers. His friend Friedrich Engels assembled the manuscripts and released the second volume in 1885 and finally, in 1894, the long-awaited Volume 3.

Volume 3 used a different rule: prices set by the cost of production, wages plus materials plus an average profit. In his 1896 essay, Zum Abschluss des Marxschen Systems, Boehm-Bawerk pressed one charge above all. It was not that Marx failed a test against data; it was that his two volumes could not both be true, an internal contradiction you can see with no data at all. Marx, he showed, had quietly dropped his own theory and slipped in the older cost-of-production theory of price associated with Adam Smith.

Boehm-Bawerk's alternative came from the Austrian school founded by Carl Menger in 1871. Labor does not put value into a thing; value is decided by how much a particular person wants it at that moment. Prices therefore come from what buyers actually want, not from the hours of work spent. Ask why a handmade horseshoe today sells for less than the labor it takes to forge, and the Austrian answer is subjective value: what a thing is worth depends on how much each buyer wants it.

The essay first appeared in a 1896 collection honoring the German economist Karl Knies. In 1904 the young Marxist Rudolf Hilferding, later Weimar Germany's finance minister, wrote the standard reply, and in 1949 the American Marxist Paul Sweezy printed both essays together in English.

For a generation the essay largely ended serious academic defense of Marx's value theory in German universities, though socialist parties kept growing and Das Kapital kept selling. The defense revived only with the Anglo-American revival of the 1940s to 1970s.

Later Marxists such as Duncan Foley offered a New Interpretation that does not defend Volume 3's original equations at all but rebuilds from other passages. Critics read that as a concession: keeping the verdict while abandoning the argument amounts to accepting the original refutation and starting over from different pages.

kirznerian-entrepreneurship-applied-jobs.context_blurb:
Why do some founders build giant companies out of technology that everyone else could have used too? Israel Kirzner, an Austrian-school economist who taught for decades at NYU, offered an answer in Competition and Entrepreneurship, published in 1973, and it can be tested on some of the most famous business stories of our time.

Kirzner learned his economics at NYU from Ludwig von Mises, who taught there from 1945 until his death in 1973 and had written the huge 1949 treatise Human Action. Kirzner became Mises's most devoted student and carried his approach to a new generation.

Two older pictures of the entrepreneur already existed. Frank Knight saw him mainly as a bearer of risk and uncertainty; Joseph Schumpeter saw him as an innovator whose new combinations destroy old industries. Kirzner's own definition differed from both: the entrepreneur is a person alert to profit opportunities that others have missed. His key skill is alertness, noticing a chance to earn money that everyone else has walked past, such as a shop nobody has opened or a product nobody has built.

Steve Jobs is one test. Touchscreens, music players and mobile phones all existed by 2006, but the market leaders, BlackBerry, Nokia and Motorola, kept their old designs. When Jobs launched the iPhone in June 2007, what he had seen was that the touchscreen, the music player and the phone could be joined in one product for a mass market.

Elon Musk is another. For forty years the launch industry threw every rocket away after one flight, like scrapping an airliner after a single trip. Musk founded SpaceX in 2002 to chase the chance everyone had missed: orbital rockets that come back, land and fly again, cutting the cost of each launch. The first Falcon 9 booster landed in December 2015, and within about a decade the company had brought back and reflown its first stages more than 300 times.

Jeff Bezos founded Amazon in a garage near Seattle on July 5, 1994, and he began with a single category: books. Books were the perfect launch product for an internet store because every copy of a title is the same, they survive shipping, they mail cheaply, and the catalog of titles is so vast that no physical shop could ever stock it.

The framework comes down to one question about any founder. The technology, the capital and the engineers were available to dozens of rivals, so what did this founder see that competitors with the same tools and money failed to act on?

Real founders mix all three theories: Bezos's choice of books was alertness, Musk's dream of Mars is Schumpeterian innovation, and both took Knightian risks. Pulling the theories apart is useful not to label a founder but to show which theory fits which particular move.

Kirzner never received a Nobel Prize, though many Austrians thought he deserved one. In 2006 he won the Global Award for Entrepreneurship Research, presented in Sweden as the field's top honor.

lightning-network-micropayments-on-top-o.context_blurb:
Bitcoin's main chain was built to be slow and secure rather than fast and cheap. It adds one block about every ten minutes, and a block has room for just a few thousand transactions, which is fine for large transfers but poor for buying a two-dollar coffee. The answer was not to change Bitcoin itself but to build on top of it.

Engineers built a second layer above the main chain, made for quick, small, everyday payments, while the base chain remains the place where final balances are settled. That fast, low-fee layer is the Lightning Network.

The design was set out in a January 2016 white paper by two developers, Joseph Poon and Thaddeus Dryja, and the network went live in March 2018.

It works through channels. Two people who expect to trade often first lock some bitcoin together in a shared account on the main chain; that step, called opening a payment channel, is done with a funding transaction. After that the pair can pay each other off the chain as often as they like, and when they finish, only the final balance is recorded on the main chain.

Channels link into a network. If Ana shares a channel with Ben, and Ben shares one with Cleo, then Ana can pay Cleo through Ben. Ben earns a small routing fee for passing the payment along; the sender pays such a fee to every go-between on the route, and each node sets its own fee in competition with the others.

In 2021 El Salvador made Bitcoin legal tender beside the US dollar, meaning money the government recognizes for paying debts and taxes. The government's Chivo phone wallet, which gave each adult $30 in bitcoin, ran on Lightning, and the developer Jack Mallers, whose Strike app sends payments over Lightning, stood beside President Nayib Bukele when the law was announced in June 2021.

A Hayekian economist sees a quiet achievement in a cheap coffee bought in San Salvador. Lightning keeps Bitcoin's settlement fully auditable while making coffee-sized payments possible at prices set by competing node operators, prices that no central rate-setter could have known how to fix.

mancur-olson-the-logic-of-collective-act.context_blurb:
Why do policies that hurt most people survive in a democracy, where the majority could vote them away? In 1965 a young economist who had grown up on a North Dakota farm answered with a short book that changed how economists and political scientists think about groups. His name was Mancur Olson.

Picture a law that hands a hundred sugar growers a million extra dollars apiece every year, funded by a one-dollar charge on each of a hundred million taxpayers. The growers battle to keep it; the taxpayers hardly notice. Economists call this pattern dispersed costs and concentrated benefits.

Olson's book, published by Harvard University Press, bears the title The Logic of Collective Action. Before it, political scientists generally assumed that people who share an interest, whether workers, consumers or taxpayers, will band together to pursue it. Olson showed that the comfortable assumption, that large groups with a common interest readily organize to advance it, is mostly false.

The reason is the free-rider problem. Think of a twenty-student class project in which everyone receives the same grade: each student is tempted to slack off and let the others finish the work. The same temptation runs through unions, taxes and climate treaties, and economists call it free-riding.

So when a subsidy would cost each of ten million taxpayers ten dollars but bring each of a hundred or so insiders a million, the side that organizes a serious lobbying campaign is the hundred insiders. A small tariff costing each family fifty dollars sails through the same way: a few domestic producers gain millions apiece, while a hundred million consumers each lose a little and never show up to object.

The arithmetic explains a whole class of politics. Policies that hand big gains to a few and spread small losses over millions survive for decades, even when their total cost exceeds their total benefit, because the winners defend them and the losers never organize.

Olson's book is often misread as saying large groups can never organize. In fact he named one mechanism that lets some succeed: selective incentives, private benefits available only to members. His classic example is AARP, whose enormous membership signs up largely for discounted insurance, hotel deals, travel savings and cheaper prescriptions.

Olson went on to write two more big books. In 1982 he asked why some nations grow rich while others stagnate, in The Rise and Decline of Nations. He died in 1998, and his students completed his last book, published in 2000 as Power and Prosperity, which explained growth through the contrast between roving bandits who plunder and stationary bandits who tax.

microstrategy-the-first-corporate-treasu.context_blurb:
In August 2020, while the Federal Reserve was creating dollars at a record pace, an American software company did something no large public company had done before. It moved its cash reserves into Bitcoin. The firm was MicroStrategy, and its founder, Michael Saylor, became the world's best-known corporate champion of Bitcoin.

Saylor's worry was simple. When a government keeps printing new money, every dollar a firm keeps in reserve slowly loses buying power, and that steady erosion is inflation. In 2020 the Fed's balance sheet expanded by trillions of dollars as it bought Treasury bonds and mortgage securities to prop up pandemic markets, and Saylor argued that this made holding cash a sure way to lose.

Bitcoin offered what dollars could not. Its supply is fixed at 21 million coins, and no one can print more, so a company's savings cannot be diluted the way dollars can.

MicroStrategy, founded by Saylor in 1989 and based in Tysons Corner, Virginia, announced on August 11, 2020, that it had turned $250 million of its existing cash, not borrowed money, into Bitcoin.

That was only the beginning. Even in the crypto slump of 2022, with the company's coins worth billions less than it had paid, Saylor kept buying, financing new purchases by selling convertible bonds again and again. By early 2026 the company held more than 200,000 bitcoin, by far the largest corporate holding in the world.

Parking a company's cash reserves in Bitcoin is now called a Bitcoin treasury strategy. MicroStrategy built its identity around it, adopting a Bitcoin-orange logo in February 2025 and changing its legal name to Strategy that August, and Saylor tells shareholders the company holds Bitcoin not as a trading chip but as a store of value for the long term.

Saylor's case sounds Austrian at almost every step. He points to the Cantillon effect, named for the eighteenth-century writer Richard Cantillon: new money reaches some people first, banks, government contractors and owners of financial assets, and they gain before prices catch up.

He also turns a corporate-finance habit upside down. Directors have a fiduciary duty to protect shareholders' value, and cash steadily loses purchasing power under a debasing central bank, so in Saylor's view fiduciary duty itself requires guarding shareholders against dollar debasement; it is no optional extra.

Others followed, and not all stayed. In early 2021 the carmaker Tesla put roughly $1.5 billion into Bitcoin, its chief executive tweeted the news and the price jumped, but within months Tesla sold much of it, and within about eighteen months it had sold roughly three-quarters of its stake.
