mises-s-critique-of-interventionism.context_blurb: By the late 1920s the Austrian economist Ludwig von Mises had spent a decade arguing that the mixed economy of subsidies, price controls, and targeted taxes was not a stable third option between capitalism and socialism but an unstable disequilibrium that must retreat toward markets or advance to further intervention. In 1929 he collected the argument in a German-language book whose title and subtitle set out the project. On April 18, 1950 Mises stood before the University Club in New York and gave the compact restatement of his three-decade case, printed days later in a financial weekly. The lecture walked the audience through a stylized milk example to show why partial intervention cannot rest: a government that caps the retail price of a food item will see the supply contract, and in response must cap the price of the feed used to produce the food item, then the price of the fuel used to transport the feed, then the wages paid in the input industries, until the state has effectively taken over every price in the economy. Mises argued that control is indivisible: either consumers direct production through the prices they are willing to pay or the state does through decree, and the middle position cannot hold. He closed with a famous short sentence that has been quoted ever since as the compact statement of the whole position. In 1987 the American economist Robert Higgs published an Oxford study of American federal growth across the twentieth century documenting a specific one-way asymmetry: governments that grew in a crisis never fully returned to their pre-crisis size afterward.

murray-rothbard-who-he-was.context_blurb: Murray Rothbard was born on March 2, 1926 and died on January 7, 1995. He entered Columbia at sixteen, earned a BA at nineteen, took his Columbia PhD in 1956 with a dissertation on the Panic of 1819, and by the late 1950s had become the second generation of the American Austrian school. His father David was a chemist who had emigrated from Poland; the family were Jewish immigrants to the Bronx. From the mid-1950s Rothbard attended Ludwig von Mises's private seminar at New York University, paid for by a classical-liberal donor fund. Mainstream American economics departments refused to hire him for the first thirty years of his career; he taught part-time at a Brooklyn engineering school from 1966 to 1986 while writing the Austrian tradition's flagship American treatise. In 1986 he finally moved to a full economics chair at the University of Nevada, Las Vegas, where he stayed until his death. He helped co-found two of the most influential libertarian institutions of the century, the Washington think tank in 1977 and the Austrian-focused academic institute in Auburn, Alabama in 1982, each as a different wing of the same movement. He coined a specific term for his own political system, a stateless private-property order defended by voluntary institutions, which distinguished his position from the minarchism of Nozick and the minimal-state objectivism of Rand. His 1973 Macmillan popular manifesto introduced his system to general readers; his four-volume history of American colonial life and the Revolution, published between 1975 and 1979 with a fifth volume assembled posthumously in 2019, is his largest work of American history.

nimby-political-economy-palo-alto-zoning.context_blurb: In Silicon Valley the paradigm case of local homeowners successfully blocking new housing is a small city that houses Stanford University, where the median home price has approached three million dollars. Roughly ninety-four percent of its residential land is zoned exclusively for single-family detached homes, which makes apartment construction practically illegal across almost the whole city. The three-letter shorthand for the pattern in which existing local homeowners organize to block new housing in their neighborhoods, even when a region's overall housing shortage produces high rents and long commutes, has become standard political-science vocabulary. Harvard urban economist Edward Glaeser and Wharton's Joseph Gyourko coined a term for the wedge between the actual construction cost of housing in supply-constrained cities and its market price, estimating it in the range of thirty to sixty percent in Bay Area cities. In Mancur Olson's framework, applied to this case, existing homeowners are the concentrated beneficiary group that organizes; the dispersed victims are families priced out to distant commuter cities or out of California entirely, who cannot vote in the city and often never knew that a specific project would have housed them. A counter-coalition began forming around 2015-16 under a different four-letter acronym. California passed a 2021 state law allowing homeowners to build a duplex on single-family lots over local objection, and the city of Minneapolis in 2018 became the first major US city to eliminate single-family-only zoning citywide. One large Sun Belt city produced actual measured rent declines through a 2019-2024 permitting boom. Japan's national zoning system, which permits substantial by-right construction, has kept Tokyo housing prices comparatively stable.

operation-twist-and-qe3-2011-14.context_blurb: On September 21, 2011 the Federal Reserve announced a program to sell four hundred billion dollars of short-dated Treasuries while buying the same quantity of long-dated ones, flattening the yield curve without expanding the balance sheet. The program borrowed its name from a Kennedy-era Treasury-Fed program of 1961 that had first tried the yield-curve-flattening technique, originally for a different policy purpose. One year later, on September 13, 2012, the Fed launched its third round of large-scale asset purchases, initially committing forty billion dollars per month in mortgage-backed-security purchases with no announced cap. A market strategist coined a now-standard nickname for the program that stuck immediately across financial media. In December 2012 the program was expanded to add forty-five billion dollars per month in longer-dated Treasury purchases, bringing total monthly Fed asset buying to a very large monthly figure. The program ran until October 2014, when a new Fed chair, the first woman to lead the Federal Reserve, announced the taper-and-end. By late 2014 the Fed's balance sheet had grown roughly fivefold from its pre-2008 level. Austrian critics warned throughout the era that an expansion of this scale was setting up a future price event once money velocity recovered, pointing to a Cantillon pattern in which asset prices rise first and consumer prices follow with a long lag. The 2021-2023 consumer-price wave, arriving more than a decade after the first round, fit the Austrian prediction. There is also a public-choice point: when central-bank monthly purchases exceed the annual GDP of several small countries, the choice of which assets to buy is inescapably political, not merely technical.

peter-schiff-and-the-gold-versus-bitcoin.context_blurb: Peter Schiff is an American stockbroker who runs the firm Euro Pacific Capital. He has been publicly bullish on gold since the early 2000s and became widely known outside the gold community after making a correct prediction about an American financial crisis on live cable television in the years just before it came true. His father, an Austrian-economics writer who died while serving a federal prison sentence in 2015, had shaped his economic worldview. Schiff wrote a 2007 book laying out the prediction he had been making on television; videos of the 2006-07 cable appearances became a viral YouTube compilation after the crash arrived. Since roughly 2013 Schiff has been Bitcoin's most persistent critic in the sound-money community. His central argument against Bitcoin points to one specific property gold has that Bitcoin does not: a long history of non-monetary use, from jewelry to industrial applications to five thousand years of recognition across cultures. His standard debate opponent since 2020 has been the executive who made the largest corporate-treasury Bitcoin purchases in history, and the two have exchanged positions in dozens of recorded conversations. His opponent's counter-argument concedes that Bitcoin is new but denies that intrinsic non-monetary value is what actually makes something money, pointing to properties like scarcity, divisibility, portability, and verifiability as the real monetary tests. Schiff reliably brings up an Austrian-tradition argument about how money must originate historically, which his opponent concedes is a substantive argument requiring serious reply. The valuable thing about the exchange is that both men state and defend their positions honestly in public.

politics-without-romance-buchanans-nobel.context_blurb: When James Buchanan sat down to describe what the public-choice school actually did, he coined a three-word phrase that has served as its shorthand ever since. The phrase was the title of a 1979 lecture Buchanan delivered at a Vienna research institute, later widely reprinted. The romance to be stripped was a widespread mid-century habit in welfare economics of comparing imperfect real markets against idealized government interventions, as if political actors somehow escaped the ordinary self-interest that economics assumes for consumers and firms. Buchanan's move was simple and devastating: if we assume ordinary self-interest for consumers and firms, we must assume it for politicians and bureaucrats too. The symmetric treatment produced a whole category of policy breakdown that mirrors the market pathologies of the welfare-economics textbooks, which public-choice calls government failure. Specific mechanisms include regulatory capture, rent-seeking, agency budget maximization, and rational voter ignorance. Thomas Sowell, writing across many books, condensed Buchanan's whole comparative move into a two-word question a critic should always ask when someone claims the market has failed and the government should act. Buchanan credited an older Hungarian-born LSE development economist for coining the closely-related phrase the romantic view of the state well before Buchanan wrote his own. The phrase works as a diagnostic test, not a slogan.

price-gouging-laws-the-generator-that-ne.context_blurb: Hurricane Fran cut power to a million people around Raleigh, North Carolina in September 1996. Four men trucked bagged ice from Goldsboro and sold it at seven times its usual price to residents without electricity for food storage; the police arrested them on the spot, and the crowd that had been waiting in line applauded as they were cuffed. Duke University economist Michael Munger wrote the night up for the Library of Economics and Liberty under a two-word title taken from what the crowd did. Most American states punish merchants who raise prices on water, fuel, and generators after a disaster. Florida's statute does not run all the time: it switches on when the governor declares a state of emergency, and defines unlawful prices in terms of a gross disparity with the previous month's average. A classic case is the Kentucky man who watched Hurricane Katrina coverage in 2005, bought nineteen generators, rented a truck, drove about six hundred miles to Mississippi, and was jailed for four days while the generators sat in police custody rather than reaching anyone who needed them. Hayek's 1945 essay on how a price change moves information through a market shows what the anti-gouging statutes actually silence. Munger has argued against the laws for two decades, and on the economics podcast EconTalk he reduced the position to one sentence about the relationship between permitting high prices now and achieving low prices later. The deep Bastiat move is to name the unseen: every generator sitting in a warehouse two states away that stays there because the signal to bring it has been criminalized.

proof-of-work-vs-proof-of-stake-the-ethe.context_blurb: On September 15, 2022 Ethereum, the second-largest cryptocurrency by market capitalization, completed the largest scheduled software upgrade ever performed on a live financial network. It transitioned off the energy-hungry consensus mechanism that Bitcoin invented and that Ethereum had itself used since launch, onto a new mechanism in which the right to add the next block is assigned not by burning electricity but by locking up a quantity of the cryptocurrency itself. Ethereum Foundation figures put the energy reduction at roughly ninety-nine point nine five percent. Ethereum's founder, who had published its white paper in late 2013, had argued for the switch since Ethereum's earliest design discussions. The most common Bitcoin-community critique of the new mechanism is that it recreates a specific pre-Bitcoin monetary property: those who start with the most tokens have the most power to add blocks, entrench their position, and shape network rules, without any external physical check equivalent to the electricity a miner must burn. The critique rests on an economist's attack called the nothing-at-stake problem, in which validators can costlessly sign multiple competing chains at once because no real-world resource is spent per signature. The chair of the US Securities and Exchange Commission in 2023 suggested that many of the new tokens could fall under US investor-protection statutes. Bitcoin remains on the original mechanism as a core design principle: the electricity cost is not a bug but an external real-world commitment that anchors the network to physical reality. Two cryptocurrencies descended from Bitcoin's codebase persisted on the original mechanism past the 2022 upgrade. The empirical verdict will take decades of live operation across attacks and crashes.

rai-stones-of-yap-the-sunken-money-still.context_blurb: For centuries, villagers on a small group of Micronesian islands used massive round limestone discs as their circulating money. Some were over twelve feet across and weighed several tons. The islands had no limestone of their own; the discs had been carved from aragonite on an island about two hundred and fifty miles away and transported home across the open ocean by outrigger canoe. Once installed, a disc was generally too heavy to move for later transactions. When ownership changed hands, the villagers simply agreed in public that the stone now belonged to someone else, while the physical stone stayed exactly where it was. In the famous Yap sunken-stone story, a canoe crew bringing a particularly large disc home ran into a storm and the disc slid off into deep water; the crew returned and testified to its size and quality, and the villagers agreed that the stone was still valuable, still ownable, and still transferable. In 1991 Milton Friedman retold the story in an essay later collected in his book Money Mischief, drawing a direct parallel to how one New York Federal Reserve staff could shift national gold-ownership entries by moving bars between drawers inside the same vault. The deep lesson, which the cypherpunks later drew too, is that money is a ledger, and the physical container of the ledger is only a secondary engineering choice. Nick Szabo pointed out that the costly open-ocean carving of a disc is a physical analog of Bitcoin's cryptographic proof-of-work.

right-to-try-and-the-fda-from-peltzman-t.context_blurb: In 1973 the Chicago-trained economist Sam Peltzman published a Journal of Political Economy paper studying the effects of a 1962 amendment to the US Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act that had imposed new efficacy requirements for FDA approval, passed in response to a specific European sedative tragedy. Peltzman found a visible benefit (prevented tragedies of that specific kind) and an invisible cost: patients dying while safe and effective drugs sat in a longer approval queue. The move is Bastiat's SEEN versus UNSEEN applied to drug regulation. In May 2018 the federal Right-to-Try Act was signed into law, giving terminally-ill patients access to drugs that had passed Phase I safety trials but not yet received full approval; George Mason University economist Alex Tabarrok has been a leading academic advocate for FDA reform in that direction. A more recent voice is a UCSF hematologist-oncologist whose 2020 Johns Hopkins book argued that many drugs approved through accelerated pathways on surrogate endpoints have not actually delivered survival improvement. His move is to require the outcome that matters rather than proxy measures that often do not translate. The FDA sits inside a two-sided error problem: approving an unsafe drug gets front-page coverage, while blocking a lifesaving one is invisible. The 2016 bipartisan Cures Act and the December 2020 emergency pathway for COVID vaccines both expanded accelerated-approval tools.

saifedean-ammous-the-bitcoin-standard-th.context_blurb: Saifedean Ammous is a Lebanese-Palestinian economist with a Columbia PhD from 2011 who, after years as a tenured professor at Lebanese American University in Beirut, has become the most widely-read modern advocate for treating Bitcoin as sound money in the Austrian tradition. His 2018 Wiley book has since become the best-selling Bitcoin book of all time, translated into more than forty languages. Its central move is to build on an older Austrian tradition that classifies goods by how hard they are to produce more of, and to apply a specific ratio from monetary economics that measures how much of a thing already exists against how much new flow is added each year. Applied to Bitcoin, the argument reaches a dramatic conclusion about Bitcoin's monetary properties over time, because new issuance is cut in half by protocol roughly every four years. In 2021 Ammous published a sequel focused on what fiat currencies have done to the world since Nixon closed the gold window in 1971, from monetary inflation to artificial-food industrialization to debased family and cultural formation. In 2020, during COVID lockdowns, Ammous parted company with the tenured position he had held, refusing the mandatory online-teaching regime; he built a subscription platform of his own to deliver his Austrian-economics course directly, which has grown into a serious teaching institution. Ammous's independent teaching work is most often compared, by his students, to the modern American home of Rothbardian Austrian economics in Alabama.

school-choice-milton-friedmans-1955-vouc.context_blurb: In 1955 the Chicago economist Milton Friedman published an essay titled The Role of Government in Education, later reprinted as a chapter of his 1962 book Capitalism and Freedom. The essay argued that government financing of schooling might be justified on externality grounds, but that government production of schooling did not follow from that justification. His proposal was for a transferable instrument parents could redeem at any accredited school of their choice, including private and religious ones, rather than for a specific district-assigned public school. Since 1970, real US K-12 per-pupil spending has approximately tripled, while scores on the National Assessment of Educational Progress long-term-trend assessment have remained essentially flat. The first urban voucher program in the United States launched in a Midwestern city in 1990, championed by a Democratic state legislator who had been a welfare mother and signed into law by a Republican governor. In 2002 the US Supreme Court upheld a Rust Belt city's voucher program on the reasoning that aid flowed through private parental choice rather than directly to religious institutions. Milton and Rose Friedman founded a foundation in 1996, in the last decade of Milton's life, dedicated to the one policy application he considered his most important. A wave of US state Education Savings Account laws in 2023-2024 made K-12 school choice broadly available for the first time in US history across several states.

silk-road-bitcoins-first-widely-known-us.context_blurb: From February 2011 to October 2013 an online marketplace operating on the Tor anonymity network sold many kinds of illicit goods, most infamously drugs, and used Bitcoin as its exclusive currency. It became the first widely known use case for Bitcoin outside hobbyist circles. The founder, a young American libertarian named Ross Ulbricht, ran the site under a pseudonym drawn from William Goldman's novel The Princess Bride, where the identity is meant to pass from one operator to the next so no single individual is ever caught. On October 1, 2013 the FBI arrested Ulbricht in a very specific public location, the science-fiction section of a San Francisco public library branch, so it could seize his laptop while it was still unlocked and logged into the site's administrator interface. He was convicted in February 2015 on seven counts including drug trafficking conspiracy and money laundering, and in May 2015 received a sentence of life in prison without parole. After nearly ten years of advocacy for his release by libertarians and Bitcoin-community activists, a US president commuted his sentence in January 2025. Within the early Bitcoin community the use of Bitcoin on the site split opinion. Some celebrated that the technology worked as designed, offering censorship-resistant payments no intermediary could block. Others worried that the association with illegal activity would damage Bitcoin's broader prospects. The episode raises questions about proportionality of sentence and about censorship-resistance as a protocol-level design property.

sowell-on-discrimination-and-disparities.context_blurb: In 2018 Thomas Sowell published Discrimination and Disparities, aimed at a line of reasoning common in the news: where two groups end up unequal, someone must have treated one of them worse. The book argues that a difference in outcomes tells you something has differed between the two groups, and not yet what that something is. Sowell's favorite kinds of counter-examples are minorities that were legally restricted, barred from professions, and sometimes attacked in riots, and that nonetheless ended up with higher measured incomes than the host populations around them. Lebanese merchant families across West Africa, Indian merchant families across East Africa, and ethnic-Chinese communities across Southeast Asia all fit this pattern. Sowell argues that the pattern reveals the portability of human capital: trading skills, business habits, educational traditions, and commercial networks travel with people and keep working in new countries. Between 1994 and 1998 he published three linked volumes on race, migration, and conquest built on fifteen years of international travel and research. His 2018 book sharpens a specific analytical move about one English word that has been quietly doing two different jobs: there is a sense of the word that means fact-based sorting on real qualifications, and a second sense that means arbitrary aversion to a group. Many disputes about antidiscrimination policy, he argues, confuse the two. His careful statistical work includes a famous observation about birth order within families and a prerequisites argument about why success requiring multiple conditions all present together is never evenly distributed.

spot-bitcoin-etfs-approved-january-10-20.context_blurb: On January 10, 2024 the US Securities and Exchange Commission approved eleven products of a specific new kind, allowing institutional pools direct access to Bitcoin for the first time without opening a cryptocurrency-exchange account. The products hold the actual asset rather than futures contracts, which is what distinguishes them from the Bitcoin futures ETFs the agency had approved in 2021. The approval was effectively forced by an August 2023 federal appeals-court ruling that the SEC could not consistently approve one kind and deny the other based on the same underlying market. The approval vote was narrow, three to two, with the chair joining the two Republican commissioners over objections from the two Democratic commissioners. The largest of the eleven products was issued by the world's largest asset manager under a specific ticker, and accumulated the largest ETF asset base in any category during its first year. By December 2024 the full group of approved funds collectively held roughly one point one million Bitcoin, about five percent of the total supply. The Cantillon-effect reading identifies the first receivers of the new institutional product: pensions, endowments, family offices, and professional retail wealth managers whose fiduciary rules had kept them out of the asset before. One prominent Bitcoin advocate has continued to criticize the product as a trade of self-custody sovereignty for institutional accessibility; the CEO who steered one of the biggest corporate Bitcoin bets has publicly framed it as a positive structural event. Bitcoin's price passed six figures for the first time in the eleven months after approval. The ETF wrapper is a regulatory technology, not a monetary change.

tarp-and-bailouts-moral-hazard-and-the-2.context_blurb: On October 3, 2008 President George W. Bush signed a seven-hundred-billion-dollar program authorizing the US Treasury to buy troubled assets from major banks and to inject equity capital into them during the financial crisis. The program has a specific name in economics for the behavioral distortion it creates in future creditors and borrowers: once creditors expect rescue in a crisis, they demand less risk premium and the system takes more risk, making the next crisis more likely. The visible benefit was preventing a cascading collapse in that specific year. The invisible cost was in the next crisis, in the changed behavior of every future creditor and bank expecting rescue. Fifteen years later, on March 10, 2023 a California-headquartered bank failed after a classic run triggered by unrealized losses on its long-duration Treasury holdings; roughly ninety-three percent of its deposits were uninsured. Two days later the Treasury, Fed, and FDIC jointly announced that all depositors would be made whole, including uninsured ones above the standard FDIC cap, invoking a systemic-risk exception. The announcement broke a settled expectation and institutionalized the 2008 precedent. The classic Victorian rule for central-bank crisis response, from Walter Bagehot's 1873 book Lombard Street, was lend freely at a high and punishing rate against good collateral, so that banks would only use the facility in true crisis. Anna Schwartz, co-author with Milton Friedman of A Monetary History of the United States, had warned in her final years that the Fed's mission had drifted from monetary stability toward defending asset prices, and that the consequences would surface in the next crisis.

thatcher-reagan-and-the-1980s-hayekian-p.context_blurb: In 1979 a grocer's daughter from the small English town of Grantham became British Prime Minister, having led the Conservative Party since 1975. Two years later, an American actor who had been Governor of California was inaugurated as the fortieth US President, and the two governments spent most of the 1980s consciously coordinating on tax cuts, deregulation, and Cold War strategy. Both leaders drew intellectual guidance from the same Austrian-born economist. At a 1975 Conservative Research Department meeting she famously interrupted a speaker urging a middle way by pulling the economist's 1960 political-philosophy book from her handbag and declaring that this is what we believe. The economist had already founded a classical-liberal scholarly society above Lake Geneva in 1947, bringing together Mises, Milton Friedman, Karl Popper, and others, and the society became the global network for the next generation of reformers. A former RAF pilot who had read a condensation of the economist's wartime book in 1945 then founded London's leading free-market think tank in 1957 on the economist's own advice. Thatcher's government privatized major state monopolies, including a 1984 share flotation that broke records; won a year-long strike against a public-sector union in 1984-85; deregulated the London Stock Exchange on a famous day in October 1986; and cut top income-tax rates in a defining 1988 budget. Reagan invited the then-eighty-four-year-old economist to the White House in November 1983 and wrote in his diary about the meeting. The story runs from 1947 in Switzerland through the policy turns of the 1980s on both sides of the Atlantic.

the-2008-great-financial-crisis-peter-sc.context_blurb: On September 15, 2008 a one-hundred-and-fifty-eight-year-old Wall Street investment bank filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection listing about six hundred and thirteen billion dollars in liabilities, the largest corporate bankruptcy in US history. One prominent stockbroker who ran a small firm had gone on cable news through 2006 and 2007 warning that the American housing boom was a Federal-Reserve-created bubble that would end in a crash. A viral YouTube compilation after the crash intercut his cable-news appearances under a title that stated the obvious. His 2007 book, released by John Wiley just before the crash, forecast the housing collapse, the banking crisis, and a declining US dollar in sequence. The Austrian reading of the whole 2003-2008 sequence tracks closely to a theory a Vienna-born economist had set out in a 1931 LSE lecture series. Under Fed chair Alan Greenspan the funds rate had been pushed down to a historic low after the dot-com bust and held there for a year. Beginning in June 2004 the Fed raised the funds rate in seventeen quarter-point steps, which reset tens of billions of dollars of mortgages and revealed malinvestment in long-duration housing projects. On March 28, 2007 the new Fed chair told Congress that the impact of subprime problems on the broader economy was likely to be contained. A Texas congressman had warned in a September 2003 House Financial Services Committee hearing that implicit government backing of the big housing-finance firms was creating catastrophic risk. The Fed's response to the crash was to cut to zero and launch three successive rounds of large-scale asset purchases. A Mises Institute historian's 2009 Regnery book was the mature Austrian post-mortem.

the-bank-term-funding-program-stealth-qe.context_blurb: On Sunday, March 12, 2023, the same weekend one New York bank was seized, the Federal Reserve announced an emergency lending facility for banks facing bond-loss pressure. The distinctive feature that made the program unusual, and that critics called stealth QE by another name, was how it valued the collateral banks pledged. The Fed's traditional discount-window operation values collateral at market price with a haircut, which ensures the Fed is over-collateralized. The new facility accepted long-duration Treasuries and mortgage-backed securities at their original face value, not at market price. A ten-year Treasury that had been bought at a one point five percent yield when ten-year yields had climbed to four percent could be pledged at a hundred cents on the dollar rather than roughly eighty cents. The implicit subsidy to banks that had loaded up on long-duration bonds was substantial. Analysts across the sound-money community publicly argued it functioned as a quantitative-easing operation under a different name; the Fed's balance sheet was rising against the then-announced quantitative tightening program because banks were borrowing directly from the facility. The program was authorized under a specific section of the Federal Reserve Act dating to 1932 that permits emergency lending in unusual and exigent circumstances. Borrowings peaked at roughly one hundred and sixty-seven billion dollars in early 2024, and the Fed let the facility expire in March 2024 without extension. The facility is a classic Bastiat seen-versus-unseen case of a visible stabilization that hides an invisible transfer, and it leaves a precedent for every future bank risk manager.

the-black-book-of-communism-1997.context_blurb: In 1997 a major French publisher released a nine-hundred-page collaborative work by six European historians documenting the death tolls of twentieth-century communist regimes country by country from the archives that opened after the fall of the Soviet Union. The lead editor was a CNRS historian who had begun his own career as a 1968 Maoist student and spent three decades reading the archives that opened after 1991. The combined total the volume reached, assembled from careful country totals, is one of the largest and most-cited figures in modern history: a range of roughly eighty-five to one hundred million people. The country breakdown reflects what the archives showed: by far the largest fraction in China, driven by the Great Leap Forward famine of 1959 to 1961 plus the Cultural Revolution and other campaigns; the second largest in the USSR, where a specific French historian wrote the chapter from post-1991 archival access; and smaller totals in Cambodia, North Korea, Africa, Afghanistan, Vietnam, and Eastern Europe. The lead editor's introduction made an argument that generated a famous internal dispute among the contributors themselves, who distanced themselves from his equation of communist and Nazi crimes while standing by the country totals they had written. Harvard University Press published the English edition in 1999, which brought the figures into standard scholarly circulation in the US. The book has been translated into roughly twenty-six languages. Other major scholarly volumes document specific pieces of the same total, including a Pulitzer-winning history of the Soviet forced-labor system and a 2008 Chinese-journalist account of the Great Leap Forward famine.

the-cobra-effect-british-delhi-and-the-b.context_blurb: German economist Horst Siebert coined a parable-name in his 2001 book Der Kobra-Effekt, drawn from a widely-retold story about colonial administration in nineteenth-century India. In the standard telling, a colonial government wanted to reduce the venomous-cobra population in the capital and offered a cash bounty for every dead snake brought in. The seen policy was simple: kill more cobras, get paid, the population falls. The unseen response was entrepreneurial: residents started breeding cobras in their back yards for the bounty, since farming dead snakes was more profitable than hunting wild ones. When the government eventually noticed the perverse incentive and canceled the bounty, the breeders released their now-worthless stock into the streets, and the final cobra population ended higher than it had been before the program began. A better-documented parallel is a rat-bounty scheme run by French colonial administration in a Southeast Asian city, which produced the same twist. In 1975 the British economist Charles Goodhart wrote a one-line formulation of the general pattern in a Bank of England paper on monetary aggregates: when a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure. In 2016 a US retail bank was fined when employees under pressure to hit a cross-sell bounty opened millions of accounts customers had not requested. The 2001-2015 US federal education law tying funding partly to standardized test scores produced the same pattern in schools. Hospitals under the Affordable Care Act's thirty-day readmission penalties responded by keeping returning patients in emergency-department observation rather than formal admission. The parable carries a general point about any policy that pays people for a measured number instead of the outcome itself.

the-cypherpunk-lineage-digicash-b-money-.context_blurb: In the early 1990s a mailing-list movement of cryptographers and privacy advocates coalesced in the San Francisco Bay Area, dedicated to building working software rather than merely writing political manifestos. The name was coined by one of the founders at an early meeting hosted by Eric Hughes, Timothy May, and John Gilmore. The lineage of digital-cash proposals that would eventually be synthesized by Satoshi Nakamoto in 2008 runs through several concrete attempts spread across the 1990s. In 1989 an American cryptographer often called the father of digital cash founded an Amsterdam company to commercialize his 1982 invention of blind signatures. Its anonymity worked, but by 1998 the company had filed for bankruptcy; the issuance of each coin still had to go through a trusted bank, which could be shut down. In November 1998 a Chinese-American cryptographer posted a two-page proposal describing a peer-to-peer money system with no central issuer; it left the problem of consensus between users who see different transaction orderings unsolved. In 1997 a British cryptographer proposed a small computational puzzle as an anti-spam measure, imposing a cost on each email sent; the puzzle had an asymmetric property that made it instantly valuable for a completely different application a decade later. In the same year a legal scholar and computer scientist who had coined the term smart contracts posted a design in which chained proof-of-work puzzles produced scarce digital tokens. Satoshi's 2008 white paper cited two of these four proposals by name. A founding essay by Eric Hughes from March 1993 opens with a line about privacy that still functions as the philosophical anchor of the whole project.

the-farm-bill-and-snap-urban-rural-logro.context_blurb: The US Farm Bill is a comprehensive multi-title federal statute reauthorized roughly every five years, most recently in 2018 and 2024. The vast majority of its combined ten-year cost per Congressional Budget Office projections is not actually spent on farms. Roughly three-quarters of the ten-year outlays go to a specific nutrition-assistance program, formerly known under a different name, that serves tens of millions of low-income American households. The 1962 Buchanan-Tullock book The Calculus of Consent identified a vote-trading mechanism that allows a bundled policy to pass when neither of its halves could pass alone, which they called a defining feature of majority-rule legislative bodies. The persistent bundling of nutrition assistance and farm programs in the same statute traces back to a 1973 legislative architecture credited to two senators from different parties: a Republican from Kansas and a Democrat from South Dakota. The coalition logic is that urban and suburban Democrats have the votes for the nutrition program but not for farm subsidies, while rural Republicans have the votes for farm subsidies but not for the nutrition program. In 2013 the House voted to strip the nutrition program out of the Farm Bill and process it as a separate statute, but the separation failed in conference and the bundle was reconstituted. The bundle template appears in other must-pass federal statutes, and the 1996 Line-Item Veto Act, which would have let a president strike individual bundled provisions, was struck down by the Supreme Court in 1998.

the-fomc-who-actually-decides-us-monetar.context_blurb: Within the Federal Reserve System, a specific committee actually decides whether to raise, lower, or hold the target interest rate. The committee is known by a three-letter acronym and holds eight regularly scheduled meetings per year on a published calendar, roughly every six to eight weeks. It has twelve voting seats drawn from two Fed bodies: seven Board of Governors members based in Washington plus five regional Reserve Bank presidents. Only one of the twelve regional Reserve Banks has a president who always votes at every meeting; the other eleven rotate through four voting seats on annual cycles. The seven Washington-based Board members are nominated by the President and confirmed by the Senate for fourteen-year non-renewable terms, which are the longest fixed terms of any federal position other than Supreme Court justices with life tenure. One famous Fed chair ran the committee from 1987 to 2006 across the 1987 crash, the 1998 LTCM rescue, the 2000 dot-com bust, and the 2004-06 rate cycle. The committee votes a target range for the overnight interbank interest rate used as the reference point for millions of adjustable loans. Friedrich Hayek's 1945 essay on dispersed knowledge frames an Austrian objection to any central rate-setting committee: no small group can gather the dispersed information needed to set the right price for credit across the whole economy. A public-choice point about the committee is that regional Fed presidents are not Senate-confirmed; they are chosen by the boards of the private-sector member banks in their districts. Traders and journalists parse the committee's statements so intensely that an informal name has grown up for the sub-profession that reads them full-time.

the-great-terror-1936-38-the-yezhovshchi.context_blurb: Stalin's peak mass-execution wave from mid-1937 through late 1938 is remembered by an English name and a Russian personal name taken from the head of the NKVD who ran it. Post-1991 archive access gave the definitive figure for the eighteen-month campaign: roughly seven hundred and fifty thousand people shot, about a thousand per day. On July 30, 1937 the NKVD issued a specific numbered order giving every regional office quotas for executions and labor-camp sentences. The campaign included a series of Moscow show trials that destroyed the surviving Old Bolsheviks who had made the 1917 Revolution; one of them, called the party's golden boy by Lenin, was tried in a March 1938 trial and shot. The pioneering 1968 Western scholarly account was treated with academic-left disdain at publication and wholly vindicated by the archives that opened a quarter-century later. The Red Army officer corps was deliberately targeted in 1937-38, which weakened the Soviet military just before World War II: three of the five Marshals of the Soviet Union were shot, along with roughly half the officer corps. The NKVD chief who ran the campaign was himself executed by his successor's NKVD in early 1940, the standard fate of the enforcer once his work was done. Ethnic-targeted operations within the wider campaign killed disproportionately in specific border-nation communities, including an operation under NKVD Order 00485 in August 1937 against ethnic Poles across the USSR. Timothy Snyder's 2010 scholarly work is now the standard integrated account of the fourteen million civilians deliberately killed in the region between 1933 and 1945 under both Soviet and Nazi policy.

the-latin-american-debt-crisis-and-brady.context_blurb: In August 1982 one of the biggest borrowing nations in the Western Hemisphere told the US Treasury it could no longer pay its foreign debts, opening a sovereign-debt crisis that would spread across Latin America and nearly take down several of the largest American commercial banks. Through the 1970s a leading US bank chairman had been famous for a confident line that sovereign borrowers could always repay because they could tax and print. By 1982 the nine largest US commercial banks held Latin American loans equal to nearly one hundred and seventy-six percent of their combined equity, according to the FDIC's official history. The crisis had been triggered in part by Paul Volcker's 1979-81 rate hikes, which broke US inflation but drove up the dollar-interest cost of Latin American debt. Rather than let the sovereign loans default, the Fed and the IMF pressured banks into a strategy called concerted lending, in which banks kept extending fresh credit so that old loans could technically stay current. The 1980s in Latin America came to be summed up by a single dismal label reflecting ten years of stagnation, hyperinflation, and social upheaval; per-capita GDP in some countries did not regain 1981 levels until the mid-1990s. In 1989 a US Treasury Secretary under George H.W. Bush proposed a new instrument that converted old sovereign loans into tradable, partially-collateralized bonds backed by zero-coupon US Treasuries. The Austrian and moral-hazard reading of the whole episode names a specific pattern: Latin American publics bore stagnation while US bank creditors were shielded from the market discipline that would have failed several of them.

the-methodenstreit-1883-1893-menger-vs-s.context_blurb: In 1883, twelve years after his founding Principles and ten years into his Vienna chair, the Austrian economist Carl Menger published a second book with a very different purpose: to attack a rival school of German-speaking economic thought, led from a Berlin chair, that held economics should be built up from mass national statistics and specific historical case studies rather than from universal principles. The rival school was called inductive in method, moving from cases to a general rule, while Menger argued economics is like geometry, with universal laws derivable from a small number of universal premises about how human beings act. The German word for the quarrel became the standard name in every subsequent history of economics; it means method-fight. The next year Menger published a passionate short reply pamphlet in the form of open letters to a friend. In the course of the fight, the Berlin economist invented a two-word label meant as a put-down for Menger's Vienna circle; the label became a name of honor and is still used today for the school. The methodological freeze that followed was serious: from his Berlin chair the leader of the inductive school controlled Prussian academic appointments through his position, his editorship of the leading journal, and his chairmanship of the national economics association, and he kept Austrian economists out of German academic chairs for a generation. Menger's direct pupils carried on the methodological fight. The personal quarrel ended when the Berlin economist died in 1917, but the methodological split it opened stayed permanent: methodological individualism on the Austrian line, historical-institutional analysis on the German line.

the-nyc-taxi-medallion-1-3m-to-100k-afte.context_blurb: New York City has capped the number of yellow-cab licenses since a 1937 statute, holding the total near eleven thousand seven hundred for decades. The license itself, called a medallion, became a tradable asset. In 2013-14, at the peak of the New York City yellow-cab market, a single medallion traded at auction for a seven-figure sum, after rising from twenty-five hundred dollars in 1947 to about two hundred thousand in 1997. In 2011 a San Francisco company launched a smartphone-based car-service app in New York City, initially registered under the state's black-car regulatory category rather than as a taxi, which let supply expand to meet demand without hitting the medallion cap. Between 2013 and 2019, after that app and similar ride-hail services had scaled up, the medallion suffered a roughly ninety-two percent price collapse. Yellow-cab economics had depended on street hails and so concentrated in Manhattan, which meant outer-borough neighborhoods had been systematically underserved for decades; the app-hail model let for-hire vehicles meet that demand. In May 2019 two New York Times reporters published a Pulitzer-finalist series documenting about nine hundred and fifty medallion-owner bankruptcies and eight driver suicides after the price crash, showing that many owner-drivers had bought medallions at peak prices using loans they could not repay. Bastiat's method reads the collapse as more than a loss for medallion owners: it reversed a transfer that had run one way, from riders and blocked drivers to cap-protected owners, for seventy-six years. When a senator defends the cap as protecting taxi drivers from cutthroat competition, the question to ask is who the cap had been quietly protecting them against.

the-petition-of-the-candlemakers-a-law-a.context_blurb: In 1845 Frederic Bastiat published, over his own name in his larger collection of satirical economic pamphlets, a mock petition addressed to the French Chamber of Deputies. In the petition a group of French lighting-industry producers beg the government to pass a law requiring certain household openings to be closed during daytime hours in order to shut out a specific ruinous competitor whose cheap output is flooding the French market and undercutting domestic lighting industries. The ruinous competitor is identified in the petition itself: it is the sun. Bastiat's satire lets the petitioners say the quiet part loud and watches the protectionist argument collapse under its own weight. The petition lists all the downstream French industries that will benefit if the sun is shut out: more tallow farms will be needed, more whaling, more imports of oil, more jobs for carpenters making shutters. It is a working example of the logical move called reductio ad absurdum, taking an opponent's principle seriously and following it to a conclusion no one would defend. Milton Friedman's 1980 book Free to Choose refers directly to the petition when arguing against twentieth-century American trade policy, pressing the diagnostic question of whether a policy treats more goods for less work as a bad thing. The eighteenth-century companion piece in economic satire was Jonathan Swift's 1729 pamphlet about Irish poverty. The phrase has become standing shorthand in modern economics writing for any argument that treats free abundance as a threat requiring policy remedy, especially any policy that would shut out cheaper substitutes to protect an incumbent producer.

the-road-to-serfdom-1944.context_blurb: In March 1944 the London publisher Routledge released a slim book by a Viennese economist working at LSE during the Blitz. It warned Britain that keeping its wartime economic controls in peacetime would carry it along the same political path that German-speaking Europe had taken from social-democratic reform in the 1920s to National Socialist dictatorship. The author opened the book with a two-word dedication to his real target audience, naming the very group he was warning. The American edition appeared in September 1944 after three American publishers had already rejected the manuscript, picked up finally by a Midwestern university press. In April 1945 an American mass-circulation magazine did something it had never done before and never did again: condensed the book into a lead feature article for its monthly issue, in a condensation by Max Eastman. A second American magazine turned the book into an illustrated picture-book version in February 1945, essentially a comic-strip summary that General Motors reprinted as a mass pamphlet. George Orwell reviewed the book in the Observer on April 9, 1944 and summarized its thesis as socialism inevitably leads to despotism. John Maynard Keynes wrote the author a warm letter on June 28, 1944 agreeing with the moral warning while disagreeing about exactly where to draw the line of legitimate state action. In the summer of 1975 the newly elected Leader of the British Opposition famously pulled the author's 1960 companion book from her handbag at a research-department meeting and declared that this is what we believe.

the-socialist-calculation-debate-the-40-.context_blurb: In 1920 Vienna, an Austrian economist published a long essay in a German social-science journal arguing that a fully socialist economy could never make rational choices between competing uses of resources because, without private ownership of the means of production, there would be no real market prices for those producer goods against which to measure. The essay opened what became a forty-year argument between two broad schools of economists. In the mid-1930s a young Polish economist teaching at the University of Chicago offered a formal reply that proposed a central board that would set and adjust prices by trial and error to mimic market behavior under public ownership; the proposal was called market socialism. In 1935 Friedrich Hayek edited an English volume that put the original 1920 essay before English-speaking economists for the first time. In September 1945 Hayek himself published a now-classic essay in the American Economic Review that moved the debate to new ground by conceding that a planning board might, in principle, perform the arithmetic, while arguing it could never aggregate the dispersed knowledge of time and place held in millions of minds. In 1949 Mises restated the argument at book length in a comprehensive Yale treatise. The empirical verdict arrived with the fall of the Berlin Wall in 1989. In September 1990 the lifelong democratic-socialist author of The Worldly Philosophers wrote in The New Yorker that the Austrian side had turned out to be right. Don Lavoie's 1985 Austrian book reconsidered the whole debate in explicit knowledge-problem terms, coining the modern phrase the knowledge problem.

the-theory-of-money-and-credit-1912.context_blurb: In 1912 a thirty-one-year-old Vienna economist published his first major book, submitting the same manuscript to the University of Vienna as the thesis he needed to earn his Habilitation. The book opened a specific puzzle Menger's 1871 marginal-utility theory had left unresolved: if the value of a good comes from its marginal usefulness to individuals, how does money, which is useful mainly because other people accept it, escape circularity? The author's answer was the regression theorem. Today's demand for money rests on yesterday's known purchasing power, and the chain can be traced back through time until it reaches a moment when the money-good was valued for a direct non-monetary use. Gold had been valued for jewelry and dentistry, silver for ornament, cattle for food and traction, salt for preservation. The book also contained the earliest statement of what would grow, under Friedrich Hayek's extension in his 1931 LSE lectures, into the full Austrian theory of the business cycle. The English translation was done in 1934, but an American edition did not appear until 1953, when Yale added a direct response to the Keynesian orthodoxy that had swept postwar Anglo-American economics. In 1963 a leading Austrian economist wrote a slim popular restatement aimed at the general reader. In the 2010s the book's regression theorem became a live question again when a new digital money called Bitcoin appeared, since Bitcoin had no clear prior non-monetary use. Several Austrian essays, including a widely-read 2013 piece by Konrad Graf, worked out how censorship-resistant value transfer across a peer-to-peer network could serve as the required prior demand.

the-vienna-diaspora-of-1934-1940-how-the.context_blurb: In the late 1920s and early 1930s the private seminar of Ludwig von Mises in Vienna gathered many of the young economists who would later carry the Austrian School into the English-speaking world. The crossing began under academic ordinary circumstances and then accelerated under the political catastrophe of the mid-1930s. Lionel Robbins, then rebuilding LSE's economics department, brought Hayek over from Vienna in January 1931 for lectures published later that year, and Hayek stayed for nearly two decades, holding LSE's senior economics professorship from 1932 until 1950. Fritz Machlup, who had studied under Mises in the 1920s, took a Rockefeller fellowship in 1933 that led to a US chair at a New York state university from 1935 to 1947, before moves to Johns Hopkins and Princeton. Gottfried Haberler worked for an international organization in Geneva from 1934 to 1936 before his own move to the United States. Oskar Morgenstern was traveling on a Carnegie Visiting Professorship in America when German troops crossed into Austria in March 1938; he stayed and took a Princeton appointment. Mises himself left Vienna in 1934 for a paid chair in Geneva he had never been offered in his own city, then left Switzerland in July 1940 as France fell, escaped through Lisbon, and reached New Jersey on August 2, 1940. He was fifty-nine, already regarded as one of the greatest economists of his generation, and no American university offered him a paid chair for the rest of his life. Seven years after the Nazi collapse Hayek gathered a small group above Lake Geneva to see whether classical liberal thought could be rebuilt. The 1974 Nobel to Hayek fully vindicated the crossing.

tim-may-s-crypto-anarchist-manifesto-198.context_blurb: In the late 1970s a young physicist at Intel helped solve one critical semiconductor problem, cashed enough stock to retire early, and moved to the hills above Santa Cruz. There he wrote. In November 1988 he brought copies of a short essay to the annual CRYPTO academic conference in Santa Barbara, handed them out, and read it aloud to the assembled cryptographers. The essay opened with a deliberate echo of a famous nineteenth-century political document, replacing one noun with another. The specter the essay predicted was not communism; it was a set of technical capabilities that would, over the next twenty years, give individuals and groups the ability to communicate, contract, and trade with each other in a totally anonymous manner, beyond state surveillance. The essay listed specific technologies the mathematics would eventually enable, including anonymous remailers, digital pseudonyms, cryptographic contracts, and untraceable payments; most of these would be built out between 1990 and 2010. In 1994 the author followed the essay with a much longer document, a book-length FAQ on cypherpunk topics that circulated widely inside the community. He did not name Bitcoin, but the untraceable-payments capability he had forecast in 1988 was realized in engineering form in Satoshi Nakamoto's 2008 white paper. When the author died in 2018, cryptocurrency-press obituaries credited him as one of the fathers of the movement from inside which Satoshi wrote. The essay itself is pure forecast; in 1988 there was no code, no infrastructure, and no working anonymous system of the kinds the essay predicted. A modern historian reads it as a physicist's bet about what the mathematics would eventually let ordinary people do.

universal-basic-income-milton-friedmans-.context_blurb: In Chapter 12 of his 1962 book Capitalism and Freedom, Milton Friedman proposed a specific cash-transfer design intended to replace the stack of means-tested US welfare programs with a single benefit that phased out gradually as earned income rose, preserving work incentives through a known constant marginal rate. The proposal was actually tested in a series of large-scale randomized-controlled experiments in the US and Canada between 1968 and 1979, including New Jersey/Pennsylvania, Seattle/Denver, and the Canadian Manitoba trial; the experiments found modest reductions in work hours in the range of five to thirteen percent for primary earners, rather than the catastrophic labor-supply collapse critics had predicted. In the 2020 US Democratic presidential primary, one tech-entrepreneur candidate centered his campaign on a universal thousand-dollar-per-month payment he called the Freedom Dividend. In 2020-2023 a large private randomized study funded by Sam Altman's OpenResearch gave a thousand dollars a month to a thousand recipients in Illinois and Texas and found roughly one-and-a-half-hour weekly reductions in work hours alongside modest health improvements. The libertarian scholar Charles Murray proposed a ten-thousand-dollar-per-adult basic income in his 2006 AEI book, structured as a universal flat payment that would replace nearly all existing US welfare and social-insurance programs. The Alaska Permanent Fund has paid every state resident an annual per-capita share of state oil-royalty returns since 1982. A Thomas Sowell-style approach reads the statutory design, not the label, because same-label proposals with different phase-out structures produce different outcomes. Friedman's version was replace; the modern universal-income version is typically add.

vietnam-after-1975-re-education-camps-an.context_blurb: On April 30, 1975 North Vietnam's forces captured the South Vietnamese capital, ending the Vietnam War. The capital would soon be renamed for Ho Chi Minh. After reunification, the new government sent former South Vietnamese officials, soldiers, teachers, journalists, and Catholic clergy to a network of camps that held an estimated one to two and a half million people between 1975 and the mid-1980s. The collectivization of southern agriculture and the state seizure of southern private commerce in 1977-78, which targeted ethnic-Chinese business families particularly hard in a specific district of the former southern capital, drove roughly eight hundred thousand Vietnamese to flee by sea in unseaworthy craft between 1975 and 1990. The UN High Commissioner for Refugees estimates a large at-sea death toll from storms, thirst, and pirate attacks in the Gulf of Thailand, in the range of two hundred to four hundred thousand. One normalization program negotiated between the US and Hanoi from 1979 allowed Vietnamese with US ties to emigrate legally. By the early 1980s Vietnam's Soviet-model central planning had produced rice shortages in the rice-exporting Mekong Delta, chronic urban shortages, and an inflation rate around five hundred percent per year by 1985. In 1986 the Communist Party itself turned toward markets under a program whose Vietnamese name means renovation, which restored household farming, legalized private enterprise, permitted foreign investment, and deregulated prices. Within three years Vietnam went from chronic rice shortage to net rice exporter.

welfare-cliffs-the-effective-marginal-ta.context_blurb: A welfare cliff is the point on the income distribution where an additional dollar of earned wages triggers the loss of one or more means-tested government benefits. Because the lost benefits can exceed the added wages, a raise that increases earned income can actually decrease total household resources. In 2018 the Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta launched an interactive online tool that lets a specific household map its cliff exposure across the stack of federal, state, and local programs it participates in. The Congressional Research Service counts roughly eighty-two separate federal means-tested benefit programs; their uncoordinated phase-outs are what produces the cliff pattern. In 1995 Thomas Sowell published a book cataloging cases where policies aimed at helping a group produced outcomes opposite their stated intentions; the book documented pre-1965 US family-structure data showing patterns that reversed after the Great Society welfare expansion. In 2012 Casey Mulligan at Chicago published a book quantifying how the safety-net expansion during the Great Recession raised effective marginal tax rates on low-wage work. Milton Friedman's 1962 Capitalism and Freedom had proposed a unified replacement for the stack of separate programs under a specific name; the closest existing US approximation to that proposal was established in 1975 as a targeted wage subsidy for low-earning working families. One of the largest and most-discussed individual cliffs in modern US policy sat at four hundred percent of the Federal Poverty Level for premium subsidies under a specific 2010 health-insurance law.

ww1-and-the-collapse-of-the-classical-go.context_blurb: In the first week of August 1914, as the great powers mobilized for war, each major belligerent did the same thing to its money within days of each other: it ended convertibility between paper notes and gold. Under a full gold standard a government could raise money for war only by taxing citizens, which is unpopular and slow, or by borrowing from lenders, which is limited by lender willingness. Suspending gold let the central banks print notes to pay for military orders directly. The result over four years of war was that monetary bases ballooned: Germany's grew roughly twelvefold, seeding the postwar hyperinflation. Only the United States, which entered the war in April 1917 roughly two and a half years late, kept relative monetary discipline. Ludwig von Mises's 1919 book Nation, State, and Economy argued the specific counterfactual that under a full classical gold standard the war could not have been fought for four years because gold discipline would have forced the belligerents to a negotiated settlement within months. In 1925 Britain returned to the gold standard at the prewar parity, which overvalued the pound and forced painful deflation; John Maynard Keynes attacked the move in a pamphlet whose title named the Chancellor directly. The 1922 Genoa Conference had tried to reduce pressure on world gold reserves by proposing a weaker version of the system in which only central banks held gold while other countries held dollars and pounds as reserves. The Austrian reading of the twentieth century holds that political catastrophe and monetary catastrophe are the same story: no four-year Great War without paper-money printing, and no paper-money printing without abandoning gold discipline.

zoning-the-housing-that-glaeser-and-gyou.context_blurb: In 1926 the US Supreme Court upheld a suburban Ohio village's power to restrict how privately owned land could be built on, giving American cities the legal authority to adopt comprehensive zoning codes. Almost every major American city has used that authority. One large US city, famously unique, has never adopted a conventional zoning code and uses private deed restrictions instead. In 2002 a Harvard economist and a Wharton economist quantified how much land-use restrictions cost city dwellers by comparing the actual construction cost of an apartment to its market price in constrained metropolitan areas. They called the gap the zoning tax, and in their 2002 Manhattan figures it already approached half a million dollars per apartment; by the 2010s the Manhattan figure was well over a million. When a homeowner argues that zoning protects neighborhood character, Bastiat's method asks what the zoning cost that no one immediately sees: the apartments and houses the code prevented from ever being built, the families priced out of the metropolitan area, and the hours of commuting those families now pay. The reason the restrictive policy persists is a political-economy pattern with a franchise twist: current homeowners vote in local elections, and would-be residents cannot. In December 2018 one large US city became the first in the country to abolish single-family-only zoning across every neighborhood. In 2021 the California legislature signed a state law allowing the by-right splitting of single-family lots into up to four units in most residential zones, giving the pro-housing movement its first big statewide preemption win. The whole arc shows the concentrated-benefit, dispersed-cost pattern applied to housing policy.
